Expert posterior probabilities are concatenated and fused using an XGBoost meta-classifier to produce the final macro-group distribution and confidence score. On 569 real-barn clips using a 455/114 train/test split, late fusion achieved 0.816 accuracy and 0.639 Macro-F1, outperforming all individual experts. Additional analyses show that the 3 s non-overlapping configuration provided the strongest fusion Macro-F1 among tested window settings, while confidence-thresholded abstention improved reliability by enabling a controllable coverage–accuracy trade-off. Calibration analysis further showed that the fusion confidence was useful but imperfect (ECE = 0.100; multiclass Brier = 0.294), supporting its use as a practical deployment-oriented confidence signal rather than a full uncertainty model. These results indicate that integrating global, local, and distributional acoustic evidence with selective prediction is an effective and pragmatic strategy for macro-behaviour recognition in noisy farm environments.

title: Workflow Signal Protocol: A Measurement Method for Deployment-Time Workflow Observability in Legal AI
authors: L. Ben
abstract: Legal AI benchmarks, citation checks, and retrieval-grounding tests primarily evaluate upstream capability: whether a model can answer, extract, or ground a legal task. Deployment asks a different question: whether a particular output remains observable enough to be deployed, reviewed, corrected, or escalated once it enters an organizational workflow. We introduce the Workflow Signal Protocol (WSP), a deployment-layer measurement method for recording workflow observability as a structured workflow-observability record. WSP encodes source status, proposition support, review state, recourse, provenance, and role-scoped disclosure. We validate WSP through controlled stress tests, public legal datasets, documented real-world failures, and a live-output pilot using three general-purpose model application programming interface (API) arms. In the main matched-vocabulary stress test, local formal/substantive routing reduced hidden-risk deployment from 93.5% under calibration-only abstention to 4.0% or below; all 192 pilot outputs were expressible as WSP records. These results support the central claim that deployment-time workflow observability is measurable within the evaluated legal-AI settings; validation in deployed institutional legal workflows remains future work.

title: Deadline-Aware DRL for MEC Task Scheduling: Balancing Offloading and Deferral to Maximize Completion Rates
authors: M. Zulfiqar; A. Ahsan
venue: 2026 International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Computer, Data Sciences and Applications (ACDSA)
abstract: Guaranteeing deadline adherence for Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication (URLLC) tasks in Mobile Edge Computing (MEC) requires intelligent scheduling, especially under environmental uncertainty. In this work, we address the challenge of deciding not only how, but also when, to offload tasks in the face of volatile wireless channels and fluctuating server loads. We propose a Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) framework utilizing Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), where an agent learns to dynamically balance immediate task offloading against strategic deferral. By operating in a continuous action space with a size-invariant state representation, our agent learns a scalable policy capable of zero-shot generalization. Simulations demonstrate that the proposed PPO agent achieves a competitive task completion rate comparable to sophisticated heuristics while reducing energy consumption by approximately 20% through intelligent deferral. Furthermore, we demonstrate that PPO significantly outperforms Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) in terms of computational efficiency, training $5 \times$ faster and avoiding the policy collapse observed in the off-policy baseline. Extensive stress tests validate the agent's robustness against network congestion and severe channel volatility, positioning it as a sustainable and deployable solution for real-time Edge Intelligence.

title: Learning-based Task Scheduling with Deferral and Dynamic K-Selection for Lunar Communication-Navigation Constellations
authors: X. Li; H. Huang; J. Xu; F. Zhang; Y. Guo
venue: IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering
abstract: Task scheduling for lunar communication-navigation integrated constellations involves four coupled decision dimensions, i.e. task selection, task sequencing, coordinated service assets determination, and satellite-to-task assignment, which are tightly coupled due to task priority, limited load for dual function, and inter-satellite coordination. Most existing methods address this NP-hard scheduling problem through rule-based heuristics or reinforcement learning with fixed resource allocation schemes, both of which lead to significant limitations in optimality. In this paper, we develop an end-to-end deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework for joint task scheduling, aiming to learn an effective joint scheduling policy for the coupled optimization problem. To better match the problem structure, we adopt a Dual-Attention Proximal Policy Optimization framework, in which self-attention and cross-attention are used to encode inter-task resource competition and task-satellite compatibility, respectively. More importantly, the proposed multiple decision heads explicitly incorporate newly designed deferral and dynamic K-selection, enabling proactive congestion control and adaptive quality-resource trade-offs, which together yield improved overall scheduling performance. The proposed scheduling framework generalizes well to constellations with the same resource-sharing structure, including those in which shared payloads concurrently support multiple service types. Numerical simulation for Elliptical Lunar Frozen Orbit satellite constellation shows that the proposed learning algorithm achieves 14.7% higher revenue than the best heuristic baseline, and 21.4% higher than a standard DRL baseline, with the gain confirmed on 20 held-out instances under a common evaluation protocol.

title: Abstention is all you need
authors: E. Schönwälder; C. Falkenberg; C. Hartmann; W. Lehner
venue: 2025 IEEE 12th International Conference on Data Science and Advanced Analytics (DSAA)
abstract: Despite their outstanding performance across various NLP tasks, Large Language Models (LLMs) still produce incorrect answers, which can be harmful in safety-critical domains like medicine and autonomous driving. To address this issue, selective prediction systems aim to reject predictions from LLMs that are likely to be incorrect. However, current approaches either rely on querying the LLM multiple times, requiring access to its internals, or fine-tuning it. Given the significant operational costs of an LLM, we propose a selective prediction system that does not involve the LLM during inference. We conduct an extensive experimental study regarding training data sizes, time consumption, utilized models, and embeddings, improving on the current state-of-the-art while treating the LLM as a black box, without accessing its internals or requiring fine-tuning.

title: Adaptive Staged Medical Diagnosis From Multimodal Information: A Quality-Constrained Sequential Three-Way Classification Approach
authors: Y. Chenglong; L. Decui
venue: 2026 23rd International Computer Conference on Wavelet Active Media Technology and Information Processing (ICCWAMTIP)
abstract: Staged diagnosis through the progressive acquisition of multimodal information can reduce unnecessary examinations while maintaining diagnostic quality. However, misclassification and deferral for further examination have different consequences, making their relative losses difficult to quantify. Moreover, because the modalities available at different stages vary in information value, a uniform deferral criterion across stages may be inappropriate. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a sequential three-way classification method that adapts deferral criteria across stages under diagnostic quality constraints. First, a sequential three-way classification model is constructed from the multimodal information accumulated at each stage. Then, stage-specific boundary losses are optimized under bootstrap-based quality constraints benchmarked against the full-examination strategy. Finally, a cost-minimizing selection rule identifies a diagnostic policy that preserves diagnostic quality. Experiments on two multimodal medical datasets show that the proposed method maintains diagnostic performance while substantially reducing examination costs.

title: Extending Six Sigma for AI Automation Across Global Industries
authors: R. U. Tekawade; D. R. Nirmal; A. S. Ohal; A. S. Banchhod; V. K. Kolekar
venue: 2026 International Conference on Sustainable and Futuristic Technologies (ICSFT)
abstract: This paper suggests a conceptual framework that invokes 6 Sigma principles of quality control to AI-driven automation, combating gaps on global adoption readiness. We introduce a Reliability-to-Adoption Curve A $(\sigma)$ that captures how developing economies (with limited infrastructure or regulatory support) typically demand higher effective reliability (sigma levels) for the same adoption likelihood as advanced economies. We outline Sigma-Gated MLOps, a governance methodology incorporating defects-per-million (DPMO) thresholds, control charts, calibration metrics (e.g., Expected Calibration Error), model abstention, and a $1.5 \sigma$ process-shift adjustment into ML deployment. We describe Human-in-the-Loop Reliability Budgeting, showing how strategic abstentions and redundancy with human review can raise an AI system's effective sigma quality in resourceconstrained settings. Lastly, we propose a Skills Bill-ofMaterials (Skills BoM), mapping needed roles and competencies to each sigma-tier and deployment context. Realworld data on digital infrastructure, trust, and workforce training are leveraged to contrast the U.S. and India (plus illustrative examples from Brazil and Germany). Results include theory-driven reliability maps and comparative tables that highlight how variable infrastructure, informality (e.g., India's 90% informal workforce), and public trust (India ~77% vs. US ~32% trust in AI) translate into different sigmaadoption thresholds.

title: Causal Representation Learning for Reliable Prediction in Safety-Critical Applications
authors: V. Kummari; K. Ramadevi; T. S; M. C D; M. Sreedevi; P. M. Raj
venue: 2026 IEEE World Skills Conference on Universal Data Analytics and Sciences (WorldSUAS)
abstract: To achieve reliable prediction in safety-critical systems, including autonomous driving, healthcare decision support, and industrial automation, the systems must resist changes in distributions, spurious correlations, and uncertainty estimates that can be relied upon. The use of conventional deep learning models uses statistical shortcuts, which do not work in unseen conditions, resulting in unsafe and unreliable behavior. In order to overcome these issues, this paper presents a causal representation learning model to ensure accurate prediction in safety-critical systems. The suggested method explicitly separates the latent representations into causal factors and nuisance factors, which will make sure that the predictions are caused by consistent causal processes and not artifacts of the environment. A counterfactual stability regularization is used to stabilize predictions when applied to out-of-distribution data, whereas cross-environment invariance constraints are used to build out-of-distribution generalization. Moreover, the selective prediction strategy with a calculated uncertainty is risk-conscious to allow abstinence in the situation of high uncertainty, minimizing the risks of the disastrous mistakes. Large-scale experimental findings indicate that the planned framework attains better out-of-distribution robustness, better calibration, and reduced selective risk than current approaches, which makes it an excellent fit to a real-world safety-critical application.

title: VisionGuard: Cost-Sensitive AI Attestation with Quorum-Verified Blockchain Enforcement
authors: S. S. M.; L. P. R.; P. S.; S. Ramamoorthy; V. Sugumaran
abstract: Web3 platforms face a critical challenge: once unsafe content is minted on-chain, it becomes immutable and irrevocable. Traditional NSFW classifiers operate off-chain without cryptographic guarantees, leaving blockchain ecosystems vulnerable to harmful content. We present VisionGuard, a unified moderation framework that integrates cost-sensitive AI decision-making with blockchain-based enforcement. Our system combines calibrated NSFW classification, abstention-based triage for uncertain cases, perceptual hashing for near-duplicate detection, and on-chain k-of-n quorum attestation using EIP-712 signatures. We establish formal guarantees for: (i) Bayes-optimal cost-sensitive thresholds minimizing asymmetric error costs, (ii) optimal abstention intervals for human review, (iii) monotone false-negative reduction under classifier-pHash fusion, (iv) quorum compromise bounds, and (v) end-to-end unsafe-mint probability. Empirical validation on a zero-shot NSFW task demonstrates 82% accuracy (AUC = 0.88), with the Bayes-optimal threshold $(\tau^{*}=0.1)$ reducing expected cost to 27,520 versus 54,942 at the F1-optimal threshold-a 50% improvement. Calibrated abstention further lowers harm (cost= 10,649.5), while a 3-of-5 quorum with oracle compromise $p=0.1$ yields break probability $P_{\text{break}} < 1\%$. Together, Vision Guard bridges decision theory, adversarial robustness, and cryptographic enforcement, providing the first provably safe AI moderation pathway for blockchain content.

title: CalibPea-CaFormer: Confidence-Calibrated Selective Prediction for Trustworthy Pea Leaf Disease Classification
authors: P. Kaushik
venue: 2026 7th International Conference on Electronics and Sustainable Communication Systems (ICESC)
abstract: Accurate pea leaf disease classification is important for early crop monitoring, but practical agricultural diagnosis also requires reliable confidence estimation. A model that has a high confidence but low accuracy may lead to a wrong disease management decision, particularly when symptoms are similar for different disease classes. In this work, we present a confidence-calibrated selective prediction (CCSP) framework, called CalibPea-CaFormer, for trustworthy pea leaf disease classification. Pea leaf images were classified into four classes: Fresh Leaf, Downy Mildew Leaf, Leaf Miner Leaf, and Powder Mildew Leaf using a pretrained CaFormer-S18 backbone. Deterministic resizing and normalization of input images were performed without any custom design disease-specific pre-processing or attention modules. Data was partitioned by grouping duplicate and near-duplicate samples to minimize optimistic bias, and the held-out test set was not used in training or checkpoint selection. The model's performance on the held-out test partition was 96.67% accuracy, 96.50% macro-F1, 96.66% weighted-F1, 96.50% balanced accuracy, 0.955 Cohen’s kappa, and 0.955 Matthews correlation coefficient. In addition to classification performance, predictive reliability was assessed with a reliability diagram and expected calibration error. The model had an ECE of 0.029, which is a good measure of the confidence–accuracy alignment. In addition, a selective prediction strategy was developed to assist with accept, review, and defer-to-expert decisions for uncertain samples. The results demonstrate that CalibPea-CaFormer offers a trust-aware diagnostic framework, integrating disease recognition with confidence-based decision support.

title: Early Recognition of Handwritten Gestures Based on Multi-Classifier Reject Option
authors: Z. Chen; E. Anquetil; C. Viard-Gaudin; H. Mouchère
venue: 2017 14th IAPR International Conference on Document Analysis and Recognition (ICDAR)
abstract: In this paper a multi-classifier method for early recognition of handwritten gesture is presented. Unlike the other works which study the early recognition problem related to the time, we propose to make the recognition according to the quantity of incremental drawing of handwritten gestures. We train a segment length based multi-classifier for the task of recognizing the handwritten touch gesture as early as possible. To deal with potential similar parts at the beginning of different gestures, we introduce a reject option to postpone the decision until ambiguity persists. We report results on two freely available datasets: MGSet and ILG. These results demonstrate the improvement we obtained by using the proposed reject option for the early recognition of handwritten gestures.

title: GBP-Audit: AI Bias Intervention with Built-In Safety-First Guardrails
authors: R. Doku; N. Y. A. Osafo; D. B. Rawat
venue: 2025 IEEE 7th International Conference on Cognitive Machine Intelligence (CogMI)
abstract: We introduce GBP-Audit, an audit-then-act post-hoc fairness layer for frozen models when retraining is impractical. GBP-Audit first diagnoses whether observed disparities are removable proxies or task-aligned using geometric coherence (κ) between bias and task directions, a stress-test injection, and multi-seed instability. It applies an edit only when statistical guardrails certify safety - AUROC non-inferiority via TOST (δ=0.005), calibration preservation (|ΔECE| ≤ ϵ=0.003), and optional fixed-FPR drift caps; otherwise it abstains and records the rationale. a Across seven public tabular classification tasks, GBP-Audit delivered safe parity gains on 3/7 datasets while maintaining utility (e.g., Adult: −55% EO; Bank: −73%) and correctly abstained on 4/7 where counterfactual edits would harm performance (e.g., Employment: EO +0.043; Taiwan: AUROC degradation). Each decision emits a machine-readable Governance Packet (baselines, diagnostics, guardrail outcomes, expected impacts) to support compliance and auditability (e.g., NYC Local Law 144, EU AI Act, SR 11–7). Deployment is attribute-free at inference, fully reversible, and adds <1 ms CPU latency per 32 examples. GBP-Audit operationalizes the question "can we fix this bias without retraining?" into a guarded decision: ship a calibrated, non-inferior mitigation - or return evidence that remediation requires upstream change.

title: Site-Aware Applicability-Domain-Guided Selective Prediction for Atmospheric Corrosion Under Environmental Domain Shift
authors: B. Wang; H. Ji; Y. Wu; Y. Zhao
venue: 2026 8th International Conference on System Reliability and Safety Engineering (SRSE)
abstract: Reliable atmospheric corrosion prediction at unseen sites requires an evaluation protocol that preserves site dependence and an output rule that distinguishes supported prediction from environmental extrapolation. This paper develops SEAD-SP, a site-aware applicability-domain and selective-prediction framework for worldwide carbon-steel exposure records. Complete programme-site groups are isolated among model fitting, calibration, and testing. Environmental support is assessed by a dual rule combining a calibrationrelative nearest-neighbour distance with a featurewise training envelope. Supported queries receive a point estimate and an empirically calibrated interval; unsupported queries are deferred for additional environmental characterization or corrosion inspection. Across ten repeated five-fold experiments, rowrandom validation altered model ranking and overstated unseensite performance. At the principal support threshold, the dual rule retained 46.8% of non-marine and 48.9% of marine predictions while reducing MAE from 5.64 to 4.75 micrometres and from 42.69 to 23.32 micrometres, respectively. Distance ablations, a nonlinear gradient-boosting baseline, programmeisolated transfer, site-macro coverage, and an independent fivesite Colombian case study further support SEAD-SP as a reproducible reliability-control layer for deployment under environmental domain shift.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Deep Learning for Safety-Oriented Triage of Occult Wrist Fractures in Radiographs
authors: H. Agarwal; E. Mishra; S. V; S. Annamalai
venue: 2026 9th International Conference on Trends in Electronics and Informatics (ICOEI)
abstract: Occult fractures of the scaphoid and distal radius remain difficult to detect on initial wrist radiographs, and false-negative interpretations can delay treatment, leading to nonunion, avascular necrosis, and long-term functional impairment. Existing deep learning systems for radiograph analysis are typically designed as closed binary classifiers that must output a definitive normal or abnormal label for every input, with no mechanism to express diagnostic uncertainty. This design assumption is misaligned with clinical practice, where ambiguous wrist radiographs routinely prompt immobilisation and referral for CT or MRI rather than a forced binary decision. This paper introduces an uncertainty-aware triage pipeline for wrist radiographs that replaces the forced binary output with a three-way policy: confident normal, confident abnormal, or deferred for advanced imaging. A ResNet-50 backbone fine-tuned on the wrist subset of MURA v1.1 is augmented with Monte Carlo (MC) dropout inference. Across T = 30 stochastic forward passes per study, the sample mean provides a calibrated abnormality score while the sample variance quantifies epistemic uncertainty. A data-driven uncertainty threshold γ routes high-variance studies directly to CT/MRI referral. At a 25% deferral rate, the system reduces missed fractures from 295 to 221—a 25.1% reduction—while accuracy on auto-diagnosed cases remains essentially unchanged. These results show that uncertainty quantification is a practical and clinically meaningful mechanism for improving patient safety in AI-assisted fracture screening.

title: Learning to Decide When Not to Decide: Coverage-Constrained Selective Classification with Abstention
authors: J. K. Petra K; J. D; D. R
venue: 2026 IEEE International Conference on AI Engineering and Innovations (AIEI)
abstract: Recently, deep neural networks (DNNs), which have been well proven in classification tasks, are overconfident when facing ambiguous or uncertain inputs and make decisions that are not reliable to be applied in serious application domains with safety issues. This issue is tackled by selective classification with an abstention mechanism that stops a classifier from generating predictions, whenever the predicted confidence is low. To concretely represent the effective use of the abstention mechanism in a neural classifier, this paper introduces a confidence-aware selective learning framework, where coverage-constrained risk minimization has been demonstrated by optimizing a common loss function, which takes both prediction accuracy and coverage into account. The proposed model is capable of learning discriminative representations and selective decision boundaries simultaneously. Experiments on the Fashion-MNIST datasets demonstrate that the proposed selective model achieved an accuracy of 95.31%, but it did not predict 27.02% of inputs that are uncertain. In contrast, we achieve an accuracy of 87.83% using a typical baseline classifier that does not have the option to abstain. The results indicate that selective prediction leads to a considerable increase in decision reliability, thus corresponding more directly to applications where a model's output should not show erratic behavior.

title: The Convergence of Explainable AI and Uncertainty Quantification in Special Education: A Scoping Review of AI-Assisted Support for Autism Spectrum Disorder
authors: R. A. Razali; F. A. Rahim; A. M. Khairuddin; N. I. Othman; R. Y. Masri; N. A. Muhamad Shaari
venue: 2026 6th International Conference on Smart Sensors and Applications (ICSSA)
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) are increasingly used to support personalized learning, intervention, and transition planning for individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). However, the opacity of advanced AI models limits their trustworthiness in high-stakes educational and vocational decision-making. Explainable AI (XAI) can improve transparency by revealing why a prediction or recommendation is generated, while Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) indicates how reliably that prediction should be interpreted. This scoping review examines the convergence of XAI and UQ in AI-assisted support for ASD education and learning-to-career transition. Following the PRISMA-ScR framework, five databases were searched and supplemented by backward and forward snowballing. Of 1,263 identified records, 17 peer-reviewed empirical studies were included in the final synthesis. The findings show that XAI-focused studies improve interpretability but rarely quantify predictive reliability, whereas UQ-focused studies estimate uncertainty or enable abstention but provide limited stakeholder-oriented explanations. Although approaches integrating XAI and UQ provide a stronger foundation for trustworthy decision support, their application remains limited, particularly in ASD educational and vocational contexts. This review therefore highlights the need to integrate XAI, UQ, and Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) oversight so that AI systems can communicate why a recommendation is generated, how reliable it is, and when human review is required. Such integration may support more transparent, uncertainty-aware, and personalized AI-assisted decision-making while preserving human oversight and the agency of autistic individuals.

title: Abstention-Aware Deepfake Screening with Multi-Model Ensembles: An Atomic Evaluation Framework
authors: C. Bernardino; C. Costa; J. Aparício
venue: 2026 International Conference on Intelligent Digitization of Systems and Services (IDSS)
abstract: The proliferation of AI-generated deepfakes poses major risks to information integrity, democratic processes, and national security. In operational settings, deepfake screening must handle both classification and model abstentions/refusals. In our experiments, a tested commercial vision-language model (VLM) exhibited safety-driven abstention behavior that can collapse automated recall under common REAL-by-default mappings. This paper presents an Atomic Evaluation Framework (AEF), developed using Design Science Research Methodology (DSRM), for abstention-aware, multi-model (LLM/VLM) ensemble screening with structured rationale outputs and auditability.We report four empirical findings: (1) self-judgment bias on own generations across five rhetorical profiles (N=100) shows +15.3% average overrating (t=18.07, p < 0.01), with independent cross-model evaluation indicating a "Safety-Induced Blind Spot"; (2) pilot results consistent with a "Safety–Security Paradox" in which a commercial VLM exhibits 100% abstention on a Face-Forensics++ subset (N=20), yielding 0% recall under REAL-by-default mapping; (3) an abstention-aware fusion policy combined with an open-source VLM achieves 57.1% effective recall on the same subset, while a supervised baseline (XceptionNet) reaches 100% recall; and (4) a pilot user study with OSINT analysts (N=15) shows 55% trust improvement and 83% faster decision-making with explainable outputs.This paper contributes to the literature with: (1) empirical quantification of LLM self-judgment bias with cross-model validation; (2) an abstention-aware formulation and measurement of safety-induced screening failures in commercial VLMs; (3) an atomic, multi-model screening architecture that supports human triage and auditability; and (4) an open, sovereignty-enabling implementation supporting on-premise deployment.

title: Towards Trustworthy Telugu Named Entity Recognition: Calibration and Selective Prediction for Transformer-Based Models
authors: S. Samarla; D. L. K. P; G. S. Dharani; G. Dhanusha; G. Manasa; K. Sravani
venue: 2026 4th International Conference on Integrated Circuits and Communication Systems (ICICACS)
abstract: Named Entity Recognition (NER) for low-resource languages such as Telugu has seen rapid progress with transformer-based models; however, their predictive reliability remains underexplored. In safety-critical and real-world deployments, accurate confidence estimation and uncertainty-aware decision-making are as important as predictive accuracy.This paper presents a reliability-oriented evaluation framework for Telugu NER built upon a transformer-based token classification model using MuRIL. Rather than introducing a new architecture, the study focuses on three complementary aspects: (i) calibration analysis using Expected Calibration Error (ECE), Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL), and Brier Score; (ii) post-hoc probability calibration via temperature scaling; and (iii) selective prediction using entropy-based uncertainty filtering.We further extend token-level uncertainty handling by introducing span-consistent selective prediction aligned with BIO tagging constraints. Experimental results on the Telugu subset of the WikiAnn dataset demonstrate that temperature scaling improves probability calibration without degrading F1-score, while selective prediction enables improved precision under controlled coverage.The study highlights the importance of moving beyond accuracy-centric evaluation toward reliability-aware metrics in low-resource NER systems. The proposed evaluation protocol provides a practical foundation for deploying trustworthy Telugu NER models in real-world applications.

title: A Geometric Abstention Mechanism for Language Models
authors: C. M. Wyss
abstract: Due to the nature of their architecture, Large Language Models (LLMs) typically produce responses even when no coherent answer exists. In this paper, we introduce a principled, geometric mechanism that enables LLMs to abstain in such circumstances. Our approach is grounded in the notion of a Continuous State Machine (CSM), which is a glass-box model of LLM inference dynamics. In particular, a CSM can be instantiated from an ontology so that the geometry of its latent semantic space reflects that ontology. This means, among other things, that input probes trace trajectories through semantic space until either converging to a concept attractor (in-domain) or remaining isolated in null space (out-of-domain), enabling the system to distinguish realizable from non-realizable input.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Deep Neural Networks for Reliable and Selective Decision-Making in Medical Image Classification
authors: K. K. Tirupati; N. K. Methuku; P. K. Chilukury; S. R. B. Reddy
venue: 2026 International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Systems, and Emerging Technologies (ICAISET)
abstract: Artificial intelligence systems used in safety critical areas tend to make overconfident predictions without knowing their own uncertainty, making them unreliable for decision making in real life. This work proposes an uncertainty-aware deep learning framework for robust medical image classification based on the DermaMNIST dataset, and employs the Monte Carlo Dropout technique within a convolutional neural network to model the uncertainty of the prediction. Besides traditional classification, the approach allows calibrated confidence estimation and selective prediction. Experimental results obtain accuracy of 0.7362 with macro F1-score of 0.4311 and good calibration of Expected Calibration Error of 0.0363. Uncertainty analysis shows just how much incorrect predictions have uncertainty which almost double (0.0020109) the uncertainty of correct predictions (0.0010636). Furthermore, selective prediction increases reliability significantly in accuracy of prediction with 0.9302 at 40% coverage and 1.0000 at 10% coverage. These findings signal the benefits of uncertainty-aware models in trustworthy, risk-sensitive, AI decision-making.

title: Trustworthy Glucose Forecasting With Physiology-Constrained Neural Dynamics, Conformal Risk Control, and Risk-Sensitive Reinforcement Learning
authors: S. Maqsood; M. A. Sarwar; E. Belousovienė; R. Maskeliūnas
abstract: Reliable short-horizon continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) forecasting is essential to prevent hypoglycemia, yet most data-driven models provide neither physiological awareness nor actionable safety guaranties. We introduce a trustworthy forecasting framework that unifies continuous-time neural dynamics, calibration-based conformal risk control (empirically validated in held-out subjects), and tail-risk-aware adaptation. First, a Neural Controlled Differential Equation (Neural CDE) encoder models irregular, multi-channel streams (CGM, insulin, carbohydrates, activity, time-of-day). A physiology regularizer anchors latent dynamics to plausible glucose responses (e.g., post-prandial rise, insulin-mediated decay) and penalizes simulator-inconsistent trends. Second, Conformal Risk Control calibrates prediction sets and provides an actionable deferral policy when uncertainty or low-glucose risk is high, achieving prediction sets calibrated to a nominal coverage target and empirically validated under subject-disjoint evaluation. Third, a risk-sensitive policy (CVaR-optimized PPO) adapts predictions to minimize tail errors, explicitly weighting under-predictions near hypoglycemia. We evaluated in BrisT1D and OhioT1DM with patient-wise splits and performed in-silico stress tests in the UVA/Padova simulator (meal/bolus perturbations, basal overrides, sensor noise). Across 30/60-minutes horizons, our method achieves MAE= 3.0–3.9 mg/dL, RMSE= 8.5–9.8 mg/dL, and MARD= 2.1–2.7%, outperforming strong baselines by 10–14 mg/dL RMSE and 10–13 mg/dL MAE on average. The risk control is calibrated at a nominal target of 90%, achieving 90.5 to 91.5% coverage with a average set width of 18-20 mg/dL and 5% to 6% deferral. Clinically, the rates of the SEG/Parkes A/B-zone increase by + 10–14 pp, and event-centric analyzes show PR-AUC= 0.92–0.95 and ROC-AUC= 0.94–0.96 with earlier warnings (9–11 min median lead-time) and a 35–45% reduction in hypoglycemia under-prediction near the threshold. To our knowledge, this is the first end-to-end framework combining physiology-constrained Neural CDEs, conformal risk control with deferral, and CVaR-PPO adaptation for CGM forecasting, delivering verifiable safety properties alongside state-of-the-art accuracy.

title: Fair-MAD:For FGKB-Guided Adjudication of Stereotype-Prone Questions
authors: Z. Dong; Z. Yu; Z. Jiang; E. Zhu
venue: 2026 International Conference on Computer Science, Machine Learning and Agents (CSMLA)
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to answer questions involving protected or socially sensitive attributes, yet many such questions do not provide the person-specific evidence required for a determinate answer. In these cases, the central safety risk is not only incorrect prediction but unsupported commitment, in which a model fills an evidential gap with a demographic stereotype. This paper presents Fair-MAD, an inference-time framework that grounds fairness adjudication in a Fairness-Grounded Knowledge Base (FGKB). Four role-specific agents assess evidence sufficiency, stereotype risk, counterfactual stability, and response mode; a constrained final judge converts their structured outputs into an answer or abstention decision with a rationale and audit trace. All agents share the same language-model backbone and differ only in role, selected rules, prompts, and output schemas. We evaluate seven inference settings on 10,458 aligned examples from nine sensitive categories. Because answer keys are permuted, abstention is evaluated through the item-specific abstention option rather than a fixed option identifier. Fair-MAD No Debate and Full attain abstention rates of 81.75% and 83.79%, compared with 62.92% for the Single-Agent Judge. On 5,148 ambiguous items, their false commitment rates are 0.04% and $\mathbf{0. 0 2 \%}$; on 5,310 answerable items, their over-abstention rates are 64.09% and 68.10%. A module-level comparative analysis shows that the main policy shift is associated with the combined FGKB-guided structured adjudication pipeline, while optional Pro-Con deliberation provides only a small additional reduction in false commitments and makes the system more conservative. The results establish strong commitment control, together with a substantial safety-utility trade-off that requires calibration.

title: Selective Hybrid Decision Support for Incoming Quality Inspection Under Scarce Industrial Defect Data
authors: B. Ajdari; A. Barutti; E. M. Cepolina
venue: 2026 IEEE 31st International Conference on Emerging Technologies and Factory Automation (ETFA)
abstract: Incoming quality inspection in manufacturing with high product variety must allocate limited inspection capacity while limiting downstream defect escapes. Scarce defect labels, rare severe events, and an existing expert rule make direct replacement by a machine learning model unsafe. We propose a governed selective hybrid policy that always inspects critical to quality (CTQ) items, recommends a change only with sufficient article-supplier evidence, and otherwise confirms or defers to the expert rule. In an industrial case with 28,208 modeling receipts, 530 recorded nonconformities, and 88 Major cases, a replacement based only on the model failed the operational gate at matched inspection volume. Over the most recent 60 scored days, the selective policy changed only 19 of 1,080 recommendations and deferred 775. These preliminary results demonstrate conservative policy behavior and motivate prospective validation in shadow mode; they do not establish operational benefit.

title: AURELIUS: Agentic Uncertainty-Reasoning & Learning with Hierarchical Bayesian Multi-Agents Unified System for Handling Non-Determinism in HealthTech
authors: M. Chandrasekaran
venue: 2025 4th International Conference on Computing, Management and Telecommunications (ComManTel)
abstract: Healthcare AI faces non-determinism owing to noisy clinical signals, incomplete records, and hetero-geneous patient trajectories that evolve over time. These challenges make current systems brittle and prone to overconfident errors when deployed in high-stakes settings such as intensive care or chronic disease management. Objective: To design an agentic AI framework that embeds probabilistic reasoning, uncertainty awareness, and governance mechanisms directly into the decision-making loop for safe, auditable, and interpretable clinical support. Methods: I propose AURELIUS, a hierarchical Bayesian multi-agent architecture that integrates multi-modal uncertainty encoders, graph-based communication, and a meta-agent for option selection under Dec-POMDP formulations. Runtime safety checks, abstention mechanisms, and compliance-aware controllers ensure that policies remain aligned with HIPAA/GDPR constraints. Results: On SepsisSim and MIMIC-IV, AURELIUS improved AUROC by 4.9 pp, reduced calibration error by 31Conclusion: Embedding governance and uncertainty propagation into memory, policy, and coordination yields measurable improvements in safety, interpretability, and efficiency. AURELIUS provides a deployable path toward trustworthy HealthTech AI.

title: Srnn: A Unified Framework For Self-Reflection, Uncertainty Calibration, and Selective Prediction In Deep Neural Networks
authors: K. Jeswanth; D. Litishkumar; V. Allin Geo A
venue: 2026 Conference on Latest Innovations in Computing and Knowledge (CLICK)
abstract: The deep neural networks are very accurate, but predictions that are inaccurate are likely to have high confidence, rendering them less useful for practical applications. Methods such as estimating uncertainty, calibration, among others have been applied to enhance the confidence alignment of the predictions although none of them provides a single framework of self-knowledge of the model. In this paper, a new model named SRNN (Self-Reflective Neural Network) which can evaluate the validity of the predictions is introduced. The framework has a reliability estimation head and a failure memory part which learns from prediction errors. Besides, it possesses a selective prediction mechanism, which enables it to evade making low confidence predictions, thus enhancing the quality of decision-making. Overconfident errors are penalized and accurate confidence estimation is encouraged by using a reliability-aware loss function. The results of the experiment show that, SRNN can give better separation for classification and reliability and high confidence level and vice versa, if the level of confidence is low, then the class is not classified correctly. This study has played a significant role towards the creation of trustworthy and self-conscious AI devices.

title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Non-Stationary Edge Task Scheduling
authors: D. Li; A. Li
venue: 2026 International Joint Conference on Neural Networks (IJCNN)
abstract: Task scheduling in edge-enabled Internet-of-Things systems becomes fundamentally harder when device capability is non-stationary: repeated execution can degrade near-term processing efficiency, while idleness enables recovery. Existing learning-based schedulers typically optimize latency or utilization under stationary or exogenous service models, which limits their ability to learn when temporary deferral is beneficial. We formulate this problem as a multi-agent stochastic game in which each device carries a time-varying processing-efficiency state governed by controlled mean-reverting dynamics. Building on this model, we develop a degradation-recovery reinforcement-learning scheduler whose main instantiation is a tabular Q-learning policy over backlog, efficiency, and shared-context variables, and we discuss a policy-gradient extension for continuous-state settings. Experiments on heterogeneous edge IoT systems show that the learned policy acquires recovery-aware behavior, executing aggressively in high-efficiency states and deferring selectively when devices are degraded. Across low, medium, and high load regimes, the proposed method reduces deadline violations by 8–31% and improves throughput by 12–19% relative to fatigue-unaware reinforcement learning, with gains increasing as degradation strength grows. The method also maintains stable backlog as the number of devices increases and achieves sub-millisecond inference with constant per-device model size. These results show that explicitly modeling endogenous degradation can substantially improve reinforcement-learning-based scheduling in non-stationary resource-constrained environments.

title: Oracle MILP and Reinforcement Learning Bidding for PV-Battery Dispatch in an Incentive-Driven Local Flexibility Market
authors: N. Gkolia; N. Dimitropoulos; V. Marinakis
venue: 2025 16th International Conference on Information, Intelligence, Systems & Applications (IISA)
abstract: Within the EU-funded Hedge-IoT project to develop a local flexibility market, we investigate explicit demand response (DR) and behind-the-meter arbitrage in residential PV-battery systems. Perfect-foresight schedulers often incur net losses once DR payments are deducted. We develop a deterministic mixedinteger linear program (MILP) oracle that co-schedules battery charge/discharge with two DR schemes-instantaneous curtailment and energy-conserving deferral-under hourly and daily activation limits. The oracle's hour-by-hour net import/export profile is embedded in a custom OpenAI Gym environment for bidding into the emerging flexibility market, using dayahead wholesale prices as a proxy. We train Proximal Policy Optimization agents to place continuous quantity and price bids using only current-hour observations. On a 108-day dataset from 10 IoT-instrumented residential prosumers (Greece, 2024), with prices from the Greek day-ahead market in €/MWh and system statistics ($182 \pm 76 \text{kWh}$ PV, $304 \pm 102 \text{kWh}$ load), RL policies achieve mean net daily profits of € 4.1 (no DR), € 5.9 (curtailment), and € 4.2 (deferral), capturing $\boldsymbol{\sim} \mathbf{6 0 \%}$ of the arbitrage potential (€ 8.0 / day) and outperforming the hindsightoptimal oracle (net no DR: - € 19.0 / day). We outline market scope, discuss limitations of the Gym-based pricing model, and highlight relevance to emerging flexibility markets. Our results show that RL bidding is a practical and robust alternative to oracle-based scheduling in DR-aware energy arbitrage.

title: Knowing when you don't: Bag of visual words with reject option for automatic visual inspection of bulk materials
authors: M. Richter; T. Längle; J. Beyerer
abstract: Visual inspection of bulk material is the thorough optical inspection of streams of granular material to assess their quality or to detect defective objects. Examples are found in mining (discovery of ores), recycling (sorting waste from reusable material) and food safety (detection of pathogens). In these applications, it is generally not feasible or even possible to provide an accurate and exhaustive training set of all the materials that can be encountered during the inspection. Instead, classification has to be performed in an open world setting, i.e., with the option to recognize and reject unknown objects. Despite the practical relevance, prior work on this topic is surprisingly sparse. Here, we present a method to augment bag of visual words object descriptors by an additional unknown word that encodes outliers. The method depends on only few parameters that have a clear interpretation and is suitable for the application in the field. We demonstrate the performance of our approach using two real-world datasets and compare it to a related method. The experiments show that our method significantly outperforms classification with a closed world assumption as well as the related method.

title: Curated Uncertainty Exchange: A Deployment Pattern for Trustworthy AI in Expertise-Curated Environments, Motivated by a Heritage-Viticulture Re-Analysis
authors: F. Marques; A. Lourenço; P. Silva; M. Mateus; D. Fernandes; N. Ferreira; S. P. Soares; D. Augusto; T. Teixeira
venue: 2026 22nd International Conference on Distributed Computing in Smart Systems and the Internet of Things (DCOSS-IoT)
abstract: Trustworthy AI in agriculture is increasingly framed around autonomy: can the system be left alone? We argue this framing is a structural mismatch for an important class of operational environments, which we name expertise-curated environments—domains characterised by expertise-as-ground-truth held by a slow-to-train expert pool, cost-asymmetric errors, and regulatory density. In such environments, autonomy-first decision-making is structurally unfit, not merely conservative to deploy. We propose Curated Uncertainty Exchange (CUE), a pattern in which the expert seeds the AI’s training by curating ground truth upstream and arbitrates its operation by reconsultation on ranked uncertainty downstream, mediated by a rank-robust gate that is tolerant of imperfect confidence calibration. We instantiate CUE for heritage viticulture as a deployment pattern over the recently published vinum-Analytics pipeline for grapevine variety identification on the Vinha Maria Teresa parcel of Quinta do Crasto. We re-read vinum-Analytics’ published evaluation through the CUE lens and argue that its three operationally-relevant findings—100% Top-5 accuracy on the in-distribution test set, residual errors concentrated among morphologically similar variety pairs, and a 14.6% detection-failure rate identified as the primary deployment bottleneck—jointly motivate a two-part escalation gate (a structural abstention mechanism for upstream perception failure and a rank-percentile uncertainty mechanism for classifier uncertainty) whose combined expert-review budget is plausibly bounded at K≈15–20%, subject to validation with per-prediction confidence traces and plant-disjoint temporal data. We close by sketching how a multi-session aerial resurvey dataset, already collected at the same site and now under analysis, will support a temporal extension of the gate in future work.

title: Evaluating the Reliability and Utility of GPT-4o as a Medical Expert Across Different Interaction Modes
authors: U. -B. Menderes; D. Morár; N. T. Vu
venue: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Bioinformatics and Biomedicine (BIBM)
abstract: Generative Large Language Models (LLMs) such as GPT-4o are increasingly explored for use in clinical decision support, yet their real-world reliability and utility remain underexplored, especially in domains where factual accuracy is critical. This paper presents an empirical evaluation of GPT-40 in a medical expert role, focusing on its ability to provide clinically useful and reliable responses across varying degrees of external control. We evaluate three interaction strategies: Default Interaction, Hard Prompting, and Retrieval-augmented Generation (RAG), using a curated dataset of 70 authentic medical queries authored by practicing physicians. The practicing medical professionals evaluate the generated responses along two key dimensions: factual reliability and clinical utility. Our findings reveal critical trade-offs across the control spectrum: while RAG and hard prompting offer more constrained and verifiable responses, the default interaction approach achieved the highest combined ratings for reliability and clinical utility, showing the lowest abstention rate among the evaluated strategies. This study contributes a practical evaluation framework for assessing the potential of LLMs as medical experts and offers actionable insights for their deployment in healthcare contexts where factual precision, usability, and trust are paramount.

title: Machine Learning Techniques for Enhancing Security in Wireless Communication Systems
authors: S. Surya; R. Trimbak Ingle; M. Saxena; J. R. Poddutoori; D. Budesh Kanwer; D. Kapila
venue: 2025 International Conference on Pervasive Computational Technologies (ICPCT)
abstract: Web of Things or IoT frameworks rely upon wireless communication systems or WCS to accumulate and send measurements, their norm of execution is in danger from security assaults. In IoT frameworks, the Steering Conventions that can be routing protocols for Lower-Power (RPL) and Misfortune Systems administration are fundamental for successful measurements move; in any case, attacks can seriously disable usefulness. Utilizing the change of steering insights, traffic fascination through maverick focuses, and information passages to destructive places, these weaknesses compromise the legitimacy of organizations. To work on RPL's security and execution quality, this examination proposes a progressive AI and ML framework. This strategy joins a support learning calculation for adaptable and versatile highways, an irregular timberland framework for exact traffic classification, and modified RPL goals that consider order results while pursuing directing decisions. Displaying shows that this approach keeps up with negligible jitter while accomplishing extensive enhancements in bundle dispersion extents, network speed, and deferral. Also, it further develops execution quality in IoT-based WCS and solidly gets the RPL convention by accomplishing an extraordinary acknowledgment rate, scarcely any misleading up-sides, and speedy responses to somewhere safe occasions. The study's conclusions provide significant additions to the area and give a thorough way to safeguard RPL against common safety risks

title: Beyond the Trolley Problem: Dostoevsky's Crime and Punishment as a Framework for AI Ethics
authors: G. Haydarova; G. Salimova
venue: 2026 11th International Conference on Computer Science and Engineering (UBMK)
abstract: Autonomous systems in transport, medicine, and defence increasingly select actions in situations where every available option harms someone, yet many decision architectures scalarise heterogeneous harms into one objective and return a confident optimum. This paper asks what design requirements follow when that confidence is itself a failure mode. Using a qualitative interdisciplinary method—hermeneutic reading of Fyodor Dostoevsky's Crime and Punishment, conceptual mapping to AI decision contexts, and targeted thematic synthesis of peer-reviewed AI ethics literature—we develop three design claims. First, consequentialist language can operate as post-hoc rationalisation; therefore, the deployed objective should be audited against its stated ethical justification. Second, some individual-level harms should be encoded as aggregation-invariant constraints rather than weighted terms. Third, responsibility gaps should be treated as design defects requiring logged and attributable human decision points. We consolidate these claims into a moral confidence threshold: an abstention rule, related to selective prediction and safe reinforcement learning, that blocks autonomous execution when the best available action exceeds a deliberatively set individual-harm ceiling or when competing actions are morally indistinguishable. The mechanism is a conceptual design proposal, not a validated result; a simulator-based validation protocol is specified. The framework's Christian-personalist basis is a stated limitation requiring cross-tradition testing.

title: Multitruck Multidrone Collaborative Delivery via EG-GAT Embedding Multiagent DRL in Rural Areas
authors: H. Qi; J. Liu; X. Deng; H. Lin; J. Gui; J. Zhang; S. Wan
abstract: The vast geographic coverage and sparse customer distribution in rural areas lead to inefficiency in traditional last-mile delivery. Truck–drone collaborative delivery systems have emerged as a promising solution to these rural logistics challenges. Accordingly, we introduce a multitruck multidrone collaborative delivery framework. Within this framework, we propose a novel graph embedding module—the edge-gated graph attention network (EG-GAT)—which incorporates multidimensional edge features into the attention mechanism and introduces a learnable gating module for adaptive multihead fusion. We further propose a graded flexible time window mechanism, which permits limited service advancement or deferral while applying graded incentive–penalty structures. This approach better captures the temporal flexibility inherent in rural customer service requirements. The resulting multiobjective truck–drone routing problem is modeled as a reward-maximization task and solved using multiagent proximal policy optimization (MAPPO) under a centralized-training with decentralized-execution framework. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms other approaches. Furthermore, studies assess the individual effects of graded flexible time window settings and objective function weight coefficients on the optimization performance of collaborative delivery. Finally, we evaluate the practical advantages of our proposed model using real-world rural road cases.

title: Optimal Planning of Distribution Network Access for Deferring Network Reinforcement
authors: Z. Lin; Y. Zhou; X. Jiang; W. Gan; W. Zhou; J. Wu
venue: 2025 IEEE Power & Energy Society General Meeting (PESGM)
abstract: Distribution network access is the procedure of connecting new demand and generation to the existing distribution network. Given the large numbers of distributed generators (DGs) requesting access of various capacities at different places, it is challenging for distribution network operators (DNOs) to decide how much the new generation and demand should be connected at each node, given a certain target of total amounts to be connected each year. In this paper, an optimal planning method of distribution network access is proposed to enable DNOs to decide the optimal amount of new demand and generation to be connected at each node across the network. The objective is to maximize the economic benefits of deferring future network reinforcement, by minimizing the net present value of the reinforcement investment given certain load and generation growth rates. The impact of the newly connected demand and generation on future reinforcement is modelled via a feasible operation region-based approach, considering both active and reactive power. Simulation results on a 13-node feeder selected from the 11kV UKGDS distribution system reveal the validity of the proposed method.

title: Mitigating Bias and Hallucinations in LLMs Through Prompt Engineering and Knowledge-Grounded Approaches in Healthcare Domain
authors: A. P. D. Ishadya; A. Withanaarachchi; S. Jayalal
venue: 2026 6th International Conference on Advanced Research in Computing (ICARC)
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied in healthcare for clinical question answering and information support, yet their deployment is constrained by risks of hallucinated content and embedded bias that can compromise patient safety. This study proposes an integrated mitigation framework that combines advanced prompt engineering with knowledge-grounded approaches, specifically Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and the Model Context Protocol (MCP), without modifying underlying model parameters. Using a mixed-methods design, parallel RAG and MCP pipelines were implemented with shared retrieval and prompting logic and evaluated on NIH-derived MedQuAD subsets (CancerQA and NIDDKQA). Structured prompting strategies including role-based prompts, chain-of-thought, and chain-of-verification were applied consistently across both pipelines. Quantitative evaluation using accuracy, semantic similarity, evidence-backed rate, abstention, recall, and demographic drift metrics shows that MCP consistently outperforms or matches conventional RAG, achieving higher F1 and ROUGE-L scores, stronger evidence grounding, and lower abstention while maintaining minimal demographic drift. Expert review further confirmed improved clinical relevance and reduced unsupported claims. These findings demonstrate that coupling structured prompting with knowledge grounding produces more reliable, safer, and fairer healthcare LLM outputs, offering a practical and scalable pathway for trustworthy AI deployment in high-stakes clinical settings.

title: Signal in the Noise: An Auditable Reliability Layer for Biomedical Text Classification
authors: M. Y. Hassan; S. Wong; W. K. Xuan
venue: 2026 14th International Conference on Bioinformatics and Computational Biology (ICBCB)
abstract: Biomedical NLP pipelines routinely presuppose clean input text, yet large-scale corpora assembled through automated PDF parsing harbour pervasive OCR-like artifacts, token splits and merges, hyphenation remnants, and character-level corruption, that systematically erode lexical evidence and degrade downstream classifiers. We introduce a conservative, fully auditable spell-correction reliability layer conceived as a safety-oriented preprocessing module rather than a maximal-accuracy corrector: under conditions of uncertainty, the system abstains from editing, in accordance with a medical do-no-harm philosophy. The deterministic architecture couples bounded edit-distance candidate generation with corpus-derived n-gram scoring and a suite of biomedical safety gates that protect domain-critical terminology. We evaluate the layer both intrinsically, on a manually curated benchmark of 2,104 token-level cases, and extrinsically, on a tri-class CORD-19 topic classifier (Prevention, Treatment, Epidemiology) spanning 10,000 examples under a principled four-run protocol (Clean, Noisy, Restored, Safety). Intrinsically, the layer attains 94.61% error-fix recall on synthetic errors with zero harmful edits on negative controls. Downstream, it recovers approximately 80.45% of the noise-induced macro-F1 degradation, elevating macro-F1 from 0.7654 (Noisy) to 0.7717 (Restored) while preserving near-clean performance (Safety: 0.7721). A supplementary case study on 103 real-world OCR-extracted abstracts classified with BioBERT confirms that transformer encoders appeared relatively robust to mild noise, motivating a future grey-box architecture that integrates bounded neural signals and UMLS lexicons without compromising auditability. The system is fully deterministic, artifact-driven, and designed with deployment and auditability in mind.

title: Persona Vectors in Controlling Hallucination of Small Large Language Models: A Safety-Oriented Analysis
authors: U. Kose; I. Uysal
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) ensured a paradigm change in artificial intelligence research and the way of human-computer interaction. However, they are not perfect yet and can easily demonstrate failures in generating senseful answers. Hallucinations are among the failures, and they are known as fabricated, false but convincing content. Reasons for hallucinations vary but the US company Anthropic showed that a latent space called as persona vectors can be one reason triggering them. So, it is seen that monitoring and controlling such vectors can help in reducing hallucinations. In this sense, this study presents an analysis of persona vectors in hallucination behaviors, by considering four different small models: TinyLlama, Qwen2, Phi-2, and Phi-3-mini. The study included use of two data sets TruthfulQA, and SQuAD v2 to test the models with four different metrics (in terms of accuracy, hallucinations, and abstention) and analyze them in a basic RAG experiment. According to the findings, the persona switches had the highest effect on abstention behaviors of the models.

title: FCD: Fallback Cognitive Deferral in Complex Human–Machine Collaboration Tasks
authors: C. He; B. Zou; J. Xing; X. Li; J. Chen; Y. Shi; H. Ma
abstract: Integrating machine learning with human expertise has become essential in human–AI collaboration, especially when models face uncertainty. A key challenge lies in determining when to defer to humans to optimize both accuracy and cost. Inspired by Kahneman’s dual-process theory, we propose the fallback cognitive deferral (FCD) framework, which models fast, automatic decisions via a machine-only module (System 1), and defers complex or uncertain cases to a human–AI hybrid module (System 2). Focusing on three alternative switching mechanisms, we introduce adaptive thresholding, reinforcement learning, and joint training—each representing a distinct deferral strategy that governs the transition between System 1 and System 2. A novel surrogate loss function is designed for System 2, incorporating expert-annotated labels and expert defer costs to mitigate excessive reliance on human input. Extensive experiments across image, text, and medical domains demonstrate favorable accuracy–coverage tradeoffs under varying levels of expert involvement. For example, on the correctional offender management profiling for alternative sanctions dataset, FCD Joint improves accuracy by 2.4% over the human-alone model and 4.1% over the machine-only baseline at 70% coverage. This work offers a cognitively grounded framework for efficient and scalable human–AI collaboration.

title: Multimodal Vision-Language Models for High- Stakes Decision Making
authors: B. Mandal; S. Sardana; D. Garg
venue: 2026 IEEE Global Symposium on Emerging and Communication Technologies (GSEACT)
abstract: Application of multimodal vision-language models (VLMs) has proven to be capable of impressive perception, reasoning, and post-discovery abilities; however, their use in high-stakes decision-making setups has been limited in regard to concerns about reliability, hallucination, as well as accountability. This paper introduces a risk-conscious procedure of trustworthy multimodal decision-making fitting evidence grounding, uncertainty quantification, and selective prediction into one remarkable structure. The proposed system makes the models explain the output using verifiable visual and textual indicators and simultaneously estimate confidence to deployment risk. A counterfactual validation mechanism is yet another method that judges how predictions do in cases of perturbations, allowing an automatic increase in prediction to human experts when the ambiguity goes beyond tolerable limits. Experiments in safety-critical situations demonstrate that unsupported claims are significantly reduced, and calibration is improved compared to standard VLM pipelines and makes them much more robust. These findings provide a viable road map to verifiable and human conformable artificial intelligence applicable in activities of actual world applications where mistakes have enormous societal, legal and economic implications.

title: Discovering and Repairing Blind Spots in LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluation of Multi-Turn AI Systems
authors: V. Gummadavelli; U. Imtiaz; P. A; S. H. Kolla; N. S. Bavirisetty; S. R. Kondapalli
venue: 2026 International Conference on Intelligent and Sustainable AI Systems (ICOSAAS)
abstract: The widespread use of Large Language Models (LLMs) as automated evaluators for multi-turn conversational AI systems is due to their scalability and adaptability. Nonetheless, LLM-as-a-judge systems often have systemic blind spots, leading to the neglect of certain flaws because to insufficient, inflexible, or biased assessment standards. This project investigates if disparities between human annotations and LLM evaluations might function as a diagnostic instrument to identify missing evaluation criteria and improve rubric design. By developing a rubric, we provide a systematic framework that may identify indications of disagreement, categorize them to uncover concealed defect patterns, and initiate new aspects of evaluation. The proposed improvements to the rubric are assessed using previously inspected datasets to verify its universality and reliability. We provide a confidence-aware abstention mechanism that detects doubtful predictions and refers them to human assessors to enhance safety and dependability. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed technique improves defect memory, optimizes the calibration of confidence and accuracy in defect prediction, decreases false alarms, and lowers total annotation costs. Our findings suggest that human disagreement should be regarded not just as noise, but as a crucial signal that might enhance LLM-based assessment systems over time.

title: Investment Deferral of Feeder Upgrades Revealed by System-Wide Unbalanced Dynamic Rating: Harvesting the Hidden Capacity of Distribution Systems Discovered by Thermal Map Technology
authors: A. Borbuev; W. Wang; H. Lu; S. Jazebi; F. de León
abstract: Dynamic thermal rating for underground cables with balanced phase currents has been extensively studied in the literature. Paradoxically, distribution feeders operate inherently unbalanced and no publications are available for unbalanced thermal rating. Because of the lack of technology, utilities operate with very conservative margins using the maximum of the three-phase currents to determine the line loading. This practice leads to the significant underutilization of underground cables. To fill the gap this paper presents a physically sound and accurate transient electro-thermal model of unbalanced three-phase distribution cables considering variations in the load and environment. Moreover, the model proposed in this paper allows harvesting the large hidden capacity of distribution systems trapped in the thermal inertia of underground cables. A convenient visual tool is developed to uncover hot spots and underutilized energy routes. This facilitates real-time network reconfiguration based on predicted load graphs and dynamic thermal conditions. The proposed model is also useful to study load growth, perhaps eliminating or deferring capital investments needed to upgrade the capacity of the existing underground feeders. The IEEE 37-bus distribution network is used as a case study. The results show that the proposed methodology has a high potential to defer investments, for instance, one could save $5M for a small system like the IEEE 37-bus distribution network which would have been necessary under current conservative practice.

title: An Holistic Approach to e-Nose Response Patterns Analysis—An Application to Nondestructive Tests
authors: M. Salvato; S. De Vito; E. Esposito; E. Massera; M. Miglietta; G. Fattoruso; G. Di Francia
abstract: Artificial olfaction is an emerging application field for machine learning practitioners. In this paper, we propose a holistic approach to pattern classification in electronic noses applications. In particular, we show how classification results based on a complete measurement cycle can be combined with an assessment provided by real-time classifiers acting on the single instantaneous measurement sample. A running classification confidence measure allows for obtaining fast and reliable outcomes. A safety critical scenario has been selected for the testing of the proposed pattern analysis strategy involving the identification and discrimination of surface contaminants on composite panels in pre-bonding nondestructive tests during lightweight aircraft assembly. A reject option has been introduced to refuse low classification confidence panels improving both FP and FN rates. Results show how this strategy can efficiently exploit two different views of the electronic nose olfactive fingerprinting process that is currently seen as alternative.

title: Deep Learning-Based Meat Freshness Detection With Segmentation and OOD-Aware Classification
authors: H. A. Bramantyo; M. A. Faridi; R. Chen; C. Harris; Y. Sun
abstract: In this study, we present a meat freshness classification framework from Red–Green–Blue (RGB) images that supports both packaged and unpackaged meat datasets. The system classifies four in-distribution (ID) meat classes and uses an out-of-distribution (OOD)-aware abstention mechanism that flags low-confidence samples as No Result. The pipeline combines U-Net-based segmentation with deep feature classifiers. Segmentation is used as a preprocessing step to isolate the meat region and reduce background, producing more consistent inputs for classification. The segmentation module achieved an Intersection over Union (IoU) of 75% and a Dice coefficient of 82%, producing standardized inputs for the classification stage. For classification, we benchmark five backbones: Residual Network-50 (ResNet-50), Vision Transformer-Base/16 (ViT-B/16), Swin Transformer-Tiny (Swin-T), EfficientNet-B0, and MobileNetV3-Small. We use nested $5\times 3$ cross-validation (CV) for model selection and hyperparameter tuning. On the held-out ID test set, EfficientNet-B0 achieves the highest accuracy (98.10%), followed by ResNet-50 and MobileNetV3-Small (both 97.63%) and Swin-T (97.51%), while ViT-B/16 is lower (94.42%). We additionally evaluate OOD scoring and thresholding using standard OOD metrics and sensitivity analysis over the abstention threshold. Finally, we report on-device latency using TensorFlow Lite (TFLite) on a smartphone, highlighting practical accuracy–latency trade-offs for future deployment.

title: A Cost-Efficient CWE-Grounded Multi-Agent LLM Pipeline for Web and API Vulnerability Analysis: Design, Statistical Evaluation, and Implications for 5G/6G Edge Deployment
authors: A. B. Zhenissov; I. Shayea; D. Marlambekov; A. Mukhanbet; Y. Nurakhov; L. Rzayeva
venue: IEEE Open Journal of the Communications Society
abstract: Software-defined fifth-generation (5G) and sixth-generation (6G) networks expose web and application programming interface layers across distributed edge infrastructure, enlarging the attack surface while commercial static analysis stays costly for small teams. This study introduces a Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE)-based multi-agent pipeline: a detector agent achieves high recall, a validator agent scores candidates, and ambiguous cases are escalated to a human analyst. Escalation is formalized as classification with a reject option, with closed-form thresholds and proof that human review does not reduce precision. The pipeline was evaluated over ten runs on the Spiracle benchmark (blinded re-annotation), and against the OWASP Benchmark, compared to CodeQL, a single-agent configuration, and a rule-plus-large-language-model baseline. Precision reached 83.3% on Spiracle and 0.683 with 0.867 recall on labeled data, costing under ${\$}0.10$ per scan. Model drift—not sampling temperature—explained most run-to-run variation. The evaluation used Java web code from two benchmarks; no 5G network function was scanned, and a deterministic analyzer outperformed the pipeline on detection.

title: SPR: Shielded Processor Reservations with Bounded Management Overhead
authors: E. Kökten; G. Parmer; B. B. Brandenburg
venue: 2025 IEEE 31st Real-Time and Embedded Technology and Applications Symposium (RTAS)
abstract: With growing hardware consolidation in modern computational infrastructures, ensuring predictable CPU allocation has become increasingly critical. Processor reservations, usually realized through rate-limiting servers, play an essential role in providing such predictability by precisely controlling when and how long each task may execute. In theory, ratelimiting servers provide strong temporal isolation, meaning that a task's timely access to its guaranteed budget is not contingent on the behavior of any other task in the system. However, in practice, these guarantees are easily undermined by the realities of actual hardware and shortcomings in naïve reservation implementations. When confronted with malicious tasks using the reservation policy itself to attack the very security and rate properties it is meant to uphold, temporal isolation breaks down in current implementations. In response, this paper presents shielded processor reservation (SPR) scheduling, a novel approach that ensures that at most two reservations are processed per scheduler invocation and integrates deferred timer handling, early replenishment processing, and processor access granularity guarantees to provide robust temporal isolation. We implement SPR and existing rate-limiting servers in the Composite operating system and evaluate its performance. The results demonstrate that SPR provides reliable rate-limiting with low overhead while also mitigating vulnerabilities that can be exploited to attack existing reservation systems.

title: An Adaptive Expert-Based Agricultural Phenomics Framework for Trustworthy Crop Disease Diagnosis Using ConvNeXt V2
authors: V. Jaiswal; S. Verma; S. Kumar; M. B. Ratnaparkhe; M. Jain; R. M. Patel
venue: 2026 International Conference on Advanced Computing Technologies (ICACT)
abstract: Plant diseases destroy an estimated forty percent of global crop production each year, imposing losses exceeding two hundred billion US dollars annually. Existing deep-learning diagnostic systems share a structural weakness: they route all crops through a single shared feature space, emit predictions without calibrated confidence signals, and produce models too large for edge field deployment. This paper presents the Adaptive Expert-Based Agricultural Phenomics Framework (AEAPF), which organizes crop disease diagnosis around six coordinated components: ConvNeXt V2 Large expert encoders, domain-adaptive self-supervised pre-training via masked reconstruction, a learned soft Adaptive Expert Router, multi-task disease intelligence, a fused Monte Carlo dropout and test-time augmentation uncertainty module, and a knowledge distillation pathway to a compact ConvNeXt V2 Nano student. Evaluated on a 1,405-image held-out unified test set spanning 21 disease classes across wheat and soybean, AEAPF achieves 93.45% accuracy, 0.913 macro-F1, and 0.998 macro-AUROC. Confidence-aware selective prediction reaches 96.1% auto-diagnosis coverage at a 5% risk ceiling (AURC = 0.0078). The distilled student model contains only 15.0 million parameters and achieves 593 frames per second on GPU at sub-2 ms latency, enabling practical field deployment.

title: RACER: Risk-Aware Conformal Expert Routing for Efficient and Trustworthy Mixture-of-Experts Language Models
authors: Y. Guo; A. Li; Q. Tang; H. Ma
venue: 2026 International Joint Conference on Neural Networks (IJCNN)
abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models promise favorable capacity–compute trade-offs, yet their routing decisions remain brittle: a single misrouted token can trigger compounding hallucinations or costly fallback heuristics, undermining reliability in real deployments. We propose RACER, a post-hoc, risk-controlled routing layer that turns a black-box MoE (or any cascaded language system) into a selective generator: the system either (i) answers with a cheap expert path or (ii) escalates to a stronger expert (or retrieval-augmented path) when its own signals indicate elevated risk. RACER is built around conformal risk control and "learn-then-test" (LTT) calibration, yielding finite-sample guarantees on selective risk under mild exchangeability assumptions. We evaluate RACER on two real tasks—TruthfulQA factuality and Natural Questions open-domain QA—using both a Mixtral-8x7B MoE system and a LLaMA-2-7B → 70B cascade. Across settings, RACER satisfies user-specified risk constraints while achieving 26–45% compute savings over always-large baselines at matched error rates, outperforming six competitive baselines including entropy thresholding, temperature scaling, and self-consistency routing. Ablations confirm robustness to calibration set size (stable with n ≥ 150), distribution shift (topic/time splits), and score function choice. Code will be released upon acceptance.

title: ARGUS-Net: An Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Agent Framework for Multimodal Deepfake Detection With Probabilistic Evidence Fusion
authors: Y. Hmimou; M. Tabaa; A. Khiat; Z. Hidila
abstract: The rapid proliferation of generative models has made deepfake media increasingly realistic and accessible, posing critical threats to digital forensics and multimedia trust. Existing detection methods predominantly rely on single-modality analysis and deterministic predictions, yielding overconfident outputs and limited robustness under ambiguous and cross-dataset conditions. We introduce ARGUS-Net, an uncertainty-aware multi-agent framework for multimodal deepfake detection based on probabilistic evidence fusion. Four independent forensic agents analyzing physiological signals (rPPG), audio-visual synchronization, spectral artifacts, and CNN-based facial manipulation produce modality-specific suspicion and confidence scores. A probabilistic reasoning module fuses this multimodal evidence to estimate deepfake probability and quantify decision uncertainty via Shannon entropy. When uncertainty is high, the ARGUS-AC mechanism triggers controlled perturbations (illumination, motion, and occlusion) to re-evaluate ambiguous cases, reducing mean predictive entropy from 0.985 to 0.935. Decision-making is strictly separated from a post-hoc LLM-based forensic explanation module, ensuring interpretability without affecting the integrity of the detection process. Evaluated on Celeb-DF v2 (AUC = 0.793) and FaceForensics++ (AUC = 0.633), and further assessed on WildDeepfake under a restricted-modality external protocol, ARGUS-Net demonstrates that probabilistic multimodal reasoning combined with active uncertainty resolution improves the reliability of deepfake detection systems while remaining strongly sensitive to domain shift.

title: Disaster Management and Information Transmission Decision-Making in Public Safety Systems
authors: G. Fragkos; E. E. Tsiropoulou; S. Papavassiliou
