Controlled anomaly simulations further showed that, when approximately 30% of satellite–epoch links were perturbed, UL-GSR retained an accuracy of (74.34% ± 5.68%) using the originally trained models and outperformed both deterministic baselines. In addition, in a within-city cross-area transfer experiment using 500 labeled target-area samples, source-domain initialization achieved 81.24% accuracy, compared with 71.64% for training from random initialization.

title: Achievable Error Exponents for Almost Fixed-Length M-Ary Hypothesis Testing
authors: J. Diao; L. Zhou; L. Bai
venue: ICASSP 2023 - 2023 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing (ICASSP)
abstract: We revisit multiple hypothesis testing and propose a two-phase test, where each phase is a fixed-length test and the second-phase proceeds only if a reject option is decided in the first phase. We derive achievable error exponents of error probabilities under each hypothesis and show that our two-phase test bridges over fixed-length and sequential tests in both Neyman-Pearson and Bayesian settings in the similar spirit of Lalitha and Javidi [1] for binary hypothesis testing. Specifically, our test may achieve the performance close to a sequential test with the asymptotic complexity of a fixed-length test and such test is named the almost fixed-length test. Our results generalize the design and analysis of the almost fixed-length test for binary hypothesis testing to account for more than two outcomes.

title: Contribution of Microgrids to distribution network reliability
authors: A. L. A. Syrri; E. A. Martínez Ceseña; P. Mancarella
abstract: The current development of distribution networks into active and smarter systems has been facilitated by the integration of novel technologies such as Microgrids (MGs) and Distributed Energy Resources. These new concepts are expected to bring about significant economic benefits at the distribution level in the form of network reinforcement deferral and increased reliability levels, among others. In this context, this paper aims at shedding light on the impacts that the use of MGs for post-contingency distribution network management can have on reliability. For this purpose, a reliability assessment tool based on sequential Monte Carlo Simulations (MCS) is presented and used for the evaluation of a real distribution network, while a framework to implement the MG services is also proposed. The results show that reliability improvements for MG users can be remarkable, while external network users and the network operator also perceive benefits. The former experience higher reliability levels, and the latter experience lower network reinforcement needs when connecting additional customers due to the services provided by MGs.

title: Confidence-Calibrated and Explainable Decision-Support System for Pneumonia Detection from Chest X-Ray Images
authors: S. Vallu; K. Gupta; C. Singh; S. Tensingh
venue: 2026 International Conference on Advancements in Smart, Secure and Intelligent Computing (ASSIC)
abstract: Pneumonia is a serious respiratory infection that needs to be diagnosed in a timely and precise manner. Although the main diagnostic tool is the Chest X-Ray (CXR) imaging, the interpretation is still very difficult and subjective. Although deep learning models are performing well, most of the existing methods are not clinically reliable and interpretable. The paper introduces a confidence-calibrated, explainable decision-support system to detect pneumonia, CXR image. The system uses a well-tuned ResNet-18 classifier, uses temperature scaling to post-hoc confidence calibration, and uses a selective prediction strategy to refer low-confidence cases to expert review. Visual explanations created by Gradientweighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM), indicating diagnostically relevant parts of the image. This framework gives a test accuracy of 90.71, decreases the Expected Calibration Error (ECE) to 0.0548, and appropriately rejects 47 among 624 test samples due to uncertainty. These results indicate that classification combined with calibration and selective deferral and explainability within the same pipeline can greatly enhance clinical plausibility of AI-assisted diagnosis of pneumonia.

title: Achievable Error Exponents for Almost Fixed-Length Binary Classification
authors: L. Bai; J. Diao; L. Zhou
venue: 2022 IEEE International Symposium on Information Theory (ISIT)
abstract: We revisit the binary classification problem where the generating distribution under each hypothesis is unknown and propose a two-phase test, where each phase is a fixed-length test and the second-phase proceeds only if a reject option is decided in the first phase. We derive the achievable error exponents of both type-I and type-II error probabilities. Furthermore, we illustrate our results via numerical examples and show that the performance close to sequential test can be achieved with the much simpler and less complex almost fixed-length test. Our results generalize the design and analysis of the almost fixed-length test for binary hypothesis testing (Lalitha and Javidi, ISIT 2016) to the more practical setting of binary classification.

title: Waiting Cost Based Long-Run Network Investment Decision-Making Under Uncertainty
authors: X. Yan; C. Gu; H. Zhang; F. Li; Y. Song
abstract: Traditional system investment decision is costly and hard to reverse. This is aggravated by uncertainties from flexible load and renewables (FLR), which impact the accuracy of network investment decisions and could trigger a high asset risk. Thus, system operators have the incentive to postpone network reinforcement, and `wait and see' whether the request of investment can be reduced or delayed with new information. This paper proposes a novel method to evaluate network investment horizon deferral based on the trade-off between waiting profit and waiting cost under FLR uncertainties. Although deferring investment leads to waiting cost, it is worthy to wait if the cost is smaller than the waiting profits. To capture the impact of FLR uncertainties on system investment, nodal uncertainties are converted into branch flow uncertainties based on a combined cumulant and Gram-Charlier expansion method. The waiting cost is quantified by the options' cost based on real options method and waiting profit is from asset present value reduction due to the deferral. Thus, by paying waiting cost, current investment cost can be reserved until uncertainties are reduced to an acceptable level. The waiting time is evaluated by Sharp ratio and expected return, determined by the waiting cost and uncertainty level. The results show that paying waiting cost is an economical way to reduce the impact of uncertainty and avoid hastily investment.

title: Economic Impacts and Mitigation for the Grid Connected Electric Vehicle Charging: A Technical and Operational Overview
authors: O. E. Ikhajangbe; H. Dhulipati; S. Liu
abstract: The rapid growth of residential electric vehicle (EV) adoption is reshaping distribution networks, shifting load patterns from relatively dispersed background demand to synchronized, high-amplitude charging events. When charging is unmanaged, these concentrated loads can exceed thermal and voltage limits, accelerate transformer aging, intensify harmonic stress, and prompt costly infrastructure upgrades. Unlike prior reviews that examine technical, economic, and coordination aspects separately, this paper brings them together within an integrated technical–economic analytical review that considers thermal limits, voltage security, and battery state-of-charge constraints simultaneously. Transformer loss-of-life, harmonic–thermal interactions, peak amplification, and renewable–EV timing mismatch are quantitatively analyzed alongside infrastructure deferral benefits and ancillary-service revenues. Economic performance is evaluated by balancing upgrade deferral, V2G revenue, battery degradation costs, and coordination overhead. A comparative assessment of ARIMA, LSTM, and reinforcement learning methods highlights practical trade-offs between forecasting accuracy and computational scalability under evolving charging behavior. Evidence from field pilots reports 10–30% peak reduction, 20–65% charging cost savings, and 100–500 per EV-year gross V2G revenue, depending on market structure and incentives. Overall, this review provides an integrated analytical foundation to support resilient and economically efficient EV–grid integration under high-penetration conditions.

title: DCWF-QA: A Domain Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Question Answering on Direct-Coupled Waveguide Filters
authors: Y. Hu; W. Zhang; F. Feng; K. Liu
venue: 2026 IEEE International Conference on Radio Frequency and Antenna Technologies (RFAT)
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for technical assistance, yet their reliability on highly specialized RF/microwave engineering queries is not well quantified. We introduce DCWF-QA, a focused benchmark for direct-coupled waveguide filters (DCWF) built from 214 peer-reviewed papers. We define six question types to cover the core information needs and typical failure modes in this domain: numeric specifications, structural/topology reasoning, transmission-zero analysis, tuning/manufacturing considerations, design-process workflows, and refusal/abstention for evidence-insufficient cases. Starting from 25680 LLM-synthesized candidates, expert screening yields 3107 curated questions with traceable paper identifiers. We evaluate representative LLMs under no-retrieval and article-level RAG settings using end-to-end answer accuracy (QA-Acc) and retrieval evidence recall (Hit@5). Results show that DCWF-QA is challenging for LLMs without retrieval, while RAG effectively improves answer correctness and achieves strong evidence coverage. Nevertheless, the overall performance of current models remains unsatisfactory with substantial room for improvement. This demonstrates that grounding is both measurable and beneficial for specialized engineering QA, and highlights the significance of DCWF-QA as a targeted evaluation framework to advance model capability in this niche domain.

title: Impact of Flexibility Services Implementation on Power Network Constraint Management
authors: C. Cruzat; S. Karim Anaya; M. G. Pollitt; R. Williams
abstract: The widespread deployment of flexibility services e.g. by generators, energy storage units and demand response, are causing novel challenges to Distribution Network Operators (DNOs) or Distribution System Operators (DSOs) when managing their power systems. The aim of this research is to understand the economic impact that these flexibility services could cause on possible future world scenarios. This paper presents the main findings obtained from the MERLIN project, which explores and compares the techno-economic impact of managing network operational constraints through traditional reinforcement and flexibility services over a ten-year forecast period. Two case studies were carried out, the realistic case (RC), which focusess on realistic load and generation forecasts, and the worst-case (WC), which is what is traditionally performed by DNO system planners to model the impact of peak demand when generation is turned off over a period of time. The analysis was conducted on the 33/11 kV network in Fort William, (Western Scottish Highlands). The study revealed insights into the anticipated costs of traditional reinforcement and influenced when flexibility services would be a more favorable investment option. Results suggest that flexibility services are preferred only to deal with thermal constraints in the 33 kV line, with no or negligible savings in the 11 kV line. The results show discounted savings of around £175k for four year deferral (by 2050), equivalent to 12% of reinforcement costs.

title: A Review on an Android Application for Medicine Availability and Location Finder
authors: S. Ghodeswar; P. Gawali; S. Chaudhari; M. Jawade; M. Gawande; S. Sawwashere

title: Probabilistic Planning for Distribution Networks including Optimal DER Regulation and Storage Allocation
authors: S. Massucco; G. Mosaico; P. Pongiglione; M. Saviozzi; F. Silvestro
venue: 2020 IEEE Power & Energy Society General Meeting (PESGM)
abstract: The increasing penetration of Renewable Energy Sources (RESs) in distribution networks is requiring smarter integration techniques, in order to guarantee secure system operation and grid reinforcement deferral. Distributed resources can contribute to voltage management through Volt/var regulation and, if storage devices are installed, to relieve congestions by leveraging smart control strategies. This work proposes a probabilistic planning formulation for the allocation of storage systems, to be optimally controlled together with other sources available along the grid feeders. The target is to minimize the number of storage modules needed to guarantee technical and quality constraints for all components. The presented approach is implemented in GAMS (General Algebraic Modeling System) and applied to the real distribution grid of Sanremo, Italy.

title: Verification of tool for allocation of harmonic current emissions considering frequency-dependent impedance
authors: T. I. Reigstad; B. I. Oftedal; T. Holm; B. N. Torsæter; H. Taxt
abstract: Simple tools with sufficient accuracy are needed to calculate the impact of new customers on voltage quality. This paper presents the results, findings and conclusions from the verification of a tool for calculating harmonic current emissions limits based on IEC 61000-3-6. The main advantage of the tool is the estimation of the frequency-dependent impedance using a simplified network model. In most cases, this allows higher harmonic current emissions limits for new customers and thus lower costs for connecting new nonlinear loads for the customer. In addition, the tool is easy to use for DSOs and can enable grid reinforcement deferral. The tool also provides more knowledge about the low-frequency resonances in the grid and can thus support the filter design and converter control. However, the simplification of modelling only the main feeders can lead to large discrepancies in cable-dominated grids or when a significant cable near the customer is not modelled. In these cases, modelling of the main branches is also required.

title: Operational load forecasts for dynamic flexibility procurement
authors: N. Wade; K. Soderquest; W. Yang; G. Williamson; A. Glennie; P. Glendinning
abstract: Changes to the management of electricity distribution networks requires the development of essential system operation functions, which include refined forecasting capabilities. The work presented here identifies the most suitable approach to optimise and de-risk the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into demand forecasting functions for operational decision making. As distribution network operators (DNOs) develop their distribution system operation (DSO) functions, a step change is required in their forecasting capability to optimise flexibility procurement. Annual, assumptions-driven models that forecast load at primary and secondary substations will not suffice; operational forecasts at the monthly, weekly and daily level are required to inform flexibility procurement and dispatch decisions that enable deferral of network reinforcement expenditure. This research develops day and week-ahead load forecasting models at primary and secondary substations, utilising the latest advancements in time-series and machine learning methods, to identify flexibility needs and bring procurement of these services closer to the time of use. Development of such capability is critical for network management and has scope for considerable cost efficiencies. Results are presented for the performance of a selection of forecasting methods, partitioned by input data quality and periods of peak demand.

title: A novel planning process approach – widening flexibility range
authors: J. Milheiro; L. M. Coelho; R. M. Bento
venue: 28th International Conference and Exhibition on Electricity Distribution (CIRED 2025)
abstract: Distribution System Operators (DSOs) are being challenged to demonstrate the need to construct new network infrastructures compared to other viable alternatives, namely the use of market-based contracting of flexibility of distributed resources. A recent experience by E-REDES with a set of flexibility use cases showed that no economic efficiency was recognized in flexibility alternatives as a mechanism for investment deferral. Instead, regarding this limitation and considering the finite investment resources that DSOs have, it is proposed to establish flexibility alternatives to guarantee power supply within regulatory and safety standards, even if the grid rated capacity does not suffice. This paper introduces a new approach to the planning process within the scope of investments justified by load growth. It is proposed that flexibility contracts, along with power flow probabilistic methodology, be taken advantage of as a risk management tool to ensure the satisfaction of consumption loads under normal operating conditions. A use case is presented where flexibility requirements are proposed to avoid expected constraints, at least until the project's conclusion.

title: Omission-Aware Evaluation of AI Agents Under Informational Incompleteness
authors: A. Koshio
venue: 2026 20th IIAI International Congress on Advanced Applied Informatics (IIAI-AAI)
abstract: AI agent evaluation has advanced from static question answering to trajectory-level measurement of tool use, task completion, latency, cost, and safety failures. These measures are necessary, but they still miss a failure mode that becomes salient when agents act under informational incompleteness: an agent may complete a task while relying on a thin, stale, homogeneous, or socially partial information ecology. It may mistake model priors for evidence, ignore stakeholders absent from the prompt, or force closure when responsible action requires clarification or deferral. This paper roposes an omission-aware evaluation layer for AI agents. The layer has two trace-level constructs: informational health, which evaluates whether the agent's action is grounded in task-appropriate, provenance-aware, uncertainty-aware, and plural information use; and absent-data awareness, which evaluates whether the agent detects and responds to missing evidence, missing stakeholders, temporal absence, structural exclusion, and frame-relative omission. We specify a scoring model combining outcome quality, informational health, and absent-data awareness, with an omission-sensitive gate for high-stakes tasks. Six benchmark patterns and small feasibility pilots illustrate how the constructs can be annotated and audited. The central claim is modest: valuable agents should not only act effectively; they should recognize when their informational basis is too incomplete for responsible closure.

title: An Intelligent Approach for the Challenges in the Evaluation of Public Accountant Firms Under Uncertainties
authors: Z. Yu
abstract: For certified public accountant (CPA) firms to maintain high levels of competent assistance, achievement evaluations are essential. However, because aspects like customer fulfilment, productivity, economic success, and legality include personal and interconnected assessments, standard approaches to assessment frequently fall short of addressing the inherent complexity and uncertainty in decision-making. To overcome these issues, this paper suggests a unique multiple-criteria decision-making (MCDM) model based on complex T-Spherical fuzzy Frank (CTSFF) operations. The approach uses complex T-spherical fuzzy Frank Weighted Averaging (CTSFFWA) and complex T-spherical fuzzy Frank Weighted Geometric (CTSFFWG) operators to manage multi-attribute assessment under unclear and uncertain circumstances. The ability to handle subjective and unclear data while integrating interconnections between several assessment requirements is lacking in the practical assessment methods currently used by CPA companies. This restriction makes obtaining trustworthy and useful information for enhancing company operations more difficult. The intricacy of contemporary CPA operations, such as the increasing requirement to consider qualitative assessments and a range of client viewpoints, calls for creating a strong and flexible structure to support decision-making. The inability of conventional fuzzy frameworks to accurately represent these subtleties necessitates using sophisticated techniques. To retain mathematical accuracy while accounting for ambiguity via membership, non-membership, and abstention degrees, the suggested model uses CTSFF logic. A thorough assessment of CPA company achievement through various factors is made possible by the improved aggregation possibilities introduced using CTSFFWA and CTSFFWG operators. Flexibility evaluation is additionally built into the framework to guarantee the findings’ reliability and pinpoint ideal factor setups. This research gives decision-makers a versatile instrument to modify the framework for various expert business sectors. It offers a methodical and comprehensive way to assess the efficiency of CPA firms. This investigation makes an essential contribution to the discipline of decision-making under uncertainty by filling in the deficiencies in the assessment methods that are currently in use.

title: Uncertainty-Aware IGBT Aging State Classification for Traction Inverters Using Bayesian Residual Networks
authors: J. Liu; S. Sahoo; X. Wei; B. Yao; Y. Zhang; Y. Liu; F. Blaabjerg; H. Wang
venue: 2026 International Power Electronics Conference (IPEC-Nagasaki 2026 - ECCE Asia)
abstract: Condition monitoring of insulated gate bipolar transistor (IGBT) modules in traction inverters is essential for reliability-oriented operation. Existing data-driven methods can classify aging levels from measured waveforms, but most are deterministic and provide only point predictions without quantifying confidence, particularly when the input lies outside the training distribution. This paper proposes a Bayesian 1D residual network for four-class IGBT aging level classification using multi-sensor time-series data acquired from a 5-kW traction inverter. By treating the network weights as probability distributions, the model preserves high closed-set classification accuracy (97.8%) while quantifying predictive uncertainty. The uncertainty is further decomposed into aleatoric and epistemic components to distinguish data ambiguity from model ignorance. Uncertainty quantification is employed not to replace aging level classification, but to provide a principled reject option for unreliable predictions: unseen aging levels and unseen mission profiles produce elevated epistemic uncertainty, whereas noise-corrupted measurements mainly increase aleatoric uncertainty. The results show that Bayesian learning can improve the trustworthiness of condition monitoring systems for safety-critical traction power converters.

title: AgroChat: A Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Assistant with Reliability-Aware Inference for Crop Diagnosis
authors: M. Deepika; P. Rishita; U. Sreehitha; P. V. Kumar; S. H. Vardhan; S. Brinda
venue: 2026 5th International Conference on Innovative Mechanisms for Industry Applications (ICIMIA)
abstract: Agriculture faces many challenges such as crop diseases, pests, and changing weather conditions. However, many farmers in rural areas still find it difficult to get proper guidance because internet access is limited and expert support is expensive. Most existing tools give general advice and do not consider local environmental conditions. For example, they may suggest spraying chemicals just before rainfall, which reduces its effectiveness. To address these limitations, we propose AgroChat, an offline-first multimodal agricultural assistant designed for lowconnectivity environments. Unlike a generic combination of CNN-based classification, retrieval-augmented generation, and languagemodel reasoning, AgroChat combines dual visual diagnosis branches for plant disease and insect recognition, retrieval-grounded advisory generation from a curated agricultural knowledge base, optional weather-aware conditioning, and a reliability-aware abstention mechanism that withholds responses when supporting evidence is insufficient. The system uses two EfficientNet-B0 classifiers, ChromaDB retrieval with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings, and a locally deployed LLaMA 3.2 1B model to generate grounded recommendations without cloud dependency. Our results show that the system achieves 91.2% response accuracy with a hallucination rate of 8.6%, demonstrating its ability to provide reliable and context-aware agricultural decision support for farmers. The source code is available at: https://github.com/Sreehitha05/Agrochat.git.

title: Mastering Linux Device Driver Development: Write custom device drivers to support computer peripherals in Linux operating systems
authors: J. Madieu
venue: Mastering Linux Device Driver Development: Write custom device drivers to support computer peripherals in Linux operating systems
abstract: Master the art of developing customized device drivers for your embedded Linux systemsKey FeaturesBook DescriptionLinux is one of the fastest-growing operating systems around the world, and in the last few years, the Linux kernel has evolved significantly to support a wide variety of embedded devices with its improved subsystems and a range of new features. With this book, you’ll find out how you can enhance your skills to write custom device drivers for your Linux operating system. Mastering Linux Device Driver Development provides complete coverage of kernel topics, including video and audio frameworks, that usually go unaddressed. You’ll work with some of the most complex and impactful Linux kernel frameworks, such as PCI, ALSA for SoC, and Video4Linux2, and discover expert tips and best practices along the way. In addition to this, you’ll understand how to make the most of frameworks such as NVMEM and Watchdog. Once you’ve got to grips with Linux kernel helpers, you’ll advance to working with special device types such as Multi-Function Devices (MFD) followed by video and audio device drivers. By the end of this book, you’ll be able to write feature-rich device drivers and integrate them with some of the most complex Linux kernel frameworks, including V4L2 and ALSA for SoC.What you will learnExplore and adopt Linux kernel helpers for locking, work deferral, and interrupt managementUnderstand the Regmap subsystem to manage memory accesses and work with the IRQ subsystemGet to grips with the PCI subsystem and write reliable drivers for PCI devicesWrite full multimedia device drivers using ALSA SoC and the V4L2 frameworkBuild power-aware device drivers using the kernel power management frameworkFind out how to get the most out of miscellaneous kernel subsystems such as NVMEM and WatchdogWho this book is forThis book is for embedded developers, Linux system engineers, and system programmers who want to explore Linux kernel frameworks and subsystems. C programming skills and a basic understanding of driver development are necessary to get started with this book.

title: Assessment of a New Constraint Satisfaction-Based Hybrid Distributed Control Technique for Power Flow Management in Distribution Networks with Generation and Demand Response
authors: T. Luo; M. J. Dolan; E. M. Davidson; G. W. Ault
abstract: Technical innovation in power distribution networks is pointing toward a decentralized control vision to deal with the issues in design and operations related to distributed energy resources. Thus, decentralized approaches to power flow management (PFM) are of significant importance from the distributed network operator (DNO) perspective. In this paper, a new hybrid distributed control approach is proposed to deal with thermal overload issues. The control algorithm is based on constraint satisfaction problem that is applied to solve the network constraint problem. The novelty of this control approach consists in the joint control of both distributed generation and demand response units for PFM in an autonomous regional control environment. The implementation of this demand-side management, integrated active network management, and distributed control technique contributes to network reinforcement deferral, economy of supply, and efficient capital expenditure. Simulation has been implemented in a medium voltage interconnected test network with a substation controller and a network simulator. The control actions successfully achieve the desired objectives and are evaluated in comparison analysis. This new hybrid distributed control technique has potential to benefit the DNO planning and operation activities in the development of future decentralized smart grids.

title: Open-Set Fault Diagnosis for Industrial Rotating Machines Based on Trustworthy Deep Learning
authors: D. Wei; M. Zuo; Z. Tian
venue: IEEE Transactions on Industrial Cyber-Physical Systems
abstract: Detecting and diagnosing faults in rotating machines is crucial for ensuring the safety and reliability of modern industrial cyber-physical systems. Traditional data-driven fault diagnosis methods have achieved significant success when dealing with a set list of known faults and working conditions. However, they become inaccurate and overconfident when faced with new fault classes outside the training set. This paper introduces a novel Evidential Abstention Classifier based on trustworthy deep learning. It can quantify prediction uncertainty and recognize new fault classes without the need for their training data. Experiment results validated the efficacy of the proposed L1 regularization in improving uncertainty quantification. They also highlighted the proficiency of the designed auxiliary training method in generating fault-discriminative features and establishing effective decision boundaries for new fault types. EAC enables accurate open-set fault diagnosis with reduced reliance on historical data, offering improved transparency in the diagnostic process.

title: Quantifying and Communicating Uncertainty in SAR-Based Flood Mapping via Density-Aware Neural Networks and Conformal Risk Control
authors: Y. Li; P. Matgen; M. Chini
venue: IEEE Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing
abstract: Accurate flood mapping from synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery is essential for disaster response and risk management. Although deep learning (DL) models have advanced SAR-based flood mapping, they typically lack mechanisms to quantify and communicate predictive uncertainty, limiting their reliability in high-stakes applications. This study proposes a unified framework that captures and conveys two key sources of uncertainty in flood mapping: uncertainty arising from the model’s limited knowledge, and uncertainty caused by noise and ambiguity inherent in the data. The former is estimated via feature density in the latent space of a density-aware neural network, while the latter is quantified using softmax entropy. These uncertainties are then communicated through conformal risk control under a user-defined risk level ( $\alpha $ , $\delta $ ): inputs associated with high model-knowledge uncertainty are flagged as out-of-distribution (OOD) and abstained from prediction, while data-related uncertainty guides the construction of set-valued predictions for in-distribution (ID) samples. Experiments on diverse real-world flood scenarios—including flooded built-up (FB) areas, flooded vegetation (FV), and flooded bare soil—demonstrate substantial gains in uncertainty quantification and predictive reliability. The proposed density-aware neural network achieves an average area under the receiver operating characteristic (AUROC) of 0.921 in OOD detection, outperforming Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) (0.684) and deep ensembles (DEs) (0.603). OOD abstention improves predictive safety, reducing the average water false negative rate from 36.9% to 28.5% under a risk level of ( $\alpha =0.05$ and $\delta =0.1$ ), while prediction sets reduce average miscoverage from 4.4% to 1.6% compared to standard singleton predictions. By explicitly quantifying and communicating the uncertainty in DL predictions, this work strengthens trustworthy, risk-informed decision support for SAR-based flood mapping.

title: Dynamic Network Tariff in Practices: Key Issues and Challenges
authors: P. P. Singh; F. Wen; I. Palu
venue: 2021 IEEE 4th International Conference on Computing, Power and Communication Technologies (GUCON)
abstract: A significant transformation in the energy sector is taking place due to power industry restructuring, ever-increasing employment of intermittent renewable generation, environmental constraints, and emergent prosumers such as electric vehicles (EVs). These factors impose the necessity of redesigning distribution network (DN) tariffs to promote renewable energy generation accommodation and to incentivize customers to promote energy efficiency. The moving loads (EVs) are also creating big challenges to the distribution system operator (DSO). The DSO has to act on network reinforcement deferral, energy losses reduction, peak power reduction, voltage control, ancillary services, improving power quality, and reduction in the load/ generation curtailment. Therefore, there is a necessity of redesigning distribution network tariffs to promote efficient network utilization and optimal customer response, for both short-term operation and long-term planning of the network. This paper critically reviews dynamic network tariffs used in several countries and provides key issues and challenges in designing the DN tariffs.

title: Dynamic Cluster Head Selection and Secure Routing Approach Industry 4.0 Framework for Precision Agriculture
authors: A. B. Manwatkar; R. K. Deshmukh; A. A. Junnarkar
abstract: As Precision Agriculture (PA) evolves through the integration of Industry 4.0 technologies, it also faces new and sophisticated threats. This paper presents an in-depth analysis and framework for threat detection in PA utilizing Artificial Intelligence (AI). The proposed framework focuses on identifying and mitigating both cybersecurity and physical threats that could compromise the efficiency, safety, and sustainability of agricultural operations. By leveraging machine learning algorithms and real-time data analytics, the framework aims to provide proactive threat detection and response mechanisms, ensuring robust protection for PA systems. This study System describes a network threats detection mechanism using machine learning for IoT-based precision farming application. In the first phase of this research detection of http threats under the large Wireless Sensor Networks (WSN). We developed a cloud-connected precision farming application & applied the data mining &machine learning algorithms for accurate Hypertext Transfer Protocol(HTTP) threats. In this paper describes an cross-layer-based clustering & routing algorithms have been intended to diminish network correspondence deferral, dormancy, &energy utilization. The boundaries of various layers like a physical, Medium Access Control (MAC) & network layer of every sensor are utilized to assess & choose ideal Optimized Cross-Layer Routing for Industry $4.0(O C L R I) \&$ productive information transmission. Initial cluster head $(\mathbf{C H})$ selection has done and then Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) proposed for secure data transmission. In experimental analysis results demonstrates the proposed OCLRI-ACO techniques improves the overall QoS parameters.

title: Secure MCP-Based Tool-Augmented RAG for Industrial IoT Diagnostics Under Indirect Prompt Injection, Retrieval Poisoning, and Modality Outages
authors: P. Ersoy; M. Erşahin
venue: 2026 6th International Conference on Electrical, Computer and Energy Technologies (ICECET)
abstract: Industrial IoT diagnostics require integrating diverse evidence streams, such as telemetry, event logs, configuration snapshots, and operational knowledge bases, while adhering to safety and security requirements. Tool-augmented retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) facilitates this integration by merging retrieval processes with the regulated use of tools. In Operational Technology (OT) settings, two primary risks associated with deployment are: (i) indirect prompt injection through retrieved materials or tool outputs, which can disrupt the model context and result in behavior that contradicts established policies; and (ii) limited visibility caused by tool failures, gaps in telemetry, and delayed logging, which diminishes evidential support and raises the chances of producing unsubstantiated outputs. This paper examines a protocol-aligned architecture that integrates MCP-exposed tools within a defense-in-depth RAG pipeline. The approach employs hybrid retrieval and reranking, instruction-aware content filtering, typed least-privilege tool mediation with audit logging, evidence-bound generation with citation enforcement, and outage-aware abstention policies. An OT-oriented stress-test suite is defined based on prior RAG security evaluations, and utility, security, and degradation metrics are reported using a proprietary multi-site IIoT dataset. The findings indicate the importance of treating retrieval and tool interfaces as distinct security boundaries in industrial diagnostic assistants.

title: A Quality Assurance Framework for Governing Reliability in Clinical AI Systems: A Case Study in EEG-Based Seizure Detection
authors: Q. Khan
venue: 2026 IEEE 14th International Conference on Healthcare Informatics (ICHI)
abstract: Automated EEG-based seizure detection has benefited from deep learning, yet challenges related to probabilistic reliability, distributional shift, alarm burden, and patient-level variability continue to limit safe clinical deployment. This work proposes a Quality Assurance (QA) framework that treats seizure detection as a continuously governed clinical AI system rather than a standalone classifier. The framework introduces deployment-oriented mechanisms for monitoring probabilistic calibration, enforcing confidence-based risk control, and detecting distributional drift using statistically grounded criteria aligned with medical device lifecycle standards. Using convolutional, recurrent, and transformer-based EEG models as representative backbones, we evaluate the framework in a proof-of-concept case study on the CHB-MIT paediatric dataset under a subject-exclusive protocol. Results show that accuracy-oriented evaluation obscures critical system-level failure modes, including unsustainable alert volumes, calibration degradation, and sensitivity to cross-session variability. Post-hoc calibration improves probability fidelity, while confidence-based filtering and drift-aware QA enable explicit control over safety–coverage trade-offs. To better reflect clinical utility, we complement window-level analysis with event-level alarm consolidation and quantify the trade-off between seizure sensitivity, false alarms, and deferral-driven review load. These findings demonstrate that QA defines a tunable design space rather than a single optimal operating point, governed by clinical risk tolerance and workflow constraints. While broader validation across diverse populations and clinical settings is required, this work establishes QA as a necessary governance layer for clinical seizure detection and provides a foundation for deployment-oriented evaluation of medical AI systems.

title: When Not to Answer: Confidence-Aware Response Control for Hallucination Reduction in Consumer Rights Question Answering
authors: A. K; K. V; D. G
venue: 2026 10th International Conference on Inventive Systems and Control (ICISC)
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains such as legal assistance and consumer rights support, where response accuracy is of paramount importance; however, a critical challenge in such deployments is hallucination-the generation of factually incorrect or unverified statements that may mislead users and cause tangible harm. This work introduces the notion of a confidence-aware response control system that aims to improve the robustness of consumer rights questions answered through the use of large language models by combining RAG with multi-signal confidence assessment, which uses three different signals: semantic similarity, lexical overlap, and context coverage. These scores are then aggregated using a weighted scoring function to obtain a final confidence score, where if the confidence score is below a certain threshold value determined experimentally through grid search using F1-optimal values then the system chooses not to reply. The threshold selection process and weight configurations are empirically justified through sensitivity analysis and an ablation study. The interpretable and scalar-valued confidence indicator also offers a lightweight version of explainability, making the decision process of the system easily understandable for the operators. In an experimental setup conducted using 30 questions related to consumer rights, the system achieved 90% accuracy and hallucinations to only $\mathbf{1 0 \%}$, thus outperforming a baseline LLM (63.3% accuracy, 36.7% hallucination rate) and a RAG-only system (80% accuracy, 20% hallucination rate). This approach requires no model retraining and introduces negligible computational overhead (under 100 ms additional latency), making it practical for real-world deployment and establishing abstention-based response control as an effective safety mechanism for LLM-based legal applications.

title: Toward High Renewable Penetration: Energy Storage Planning in Medium-Voltage Distribution Networks
authors: J. Huan; Z. Zuo; Y. Wang; W. Wu; R. Fan; Z. Yu
venue: 2026 IEEE 3rd International Conference on Electrical Power Systems and Intelligent Control (EPSIC)
abstract: Facing the consumption and operational challenges from high-penetration wind and PV integration, this study develops a storage planning method that jointly considers intelligent prediction and cooperative optimization for medium-voltage distribution networks. Traditional planning research mostly focuses on the capacity configuration of energy storage and fails to systematically address the core issue of the collaborative optimization of "site selection - capacity determination". In view of the above limitations, this study constructed a two-stage planning framework. Firstly, To obtain accurate short-term forecasts for wind and solar power, the Extreme Learning Machine (ELM) artificial intelligence algorithm is introduced, providing reliable input data for subsequent optimization and effectively enhancing the accuracy of the planning premise. Secondly, an optimization model for the location and capacity determination of energy storage stations in 35kV and below medium-voltage distribution networks, aiming at maximizing the comprehensive benefits of the system, was established. This model balances economic considerations (encompassing storage lifecycle costs and grid upgrade deferral value) with strict safety constraints, including system power balance, equipment operational boundaries, and energy storage SOC limits. Through simulation verification of the improved IEEE 30 nodes, the schemes planned by the method proposed in this paper can significantly enhance the peak shaving adequacy of the system, effectively alleviate branch congestion, and promote the local consumption of new energy.

title: WASCO Routing Protocol: Enhancing Security in Vehicular Adhoc Networks (VANETs) using Weighted Average Sandpiper Coot Optimal Approach
authors: A. N. Patil; S. V. Mallapur
venue: 2024 4th International Conference on Innovative Practices in Technology and Management (ICIPTM)
abstract: In today’s interconnected society, improving security in Vehicular Adhoc Networks (VANETs) is critical to protecting the network’s integrity, confidentiality, and availability. Conventional approaches suffer a variety of security challenges and vulnerabilities in terms of vehicle occupant privacy and safety. To address these security issues, the present study presented the Weighted Average Sandpiper Coot Optimal (WASCO) Routing Protocol for VANET security enhancement. In this study, the Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) approach is used to secure traffic emergency information, and asymmetric approaches are used to generate keys in a system with a reliable structure. The Sandpiper optimization technique and the Coot optimization algorithm are used in this work to improvise the outcomes of the WASCO protocol. The WASCO routing protocol’s performance is evaluated by examining its effectiveness based on important metrics such as detection accuracy, authentication latency, Packet-Delivery-Ratio (PDR), start to finish deferral and throughput, contrasting it with existing methodologies. The exploratory outcomes show the proficiency of WASCO routing protocol for enhancing security in VANET systems.

title: Guest Editorial Special Section on Industrial and Commercial Demand Response
authors: J. P. S. Catalão; P. Siano; F. Li; M. A. S. Masoum; J. Aghaei
abstract: The eleven papers in this special section focus on the industrial and commercial potential of demand response (DR). Customers from this non-residential market base have great potential in providing flexibility for power systems through diverse demand response (DR) programs. Intelligent energy management can be carried out with DR in industrial and commercial facilities, especially if onsite control, information, and communication technologies are available, enabling also the inherent automation capabilities of heating, ventilation, and air conditioning systems. In the dawn of the Smart Grid era, with increasing distributed generation and the conversion of traditionally passive consumers to newly active energy players in the market, DR is being effectively considered for outage management and network reinforcement deferral.

title: Learning to Defer: A Survey
authors: Strong, Joshua; Sun, Emma; Harry Rogers; Helen Higham; Noble, Alison
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Learning to defer (L2D) enables AI systems to choose between autonomous prediction and deferral to experts. This survey consolidates the fast-growing literature through a four-branch taxonomy: methodological frameworks; optimization and theory; task generalizations; and real-world adaptations. We outline contrasts between score-based and predictor–rejector formulations; one-stage, two-stage, and post-hoc training; unify surrogate losses with theoretical guarantees; and synthesize extensions to regression, multi-task prediction, top-$k$ committees, sequential settings, and causal pipelines. Practical considerations include limited annotations, dynamic expert pools, workload/budget control, fairness, interpretability, robustness, and uncertainty handling, concluding with open challenges for reliable human–AI decision systems.Note: This is the preprint version of a manuscript currently under review. It has not undergone peer review.

title: Post-Hoc Estimators for Learning to Defer to an Expert
authors: Harikrishna Narasimhan; Wittawat Jitkrittum; Aditya Krishna Menon; Ankit Singh Rawat; Sanjiv Kumar

title: A Causal Target for Learning to Defer Under Hidden Confounding
authors: Yanmin Li; Lihua Liu; Xin Eric Wang; Zhilong Mao; Jibing Wu; Weidong Bao
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Learning decision policies from confounded observational data is a challenging task in causal inference, as unobserved confounders can lead to biased or suboptimal actions when relying solely on machine learning models. A synergistic approach is learning to defer, which decides when to act itself and when to defer to a human expert with access to unobserved information. However, constructing the learning target, which defines the probability of choosing each action or deferral, remains a core challenge. To address this, we propose causal-target-based learning to defer (CTLD) framework, where the causal target is constructed from sharp bounds on potential outcomes. Specifically, the degree of overlap between these bounds determines the probability of deferral, while their relative positions and widths define the probabilities over actions. CTLD aligns model predictions with this causal target to make probabilistic decisions over actions and deferral. We present comprehensive theoretical guarantees for the learned policy and demonstrate the effectiveness of CTLD on synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets.

title: A Simple Heuristic for Controlling Human Workload in Learning to Defer
authors: Andrew Ponomarev

title: A benchmarking framework and dataset for learning to defer in human-AI decision-making
authors: Jean V. Alves; Diogo Leitão; Sérgio Jesus; Marco O. P. Sampaio; Javier Liébana; Pedro Saleiro; Mário A. T. Figueiredo; Pedro Bizarro
abstract: Learning to Defer (L2D) algorithms improve human-AI collaboration by deferring decisions to human experts when they are likely to be more accurate than the AI model. These can be crucial in high-stakes tasks like fraud detection, where false negatives can cost victims their life savings. The primary challenge in training and evaluating these systems is the high cost of acquiring expert predictions, often leading to the use of simplistic simulated expert behavior in benchmarks. We introduce OpenL2D, a framework generating synthetic experts with adjustable decision-making processes and work capacity constraints for more realistic L2D testing. Applied to a public fraud detection dataset, OpenL2D creates the financial fraud alert review dataset (FiFAR), which contains predictions from 50 fraud analysts for 30 K instances. We show that FiFAR's synthetic experts are similar to real experts in metrics such as consistency and inter-expert agreement. Our L2D benchmark reveals that performance rankings of L2D algorithms vary significantly based on the available experts, highlighting the need to consider diverse expert behavior in L2D benchmarking.

title: Learning-to-Defer Inference for Computer Agriculture Irrigation Advisories Under Conflicting Human-Agent Competence: An Artificial Intelligence Deferral-Regret Evaluation
authors: Akosua Nyarko-Mensah
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Irrigation advisories generated by artificial intelligence agents are increasingly paired with farmer judgement, yet the two sources of competence are rarely aligned: the agent may be better informed about soil-moisture dynamics while the farmer is better informed about local water availability, crop condition and institutional constraints. the present analysis formalises the resulting decision problem as a learning-to-defer inference task in which a deferral policy routes each advisory instance either to the agent or to the human expert, and it evaluates the policy through a deferral-regret criterion rather than through predictive accuracy alone. The analysis is theoretical and methodological: no observational data are used or claimed. A before-after-control-impact design is characterised under a declared variance structure with between-cluster standard deviation 6.0, residual standard deviation 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64, and power is estimated across 2000 design cells for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design requires 54 clusters to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80 per cent power. The paper derives a deferral-regret decomposition that separates the regret attributable to agent error from the regret attributable to human error and from the regret attributable to misrouted deferral, and it shows that the three components have different sample-size requirements. The contribution is a formal criterion and an evaluation design for deferral policies in irrigation advisory systems, together with the boundary conditions under which deferral improves on either agent-only or human-only advice.

title: How can humans leverage machine learning? From Medical Data Wrangling to Learning to Defer to Multiple Experts
authors: Daniel Barrejón; Pablo M. Olmos; Antonio Artés-Rodríguez
abstract: Medical data sets are usually corrupted by noise and missing data. These missing patterns are commonly assumed to be completely random, but in medical scenarios, the reality is that these patterns occur in bursts due to sensors that are off for some time or data collected in a misaligned uneven fashion, among other causes. This paper proposes to model medical data records with heterogeneous data types and bursty missing data using sequential variational autoencoders (VAEs). In particular, we propose a new methodology, the Shi-VAE, which extends the capabilities of VAEs to sequential streams of data with missing observations. We compare our model against state-of-theart solutions in an intensive care unit database (ICU) and a dataset of passive human monitoring. Furthermore, we find that standard error metrics such as RMSE are not conclusive enough to assess temporal models and include in our analysis the cross-correlation between the ground truth nd the imputed signal. We show that Shi-VAE achieves the best performance in terms of using both metrics, with lower computational complexity than the GP-VAE model, which is the state-of-the-art method for medical records.

title: Learning-to-Defer for Artificial Intelligence Agriculture Disease Triage Under Asymmetric Referral Costs: A Computer Regret-Bound Evaluation
authors: Chanda Mwila-Kabaso; Mutale Chileshe Bwalya; Nchimunya Hamoonga
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Agricultural disease triage systems that combine automated inference with human expert referral must decide, for each case, whether the cost of deferring to a scarce plant pathologist is justified by the expected gain in diagnostic accuracy. Existing learning-to-defer formulations assume symmetric referral costs and evaluate deferral policies by their average accuracy, which misstates the decision problem when a missed epidemic-class disease costs far more than an unnecessary referral. The triage problem is formalised as a cost-sensitive contextual bandit in which the deferral cost depends on the true disease class, and a cost-weighted regret is defined against the best policy in a restricted deferral class. A bound is derived that decomposes regret into an estimation term scaling with the square root of the number of triage cases and a misspecification term controlled by the asymmetry ratio between false-negative and false-positive referral costs. The bound is evaluated on a declared design grid of 8, 16, 24 and 32 clusters, effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, and 2000 replications per cell, with an intraclass correlation of 0.64, between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0 and residual standard deviation of 4.5. Power reaches 80 per cent at 52 clusters for a 5 percentage point effect. Asymmetric referral costs shift the optimal deferral threshold and that the regret bound tightens as the asymmetry ratio grows, which has consequences for how triage systems should be calibrated before deployment.

title: Classification with reject option for software defect prediction
authors: Diego Parente Paiva Mesquita; Lincoln S. Rocha; João P. P. Gomes; Ajalmar R. Rocha Neto

title: Conformal selective prediction with cost aware deferral for safe clinical triage under distribution shift
authors: Hyun Kwon; Dae-Jin Kim
abstract: We propose a selective prediction framework for clinical triage that combines calibrated probabilistic modeling, conformal prediction, and cost-aware deferral to prioritize patient safety. The system produces set-valued predictions with finite-sample coverage control and defers low-confidence cases to clinicians when doing so reduces an explicit expected clinical cost. We construct prediction sets using split conformal prediction, a group-conditional Mondrian variant for gender-stratified coverage, and an importance-weighted variant to improve robustness under distribution shift, and we select a single deferral threshold by minimizing expected cost on a held-out calibration set. On temporally separated in-distribution and out-of-distribution test splits for early sepsis prediction, selective deferral yields a favorable risk-coverage trade-off, reducing error on retained cases by 49.6% on the in-distribution (ID) test split and 46.7% on the out-of-distribution (OOD) test split, both at 80% coverage, while achieving low expected cost on both splits with only a moderate increase under shift. Calibration remains strong with low expected calibration error on both test sets, and rule-out performance is conservative, attaining near-perfect negative predictive value at a 95% sensitivity target. Coverage stays close to the nominal 90% target in-distribution and degrades only slightly out-of-distribution, with the weighted method most robust, and the Mondrian method reduces the gender coverage gap to 1.4 percentage points. These results indicate that conformal uncertainty quantification combined with cost-aware deferral can provide transparent and safer clinical decision support that degrades gracefully under temporal distribution shift.

title: Calibrated Abstention and Clinical Deferral in Small Language Models via RLVR and GRPO
authors: Narendra Bayutama Wibisono
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract The deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) in clinical settings is fundamentally limited by their propensity for epistemic overconfidence. This paper investigates the efficacy of Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) combined with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to instill 'Calibrated Abstention' in a Small Language Model (SLM), specifically Gemma 4 2B. By enforcing a verifiable clinical reasoning protocol (SOFA) and a routing protocol (Cactus Signal), we trained the model to recognize internal uncertainty and perform clinical deferral (escalation) when presented with ambiguous data. Our results demonstrate a pronounced 'Alignment Tax' on raw accuracy (decreasing from 44.0% to 35.5% on MedQA-USMLE). However, this is offset by a critical +129% Safety Gain in the Abstention Rate (from 3.5% to 8.0%). This study concludes that in high-stakes triage, prioritizing safety through conservative deferral yields a more reliable clinical assistant than maximizing raw benchmark performance. Core Methodology Algorithmic Framework: Leveraged Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to train the model without the need for a memory-intensive critic model, enabling successful alignment on resource-constrained hardware (Dual NVIDIA T4 GPUs). Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR): Embedded a clinical "constitution" using the SOFA (Sequential Organ Failure Assessment) protocol and Cactus Signal as verifiable constraints to suppress hallucinations. Phased Training Strategy: Implemented an adaptive strategy by increasing group size ($G=2 \to G=4$) and context window ($512 \to 1024$ tokens) to maintain gradient stability and reasoning completeness. Key Performance Metrics Evaluations were conducted on 200 strictly unseen samples from the MedQA-USMLE dataset: Metric Outcome Clinical Interpretation Abstention Rate +129% Gain The model is 2.3x more likely to escalate in ambiguous cases. Raw Accuracy -8.5% (Alignment Tax) An acceptable performance trade-off for the elimination of hallucinations. Safety Matrix Calibrated & Cautious Behavioral shift from "speculative guessing" to "clinical deferral". Operational Insights This research demonstrates that robust safety alignment is achievable in parameter-constrained models (2.6B) through deterministic reward signals. While inference latency challenges remain due to structured rambling (~153 seconds), the successful convergence at low group sizes ($G=4$) proves that verifiability can effectively substitute for compute scale in developing trustworthy medical AI.

title: Conformal validation: A deferral policy using uncertainty quantification with a human-in-the-loop for model validation
authors: Paul Horton; Alexandru Florea; Brandon Stringfield
abstract: Validating performance is a key challenge facing the adoption of machine learning models in high risk applications. Current validation methods assess performance marginally over the entire testing dataset, which can fail to identify regions in the distribution with insufficient performance. In this paper, we propose Conformal Validation, a systems-based approach with a calibrated form of uncertainty quantification using a conformal prediction framework as a part of the validation process to reduce performance gaps. Specifically, the policy defers a subset of observations for which the predictive model is most uncertain and provides a human with informative prediction sets to make the ancillary decision. We evaluate this policy on an image classification task where images are distorted with varying levels of gaussian blur for a quantifiable measure of added difficulty. The model is compared to human performance on the most difficult observations, i.e., those where the model is most uncertain, to simulate the scenario when a human is the alternative decision-maker. We evaluate performance on three arms: the model independently, humans with access to a set of classes the model is most confident in, and humans independently. The deferral policy is simple to understand, applicable to any predictive model, and easy to implement while, in this case, keeping humans in the loop for improved trustworthiness. Conformal Validation incorporates a risk assessment that is conditioned on the prediction set length and can be tuned to the needs of the application.

title: Robust classification with reject option using the self-organizing map
authors: Ricardo Sousa; Ajalmar R. Rocha Neto; Jaime S. Cardoso; Guilherme A. Barreto

title: The Coverage-Deferral Trade-Off: Fairness Implications of Conformal Prediction in Human-in-the-Loop Decision Systems
authors: Davut Emre Tasar
abstract: Conformal prediction (CP) provides distribution-free uncertainty quantification by constructing prediction sets with guaranteed coverage. In human-in-the-loop (HITL) decision systems, these sets naturally define deferral policies: cases with singleton sets proceed automatically, while those with multiple labels require human review. Mondrian CP, which calibrates separately per group, has been proposed to achieve group-conditional coverage validity, ensuring each demographic group meets the target coverage level. However, we demonstrate through extensive experiments (832K evaluations across 14K configurations, 6 datasets, 100 seeds) that improving coverage validity comes at a significant cost: Mondrian CP increases deferral disparity by 143% compared to global CP, despite reducing coverage disparity by 26% on average. This coverage-deferral trade-off is fundamental: it persists across all datasets (p < 0.001), is invariant to HITL parameters, and exhibits monotonic behavior with respect to the shrinkage interpolation parameter γ. We prove an analogous impossibility result for conformal prediction: under specific conditions, coverage parity and deferral parity cannot be simultaneously achieved when base rates differ between groups. We further demonstrate that standard fairness metrics (Equalized Odds, Average Odds Difference) are invariant to CP method choice, identifying deferral gap as a critical operational fairness metric that captures CP’s unique impact on who receives human review, a dimension invisible to standard EO metrics. Our findings provide actionable guidance: use Mondrian for group-conditional coverage validity, global CP for deferral fairness, or shrinkage for balanced trade-offs.

title: Selective-Prediction Evaluation for Computer Agriculture Fertilizer Advisories Under Soil-Test Sampling Gaps: An Artificial Intelligence Abstention-Risk Bound for Over-Application Safety
authors: Tesfaye Wolde Selassie; Getachew Mekonnen Ayele
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Fertilizer advisory systems built on machine learning must issue a recommendation for every field, yet soil-test sampling gaps mean that many fields arrive with covariates that are only partially observed. The framework treats abstention as a first-class output, defines the abstention-risk profile as the conditional over-application rate among retained cases, and proves that under a bounded calibration gap the profile is controlled by the abstention threshold and the sampling-gap severity. A design-based evaluation is characterised under a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD 6.0, residual SD 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64; power was estimated across 2000 design cells for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design requires 52 clusters to detect a 5 percentage-point effect at 80% power. The bound converts an evaluation target into an auditable abstention rule, and the paper argues that advisory evaluations should report abstention-risk profiles alongside aggregate accuracy.

title: Clinical Computer Vision for Dengue Warning-Sign Recognition Under Variable Capillary Refill Assessment Skill: A Human-in-the-Loop Deferral Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence Triage Safety
authors: Amina Abdirahman Farah; Abdiqani Yusuf Hassan
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Dengue warning-sign recognition depends on capillary refill assessment, a bedside skill whose reliability varies widely among clinicians. Computer vision systems that estimate refill time from smartphone video could standardise triage, but their safety depends on how they interact with the variable skill of the humans who defer to them. The framework characterises triage safety through a deferral operating characteristic and derives the conditions under which machine deferral reduces, rather than redistributes, triage error. A design-based evaluation of the before-after-control-impact estimator was conducted under a declared variance structure with between-cluster standard deviation 6.0, residual standard deviation 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64, across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The analysis indicates that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5 percentage point effect at 80 percent power. The framework proposes that deferral safety is governed not by model accuracy alone but by the covariance between model and clinician errors, and that this covariance is itself a function of clinician skill. The contribution is a formal account of when human-in-the-loop deferral improves triage safety for dengue warning-sign recognition under variable capillary refill assessment skill.

title: Message Classification with Reject Option in a customer contact system.
authors: T.J. Selier
abstract:
CaseDriver is a multi-user multi-division customer contact system.
Currently, the labelling and distribution of messages in CaseDriver is per- formed manually, i.e. a supervisor has to determine whether a message should be deleted, or which employee and stream the message has to be assigned to. This research focuses on automating this process. Automating this process allows the messages to reach the employees faster and will save time of the employee who has to perform the classification. Three big challenges arise in this research, the first being: how to pre-process the data. The second is finding the best classi- fication algorithm in the huge classification and hyper-parameter search-space. The last challenge is deciding what to do with a prediction; when the confidence of a prediction is low, or not high enough, it is unwise to automatically label
the message.
The first challenge is addressed with common data-mining techniques. Find-
ing an optimal classification algorithm is done with Auto-Weka [14] which uses Sequential Model-based Algorithm Configuration (SMAC [10]). Finally, the last challenge is solved by providing a mean to make a trade-off decision between the proportion that is automatically classified and the accuracy of the classification.
The trade-off is generated by considering four different reject-measures (which conclude to multiple types of reject rules), and selecting only the best reject- rules. Selecting the best reject-rules is done by selecting the reject-rules whose performance lies on the Pareto-front. It turns out that three (out of four) reject- measures have a representative amount of reject-rules in the Pareto-front, so all these reject-measure contribute to a better trade-off.

title: Abstention and Threshold Identification for Uncertainty Management in Clinical Decision Tools: A Case Study using Human-In-The-Loop Pediatric Autism Classifiers
authors: Aiden Ko; Aaron Kline; Kaitlyn Dunlap; Saimourya Surabhi; Parnian Azizian; Peter Yigitcan Washington; Dennis Paul Wall
abstract: Uncertainty quantification remains an underdeveloped aspect of AI-based clinical decision tools. As AI systems become increasingly prevalent in healthcare, it is essential not only to measure uncertainty but also to manage it in ways that support clinical decision-making. In this study, we investigate abstention as a practical mechanism for managing uncertainty in diagnostic classifiers. To stress-test this approach, we deliberately evaluate abstention performance on a purposefully noisy dataset of pediatric autism video assessments comprising heterogeneous video sources and a diverse range of human raters. We apply abstention strategies to existing autism classifiers trained on diagnostic assessment data, comparing baseline performance to a range of thresholding configurations that trade off retained sample coverage against key clinical metrics. We compare performance gains from prioritizing sensitivity or specificity to targeting a balanced increase in Youden's J to demonstrate a wide variety of use cases that abstention can enable. This work demonstrates a concrete use case of introducing abstention into the output range of clinical decision models, enabling both uncertainty quantification and management in diagnostic classifiers.

abstract: This paper focuses on the applications of the battery energy storage system (BESS) to be installed in distribution systems for deferment of the distribution reinforcement investment in the short-term power distribution planning. The existing system is 22-kV voltage level includes 115/22 kV substation, the 45-km. distribution feeder, 1 photovoltaic plant and 8 load points with mixed customer types. The technical problem often occurred in 22-kV distribution feeders is the power demand exceeds the line thermal limit in short time (1-4 hour per day) every day. Following PEA’s standard and criteria, distribution network owners (DNO) has 2 choices to solve this problem; taking the risk of fault or reinforce feeders. Nowadays, energy storage technologies play the interested role in smart grid era. It illustrates from the analysis that BESS can solve this problem and postpone the time of system reinforcement such as construction of the new distribution line with worthy investment. Power flow of the study system is calculated by DIgSILENT PowerFactory software. The best alternative is chosen based on the maximum net present value (NPV).

abstract: When machine learning is applied in safety-critical or otherwise sensitive areas, the analysis of feature relevance can be an important tool to keep the size of models small, and thus easier to understand, and to analyze how different features impact the behavior of the model.In the presence of correlated features, feature relevances and the solution to the minimal-optimal feature selection problem are not unique.One approach to solving this problem is identifying feature relevance intervals that symbolize the range of relevance given to each feature by a set of equivalent models.In this contribution, we address the issue of calculating relevance intervals -a unique representation of relevance -for reject option support vector machines with a linear kernel, which have the option of rejecting a data point if they are unsure about its label.

title: Virtuous Deferral
authors: J. Adam Carter; Jesper Kallestrup
abstract: ABSTRACT Virtue epistemology has long struggled with the “Creditability Dilemma”: how can knowledge gained through deference be creditable to the knower if it primarily depends on others’ cognitive work? We propose a novel solution by developing a telic account of doxastic deference as a distinctive kind of social‐epistemic performance. On our view, such deference succeeds when a deferrer forms a true belief that p in domain d , which answers their query, on the basis of the fact that a deferee states that p because of their epistemically superior competence in d . Drawing on Sosa's framework of performance assessment, we identify a metaphysical hierarchy of increasingly creditable achievements in deferential belief‐formation, from mere accurate doxastic deferral through to fully apt doxastic deferral. This hierarchy reveals that the apparent tension between individual credit and epistemic dependence rests on an “inverse creditability” thesis which fails to apply in cases of deferential belief. Instead, the highest forms of deferential achievement often align with and track the cognitive achievements of those deferred to. This framework also illuminates expert identification and epistemic trespassing as problems of exercising deferential skill under suitably normal conditions.

title: Governed OMR–Vision Capture and Validation Pipeline for Hand-Marked Survey Instruments: A Calibration–Validation Firewall with Selective-Prediction Deferral and Honest-Denominator Reporting
authors: Christopher A. Clemons; Jason D. McKibben; Harber, Steven, C.; Joseph P. Lash; James R. Lindner
abstract: This deposit provides a governed, human-in-the-loop pipeline for optical mark recognition (OMR) and computer vision. The detection of hand-entered marks (checkboxes, radio buttons, tick marks) on scanned paper survey instruments is distinct from optical character recognition (OCR), which reads printed or handwritten text. Rather than treating every machine prediction as an accepted observation, the pipeline separates calibration from validation, defers predictions that do not satisfy a selective-prediction (reject-option) gate, and reports performance on an honest denominator (confident-capture accuracy alongside coverage and commission).Validation spanned three instruments of increasing mark difficulty: printed marks (Instrument A pilot; confident-capture accuracy 0.858), printed radio circles (Instrument B; 96.8% held-out confident capture), and faint handwritten audiometry ticks (Instrument C; defer-dominated. No operating point cleared the acceptance gate, and the 106-form held-out set was sealed and remained outside of scoring). Human-verified reference standards established the validation baseline; inter-rater reliability on Instrument C was high (Cohen's kappa = 0.941; Fleiss' kappa = 1.000). The deposit also includes a human-versus-machine time-on-task comparison, the frozen pipeline configuration, and synthetic-test artifacts for reproducibility. Participant data are not included.

title: HITL-IoT: Human-in-the-Loop Intrusion Detection Dataset
authors: Wakili, Abubakar
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract: HITL-IoT is the first intrusion detection dataset for IoT environments that integrates human analyst decision metadata with traditional benign/attack labels. The dataset includes network traffic covering twelve IoT attack categories, complemented by 10,227 human-annotated samples produced by security analysts across three expertise levels (expert 80.5%, intermediate 14.4%, novice 5.1%). Each annotation includes the analyst's decision, confidence score (0-1 scale), decision latency, and justification text, enabling detailed study of human decision behavior, human-AI collaboration, and oversight mechanisms. The dataset provides 54 CICFlowMeter-style features per flow and covers 12 IoT device types, including cameras, thermostats, doorbells, and speakers. The dataset release includes baseline benchmarks for nine classical and deep learning models (best: XGBoost 99.59% accuracy, 1.67s training), together with preprocessing utilities and evaluation protocols to ensure reproducible experimentation. Human annotation performance ranges from expert (92.2% accuracy, ECE=0.152) to novice (76.9% accuracy, ECE=0.256), demonstrating the importance of expertise stratification in HITL systems. HITL-IoT enables research in human-centered intrusion detection, selective-deferral strategies, confidence calibration, and regulatory oversight analysis aligned with EU AI Act Article 14 requirements. All dataset files, metadata, baseline code, and documentation are openly available under CC BY 4.0 license to support transparent, extensible research in trustworthy, human-aligned IoT cybersecurity.
