title: Vaccination Recommendation Patterns and Associated Factors Among Children with Special Health Care Needs: A Cross-Sectional Study in District-Level Immunization Services in China
authors: Chenglian Wang; Li Zhang; Binyue Xu; Xiaolan Fu; Li Fu; Bowen Li; Wang Ju; Qingyu Li; Sitong Luo
abstract: Background: Children with special health care needs (CSHCN) are at heightened risk of delayed or missed vaccinations because of clinical complexity and provider uncertainty. Although China has issued expert consensus guidelines and established immunization advisory services, little is known about vaccination decision-making within routine district-level immunization services. This study examined vaccination recommendation patterns and factors associated with deferral or non-recommendation among CSHCN in these settings. Methods: This cross-sectional study was conducted between 1 April 2023, and 31 March 2024, in Changshou District, Chongqing, China, encompassing 18 primary health centers, five general hospitals and one special hospital. Children aged 0–18 years identified by physicians as having conditions potentially affecting vaccination decisions and with at least one documented vaccination-related consultation were included. Clinical characteristics and physician recommendations (“recommended,” “temporarily deferred,” “not recommended”) were recorded via the national Epidemiological Dynamic Data Collection (EDDC) system; subsequent vaccination uptake was verified using the Chongqing Immunization Information Management System. Logistic regression identified factors associated with deferral or non-recommendation. Results: A total of 761 participants were included in the analysis, with a median age of 12 months (IQR: 1–47). Among all vaccine-specific recommendations, 55.2% were classified as “recommended,” 43.4% as “temporarily deferred,” and 1.5% as “not recommended”. Deferral proportions varied markedly, highest in respiratory (73.6%) and immunologic (42.1%) conditions and lowest in neonatal disorders (4.0%). Compared with 0–6-month-olds, children aged 7–12 months (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 5.26, 95% CI 2.30–12.33) and >13 months (aOR = 13.48, 95% CI 6.69–28.34) were more likely to receive deferral or non-recommendation; multimorbidity also increased odds (aOR = 20.68, 95% CI 11.26–40.10). Consultations at primary health centers were associated with a lower likelihood of deferral or non-recommendation (aOR = 0.26, 95% CI 0.15–0.45). Conclusion: Vaccination recommendations for CSHCN vary considerably across clinical profiles and facility types in routine immunization settings. Despite national initiatives, many vaccine doses remain deferred or not recommended. Disease-specific guidelines, enhanced provider training, and context-adapted decision-support tools are needed to promote timely and equitable immunization for this medically vulnerable population.

title: Prevalence And Causes Of Donor Deferrals In National Blood Centre
authors: Syazwana Syirin Ibrahim
venue: Universiti Sains Malaysia Institutional Repository (Universiti Sains Malaysia)
abstract: Introduction: Blood donor deferral was established to ensure the safety of blood donors and patients. This research evaluated the prevalence and causes of blood donor deferrals in National Blood Centre, Malaysia. Methods: A cross-sectional study was performed on 1103 whole blood donors that had been deferred from 1st January 2018 to 31st December 2020. Data were extracted from donor deferral reports and the blood bank information system. Simple and multiple logistic analysis were used for statistical analysis, and a p-value of < 0.05 was considered significant. Results: A total of 732,756 blood donor were registered and 167,855 were being deferred. The prevalence of donor deferrals rate was 22.9%, in which 95.4% was temporary deferred and 4.6% was permanently deferred. From 1103 of deferred donors, more than half of the temporary deferrals were female donors (66.3%). In contrast, male blood donors were majority of being permanent deferred (76%). The most common reason for temporary deferral was low haemoglobin (52.3%), followed by high blood pressure (12.3%). However, for permanent deferrals, medical illnesses were the most frequently deferred (36%), followed by high risk behaviour (30%). Female (adjusted OR = 5.220, 95% CI 2.657 – 10.25, p <0.001) and regular/ repeat donors (adjusted OR = 6.470, 95% CI 1.929 – 21.70, p<0.002) were significantly associated with deferrals. Conclusion: Female donors and regular/repeat donors were significantly associated with deferral. Blood donor awareness, education, and pre and post donation care are crucial in reducing blood donor deferrals and preventing blood donor loss.

title: The Necessary Non-Action: When Hesitation Becomes Correctness — and When It Becomes Failure
authors: Rogério Figurelli
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: An apparent absence of action can denote successful restraint, an already satisfied goal, an epistemically necessary pause, an authorized refusal, a missed obligation, or a false statement of completion. These states are not interchangeable. Treating a zero-tool step as a generic failure hides correct non-action; treating a declaration of hesitation as sufficient justification protects inaction that has become avoidable, unsafe, or strategically convenient. This paper develops a conditional, evidence-relative theory of necessary non-action in tool-using language-model agents. It reconstructs a documented conceptual lineage from intention-gated computation and computable hesitation to agentic claim–state qualification, while positioning that lineage against established selective prediction, sequential decision theory, supervisory control, agentic abstention, and formal verification. The proposed framework separates goal satisfaction, action necessity, admissibility, observability, temporal opportunity, and report validity. Twelve normative principles support ten bounded propositions about no-op success, non-identifiability, obligation-sensitive idleness, reversible hesitation, deadline effects, and the impossibility of evaluating non-action from tool counts alone. A typed Non-Action Warrant is proposed as a challengeable record, not as a new security primitive or a guarantee of correctness. A limited secondary audit of a public research package of 64 controlled agent sessions confirms that zero-call records are numerous and denominator-sensitive, but cannot label them as justified or unjustified without task-state ground truth. An adversarial validation agenda specifies positive and negative controls, matched conventional baselines, explicit opportunity costs, and falsification conditions. No new live-model trials, causal treatment effects, or unique Field-specific advantage are claimed. The scientific target is a narrower question: under which stated conditions is not acting the correct operational decision, and when must hesitation stop being credited as responsible behavior?

title: Value-Grounded Neural Networks: An Architectural Approach to Behavioural Control in AI Systems
authors: Baby Gobin
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are now widely deployed in domains involving consequential decisions, including healthcare, law, education, agriculture, and mental health. While these systems demonstrate high fluency and strong task performance, their behaviour in use reveals persistent interaction-level risks. Existing alignment approaches such as reinforcement learning from human feedback, instruction tuning, and post-hoc safety constraints have reduced overtly harmful outputs and improved instruction following, but they primarily regulate generated content. They do not directly control how authority, guidance, or influence are exercised during interaction. This paper argues that many alignment failures arise not from unsafe content, but from inappropriate behavioural authority in high-stakes or uncertain contexts. This gap motivates an architectural reframing of alignment: not only controlling what systems say, but deciding when and how guidance is appropriate. Alignment is reframed as a problem of behavioural admissibility that is, determining whether guidance should be given, rather than content safety alone. Value-Grounded Neural Networks (VG-NN), a conceptual architectural framework in which action selection is constrained prior to generation is presented. Refusal, deferral and escalation are treated as first-class outcomes rather than failure modes. By separating cognitive capability from decision authority, VG-NN aims to preserve reasoning capacity while limiting inappropriate influence in sensitive interactions. This work is intended as a conceptual and architectural position paper and does not aim to provide benchmark-level empirical evaluation.

title: Prognostics and Remaining-Useful-Life Estimation for the Consumable Centrepost: A Dual-Channel Fluence-Driven Framework Scheduling Cartridge Replacement in a Spherical-Tokamak Breeder
authors: Priyanca Ford; Robert J. Weggel; C Weggel
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The inboard centrepost of a compact spherical-tokamak (ST) breeder is not a lifetime component: behind a practical inboard shield the fast-neutron fluence degrades the no-insulation REBCO conductor and its copper stabiliser to end of life within a fraction of a full-power year, so the machine is designed to swap the centrepost as a scheduled consumable cartridge. When to swap it is therefore a control decision, and a single worst-case interval wastes life or courts an unplanned outage. We formalise that decision as a prognostics problem. We derive a state-space damage model in which a physics channel integrates the fast-fluence load into a cumulative-damage variable by a linear (Miner) accumulation with a fracture-mechanics second mode, and cast the remaining-useful-life (RUL) estimate as a Bayesian posterior propagated by a particle filter that fuses the deterministic physics trajectory with a damage-correlated in-situ observable. To run the physics channel at control latency we train a multi-fidelity neural-operator surrogate that emulates the Monte-Carlo fluence field, fusing a cheap reduced-order transport model with the full-height three-dimensional runs by a control-variate correction with quantified uncertainty. The load-bearing safety feature is an out-of-distribution (OOD) backstop: when the live signals leave the calibrated envelope — flagged by a Mahalanobis regime score that separates epistemic from aleatoric uncertainty and made rigorous by a distribution-free conformal wrapper — the estimator abstains and returns the conservative physics-fluence bound rather than extrapolating a data model past its support. We cast this abstention as a runtime-assurance (Simplex) switch to a certified baseline, log every served estimate and every abstention to an append-only hash-chained provenance ledger under a goal-structured assurance case, and federate the degradation prior across the four-unit breeder fleet without centralising raw telemetry. Grounded in the frozen de-risking gates for the Hyperion breeder (I_p=9.66 MA, Q=3.076, P_fus=85.04 MW, negative triangularity δ=-0.30, B_0=8 T, centrepost peak field 16.84 T), the framework converts a life estimate that spans more than three orders of magnitude across modelling bases (0.0003–0.765 fpy) into a live, confidence-bounded schedule that tracks the register-resolved design life of 0.58 fpy behind a 45 tungsten-carbide shield, drives a cartridge-swap cadence of order five swaps per full-power year, and feeds the fleet-availability tiers. The one honest open item is the neutron tolerance of the in-winding observable, degraded by up to 39× against the demonstrated diamond-sensor state of the art; the framework is designed so that the protective function survives it by falling back to the physics bound. This is a methods contribution — a prognostics architecture — distinct from the structural-integrity, quench-detection and swap-logistics papers of the series. Key results (frozen anchors): Q = 3.076; delta = -0.30; dotd = 0.0093. Methods & codes: OpenMC, DAGMC, ENDF/B-VIII.0, STEP. title: Mapping HIV-related figures of risk in Europe’s blood donation regime
authors: Agata Dziuban; Todd Sekuler
abstract: Grasping blood donation as contested grounds for enacting notions of belonging, responsibility and citizenship, this article analyses the role of donor deferral policies in the emergence of a European blood donation regime. We demonstrate how shifts in the moral economy of blood donation that followed from the outbreak of the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) epidemic led to the prioritisation of donor deferral policies in efforts to enhance blood safety across Europe. We propose the notion ‘figures of risk’ – condensed figurations of those understood to pose risks of HIV infection to themselves and to others – to describe the categories of persons implicated in changing European donor restriction policies. We explore how the Council of Europe’s annually revised Guide to the preparation, use and quality assurance of blood components, first published in 1992, came to legitimise and sustain increasingly contested deferral practices, which have produced shifting groups of persons as European ‘figures of risk’. Qualitative analyses of the Guide’s 19 editions reveal 3 dimensions through which these figures have become increasingly stabilised over time: in terms of their ontology, temporality and risk-related exceptionality. We conclude by asking how collectivising figurations of donors, framed through literature on ‘profiling’, shape notions of European citizenship.

title: Ключевые факторы риска абсолютных отводов доноров крови: ретроспективный когортный анализ за 2014–2024 гг.
authors: O. V. Karpova; О.Д. Духанина
abstract: Введение. Учитывая критическую роль анализа причин донорских отводов в обеспечении безопасности гемотрансфузий и значительную глобальную вариабельность подходов к отбору доноров в зависимости от уровня благосостояния стран, новизна данной работы заключается в проведении анализа многолетней динамики абсолютных отводов в регионе со средним уровнем дохода. Цель исследования: проанализировать динамику абсолютных отводов доноров за 2014–2024 гг. и выявить факторы риска. Материалы и методы. Выполнено ретроспективное исследование базы данных отделения переливания крови (n = 1116 абсо­лютных отводов из 101960 донаций). Анализировались социально-демографические характеристики, вид донации и причины отвода от донорства — превышение норм аланиаминотрансферазы (АЛТ), выявление маркеров гепатита B (ВГВ), гепатита C (ВГС), сифилиса, вируса иммунодефицита человека (ВИЧ). Расчет относительных рисков (ОР) и соответствующих долей осуществлялся с использованием данных по совокупному числу донаций (n = 101960). Результаты. За период 2014–2024 гг. на фоне четырехкратного роста ежегодного объема донаций (с 3388 до 13406) зафиксировано десятикратное снижение частоты абсолютных отводов — с 3,66 до 0,36% (p < 0,001). Ключевыми факторами риска абсолютного отвода от донорства стали мужской пол (отношение шансов (ОШ) = 1,878; 95% доверительный интервал (ДИ) = 1,639–2,151) и статус первичного донора (ОШ = 8,58; 95% ДИ = 7,61–9,67), тогда как донорство плазмы и тромбоцитов ассоциировалось со значительно более низкими шансами абсолютного отвода по сравнению с забором цельной крови (ОШ = 0,592; 95% ДИ = 0,487–0,718 и ОШ = 0,391; 95% ДИ = 0,320–0,477, соответственно; p < 0,001). Этиологический профиль отводов претерпел коренную трансформацию: доминировавшая в 2014 г. доля повышенной активности АЛТ (75,0%) к 2024 г. сократилась до 4,2%, уступив ведущую роль маркерам ВГС (41,7%) и ВГВ (29,2%), а также впервые верифицированным случаям ВИЧ-инфекции (6,3%). Заключение. Основными независимыми факторами риска абсолютного отвода являются мужской пол и статус первичного донора. Наблюдаемая трансформация структуры причин отвода (замещение суррогатного маркера АЛТ специфическим выявлением ВГС и ВГВ) отражает переход к современной парадигме обеспечения трансфузионной безопасности. Достигнутый уровень отводов (0,27–0,36%) соответствует международным стандартам и свидетельствует об эффективности оптимизированных алгоритмов отбора доноров в условиях мегаполиса со средним уровнем дохода. Introduction. Given the critical role of analyzing blood donor deferral causes in ensuring transfusion safety and the signifi­cant global variability in donor selection approaches based on country income levels, the novelty of this study lies in conducting analysis of the long-term changes in permanent deferrals in a middle-income region. Aim: to analyze the dynamics in absolute donor deferrals from 2014 to 2024 and identify key risk determinants. Materials and Methods. This retrospective cohort study used the blood transfusion center’s database from January 1, 2014, to December 31, 2024. All permanent deferral cases (n = 1116) were included. Data on sociodemographic characteristics, donation type, and deferral reasons — alanine aminotransferase (ALT), hepatitis B (HBV), hepatitis C (HCV), syphilis, and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) were collected. Relative risks (RR) and proportions were calculated using total donations (n = 101,960). Results. From 2014 and 2024, the permanent deferral rate decreased tenfold (3.66% to 0.36%; p < 0.001) amid a quadrupling of annual donations (3,388 to 13,406). Male sex (odds ratio (OR) = 1.88; 95% confidential interval (CI) = 1.639–2.151) and first-time donor status (OR = 8.58; 95% CI = 7.61–9.67) were key risk factors for deferral, while plasma and platelet donations carried significantly lower odds of deferral compared to whole blood (ОR = 0,592; 95% CI = 0,487–0,718 and ОR = 0,391; 95% CI = 0,320–0,477, respectively; all p < 0.001). The etiological landscape shifted fundamentally from dominant ALT elevation (75.0% to 4.2%) to prevalent HСV (9.7% to 41.7%) and HBV (5.6% to 29.2%) markers, with newly detected HIV cases emerging at 6.3% in 2024. Conclusion. Male sex and first-time donor status were identified as primary independent risk factors for permanent deferral. The observed transformation in deferral etiology (shifting from the surrogate marker ALT to specific detection of HCV and HBV) reflects a transition towards a contemporary transfusion safety paradigm. The achieved deferral rate (0.27–0.36%) aligns with international standards and underscores the efficacy of optimized donor selection algorithms within a middle-income metropolitan setting.

title: Robust PV fault diagnosis under data constraints using a hybrid vision transformer with cross-attention fusion and uncertainty-aware explainability
authors: Mohammed H. Alqahtani; Ali S. Aljumah; Abdullah Mohammed Shaheen; Mohammed A. Atiea
abstract: Solar photovoltaic (PV) systems are crucial in modern energy infrastructures for the shift to sustainable renewable energy, making accurate and reliable fault diagnosis essential for maximizing energy yield, operational efficiency, and system availability. However, reliable automated fault diagnosis faces challenges like data scarcity, class imbalance, and lack of calibrated uncertainty in deep learning models. This paper introduces HyViX-PV, a hybrid deep learning framework that integrates EfficientNet-B3 and Vision Transformer (ViT-B/16) through a novel cross-attention fusion mechanism to enhance renewable PV monitoring and its associated energy efficiency. Unlike conventional static fusion approaches, the proposed HyViX-PV module dynamically combines local texture features and global contextual representations via learnable query-key interactions, enabling adaptive feature prioritization based on input characteristics. The presented framework incorporates Monte Carlo dropout for uncertainty quantification, facilitating confidence-aware decision-making and selective prediction abstention. In addition, a multi-granularity explainability pipeline, combining Grad-CAM, attention roll-out, and fusion weight analysis, provides transparent and interpretable diagnostic insights aligned with domain expert reasoning. The proposed model is evaluated using a five-fold cross-validation, a locked test set, and hash-based data leakage prevention. Experimental results demonstrate that HyViX-PV achieves 92.22% accuracy and 0.9230 macro F1-score, outperforming state-of-the-art CNN, ViT, and hybrid baselines while maintaining efficient inference. Cross-dataset validation shows strong generalization with only a 1.05% performance drop. Furthermore, it attains 92.66% accuracy and 0.9364 macro F1-score robustness under severe class imbalance realistic scenarios. By enabling dependable, interpretable, and uncertainty-aware fault diagnosis, the proposed framework supports improved reliability, reduced maintenance costs, and enhanced operational performance of solar PV installations, contributing to the broader adoption and effective utilization of renewable energy systems.

title: Policies for Rapid Mitigation of the Crisis’ Effects on Agricultural Supply Chains: A Multi-Criteria Decision Support System with Monte Carlo Simulation
authors: Tomas Baležentis; Mangirdas Morkūnas; Agnė Žičkienė; Artiom Volkov; Erika Ribašauskienė; Dalia Štreimikienė
abstract: This paper proposes an integrated approach towards rapid decision-making in the agricultural sector aimed at improvement of its resilience. Methodologically, we seek to devise a framework that is able to take the uncertainty regarding policy preferences into account. Empirically, we focus on the effects of COVID-19 on agriculture. First, we propose a multi-criteria decision-making framework following the Pugh matrix approach for group decision-making. The Monte Carlo simulation is used to check the effects of the perturbations in the criteria weights. Then, we identify the factors behind agricultural resilience and organize them into the three groups (food security, agricultural viability, decent jobs). The expert survey is carried out to elicit the ratings in regard to the expected effects of the policy measures with respect to dimensions of agricultural resilience. The case of Lithuania is considered in the empirical analysis. The existing and newly proposed agricultural policy measures are taken into account. The measures related to alleviation of the financial burden (e.g., credit payment deferral) appear to be the most effective in accordance with the expert ratings.

title: A Review of Fault Diagnosis and Intelligent Operations and Maintenance for Agricultural Machinery: Fault Mechanisms, Key Technologies, and Practical Recommendations
authors: Yu Zhang; Xingzhu Qian; Ruifan Tang; Chenyu Xi; Tingrui Cui; Zhong Tang
abstract: Agricultural machinery operates under variable loads, impacts, dust, and changing soil-crop interactions, allowing faults to propagate through energy, material, information, and control pathways. This qualitative review synthesizes 195 research publications across fault formation, trustworthy diagnosis, prognostics and proactive risk control, maintenance and recovery, and case-based evidence assessment. Empirical findings are reported separately from review-derived recommendations, the authors' conceptual requirements, and mandatory provisions of applicable standards or law. The literature most consistently supports controlled-fault identification, selected single-machine field monitoring, and localized operational compensation. Evidence is weaker for transfer across machines and seasons, calibrated prognostics, safety authorization, post-repair verification, and fleet-scale deployment. On this basis, the review recommends mission profile-specific fault boundaries, traceable diagnostic outputs, explicit uncertainty and abstention, and risk decisions linked to remaining work and resources. It also proposes a diagnostic passport, risk evolution trajectory, repair-effectiveness label, case-evidence matrix, and closed-loop repair workflow as review-level organizing constructs. No included study continuously followed the same machine or fleet through diagnosis, prognosis, authorization, maintenance, acceptance, and feedback; the framework therefore connects evidence-supported stages theoretically rather than claiming end-to-end validation.

title: Causes of pre and post-donation deferrals among blood donors, at Kwale Satellite Blood Transfusion Center, Kwale County, Kenya, 2018–2022
authors: Gibson Waweru Nyamu; Matano Ali Shee; Polly Kiende; Benson Muithya Muthiani; Rocky Jumapili Nakazea; Narcis Mwakidedela Mwasowa; Frendrick Odhiambo; Jacintah Mueni King’oo; Ronald Nyarambe Wigina
abstract: BACKGROUND: Both pre-donation and post-donation deferrals pose challenges to blood safety and availability. This study delved into the deferral rates before donations and their underlying reasons, as, transfusion transmissible infections (TTIs) leading to post-donation deferrals among potential blood donors at the Kwale Satellite Blood Transfusion Centre (KSBTC) in Kenya. METHODS: We performed a retrospective electronic record review of pre- and post-donation deferrals among blood donors at KSBTC, 2018-2022. The pre-donations deferral rate and reasons for deferral were analyzed. Accepted donations were analyzed to determine the prevalence of HIV, hepatitis B (HBV), hepatitis C (HCV), and syphilis. Descriptive statistics were calculated and both crude odds ratio (COR) and adjusted odds ratio (AOR), and their 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated. Variables with p < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. RESULTS: A review was conducted on 12,633 blood donation records. Among these, individuals 2,729/12,633 (21.60%) were deferred from donating with the primary reason being low hemoglobin levels, constituting 51.86% of deferrals. Around 773/9,904 (7.80%) of blood units, were discarded due to at least one TTI. Among these, HBV accounted for 4.73%, HIV for 2.01%, HCV for 1.21%, and Syphilis for 0.59% of cases. The adjusted odds ratio for male donors were, (aOR = 1.3, 95% CI 1.01-1.57), donors with none or primary education level (aOR = 1.4 95% CI 1.11-1.68), first-timer donors (aOR = 1.2, 95% CI 1.01-1.44), and static strategy for blood collection (aOR = 1.4, 95%CI 1.12-1.63) were independently potentially associated with testing positive for at least one TTI. CONCLUSION: The study indicates that TTIs continue to pose a risk to the safety of Kenya's bloodstock, with a notable prevalence of HBV infections. Male donors, individuals with limited education, first-time donors, and utilizing a fixed strategy for blood collection were identified as potential risk factors independently associated with TTIs.

title: Barriers and enablers to source plasma donation by gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men under revised eligibility criteria: protocol for a multiple stakeholder feasibility study
authors: Elisabeth Vesnaver; Mindy Goldman; Sheila F. O’Brien; Paul A. MacPherson; Terrie Butler‐Foster; Don Lapierre; Joanne Otis; Dana V. Devine; Marc Germain; Andrew Rosser; Richard MacDonagh; Taylor Randall; William Osbourne‐Sorrell; Broderic Clement-Thorne; Taim Bilal Al‐Bakri; Kyle A. Rubini; Nolan E. Hill; Justin Presseau
abstract: BACKGROUND: Blood donation policy in Canada for gay, bisexual and other men who have had sex with men (gbMSM) has changed progressively in the last decade from indefinite deferral to 3-month deferral from last male-to-male sex. Driven by safety data and overseen by the national regulator, more inclusive policies continue to redress the disparity in donation for gbMSM. At the same time, the need for source plasma to prepare fractionated blood products is growing worldwide. The collection and processing of source plasma ensures greater safety compared to whole blood donation with respect to transfusion-transmitted infection. This greater safety offers an opportunity to evolve policies for gbMSM from time-based to behaviour-based deferral using revised eligibility criteria. However, changing policies does not in itself necessarily guarantee that gbMSM will donate or that staff in donor clinics are ready to support them to do so. In anticipation of a move to behaviour-based donation screening for gbMSM in Canada, we aim to assess the acceptability of and perceived barriers and enablers to source plasma donation using revised screening criteria for gbMSM among key stakeholders to inform policy implementation strategies. METHODS: This mixed-methods feasibility study will involve gbMSM and donor centre staff to understand modifiable barriers to implementing more inclusive eligibility criteria. Key informant interviews and surveys will be rooted in the Theoretical Domains Framework to identify modifiable factors associated with source plasma donation motives in gbMSM and training needs in donation centre staff. We will use an integrated knowledge translation approach involving a partnership between researchers, the national blood operator and gbMSM, situating knowledge users as key research team members to ensure their perspectives inform all aspects of the research. DISCUSSION: Our integrated knowledge translation approach will provide a more comprehensive and collaborative understanding of blood operator and gbMSM needs while accelerating the implementation of study findings. Given the historical backdrop of the decades of exclusion of sexually active gbMSM from blood donation, this study has the potential not only to inform a process and policy for gbMSM to donate source plasma, a blood product, but also offers opportunities for new relationships between these knowledge users.

title: Post-Training on the Clock: Specializing a Small Language Model on a Consumer GPU
authors: Uygar Kurt
abstract: Abstract How should a language model be specialized for a target task when training is limited to one consumer GPU and a few hours? We study the allocation of a nominal three-hour training budget, with up to 0.3 additional hours, between supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). We use tool calling as a case study because of its practical relevance to language-model agents and its verifiable outputs. Using Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct with low-rank adaptation on an RTX 5060 Ti with 16 GB of memory, we compare SFT, GRPO, and six sequential SFT-to-GRPO allocations. Training uses a filtered mixture of xLAM function-calling examples and Hammer irrelevance examples, covering both call construction and abstention when no offered tool is suitable. Evaluation reports xLAM exact tool-call and function-name accuracies for local call construction, BFCL-v3 Single-turn FC (agg) for external function calling, BFCL-v3 Irrelevance (agg) for abstention, and MMLU, MATH-500, and IFEval for selected general capabilities. The suffix (agg) denotes study-specific averages of selected subset accuracies weighted by subset size. At the last evaluated checkpoints within 3.3 reported hours, SFT achieves the highest xLAM exact tool-call accuracy (82.82%), compared with 69.13% for GRPO alone. Selected hybrid allocations improve external function-calling accuracy over SFT, with different abstention trade-offs. Most sampled GRPO groups have constant rewards and provide no relative task-reward signal. We release the prepared mixed dataset, all allocation-study checkpoints, and Post-Training Lab, an editable training and evaluation codebase with CUDA and MLX implementations.

title: The logic of stasis: asylum seeker drawings and the refusal of the gutter in Safdar Ahmed’s Still Alive
authors: Mike Lehman
abstract: This essay argues that the asylum seeker drawings in Safdar Ahmed’s Still Alive: Graphic Reportage from Australia’s Immigration Detention System (2022) refuse the panel-gutter-panel structure through which Ahmed’s reportage narrates the detention system. While traditional comics theory positions the gutter as a generative space of narrative closure, and refugee comics scholarship has focused on empathetic narration and the gutter’s capacity to invite readers into migrant experiences, I suggest that the drawings contributed by detained asylum seekers do not participate in this sequential logic. Whether as single images or loose clusters, the detainees’ drawings visualise what I call a logic of stasis, or a visualisation of indefinite deferral, the temporal condition in which movement is demanded but arrival is structurally denied. Extending recent critiques of gutter theory, the essay shows how these non-sequential drawings expose the limits of sequential form for representing indefinite detention. In my readings of Mazhar’s knots, the confrontational gaze of unnamed detainees, and his drawing ‘The Boat,’ I demonstrate how the absence of a next panel formally registers the temporal foreclosure that defines indefinite detention.

title: Evidence in Norwegian child protection interventions – Analysing cases of familial violence
authors: Audun Gabriel Løvlie
abstract: Abstract How is expert evidence used in care order proceedings when children are considered for foster care placement because of familial violence? What are important factors and how do the decision‐makers use and evaluate evidence from specialists and experts? In this in‐depth analysis of 104 published care order decisions from the Norwegian County Boards, I investigate how decision‐makers use and evaluate evidence from expert witnesses to determine whether a care order may be granted. The analysis shows that the evidence largely revolves around social functioning, care context and topics about how parents and children relate to each other. Led by the law, the decision‐makers use this evidence to determine whether the child's situation is harmful, whether support services are viable and whether a care order is in the child's best interests. I find that decision‐makers draw unevenly on evidence with regards to these legal requirements, and that the use predominantly defers to expert authority. However, there is also evidence of independent reasoning, where deferral to the epistemic authority of the experts is weakened. This is shown through evaluative and critical assessments and scrutiny of the disciplinary evidence.

title: Hak Asasi Manusia Kaitannya dengan Penolakan Donor Darah Sesuai Hukum Kesehatan di Indonesia
authors: Suminah; Leony Ciputri; Kimberly Ciputri; Nabila Asy-Syifa Taufik
venue: JUSTLAW : Journal Science and Theory of law
abstract: Blood donation constitutes an essential humanitarian parctice conducted voluntarily and without coercion, providing a critical source of blood for patients requiring transfusion. Despite its humanitarian nature, blood donation requires a rigorous screening process to ensure that prospective donors meet established eligibility criteria. This screening is essential to maintain the quality and safety of donated blood and to minimize the risk of transfusion-transmitted infection and other adverse health outcome in recipients. This article aims to examine the principles governing safe and appropriate blood donation practices and to analyze appropriate approaches to communicating donor deferral decisions while respecting human rights. This study employed a qualitative descriptive method through a review of relevant literature, books, and applicable laws and regulations. The finding indicate that blood donation should be conducted in accordance with the principle of humanity, safety, and respect for the rights of both donors and blood recipients. Only individuals who fulfill the established health and eligibility criteria should be permitted to donate blood. In cases of permanent donor deferral, the decision should be communicated clearly, respectfully, and transparently, while ensuring that the donor’s human rights and dignity are upheld.

title: Stakes-Blindness in Vision-Language Models as Visual Assistants for Blind and Low-Vision Users
authors: San Hong
abstract: Title. Stakes-Blindness in AI Visual Assistance: Benchmarking Safety-Critical Uncertainty Communication for Blind and Low-Vision UsersResearch questions.RQ1 (Discrimination): How accurately do vision-language models (VLMs) discriminate answerable from unanswerable situations in safety-critical visual questions?RQ2 (Stakes-sensitivity): Is response conservativeness (abstention criterion, hedging, referral to human verification) adjusted according to the severity of consequences?RQ3 (Recovery orientation): When abstaining, do models attribute the cause of failure and provide recovery paths executable without vision?Key construct. Stakes-blindness: the state in which a model's response conservativeness reacts only to visual difficulty and is insensitive to the severity of consequences.

title: Fractional Flow Reserve: Scoping Review with ☸️SAIMSARA
authors: SAIMSARA
abstract: To synthesize the structured evidence on fractional flow reserve (FFR), emphasizing its role in lesion assessment, revascularization guidance, deferral safety, prognostication, noninvasive and angiography-derived alternatives, and integration with plaque and microvascular evaluation. The review uses 615 references and builds its evidence map from 3488 original studies with 42464789 total participants/sample observations (topic-deduplicated ΣN). Across the mapped evidence, FFR emerges as a clinically actionable physiologic reference that reclassifies angiography-based decisions in roughly one-third to nearly one-half of patients and supports safer, more selective revascularization, with FFR-guided PCI reducing long-term events versus medical therapy alone (13.9% vs 27.0% at 5 years) and enabling generally safe deferral above the 0.80 threshold. However, the recurrent signal of residual risk in acute coronary syndromes, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, microvascular dysfunction, and vulnerable plaque indicates that a single hyperemic pressure cutoff is insufficient for comprehensive risk stratification. Angiography- and CT-derived FFR alternatives show promising diagnostic and workflow value but have not uniformly matched wire-based FFR for deferral outcomes. This supports a role for integrating FFR with plaque imaging and microvascular indices in routine practice, while future research should prioritize endpoint-powered trials defining when standard FFR thresholds require contextual personalization.

title: Your silence speaks volumes: Weak states and strategic absence in the UN General Assembly
authors: Julia C. Morse; Bridget L. Coggins
abstract: Abstract Country participation in one-state, one-vote forums like the United Nations General Assembly often reflects underlying power asymmetries and endogenous political processes. Voting alignment is undoubtedly an important preference indicator. However, this paper contends that it is incomplete; silence is politically significant as well. Weak states use absence as a form of institutional power that shields them from geopolitical pressure and competing-principals problems. While abstention is a public signal of neutrality that undercuts voting unanimity, the ambiguous intent of absence makes it a distinct form of political expression. We examine the politics of absences at the General Assembly, highlighting how states may be strategically absent from select votes for political reasons. Building on the Bailey et al. Journal of Conflict Resolution, 61 (2), 430–456, 2017 roll-call voting data, we distinguish strategic absences from other types of absence and provide evidence that such behavior is linked to US interests and competing-principals problems. Taking these non-random reasons for missingness into account provides a fuller picture of how weak states engage with international institutions and highlights how silence can be a consequence of larger political processes.

title: Stage Four of BioSNN-Plug: What the Cognitive Components Actually Support
authors: lzmd-arch
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: What this is. A technical report on phase four of BioSNN-Plug: multi-timescale working memory, delayed paired-associate episodic memory, a metacognitive gate, a world model, and the end-to-end delayed-recall task. It records both the results that pass their preregistered criteria and the exact boundaries under which each claim holds. What it finds. Two end-to-end results survive. A sequential working-memory to DPAR composition reaches 6/6 criteria (R^2 0.99995, selective MSE 6.16e-05, OOD abstention 0.9492). A shared-state dual-bank design with a bank-W scale gate reaches 6/6 on its primary condition (WM R^2 0.9938, OOD AUROC 0.9562, abstention 0.9368), but a follow-up sweep shows it covers only OOD scales of at least 3x and DPAR K at most 4: at 2x abstention falls to 0.720, and at K=8 working-memory R^2 is 0.89975 against a 0.90 floor. Negative results retained. Pure class-incremental learning fails (ACC 0.0876, AF 0.290); the phase-three gate was opened by task-aware CIL (0.8195 / AF 0.0, constructive). Relearn 3x remains unmet (paired median 0.957). Spiking working memory is not ready (about 0.21 / 0.19). Local Hebbian DPAR is 0.311 against 0.938 for literal nearest-neighbour and 0.828 for non-local pseudo-inverse. Closed-loop world-model termination is 0.632-0.665. The metacognitive gate is scale-specific: a valid sign-quantization OOD (6.38x in-dist error) is answered with AUROC 0.4876, and a higher-moment replacement reaches 0.5024. What this is not. It is not a claim of general OOD detection, lifelong episodic memory, stage-four overall acceptance, or bus/plugin integration. The shared-state result is a scale-gated, K<=4 result; the sequential result does not share a final state. Related records. P2 preprint 10.5281/zenodo.23429379; P4 preprint 10.5281/zenodo.23613539; P4 design notes 10.5281/zenodo.23603639; architecture and decision record 10.5281/zenodo.23603642; findings record A 10.5281/zenodo.23428426. Every preregistration and result README is in the repository. Licence. The report is CC-BY-4.0. The attached Markdown is the source; the PDF is rendered from it.

title: Investigating the Influence of AGI-Capable Multi-Agent Systems on Cogent Analysis and Ontological Semantics in Sudanese Genetic, Linguistic and Migration Networks
authors: Sirag-Eldin Elnour; Rekha Sukhani Shewakramani
abstract: This research investigates whether a HIDAYA-inspired, AGI-capable multi-agent system, supported by a provenance-aware spatial-temporal ontology, can improve cogent analysis and ontological semantics when reconciling contested Sudanese, Sahelian and Nile Basin genetic, linguistic, geographic and migration evidence. The empirical specimen is the unresolved chronology of Y-chromosome haplogroup R1b-V88. The central methodological claim is that lineage coalescence, autosomal admixture, inferred migration and language dispersal are distinct chronological constructs and should not be compared as if they were measurements of one event. The study uses a pragmatic, abductive, longitudinal design-science methodology for over twenty-four months. It adopts an embedded mixed-method design with concurrent timing and a dominant quantitative strand (QUAN + qual). The quantitative strand compares the multi-agent artefact with manual synthesis and a single-agent baseline on fixed held-out chronology-reconciliation tasks. The embedded qualitative strand uses structured expert appraisal to evaluate cogency, semantic adequacy, historical plausibility, uncertainty communication and cultural sensitivity. Integration occurs through joint displays that preserve agreement and divergence rather than averaging them away. The contribution is explicitly separated from the artefact. The theoretical contribution is the framing of contested population-history chronologies as ontology-mediated reconciliation problems; the empirical contribution is evidence about whether formal construct separation improves reasoning and semantic quality; and the methodological contribution is a transferable evaluation protocol combining provenance-aware ontologies, calibrated confidence, abstention, independent verification and Expert-in-the-Loop governance. The project is designed to support rather than replace disciplinary expertise and to treat uncertainty and justified abstention as analytical outcomes.

title: AI Bias Mitigation in Insurance Pricing and Claims Decisions
authors: Komal Manohar Tekale; Nivedita Rahul
venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence Data Science and Machine Learning
abstract: Insurers are increasingly using artificial intelligence to underwrite, price, triage fraud and assess claims, although historical data and proxy variables can reinforce unjust inequalities among groups of customers. In this paper a, end-to-end framework that considers bias mitigation as an engineering and governance field is proposed. The bias entry-points of the lifecycle problem framing, data collection and labelling, feature design, training, decision thresholds, and human overrides and propose layer controls: (i) pre-processing audits, re-weighting, and proxy sanitization, (ii) in-processing approaches such as fairness-constrained optimization, adversarial debiasing, and monotonic/shape-constrained models, and (iii) post-processing (e.g. groupwise calibration, adjusting thresholds, and reject-option classification). Fairness is assessed by multi-metric dashboards (adverse impact ratio, statistical difference of parity, error-rate balance, and calibration-between-groups) and counterfactual tests on individuals. Incorporate explainability (global and local stories) and human in the loop review of edge cases which are operationalized through MLOps through versioned model cards, drift detection, audit trails, and stress tests. Comparative analysis depicts significant parity benefits (an increase in AIR, a decrease in parity and TPR differences) at a scale of small utility losses (AUC/MAE) without endangering actuarial plausibility. Place the approach in the context of the changing regulatory frameworks (e.g., NAIC principles, EU AI Act) and comment on the possible practical implication concerning compliance, customer confidence and resilience of portfolios. The outcome is that a repeatable process of achieving more equitable pricing and claims decision-making is possible without damaging economic performance

title: The potential for peak shaving on low voltage distribution networks using electricity storage
authors: Andrew J. Pimm; Tim Cockerill; Peter Taylor
abstract: Co-location of energy storage with demand provides several benefits over other locations, while still being able to provide balancing services to the grid. One of these additional benefits is deferral of distribution infrastructure reinforcement, allowing increased load growth. This paper considers the potential of electricity storage for peak shaving on distribution networks, focusing on residential areas. A demand model is used to synthesise high resolution domestic load profiles, and these are used within Monte Carlo analysis to determine how much peak shaving could be achieved with storage. An efficient method of finding the potential peak shaving using electricity storage is developed for this purpose. It is shown that moderate levels of storage capacity can deliver significant demand reductions, if suitably coordinated and incentivised. With 2 kWh of battery storage per household, the peak demand at low voltage substations could potentially be halved. The effects of PV capacity, household size and C rates are considered. With 3 kW PV per house, 4.5 kWh of batteries could keep peak flows at the same level as before the addition of PV. It is also shown that 3 kWh of battery storage per household could allow provision of all heating from heat pumps without increasing the peak demand.

title: Blood donor eligibility criteria for medical conditions: A BEST collaborative study
authors: Cyril Jacquot; Pierre Tiberghien; Katja van den Hurk; Alyssa F. Ziman; Beth H. Shaz; Torunn Oveland Apelseth; Mindy Goldman; The Biomedical Excellence for Safer Transfusion (BEST) Collaborative
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Donor eligibility questions and criteria for medical conditions vary between blood centres, suggesting that they are based more on local regulations or experience, rather than on published data, which are limited. As the donor population ages, medical conditions become more common. We assessed donor health assessment criteria at blood centre members of the Biomedical Excellence for Safer Transfusion (BEST) Collaborative. Our aim was to compare eligibility criteria and determine their underlying basis. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A REDCap survey was sent to blood centre participants, based on medical conditions of greatest interest suggested by the Donor Studies Team of the BEST Collaborative. Participants were asked about current donor health assessment questions, deferral criteria and the basis for their deferral policy (donor risk, recipient risk or both) for 20 medical conditions. RESULTS: Complete responses were received from 26 blood donor centres (24 separate responses) representing a combination of hospital-based centres, large regional centres and community/national blood centres in 14 different countries. Most centres specifically ask about heart and lung conditions, whereas fewer than half inquire about kidney, gastrointestinal or neurological conditions. North American blood centres tended to be less restrictive, while regulatory restrictions are more prevalent in Europe. Most participants felt that the criteria were based on regulatory requirements or experience, rather than on published data. CONCLUSION: There is considerable variability in criteria by region. Ideally, criteria would be more evidence-based rather than based on regulatory requirements or experience. Deferral criteria must balance donor and recipient safety and maintain an adequate blood supply.

title: Exploring Infant Teachers’ Perceptions of the Null Curriculum in Classroom-Level Curriculum: A Q Methodological Study
authors: The Korea Associantion For Early Childhood Education Administration; Jinseol Choi; Yujin Yang
venue: The Korea Association for Early Childhood Education and Educare Welfare
abstract: This study aimed to explore infant teachers’ subjective perceptions of the null curriculum manifested in the classroom-level curriculum using Q methodology. To this end, 40 Q statements were developed through a review of previous studies, in-depth interviews with infant teachers, and expert review. The P-sample consisted of 26 infant teachers with at least one year of experience teaching classes of infants aged 0–2 years. The collected data were analyzed using the Ken-Q Analysis program. The results identified three distinct types of perceptions. Type 1 was labeled “Curricular Reconstruction of Unimplemented Experiences,” Type 2 “Deferral of Experiences Based on Teacher Judgment and Structural Conditions,” and Type 3 “Invisibility of Educational Experiences According to Practical Competence.” The findings indicate that the null curriculum in infant classrooms is formed not merely through the omission of activities but in various ways, including the reconstruction of unimplemented experiences, the deferral of particular experiences, and the invisibility of educational experiences. This study is significant in identifying the teacher-related and structural factors that shape the null curriculum in infant classrooms and providing foundational information for supporting infant teachers’ curriculum implementation.

title: Prise en charge d’une lésion kystique du pancréas de découverte fortuite
authors: Sahar Mack; Léon Finci; Caroline Bastid; Emmanuel Coron; Philippe Bichard; Jean-Louis Frossard
abstract: Pancreatic cysts (PC) are common and often discovered incidentally. The distinction between PC is essential, because of the potential malignancy of some lesions requiring surgical resection. The clinical orientation will depend on the clinical history and the radiological characteristics. Indeed, in front of all PCs, it is essential to characterize them using cross-sectional imaging (MRI) in order to highlight the worrisome features requiring further examinations by endoscopic ultrasonography and fine needle aspiration of the cysts to guide the diagnosis. Referral to an expert center will allow to propose to each patient an adequate approach: surgical resection, surveillance according to the recommendations or therapeutic abstention.

title: Condensation Nuclei and Recoherence Failure Why Knowing Isn't Acting
authors: John Richard Smith; SHAI / HATI2
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract The companion paper SIP-EP-02 diagnosed latency as regulatory failure — the cost of "we didn't know" in civil governance and research. This paper asks the harder question: Why doesn't recoherence happen even when latency is reduced? Why do systems that possess the information, authority, and mechanisms to act nonetheless fail to act? We propose that recoherence requires a condensation nucleus: a triplet N = {A, D, C} representing Authority (correctly assigned), Deliberation (appropriately bounded), and Commitment (mechanistically triggered). Modern governance systematically disrupts nucleation through sequential bottlenecks, while Aboriginal Australian fire management systems achieved nucleation probability P ≈ 1 through architectural integration spanning 65,000 years. The mathematical framework introduces a sequential activation coefficient derived from signal detection theory: α = P(A) × P(D|A) × P(C|A,D) × η(Φ) This formulation explains why adding authority without fixing deliberation produces no improvement (Lahaina), why infinite deliberation with absent commitment produces permanent deferral (string theory), and why systems where deliberation equals action achieve near-certain nucleation (Aboriginal fire management). Version 1.1 extends the framework with: (1) the η(Φ) information sufficiency term derived from Poisson signal arrival; (2) nucleation fidelity (β) distinguishing action occurrence from action appropriateness; (3) Relational Authority as an alternative to role-based authority, drawn from Aboriginal governance; and (4) implementation evidence from aviation safety and healthcare incident reporting. We introduce the Teacher Problematic: the pathological case where the person nominally responsible for nucleation is themselves the source of decoherence. Design principles are provided with quantitative targets for emergency response (P(D|A) 0.95).

title: An integrated deep learning framework for real-time badminton action recognition and pose estimation with shot-level semantic refinement
authors: Le Luo; Lisha Zhang; Hongzhi Liu
venue: Australian Journal of Electrical & Electronics Engineering
abstract: With the increasing demand for intelligent analysis in sports scenarios, this paper proposes a comprehensive badminton action analysis framework that integrates human pose estimation and temporal tracking based on deep learning. We design a multi-stage experimental evaluation pipeline incorporating enhanced YOLOv8 detection networks, pose-guided skeleton fusion modules, and trajectory modelling under real-world badminton match conditions. The proposed model, composed of YOLOv8(HGNet)+ACmix+FocalModulation, outperforms existing baselines in both accuracy and robustness of pose keypoint detection. Quantitative experiments on benchmark sequences demonstrate that our method achieves an F1-score of 87.5%, surpassing prior works such as HD-T and SRA, with a reduced temporal error of 2.14 frames. Additionally, the abstention-aware recognition module attains 94.6% accuracy in ignoring irrelevant frames.

title: Calibrated-Uncertainty Detection for Counter-UAS: Order-Invariant Evidential Fusion with Guaranteed-Containment Tracking
authors: Lucas Damián Alaniz Pintos
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: AEGIS: Calibrated-Uncertainty Detection for Counter-UAS AEGIS is a detection-only, human-in-the-loop counter-UAS (C-UAS) software pipeline built around calibrated, honest uncertainty — a system designed to know when it does not know. It discriminates drones from birds, clutter and empty scenes under noisy and sometimes contradictory sensor evidence, and is engineered to surface disagreement as calibrated uncertainty and to abstain under genuine conflict rather than emit a confident wrong answer. AEGIS performs detection, classification, tracking and alerting only; a human makes every decision, and the system has no countermeasure or targeting capability. The pipeline combines four components: order-invariant n-ary evidential fusion (PCR6) that removes the order dependence of iterated pairwise combination and retains more declared ignorance under multi-source conflict at equal discrimination; guaranteed-containment set-membership (zonotope) tracking whose position-containment guarantee is validated against real UAV flight trajectories, including aggressive fixed-wing manoeuvres that violate the tracker's own acceleration assumptions in 10–13% of ticks; runtime verification of bounded temporal-logic safety properties; and hardened calibration metrics with an explicit abstention outcome. Every run is deterministic under a fixed seed and is written to a canonicalised, hashable audit trail, making results bit-reproducible and independently checkable across platforms. This deposit contains the reference implementation, the reproducible synthetic testbed, the real-flight validation experiments, and the documentation, including an honest account of the system's measured limits (data-independent set width, position-only consistency monitor, weakly observable velocity) and the sensor that would close them. title: Residual infectious risks in blood transfusion
authors: Ryanne W. Lieshout‐Krikke
abstract: Blood transfusion in developed countries is extremely safe. However, a residual risk remains of infectious donations slipping through, because of imperfect donor selection and the diagnostic window period. A myriad of regulations and safety measures is in place to guarantee the high level of safety. The boundary between risks that should be covered by safety measures, and residual risks that are acceptable, is unclear. This thesis focuses on the yield of safety measures that cover small infectious risks. Occult HBV infected donors and previous donations from seroconverting donors may be infectious. The risk of transmission was assessed by lookback procedures. Transfusion transmissible infections (TTIs) are more common among new donors than repeat donors, as a result of the accumulation of chronic, yet undiagnosed infections. Because of the possibility of acute infections among new donors (eg. among ‘test seekers’), the value of predonation screening without actual donation was assessed. Temporary geographical deferral for donors who travelled to countries where (re)emerging infectious agents are prevalent is commonly practiced. The yield of donor deferral after travelling, by estimating the number of infected donors returning from affected areas, was assessed and the consequences for donor availability were calculated. The European Up-Front Risk Assessment Tool (EUFRAT) quantifies the transfusion transmission risk of donations from donors returning from affected areas where an emerging infectious disease is prevalent. An EUFRAT estimation of dengue infections among Dutch donors travelling to Suriname or the Dutch Caribbean was validated with the actual number of dengue infections detected among Dutch travellers.

title: Методи оцінювання невизначеності прогнозів у системах підтримки прийняття рішень на основі моделей машинного навчання / Uncertainty Estimation Methods for Machine Learning Predictions in Decision Support Systems
authors: Anatolii Holovchenko
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract: The paper addresses the reliability of machine learning predictions in decision support systems (DSS) by integrating model predictive performance, prediction uncertainty, and explainability. Moving beyond average benchmark metrics, the author conceptualizes a unified triplet characterization Q(x)=(P(x),U(x),E(x)) and formulates a decision rule R(x) that dynamically routes predictions into three operational modes: primary algorithmic recommendation, mandatory secondary verification, or deferral to expert review. The framework incorporates conformal prediction sets and counterfactual explanations to establish quantifiable confidence boundaries, enhancing overall decision-making safety in critical domains. Keywords: decision support systems, machine learning, uncertainty estimation, conformal prediction, explainable AI, prediction sets, decision routing, algorithmic reliability. title: Two Lawyers, Three Opinions: Can Output-Based LLM Uncertainty Find the Cases Where Experts Disagree?
authors: Laura Braun; Matthias Aßenmacher; Martin Hohenadler; Goeran Kauermann
abstract: Legal natural language processing (NLP) tasks often lack a single objective ground truth, as reflected in label variation across experts' annotations.We test whether two uncertainty signals based on outputs of large language models (LLMs), sampling entropy and verbalized probability, can identify posts where legal experts disagree.On 1,564 German social media posts annotated by three legal experts for punishability under the German Criminal Code, we evaluate four open-weight LLMs, with reasoning either enabled or disabled, and observe a drop in F1 score on contested posts.Sampling distributions collapse to near-deterministic judgments in most conditions, while verbalized probabilities track expert disagreement in aggregate and support deferral of model errors.Neither signal, however, reliably identifies individual contested posts: both detect the model's own errors (AUROC up to 0.83) better than expert disagreement (up to 0.76), and which signal is more informative depends strongly on model and activation of reasoning mode.

title: Amortization of R and E Expenditures under the TCJA: Unintended Consequences and Policy Lessons for Innovation Incentives
authors: Victory Ifunanya Ejim; Hossana Adeyerimi Olaomotito
venue: World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews
abstract: This article examines the mandatory capitalization and amortization of research and experimental (R&E) expenditures under amended Internal Revenue Code §174, as a retrospective case study in unintended tax policy consequences. Before the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) of 2017, firms could immediately deduct R&E expenditures in the year incurred, preserving liquidity and maximizing the present value of associated tax shields. The TCJA eliminated this option, requiring domestic R&E costs to be amortized over five years and foreign R&E costs over fifteen, generating immediate and material distortions for innovation-intensive firms. Drawing on statutory analysis, corporate finance theory, firm-level case studies, and industry advocacy evidence, this article makes three principal contributions. First, it reframes the amortization mandate as an intertemporal tax policy intervention, quantifying how deduction deferral reduces the present value of tax shields and raises effective hurdle rates, particularly under risk-adjusted discount rates reflective of innovation uncertainty. Second, it extends R&E incentive research by analyzing the consequences of withdrawing a longstanding preference rather than introducing new benefits. Third, it situates the episode within broader debates on tax stability, liquidity constraints, and cross-provision interactions, especially with qualified small business stock under §1202 and deferred tax accounting under ASC 740, and offers evidence-based lessons for innovation-oriented tax design. The 2025 reversal through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, while substantially corrective, left legacy harms that illustrate the durable costs of budget-driven policy misalignment with the distinctive economics of R&E investment.

title: Righting anachronistic exclusions: The ethics of blood donation by men who have sex with men
authors: Kavita Shah Arora
venue: Sexual and Gender Diversity in Social Services
abstract: Recently, the FDA announced that it would soon lift the long-standing lifetime ban on blood donation by men who have sex with men (MSM). Re-examining blood donation by MSM, it is clear that there are several ethical goods that must be balanced. Through balancing the primary duty to safety with the imperatives to craft a policy that is formally equal, upholds the public's trust, and is non-discriminatory, an ethical blood donation deferral guideline may be advanced, both for MSM and the population at large.

title: BOTANICAL PROVENANCE VARIABILITY AND CHEMICAL FINGERPRINTING AT THE LIMIT is an exactly 777-page prospective, high-density English research working monograph concerning the scientific distinction between botanical source identity, chemical fingerprint patterns, and independently qualified raw-material batch quality. Chinese title: 本草原料產地差異與化學指紋極限 Its central falsifiable question is whether a model can reduce the percentage of incorrect assignments on geographically independent, masked and previously withheld botanical source lots after instrument batch, harvest stage, plant taxonomy, cultivar, handling, extraction solvent and analytical platform are explicitly challenged. Its core three-coupling is Botanical Provenance x Chemical Fingerprinting x Batch-Quality Verification. The familiar Mahalanobis expression d_M^2=(x-mu)^T Sigma^(-1)(x-mu) is a conditional multivariate distance, not a certificate of geographic origin; a robust, source-representative covariance reference and honest class-rejection policy remain necessary. The book begins with voucher-authenticated botanical taxonomy, preservation of plant-part identity, accurate geographic granularity, independent source custody, harvest and storage records, and hard vetoes for unpermitted source materials or prohibited contaminants. It separates genuine regional chemistry from plausible alternative causes: elevation, soil environment, irrigation, genetic cultivar, harvest season, drying and shipping history, extraction chemistry, chromatographic alignment, ion suppression, adduct formation, baseline correction, spectral scatter, pooled-QC choice and instrument drift. The strongest adversary may be a model based solely on acquisition date and instrument ID. Multiple injections of one vial are not equivalent to independently collected botanical lots. Thirty mathematically diverse candidate plates include robust Mahalanobis distance, variance components, compositional log-ratios, matrix-matched recovery, Beer-Lambert response, relative retention, mass accuracy, isotope ratios, detection-limit estimation, chemical mass balance, dilution, degradation kinetics, Arrhenius sensitivity, mixed-effects modelling, Bayes posterior classification, farm-level classification loss, probability calibration, conformal abstention, entropy, cosine similarity, distribution divergence, spectral optimal transport, PCA, Fisher discrimination, batch offset, propagated covariance uncertainty, multivariate energy distance, isotope mixing, likelihood ratio and sequential reference drift monitoring. Every plate states mathematical construction, variables and units, conditions for identifiability, a blinded refuting test and linked chapters. Eighty-two independently scoped chapters each include a formula-bearing scientific entry plus five single-page investigations on specimen truth, rival chemistry or physics, blinded factorial challenge, uncertainty and hard refusal, and second-laboratory reconstruction. Two hundred Research Gates formulate distinct future experiments, with Chapter-specific experiments and additional cross-chapter fault injections: blind voucher swaps, harvest-stage masking, source-to-run recrossing, instrument-only rival models, cross-platform transfers, novel-origin abstention, confidential supplier-data handling, contaminant vetoes and preservation of negative or failed evidence. Thirty-three distinct Phoenix Answer Embryos propose implementable scientific artifacts including voucher-to-spectrum identity bridges, reference QC kits, chromatographic alignment witnesses, metadata-only adversaries, grouped-validation firewalls, independent safety sentinels and successor provenance atlases. The methodological mother lineages are M1 / 10.5281/zenodo.23480803 (heterogeneity and ambiguous-state caution), M2 / 10.5281/zenodo.23486020 (replayable engineering and hard release decisions), and M3 / 10.5281/zenodo.23318840 (sample chain and hybrid human-controlled handling). These are research-method ancestries, not direct experiments on F19 botanical geographic classification. The external method DOI bibliography cites botanical voucher requirements, chromatographic fingerprinting and chemometrics reviews, pooled-QC and inter-batch comparability, drift control and herbal product authentication. Individual source claims and scopes are preserved in the end-of-book evidence pages. Bibliography material does not establish the completed efficacy of the integrated system.

title: Money and Salvation
authors: Vincenzo Ruggiero
abstract: Although engaged in economic activity, the Christian elite continued to officially scorn those whose operations in the market violated Christ’s precept of fraternity among humans. These individuals remained sinners, because their earnings relied upon the exploitation of time, their goods and finances being valorized through deferral. This was a sacrilege: time belongs to God. This chapter follows the trajectory, within the Christian sensibility, whereby wealth appropriated by the rich slowly ceased to be scandalous. This became apparent between the eleventh and twelfth centuries, when in Europe money achieved some form of legitimacy and, despite the awareness of its dangerousness, of its being an obstacle on the way to Salvation, it found its place in the moral economy.

title: Separating instrument limits from model error in VLM plankton visual trait scoring
authors: Anthony J. W. Lindley; Kathryn Barbara Cook
abstract: General-purpose vision–language models (VLMs) can now answer morphological questions about plankton images in ordinary language, at near-zero cost and with no task-specific training, and operational monitoring programmes are likely to adopt them. It is not yet known when their trait calls can be trusted. The distinction matters because, when a VLM's morphological call is wrong, the error can have two quite different causes: the diagnostic feature may not be resolvable in the image (a limit of the instrument), or it may be resolvable and the model has misread or invented it (a limit of the model). These demand different responses and cannot be separated from a class label alone. This project audits the morphological trait calls of a general-purpose VLM on Imaging FlowCytobot (IFCB) imagery of marine plankton — a 22-class subset of the public WHOI-Plankton benchmark (here "WHOI22"), imaged as small grayscale regions of interest at roughly 2.7 pixels per micrometre. For each image the model scores fourteen visibility-grounded morphological concepts (eleven binary: yes / no / unclear; three multi-category, two of them ordinal). Its calls are compared against two independent references: the canonical biology of each class, compiled from the primary taxonomic literature with every value sourced; and per-image visibility labels assigned by an experienced taxonomist who records only what can be seen in the image, not what the organism is known to possess. Agreement is quantified with prevalence-robust statistics — observed agreement, Gwet's AC1, and Krippendorff's alpha with ordinal weighting — each with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals resampled by image, and with abstention ("unclear") analysed separately from agreement on committed calls. This is a registration of the confirmatory analysis. The imagery is public, and the analysis pipeline — the training-free VLM scoring procedure (a fixed structured prompt, fixed model, temperature 0, JSON-constrained output), the fourteen-concept list, the canonical-biology table and the statistics — was developed and frozen on a development set of non-expert pilot labels created by the first author. That development set exists only to build and test the method and is reported nowhere as a result. The held-out confirmatory test is the comparison against an independent expert reference that has not yet been collected: a senior plankton taxonomist (and, if available, a second reader) will label the evaluation images blind to class and in randomised order, using a self-contained offline tool. We register six confirmatory hypotheses (H1–H6; stated in full in the Hypotheses field), fixed before the expert labels exist, grouped under three themes. Faithfulness: when the model and the expert both commit to a value their per-concept calls agree well above chance, and per-concept VLM–expert agreement tracks human–human agreement. Abstention: the model answers "unclear" far less often than the expert, and this gap is larger on the visibility-limited concepts. Instrument versus model error: the model's divergence from canonical biology concentrates on the pre-specified visibility-limited concepts (e.g. striae, flagella) and co-localises with the expert's own "unclear" rate, indicating an instrument rather than a model limitation. All other analyses are exploratory and will be labelled as such. The expected outcome is high agreement when both parties commit, a systematic under-abstention gap, and divergence concentrated on the pre-specified low-visibility features. The method is training-free and model-agnostic; the deliverable is a cheap, transferable way to map where automated plankton trait scoring can be trusted and to separate instrument limits from model error.

authors: Tomislav Vuk; Karin Magnussen; Wim L.A.M. de Kort; Gilles Folléa; Giancarlo Maria Liumbruno; Harald Schennach; Giovani Vandewalle; Veerle Compernolle; Natalia Masharova; Georgia Karakatsiani; Isabella Argyrou; Vít Řeháček; Gulara Khanirzajeva; Johanna Castrén; Bruno Danic; Rachid Djoudi; Geneviève Woimant; Markus M. abstract: Transfusion of blood components is an irreplaceable form of treatment for many patients1. However, besides providing sufficient amounts of blood components of excellent quality, blood transfusion services should protect the safety of blood donors. Numerous studies have proven that iron deficiency is common in frequent blood donors, particularly women2–5. Determination of the haemoglobin concentration is a routine part of the donor selection process both in order to ensure adequate quality of red cell concentrates collected and to protect the potential donor’s health. Indeed, low haemoglobin is globally the most common reason for deferral of prospective blood donors. Nevertheless, only cases of manifest low haemoglobin levels and imminent anaemia are detected using this approach. More sensitive tests are needed to assess depletion of iron stores, particularly in non-anaemic individuals, with ferritin measurements being used most frequently.
