title: Uncertainty Decomposition & Probabilistic Reasoning: When Does Decomposed Uncertainty Add Decision Value — and How Should It Survive Heterogeneous Models, Providers and Tools?
authors: Mark Lamont
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: R146 is Thesis 06 in an eighteen-thesis independent research programme examining uncertainty decomposition and probabilistic reasoning. It asks when explicit decomposition into epistemic, aleatoric, model-form, disagreement and higher-order uncertainty creates incremental decision value across heterogeneous models, providers, tools and human interfaces, compared with calibrated predictive probabilities, prediction sets and intervals, conformal risk controls, out-of-distribution indicators, selective prediction, aggregation rules and direct decision-loss methods. The evidence synthesis spans Bayesian and approximate Bayesian uncertainty, calibration and proper scoring, conformal inference, model misspecification, expert/model aggregation, imprecise probability, distribution shift and OOD detection, LLM/agent/tool uncertainty and human reliance. R146 SOURCE v1.0 contains 223 discovered Works and a conservative 144-Work source-open substantive corpus. The thesis freezes 38 material claims and records 24/24 conclusion-bearing high-leverage verification checks. The central conclusion is conditional: richer uncertainty decomposition is justified where distinct components remain semantically defensible, survive shift and dependence, and improve consequential decisions over strong simpler alternatives after complete cost is included. The thesis does not establish a universal uncertainty engine and does not authorise implementation in Mazikeen, Nova or any other system. A fourteen-experiment E1-E14 falsification programme is proposed; the experiments have not been executed. ChatGPT was used as an AI-assisted research, drafting, analytical and quality-assurance environment under author direction; AI output is not treated as scientific evidence or independent corroboration. Evidence cut-off: 2 October 2026. Version 1.0.

title: A Trigger Aware, Event Centric, and Uncertainty Calibrated Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Actionable Cyber Threat Intelligence from Indonesian Online News
authors: Elia Setiana; Muhamad Achya Arifudin; Nur Alamsyah
venue: Bulletin of Intelligent Machines and Algorithms
abstract: Online news can provide timely cyberthreat signals, but duplicative reporting, fragmented event descriptions, resource-constrained Indonesian language text, and uncalibrated model confidence limit its operational use. This study presents A Trigger-Aware, Event-Centric, and Uncertainty-Calibrated Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Actionable Cyber ​​Threat Intelligence from Indonesian Online News (TRACE-CTI-ID), a proof-of-concept framework that integrates exact deduplication, event-centric clustering, trigger-aware semantic representation, neuro-symbolic fusion, ordinal risk estimation, conformal uncertainty, mitigation mapping, and an event-centric knowledge graph. The experiment used 711 Liputan6 records collected on March 14, 2025. Exact deduplication reduced the corpus to 79 unique headlines, which were automatically consolidated into 26 events. Splitting the separate events resulted in 30 training articles, 5 calibration articles, and 44 test articles with zero event leakage. The calibrated neuro-symbolic model achieved a micro-F1 of 0.283 and a macro-F1 of 0.441, outperforming the baseline TF-IDF of 0.074 and 0.013, respectively. However, ordinal severity prediction remained weak with an accuracy of 0.136, a macro-F1 of 0.138, and a mean absolute error of 2.023. Conformal coverage was also unstable, and the abstention mechanism did not direct uncertain articles to human review. These findings demonstrate the technical feasibility of the integrated pipeline while also demonstrating that silver labeled, title only, and single source data are insufficient for final operational validation. Therefore, the key contribution is a transparent, leak aware evaluation architecture and protocol that can be strengthened through full text collection from multiple sources and independent expert annotation.

title: Young paediatricians on the frontline: awareness of neonatal stabilization in congenital diaphragmatic hernia prior to surgical referral
authors: Saima Ghafoor; Khowla Rabbani; Maryam Ghaffar; Shabana Tehreem; Waqas Ali; Fahad Iqbal; Muhammad Zaeem Khalid
venue: International Journal of Research in Medical Sciences
abstract: Background: In congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH), survival and morbidity hinge on meticulous cardiopulmonary stabilization during the minutes to hours after birth often led by young paediatricians. Core elements include no bag-mask ventilation, early endotracheal intubation, orogastric decompression, titrated oxygen to preductal saturation milestones, gentle ventilation with permissive hypercapnia, hemodynamic optimization for PPHN, transport readiness and deferral of surgical repair until physiologic stability. Objective: To evaluate young paediatricians’ knowledge and practices in early CDH stabilization, quantify guideline fidelity, identify gaps (including beliefs about early surgery) and determine educational/system factors associated with high performance. Methods: Multi-centre cross-sectional survey of junior paediatricians across labour wards, EDs and NICUs. A validated 48-item tool generated a stabilization fidelity score (SFS, 0–20). Multivariable models assessed associations between training exposures and high SFS (≥16/20). Results: Among 312 respondents (mean age 28.4 years; 62% female, 61% tertiary centres), recent NRP was 68%, NICU ≥6 months 54%, CDH simulation 41%. Mean SFS was 13.8±3.4, 29.5% achieved ≥16/20. Strengths: intubation priority (84%), OG decompression (79%), transport checklists (74%). Gaps: avoidance of bag-mask ventilation (58%), correct preductal SpO₂ targets (46%), permissive hypercapnia (39%), stepwise PPHN management (41%). Notably, 35% believed earlier repair helps even when unstable; 18% were unsure. NRP, NICU time, simulation and unit checklists independently increased odds of high SFS. Conclusions: Young paediatricians execute procedures well but often miss numeric targets and algorithmic PPHN therapy; misconceptions about early surgery persist. Low-cost levers checklists, simulation that drills the numbers, NRP reinforcement and explicit myth-busting (“stabilize first, repair later”) can raise fidelity and pre-operative readiness.

title: Trustworthy Agentic AI in Bioinformatics: From Workflow Automation to Traceable and Validated Biological Inference
authors: Mia Yang Ang; Leonard Lipovich; Siew Woh Choo; Li Chen; Lanni Song
abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence is extending bioinformatics beyond conversational assistance by enabling systems to select tools, execute code, revise analytical plans, and interpret biological data. These capabilities may accelerate research, but they also redistribute decisions that determine whether biological conclusions are valid. We conducted a targeted, structured PubMed search in July 2026 and identified 11 peer-reviewed agentic bioinformatics systems for descriptive review based on predefined eligibility criteria for analytical decision-making, tool or code execution, iterative evaluation, or coordinated agent activity. The evidence base covered single-cell transcriptomics, microbial genomics, cancer genomics, and omics applications, together with methodological literature on reproducibility and biological validation. We examined how current systems report delegated authority, provenance, validation, evidence, abstention, and human oversight. Existing platforms implement safeguards such as sandboxed execution, restricted commands, interaction logs, evidence identifiers, automated checks, critic agents, quality scores, and expert assessment. However, published reports rarely provide a connected account linking the original biological question to samples, reference resources, analytical decisions, computational actions, statistical results, supporting evidence, validation outcomes, and final claims. We distinguish inherited bioinformatics errors, errors amplified through autonomous action, and emergent failures arising from memory, retrieval, tool interaction, or agent coordination. We further propose a multidimensional decision-rights profile, consequence-sensitive validation gates, and a claim-to-evidence provenance architecture organized through the Traceable History of Research Evidence, Agent Actions, and Decisions in Bioinformatics (THREAD-Bio) framework. Illustrative cases show that technically successful execution may still support misleading inference. Trustworthy agentic bioinformatics therefore requires claims to remain reconstructible, challengeable, validated, and proportionate to the evidence.

title: A Survey on Hallucination in Large Language Models: Definitions, Detection, and Mitigation
authors: Seyed Mahmoud Sajjadi Mohammadabadi; Burak Cem Kara; Can Eyüpoğlu; Oktay Karakuş; Mahsa Borhani Peikani
abstract: Despite the strong capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) across a wide range of natural language processing tasks, their outputs can still be unreliable. Hallucination is widely used as an umbrella label for several related failures, but its operational meaning varies across tasks and studies. This work provides a comprehensive review of recent advances in understanding, detecting, and mitigating hallucinations in LLMs. We first distinguish hallucination from the separate evaluation dimensions of factuality, faithfulness, and internal consistency. We then introduce an author-proposed organisational taxonomy covering manifestations commonly discussed under hallucination, including factual contradictions, context conflicts, fabrication, self-contradiction, and emerging failures in reasoning traces and agentic trajectories. We review detection methods based on level of access to the model, ranging from white-box approaches to grey-box uncertainty estimation and black-box consistency and verification methods. We further organize these approaches according to the signals they exploit, including uncertainty, semantic consistency, external evidence, and internal representations, and discuss their strengths and limitations across different deployment settings. Finally, we survey mitigation strategies across the LLM lifecycle, including (1) data-centric approaches such as data curation and retrieval-augmented pre-training, (2) model-centric approaches such as supervised fine-tuning, preference optimization, abstention-aware reinforcement learning, and knowledge editing, and (3) inference-time approaches such as retrieval-augmented generation, self-verification, and decoding or activation-level interventions. Rather than viewing these strategies as isolated solutions, we argue that reliable hallucination mitigation requires complementary controls across multiple stages of the model lifecycle. Key challenges include scalable and provenance-aware data curation, the alignment–capability trade-off, reliable composition of mitigation techniques, and the need to evaluate and modify reasoning and agentic processes rather than only isolated factual associations.

title: Predictive Maintenance Using Tiny Machine Learning
authors: G. JayaLakshmi; Ch. JayaLakshmi; M.V. Ramesh
abstract: Predictive maintenance using tiny machine learning is a pioneering approach that harnesses the influence of machine learning to predict equipment failures, enabling convenient maintenance and minimizing complexity. This method involves training machine learning models on sensor data collected from devices and deploying these approaches on low-power devices such as microcontrollers. By adopting this approach, organizations can shift from traditional unconsidered maintenance, which often results in costly repairs, production losses, and safety risks, to an additional cost-effective and efficient solution. The benefits of this approach are important, including extended device lifespan, improved workplace safety, compact maintenance costs, and enhanced equipment consistency and performance. It also allows enterprises to transition to a proactive continuance strategy, minimizing unanticipated failures and their impact on production schedules. The working process of predictive maintenance using TinyML follows four main steps: data collection, model training, deployment, and real-time monitoring. Initially, sensor data is collected from the sensor devices, and machine learning models are trained to classify patterns or anomalies to may designate potential failures. These models are then organized on microcontrollers, which incessantly monitor the equipment in real time, predicting maintenance needs prior to failures occur. This approach has been effectively applied across diverse industries. For example, in automotive applications, accelerometers attached to every wheel can analyze vibrations to distinguish damage in the wheel or deferral system. Similarly, in engine maintenance, microphones are used to monitor engine sounds, identifying anomalies that could signal essential issues. Tools such as Edge Impulse Studio aid the development along with use of machine learning models on edge devices, while hardware like the Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense offers a compressed, energy-efficient platform for executing these models. As the TinyML ecosystem continues to grow, predictive maintenance is hovering to revolutionize equipment executive by reducing costs, enhancing safety, as well as improving operational efficiency, driving its approval across an ample range of industries.

title: A heuristic mixed real-time task allocation of virtual utilization in multi-core processor
authors: Hongbiao Liu; Mengfei Yang; Tingyu Wang; Chenghao Song; Shenghui Zhu; Xi Chen
abstract: Multi-core processor is widely used as the running platform for safety-critical real-time systems such as spacecraft, and various types of real-time tasks are dynamically added at runtime. In order to improve the utilization of multi-core processors and ensure the real-time performance of the system, it is necessary to adopt a reasonable real-time task allocation method, but the existing methods are only for single-core processors or the performance is too low to be applicable. Aiming at the task allocation problem when mixed real-time tasks are dynamically added, we propose a heuristic mixed real-time task allocation algorithm of virtual utilization VU-WF (Virtual Utilization Worst Fit) in multi-core processor. First, a 4-tuple task model is established to describe the fixed-point task and the sporadic task in a unified manner. Then, a VDS (Virtual Deferral Server) for serving execution requests of fixed-point task is constructed and a schedulability test of the mixed task set is derived. Finally, combined with the analysis of VDS's capacity, VU-WF is proposed, which selects cores in ascending order of virtual utilization for the schedulability test. Experiments show that the overall performance of VU-WF is better than available algorithms, not only has a good schedulable ratio and load balancing but also has the lowest runtime overhead. In a 4-core processor, compared with available algorithms of the same schedulability ratio, the load balancing is improved by 73.9%, and the runtime overhead is reduced by 38.3%. In addition, we also develop a visual multi-core mixed task scheduling simulator RT-MCSS (open source) to facilitate the design and verification of multi-core scheduling for users. As the high performance, VU-WF can be widely used in resource-constrained and safety-critical real-time systems, such as spacecraft, self-driving cars, industrial robots, etc.

title: Benefits of Decentralized Residential Batteries for System-Level Energy Management
authors: Shubham Kumar Yadav; Bhavna Jangid; Chandra Prakash; Ajay Verma; Arun Nayak; Rohini Haridas; Swasti Swadha; Shivani Garg; Parul Mathuria; Rohit Bhakar
abstract: Renewable energy sources have enabled the energy transition to carbon-free generation. This has led to high penetration of distributed energy resources like rooftop solar photovoltaic and electrical vehicles into the grid at the distribution side. It causes greater net load imbalances and requires continuous infrastructure reinforcement as well as increased grid flexibility. It is important to address these challenges to secure a reliable power system. Battery energy storage solutions deployed behind the meter have the potential to overcome these challenges. Earlier, batteries installed at the consumer end stored energy from the grid to fulfill individual needs during power outages. This chapter identifies the possible benefits for residential consumers, utilities, and system operators from the deployment of decentralized residential batteries. Residential consumers account for more than one third of the total energy consumption in most developed countries. The advent of rooftop solar panels in households has increased the need to store surplus generation. This revolution is converting consumers into prosumers, enabling them to inject energy into and withdraw energy from the grid. It provides monetary benefits to consumers, and they are less reliant on the grid for their needs. This chapter analyzes how the benefits directed from the consumers’ end can further benefit utilities and system operators, thus leading to system-level energy management. The deployment of batteries behind the meter flattens the peak demand curve, leading to transmission and distribution network capacity deferral. Thus, it is concluded that it benefits all the major stakeholder groups, including consumers, utilities, and system operators. The benefits are directed from the residential consumers’ side, which necessitates their involvement with decentralized residential batteries to provide system-level benefits.

title: Malaria Screening among Blood Donors in Non Endemic Malarial Regions: Role of Donor History Questionnaires and Rapid Malaria Diagnostic Test
authors: Doaa Abdel-Badie Salem; Azza Baiomy
venue: American journal of infectious diseases and microbiology
abstract: Malaria is one of the most important parasitic diseases responsible for some cases of transfusion transmitted disease in the world. Malaria screening test of blood donor may increase the safety of blood donations. In response to the information about a Plasmodium vivax malaria outbreak in the Aswan Governorate in Egypt 2014 and in the absence of a licensed test for donor screening, our aim was to assess the value of malaria donor history questionnaires and rapid malaria diagnostic test in malaria screening among blood donors to increase the safety of blood donation. Out of two hundred and fifty two healthy blood donors attend the Mansoura University blood bank unit for blood donation, between July to August, 2015, twelve donors were deferred, one from a malaria endemic area and one with a history of travel to a malaria endemic area, the rest was deferred for other reasons. All donors were checked for weight, pulse rate, blood pressure, temperature, hemoglobin levels and malaria donor history questionnaires. Screening for malaria was done by Microscopic Examination of Thick Blood Films stained with diluted Giemsa stain and by using the individual rapid malaria test OptiMAL-IT (BIO-RAD, France) for all blood donor samples. No positive samples of blood donor volunteers were detected neither by microscopic examination, nor by rapid malaria test OptiMAL-IT. Our study support that, in a non endemic malaria region, donor deferral by malaria donor history questionnaires and screening of blood donors for malaria by using thick blood films or by rapid malaria test OptiMAL-IT is enough for safe blood donation, but clear guidelines are mandatory.

title: Systemic Challenges in EHR Alert Design: A Thematic Analysis of Physician Discourse on X (Formerly Twitter)
authors: Guy Vishnevsky; Jacob N. Ablin
abstract: Abstract: BACKGROUND: Electronic health record (EHR) clinical decision support (CDS) systems generate excessive, non-contextual alerts, causing clinician desensitization with override rates exceeding 90%. This alert fatigue disrupts workflows, contributes to burnout, and creates patient safety risks. Traditional survey-based methods fail to capture real-time end-user feedback at scale. Abstract: OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to evaluate real-world CDS usability signals by analyzing physician discourse on X (formerly Twitter) and identify physician-perceived sociotechnical pain points to inform future, hypothesis-driven EHR optimization. Abstract: METHODS: X was systematically searched in August 2025 using Grok 4 (2025-08 build) via an internal API (Application Programming Interface). The AI temperature was set to 0.7 for search generation to ensure a broad retrieval of relevant discourse, utilizing keywords including "EHR alert fatigue," "clinical decision support usability," "EMR burnout," "override EHR," and "alert fatigue doctors," yielding 117 posts from 106 self-identified physicians after manual curation (spanning from 2016 to 2025). Only the first post per author was included in the final analysis of 106 posts. We applied Braun and Clarke's reflexive thematic analysis, with artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted coding verification. Sentiment classification was conducted as a secondary assessment. Abstract: RESULTS: Six CDS usability failure domains were identified: Alert Overwhelm (38.7%, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 30.0-48.2%), Burnout and Fatigue (43.4%, 95% CI: 34.4-52.9%), Patient Safety Threats (9.4%, 95% CI: 5.2-16.5%), Regulatory and Billing Pressures (17.0%, 95% CI: 11.0-25.3%), Mitigation Strategies, including AI prioritization (36.8%, 95% CI: 28.2-46.3%), and Lack of Customization (7.5%, 95% CI: 3.9-14.2%). Sentiment was 76.4% (95% CI: 67.5-83.5%) negative. Co-occurrence analysis showed 50.0% of safety posts co-occurred with alert overwhelm, and 19.6% of burnout posts co-occurred with regulatory and billing pressures. Abstract: CONCLUSION: Physician discourse on X provides valuable, exploratory usability signals. The prevalence of alert overwhelm and burnout themes highlights recurring pain points in current EHR architectures, generating hypotheses for future user-centered CDS redesign such as tiered alerting, role-based routing, and alert deferral mechanisms.

title: CRuSE-Heart: explainable AI for risk-controlled selective ensembles in heart-attack screening
authors: Muhammad Asad; Md Tanvir Rahman Khan; Md. Serajul Kabir Chowdhury Rubel; Sumayya Jahan; Md Tohfatul Islam; Md Rana Hossain; Ponchanon Datta Rone
abstract: Cardiovascular diseases remain the leading cause of global mortality, highlighting the need for reliable and scalable tools for early heart-attack risk screening. However, many existing machine learning models for cardiovascular risk prediction are limited by severe class imbalance, lack of uncertainty awareness, and poor interpretability, which restrict their reliability in real-world clinical screening. To address these challenges, this paper proposes CRuSE-Heart, an explainable risk-controlled selective ensemble framework for heart-attack screening using large-scale population health data. The proposed method combines LightGBM and XGBoost through a weighted ensemble. Further, it incorporates a conformal prediction-based selective mechanism that abstains from low-confidence predictions to control error on accepted cases. In addition, SHAP and LIME are integrated to provide global and local explanations, thereby improving model transparency and clinical interpretability. Experiments conducted on the BRFSS Personal Key Indicators of Heart Disease dataset, comprising approximately 319,795 records, show that the proposed selective model achieves 97.28% accuracy, 95.01% sensitivity, and 97.41% specificity, outperforming several baseline methods. The selective prediction setting also provides a practical coverage–risk trade-off, improving reliability in high-stakes screening scenarios. These results demonstrate that CRuSE-Heart offers an effective, interpretable, and safety-aware framework for population-scale heart-attack risk assessment.

title: Telemedicine pre-screening for blood donor
authors: Mariana Lorenzi Savioli; Araci Massami Sakashita; ANF Cipolletta; Rosane Camargo Tokimatsu de C. Brandão; José Mauro Kutner
abstract: INTRODUCTION: The COVID-19 pandemic had an important impact on blood bank services. The onset of the pandemic led to a decrease in the number of blood donors. A remote interview would avoid deferred donors from having to travel to the blood bank. We evaluate the feasibility of using telemedicine as an alternative to a face-to-face interview as a first blood donor screening. METHODS: Our retrospective study included 404 whole blood and platelets donors, who underwent the clinical interview remotely via telemedicine. The deferred donor would not need to go to the blood bank and eligible candidates were required to donate within 7 days. On the day of donation, a mini-interview was held to ensure donor and blood safety. RESULTS: The appointments were made from June 2020 to June 2022, including 263 candidates for whole blood (WB) and 141 for platelets (PLTs). At the end of the telemedicine interview, 285 (70.6 %) candidates were considered eligible. Telemedicine was not performed for 60 (14.8 %) candidates due to technical problems (with audio or video) or absences. The deferral rate among candidates who underwent telemedicine pre-screening was 14.6 % and, among eligible donors after telemedicine, only 7 (2.9 %) were unable to donate blood. CONCLUSION: Telemedicine is a viable alternative and a welcome convenience for potential donors to avoid unnecessary travel.

title: Nebulous Intentioning – Acute hospital nurses’ struggle to deliver core nursing care
authors: Aoife Lane; Margaret G. Landers; Tom Andrews
abstract: AIM: To explore the influences on nursing practice in acute hospital care. DESIGN: A Classic Grounded Theory study. METHODS: Data collection (2013-2015) was through interviews and non-participant observations. Analysis was undertaken using constant comparative data analysis and theoretical sampling. Memo writing was used as an aid to understanding and conceptualizing data during analysis. Theoretical coding served to integrate emerging concepts. RESULTS: This theory explains core nursing as a nebulous intention, an idea which acute care nurses retain throughout each shift, that they will nurse their patients fully when they have the opportunity. It reveals this as the resolution of their main problem which is the constant deferral of core nursing care. This study explains its two sub-core categories, accommodating and integrity eroding. CONCLUSION: The theory highlights nurses' attitudes towards their role, demonstrated by deferring it to accommodate the work of others, but offers a new perspective on the significant contribution nurses make to the safe and cohesive transition of patients through the acute healthcare system. IMPACT: The theory adds a new understanding of the unique contribution nurses make to patient health and safety in acute care environments. It also provides insight into nurses' attitudes towards their own professional work. It explains the consequences of attitudes which undermine core nursing when it competes for priority with accommodating. Accommodating indicates a greater workload for nurses than has been previously understood in explaining the activities, additional to core nursing care, which nurses undertake to contribute safety and cohesion to the patient's acute care journey. These new insights suggest a role for managers in recognizing accommodating in decisions about staffing and resources and for educators in improving the profession's regard for its theoretical underpinnings and for its self-image.

title: Negative Control
authors: Amir Habibdoust; Anita Keshmirian; Xing Song; Moritz Willig
abstract: This research project examines whether large language models (LLMs) can apply causal reasoning when proposing negative control outcomes and negative control exposures for observational studies, or whether they primarily retrieve familiar examples encountered in biomedical literature. Negative controls are used in epidemiology and causal inference to detect residual confounding and other sources of bias. A valid negative control should have no causal relationship with the relevant exposure or outcome while sharing important sources of unmeasured confounding. The study will evaluate multiple LLMs across several prompting strategies, including zero-shot prompting, a role-based epidemiologist prompt, and a falsification-focused prompt with self-refutation. Models will be tested using four types of study contexts: real observational-study contexts, semi-fictional contexts in which a key field is replaced, fully fictional contexts without sufficient causal information, and flipped contexts in which the exposure and outcome are reversed. These conditions are designed to assess whether model suggestions appropriately change when the information required to identify a valid negative control is altered or removed. Model-generated candidates will be evaluated using a structured rubric. In contexts where validity can be assessed, expert reviewers will classify candidates as plausible, uncertain, or invalid based on the no-effect and shared-confounding requirements. In fictional contexts, outputs will be categorized according to whether the model abstains, proposes a recognizable real-world control, or invents a context-specific candidate. The study will also assess repetition across contexts, novelty, productive yield, abstention, and consistency across repeated generations. A preregistered LLM judge will independently evaluate candidate validity, allowing comparison between automated evaluation and expert human ratings. Statistical analyses will account for repeated observations across models, prompts, study contexts, candidates, and reviewers. The expected outcome is a systematic characterization of when LLMs produce context-sensitive negative controls, when they rely on familiar biomedical examples, and whether they are more reliable at evaluating negative controls than generating them. The project is intended to inform the responsible use of LLMs in epidemiologic study design, causal-inference workflows, and AI-assisted observational research. The study evaluates observable model outputs rather than making claims about models’ internal reasoning processes.

title: S1727 Mirikizumab Demonstrates Rapid and Sustained Improvements in Bowel Urgency Measures and Clinical Measures in Moderately-to-Severely Active Ulcerative Colitis: 28-Week Results from the Phase 3b LUCENT-URGE Trial
authors: Silvio Danese; Axel Dignass; David Laharie; Jimmy K. Limdi; Radoslaw Kempinski; James D. Lewis; Ziad Younes; Erica R. Cohen; Karla Alaka; William J. Eastman; Tian Tian; Isabel Redondo; David T. Rubin; Marla C. Dubinsky
abstract: Introduction: LUCENT-URGE is a Phase 3b, open-label, single-arm 28-week (W) study in adults with moderately-to-severely active ulcerative colitis (UC) and bowel urgency (BU, Urgency Numeric Rating Scale [UNRS] ≥3) at baseline treated with mirikizumab (MIRI). Here, we report W28 results from LUCENT-URGE. Methods: Patients (pts) received intravenous MIRI 300 mg at W0, 4 and 8, followed by 200 mg subcutaneous at W12, 16, 20, and 24. Primary objective: UNRS improvement at W12. Secondary objectives: UNRS improvement at W28, Stool Deferral Time (SDT) and Bowel Urgency Frequency (BUF) improvement at W12 and W28, proportion of participants achieving clinical remission and an UNRS score of ≤1 (BU remission) at W12 and W28, and those achieving clinical response and an improvement in UNRS score ≥3 (clinically meaningful improvement [CMI] of UNRS) at W12 and W28. UNRS and BUF were measured using a daily diary where pts recorded the number of times they experienced BU in the past 24 hours, averaged over a 7-day period. The shortest weekly SDT was used. Results: 172 pts were enrolled from 8 countries. Baseline modified Mayo score (MMS; mean ± standard deviation [SD]) was 6.8 ± 1.3, and 64.0% pts had severe disease activity (MMS 7-9). Baseline mean duration of UC was 8.0 years, mean UNRS score was 6.9 and mean BUF was 6.9 times/day. Mean UNRS and BUF improved from baseline (3.6) to W28 (3.8). The proportion of pts with SDT defined as “≥15 minutes or no urgency” was 4.1% at baseline and improved to 29.7% at W28. W12: 36 (20.9%) pts achieved clinical remission, 54 (31.4%) achieved endoscopic remission, and 92 (53.5%) achieved CMI of UNRS. W28: 62 (36.1%) pts achieved clinical remission, 76 (44.2%) achieved endoscopic remission, and 100 (58.1%) achieved CMI of UNRS. 76 (44.2%) pts achieved both clinical response and CMI of UNRS at W12, and 86 (50.0%) pts at W28. W12 and W28: 8 patients (4.7%) and 28 patients (16.3%) achieved both clinical remission and BU remission, respectively. The safety profile of MIRI in LUCENT-URGE was consistent with previous studies, with no death reported and similar frequency of treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs). Most common TEAEs: ulcerative colitis exacerbation (5.2%) and upper respiratory tract infection (5.2%). Conclusion: MIRI showed an early and sustained improvement on BU severity, frequency and stool deferral time through W28 in LUCENT-URGE. MIRI consistently improved clinical outcomes in pts with moderately-to-severely active UC.

title: Multiple treatment modalities for brain metastasis in patients with EGFR-mutant non-small-cell lung cancer
authors: Haiyang Wang; Xiaoqing Yu; Yun Fan; Youhua Jiang
abstract: Background: There are many controversies concerning the best management of epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutant non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients with brain metastases (BMs). The use of upfront EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) and the withholding of local therapies or upfront radiation therapies (RTs) remain controversial. Available treatment options include local therapies such as whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT), stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) and surgery, EGFR-TKIs, and chemotherapy. However, the optimal management of combination therapies is still under consideration. Patients and methods: A total of 45 EGFR-mutated NSCLC patients with BMs were included. All patients successively received EGFR-TKIs, RT (WBRT or SRS), and chemotherapy between 2010 and 2015 at Zhejiang Cancer Hospital. Patient follow-up was conducted by telephone until February 2017. The treatment response was evaluated, and survival data were collected and analyzed by Kaplan–Meier analysis and the Cox regression method. Results: The median overall survival (OS) was 28 months. Patients with the exon 19 deletion showed the strongest trend toward a longer median OS compared to patients with the exon 21 L858R mutation (not reached vs 26.5 months, P =0.0969). There was no difference in OS between the upfront RT group and the deferral group (26.5 vs 28 months, P =0.57), and similar results were found between the first-line chemotherapy group and the EGFR-TKI group (28 vs 23.2 months, P =0.499). In multivariate analysis, the prognosis correlated with EGFR mutation type ( P =0.017). Conclusion: EGFR-mutant NSCLC patients with BM benefited from the combination and sequential therapies of EGFR-TKIs, chemotherapy, and RTs. Patients with the EGFR exon 19 deletion may have a better OS. However, the optimal timing of RT interval remains to be explored. Keywords: epidermal growth factor receptor, tyrosine kinase inhibitors, brain metastases, non-small-cell lung cancer, pemetrexed, whole-brain radiation therapy

title: A Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis for Rigless Job Scope Prioritization: Framework for Strategic Rigless Well Candidate Selection
authors: Harry Kurniawan; Pri Hermawan
abstract: Rigless well intervention is essential for restoring production and maintaining well integrity in upstream oil and gas operations. However, companies often face dynamic environments where multiple intervention candidates arise simultaneously, while execution capacity is limited by budget, resources, or financial constraints. Without a structured prioritization framework, Rigless execution decisions tend to be inconsistent and heavily reliant on judgment, especially under financial pressure or overly aggressive strategies. This research aims to develop a systematic decision‑support framework for prioritizing Rigless well intervention programs by applying the Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP). The framework integrates multiple technical, operational, economic, and risk‑related criteria to determine the relative priority of Rigless program objectives. Expert judgments are collected and synthesized to establish a clear priority hierarchy among these alternatives including Lost Production Opportunity (LPO) Reduction, Integrity Restoration, Well Development and Stimulation. The results indicate that LPO Reduction emerges as the highest priority due to its direct and immediate impact on production recovery, followed by Integrity Restoration as a critical prerequisite for safe and sustainable operations. Based on these results, a Rigless Prioritization Guideline is also proposed as the primary business solution which translating analytical rankings into practical execution and deferral rules applicable under concurrent candidate conditions and financial or operational constraints. The main contribution of this study is translating analytical prioritization into a practical business decision framework that supports consistent, transparent, and defensible Rigless execution. This framework enables companies to adapt their execution strategy under aggressive targets or financial constraints without adding operational complexity.

title: Trust-Aware Multi-Axis Reliability Auditing for NLP Classifiers: A Theoretical and Empirical Framework
authors: Noor Islam S. Mohammad
abstract: Accuracy remains the dominant criterion for selecting NLP classifiers, yet it fails to characterize the operational reliability required for deployment under class imbalance, distribution shift, and demographic heterogeneity.We introduce TNMM++ (Trustworthy NLP Multi-axis Monitoring, extended), a theoretically grounded reliability audit that evaluates classifiers along seven complementary axes, utility, calibration, robustness, safety, fairness, selective prediction, and uncertainty quantification, and formalises model selection as constrained multi-objective optimization.Beyond metric aggregation, TNMM++ contributes six algorithmic results: a reliability tensor, a Pareto convex-hull theorem, varianceadaptive weighting, a boundary-predictor criterion with exclusion rule for majority-class collapse, a Bayesian risk decomposition, and the TAMS algorithm with optimality bound.Evaluating eight lightweight Transformer encoders (MiniLM, ELECTRA, mBERT, DistilBERT, MobileBERT, ALBERT, RoBERTa, XLM-R) and excluding models that failed to learn the task, we find that properly trained mid-tier models exhibit balanced utility and calibration superior to collapsed high-accuracy counterparts.TrustScore identifies mBERT (0.6685), ELEC-TRA (0.6630), and DistilBERT (0.6627) as deployment-reliable.Sensitivity analysis under 1,000 Dirichlet weight perturbations confirms ranking stability in 92.4% of configurations, and multi-seed evaluation (5 seeds) demonstrates conclusions are not seed artifacts.Our findings establish that single-metric selection is statistically unreliable and motivate multi-axis reliability auditing as the default protocol for trustworthy NLP deployment.

title: Pedagogical conditions for the development of risk management in educational design among university students
authors: Причинин Алексей Евгеньевич; Irina G. Dolinina
venue: Uchenye zapiski universiteta imeni P F Lesgafta
abstract: The purpose of the study is to identify the pedagogical conditions for the development of risk management in educational design among university students who are future educators. Research methods and organization. Methods of observation, testing, surveying, expert evaluation, assessment of project work, and evaluation of case study solutions were employed. The developed pedagogical conditions were tested in the educational process for higher education programs in "Pedagogical Education" (bachelor's and master's degrees). The dynamics of changes in risk management criteria were recorded among undergraduate and graduate students studying pedagogical fields. Research results and conclusions. It has been revealed that the reliable development of risk management in the educational design of university students is possible under the implementation of a number of pedagogical conditions: the educational process is built on the basis of a developed risk management system, which includes four components – target, conceptual-content, structural-functional, and procedural-resultant; didactic units reflecting elements of the risk management system are integrated into all educational blocks of the educational programs and cover the entire period of study; each didactic unit is structured into three main parts – cognitive, practical, and control; consideration of factors related to the deferral of risks in educational projects in the educational process. The construction of the educational process, taking into account these pedagogical conditions, has led to statistically significant changes in the development of risk management among university students. The results of the experimental study suggest that the identified pedagogical conditions and their implementation contribute to the development of risk management in educational design among students.

title: Role of Well Integrity in Meeting Production Mandates: Prevention of Well Barrier Failures
authors: Andrey Yugay; Faiz Issa; Aidar Zhukin; M. A. Al Mehyas; F. G. Tawfik
venue: SPE Annual Technical Conference and Exhibition
abstract: The global oil and gas industry is increasingly challenged to sustain and maximize production under heightened economic, environmental, and regulatory pressures. Within this context, well integrity emerges not only as a safety-critical discipline but also as a central enabler for production efficiency, asset longevity, and operational continuity. This paper explores the role of well integrity in achieving production mandates, emphasizing the significance of preventing integrity failures through proactive methodologies such as Root Cause Analysis (RCA). Well integrity, defined by ISO 16530-1 as "the application of technical, operational, and organizational solutions to reduce the risk of uncontrolled release of formation fluids," directly affects an operator's ability to maintain stable production. An integrity-compromised well can lead to shut-ins, production losses, environmental hazards, and expensive remediation activities. Main well integrity concept assumes continuous maintaining of two barriers between the pressure source and the environment. Those barriers might degrade with time due to insufficient material resistance to the environment, resulting in issues such as sustained casing pressure (SCP), casing corrosion, poor cement bonds, and equipment malfunction. Those well barrier failures have historically contributed to non-productive time (NPT) and deferred production. Based on the case studies reviewed, wells with barrier failures contributed to significant downtime and production deferral. As a result, improving well integrity processes becomes a strategic production assurance imperative.

title: Detecting Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models without Generating a Single Token
authors: Association for Computational Linguistics 2026; Sripadha Vallabha E G; Sai Akhil Kogilathota; Luzhe Sun; Jiawei Zhou
abstract: Hallucinations remain a persistent challenge for vision–language models (VLMs), which of ten describe nonexistent objects or fabricate facts. Existing detection methods typically operate after text generation, making intervention both costly and untimely. We investigate whether hallucination risk can instead be predicted before any token is generated by probing a model’s internal representations in a single forward pass. Across a diverse set of vision–language tasks and eight modern VLMs, including Llama-3.2-Vision, Gemma-3, Phi-4VL, and Qwen2.5-VL, we examine three families of internal representations: (i) visual-only features without multimodal fusion, (ii) vision token representations within the text decoder, and (iii) query-token representations that integrate visual and textual information before generation. Probes trained on these representations achieve strong hallucination-detection performance without decoding, reaching up to 0.93 AUROC on Gemma-3-12B, Phi-4-VL 5.6B, and Molmo 7B. Late query-token states are the most predictive for most models, while visual or mid-layer features dominate in a few architectures (e.g., ∼0.79 AUROC for Qwen2.5-VL 7B using visual-only features). These results demonstrate that (1) hallucination risk is detectable pre-generation, (2) the most informative layer and modality vary across architectures, and (3) lightweight probes has the potential to enable early abstention, selective routing, and adaptive decoding to improve both safety and efficiency.

title: IntelliLayer: A Deep Learning Architecture for Dynamic Decision Intelligence
authors: Gundeti Mounika; Vimula Shwetha; Dr K Sridhar
abstract: Organizations increasingly use data-driven systems to support operational decision-making in dynamic environments. However, many existing deep learning models focus primarily on predicting outcomes rather than recommending reliable actions. These models often provide limited information about prediction confidence, may experience performance degradation when data patterns change, and offer insufficient explanations for their decisions. Previous studies have addressed these challenges independently through improved prediction models, uncertainty estimation, calibration techniques, data drift detection, and explainable AI methods. To address these limitations, this paper introduces IntelliLayer, a five-layer deep learning architecture that combines these capabilities within a unified decision-making framework. The proposed architecture integrates static data and sequential events using Transformer encoders and a learnable gated fusion mechanism. It estimates calibrated outcome distributions through a deep ensemble and selects actions based on expected utility, while uncertain cases are referred to human reviewers. To handle changing data patterns, the framework employs adaptive windowing for drift detection and updates the model using replay techniques and elastic weight consolidation. Additionally, integrated gradients are used to explain individual predictions, and an audit record is maintained for every decision to support transparency and accountability. The paper describes the architecture of each layer, outlines the online decision-making algorithm, and presents a reference implementation stack. It also defines a reproducible evaluation framework covering predictive performance, calibration, decision-making costs, selective prediction coverage, recovery from data drift, and processing latency. Since experimental results have not yet been obtained, the proposed evaluation protocol and results template provide a structured basis for future validation of the IntelliLayer architecture.

title: DIGITAL IDENTITY AND INTERGENERATIONAL MAINTENANCE OF RECONFIGURABLE HABITATS AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page English Research Working Edition in the STARLI YULI Nano Supercar Trilogy (Research Institute XXXVI, Flagship 58 of 90). Its central question is how an autonomous reconfigurable habitat can retain a truthful, independently recoverable history when structural parts, material batches, control firmware, sensors and maintenance responsibility change across generations. The three-way coupling is Digital Identity x Structural Genealogy x Intergenerational Maintenance. The study is strictly prospective, scaled, unoccupied and non-clinical; it does not assert that an actual residence has been certified safe. The falsifiable proposal is that, with matched materials, sensing, operator time, computation and energy, a preregistered physical-digital lineage system improves genuine identity reconstruction without worsening the depth or effectiveness of safe retreat. Strong comparators include conventionally documented building maintenance, controlled strip-down requalification and a competent digital-twin inventory. Adversarial trials introduce counterfeit asset labels, unlogged repairs, swapped connectors, stale calibration, clock partitions, false histories, obsolete data schemas, physically ineffective stop commands and material fatigue. Missing genealogy or weak physical evidence requires abstention, quarantine or retirement, rather than a cosmetic digital pass. Thirty mechanism-distinct mathematical plates address identity relations, conditional entropy, graph-edge confirmation, partial event order, tamper-evident logs, mass disposition, fatigue damage, crack growth, weak stiffness modes, environmental exposure, correlated uncertainty, selective risk and coverage, physical-stop latency, compatible safety actions, replay proportions and noncompensatory acceptance logic. Each plate states the construction, units or type premises, a concrete concealed falsifier and related chapters; no plate is presented as a newly discovered natural law. Eighty-two chapter objects contain 410 separately paginated experimental investigations on material ancestry, repair and replacement custody, calibration transfer, cross-version digital twins, longitudinal load histories, authorization, retirement, privacy and founder-independent succession. Two hundred Research Gates ask distinct blind-fault, resource-matched comparator or intergenerational transfer questions, while 33 distinguishable Phoenix Answer Embryos propose future instruments and evidence interfaces with specific ways to fail. The book reports research designs, not achieved experimental outcomes; failed, refused and incomplete cases remain part of the evidence population. The research scope remains unoccupied bench coupons, guarded modular prototypes, modelled asset histories and hardware-in-the-loop exercises. Neither an authenticated digital record nor a high identity score proves structural capacity, fire safety, ventilation, water quality, rights or real-world occupancy approval. Methodological DOI ancestry includes NIST Digital Identity Guidelines (10.6028/NIST.SP.800-63-4), secure software development (10.6028/NIST.SP.800-218), security controls (10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), self-deploying structures (10.1038/s44172-026-00725-1), urban-transit predictive maintenance (10.1038/s41598-026-60575-x), and morphing robots (10.1038/s41578-024-00711-z). The author-provided Flagship 13 identifiers (10.5281/zenodo.23318840; 10.5281/zenodo.23318839) are retained as metadata-unconfirmed research-lineage references, not verified supporting results. title: Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence in Mental Health Nursing: Clinical Augmentation, Therapeutic Relationships, and Responsible Governance
authors: Kaianny Cardoso Pereira
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is entering mental health nursing through prediction, natural language processing, digital phenotyping, conversational agents, and generative documentation. This integrative narrative review examines how these functions can support care while preserving therapeutic relationships, recovery, professional accountability, and patient rights. A targeted literature and regulatory update was completed on October 26, 2026; the revised bibliography comprises 35 sources, including six contemporary nursing or nursing-education reviews. Sources were synthesized thematically, without pooled effects or a claim of exhaustive systematic retrieval. Recent reviews establish substantial conceptual overlap and identify persistent limitations in external validity, person-centred outcomes, sustained engagement, and implementation evidence. Accordingly, this article contributes an author-developed nurse-led implementation and assurance framework that connects relational nursing theory, sociotechnical safety, evidence maturity, intended-use risk, and Brazilian governance. Operational requirements include calibration, prevalence-sensitive predictive values, prospective silent validation, measurable escalation, competent human review, abstention, version control, incident grading, and controlled revalidation. Documentation benefits must be assessed through total verification workload and protected therapeutic time. The risk matrix is a conceptual proposal, not a validated clinical instrument or binding legal classification. The framework has not been prospectively evaluated. AI adoption is defensible only when local evidence, service capacity, equity, privacy, and patient choice support the intended use; technical performance alone cannot establish clinical benefit.

title: A Formal Study of InternalReliability Signals inRetrieval-Augmented Generation : A Formal Study of InternalReliability Signals inRetrieval-Augmented Generation
authors: Ravindra Kumar
venue: KTH Publication Database DiVA (KTH Royal Institute of Technology)
abstract: Deployed Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems rarelyprovide a validated per-query indication of answer reliability. Thisthesis investigates whether observable RAG pipeline signals canrank generated answers by estimated reliability without requiringa gold reference answer at inference time. HEMMIR (HierarchicalExplainable Multimodal Information Retrieval) was developed asthe experimental RAG system for text, table, and figure content. Four signals are evaluated: evidence quality (S1), claim-level faithfulness (S2), answer completeness (S3), and evidence support ratio (S4). They are combined into a composite ranking reliability scoreC, with corpus-specific weights estimated offline from correctnesslabelled data without fine-tuning the retriever, generator, or judgemodel.The framework was evaluated on the Scania industrial corpus (103questions), SPIQA TestC (218 questions), and Vectara OpenRAG (3,045 queries) using AUROC, permutation testing, and out-ofsample validation. The composite achieved AUROC values of0.705 on Scania, 0.798 on SPIQA, and 0.828 on Vectara (p < 0.001for all), with validated AUROCs of 0.667, 0.727, and 0.831, respectively. Across datasets, requirement-level completeness andevidence coverage were more stable discriminators than claim-levelfaithfulness: S3 was significant on all three corpora, whereas S2was significant only on Scania and contributed more consistentlythrough the HallucinationCap safety mechanism. A 16-case Scaniaexpert evaluation provided preliminary practical support: all 14correct or partially correct answers had C ≥ 0.67, while both unreliable or abstained cases had C < 0.45. These findings support usingC for ranking, triage, and abstention rather than as a calibratedprobability of correctness

title: Hemodynamic profile of pulmonary arterial hypertension in a Tunisian center.
authors: Amira Jamoussi; Nacef Ben Mrad; Emna Rachdi; Fatma Jarraya; Sarra Zairi; Kaïs Ben Romdhane; Mohamed Besbes; Samia Ayed; Jalila Ben Khelil
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) management can only be conceived in a specialized center. We aimed to report the experience of a Tunisian ICU about PH invasive hemodynamic exploration and to describe consequent therapeutic decisions. METHODS: Retrospective descriptive study including all patients admitted to the medical ICU of Abderrahmen Mami Hospital for right heart catheterization (RHC), between 2005 and 2019 as part of the investigation of PH. Patients' characteristics, procedure safety and arising therapeutic decisions were then reported. RESULTS: Forty patients were admitted for hemodynamic evaluation. RHC confirmed PH in 31 patients and exploration was then completed with NO reactivity test. Mean age was 41.3±15 years, gender ratio M/F was 1.06. PH was classified into: group 1 (n=13), group 2 (n=14), group 4 (n=2) and group 5 (n=2). NO vasoreactivity test was positive in 50% of post-capillary PH and in 28% of pre-capillary PH. The therapeutic decision following the reversibility test was: prescription of calcium channel blockers (n=5), a specific pulmonary vasodilator (n=10), operability (n=6), heart-lung transplant (n=3) and therapeutic abstention (n=7). Two minor complications were reported. CONCLUSION: The medical ICU in Abderrahmen Mami Hospital represents an experienced team in hemodynamic investigations despite low annual RHC number. NO reactivity test is an indispensable tool that enables important decisions during PH management.

title: Physical Interaction Through Non-Intervention: A Process-Regulation Framework for When Embodied AI Should Act, Defer, or Deliberately Remain Physically Inactive
authors: Alen Širola
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Embodied artificial intelligence is commonly evaluated by what it can perceive, plan, and do. Human-robot interaction research, however, increasingly shows that capability is not sufficient: an agent must also determine when action would interrupt a human, when assistance can be offered without disrupting an ongoing plan, when an instruction should be refused or clarified, and how interaction should adapt to the user and the history of the relationship. These problems are usually studied under separate labels such as interruptibility, non-intrusive assistance, abstention, expertise alignment, shared autonomy, mutual adaptation, and relational memory. This conceptual paper proposes a process-regulation view that treats these not as identical problems, but as neighboring manifestations of a common pre-action question: what transition should the human-AI system permit now? The proposed decision space contains three distinct outcomes: physical action, deliberate physical non-intervention, and defer/clarify. The framework is derived from longitudinal human-LLM work with AWM (AI Working Method) and conditionally transferred to embodied AI. Its central proposal is that the relative weight of human, agent, environmental, and historical signals should vary locally with the current goal, domain-relevant competence, preserved trace, safety constraints, and feedback from actual consequences (R_d). The paper connects this proposal to existing work and derives testable propositions and evaluation measures for future HRI experiments.

title: Utility of the Hypercoagulable Panel in Decision Making for Cryptogenic Stroke and Patent Foramen Ovale (P11-14.015)
authors: Riana L. Schleicher; Jordan Houser; Bichun Ouyang; Zain Ashary; Rima M. Dafer
abstract: Objective: To assess the utility of thrombophilia screening in determining candidacy for patent foramen ovale (PFO) closure for cryptogenic stroke patients <60 years old. Background: The predictive value of obtaining a hypercoagulable panel has been drawn into question, given its high cost and relatively low yield in altering clinical management. We report hypercoagulable panel findings and PFO closures in cryptogenic stroke patients < 60 with PFO to further assess the utility of thrombophilia screening in these patients. Design/Methods: This was a single-center retrospective chart review of 52 patients under the age of 60 with cryptogenic stroke found to have a PFO on transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE). Clinical and demographic data were collected, including normalcy of the hypercoagulable panel and PFO closure status. Association between an abnormal hypercoagulable panel and PFO closure was assessed using a two-tailed t-test at α < 0.05. Results: A total of 45 patients underwent analysis. Hypercoagulable panel findings were abnormal in 25 patients (55.5%). These included abnormal levels of atherosclerotic markers which, given their transient nature, were deemed insignificant and were excluded from analysis (n=20). A remaining 5 patients had thrombophilic abnormalities. A total of 21 patients (46.7%) underwent PFO closure, 20 (95%) of whom had normal hypercoagulable panels. There was no significant difference in decision for PFO closure between patients with normal vs. abnormal panels (p=0.58). No evidence was found in documentation of PFO closure deferral due to abnormal hypercoagulable panel. Conclusions: In young patients with cryptogenic stroke due to PFO, hypercoagulable panel findings were largely normal. Abnormalities noted were transient and did not alter the decision for PFO closure. This suggests that obtaining a hypercoagulable panel in this population may be low-yield and is a possible target for cost reduction. title: Cognitive Jurisdiction: Formal Limits on Artificial Intelligence Participation in Human Decision Domains
authors: Teodor Minchev
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract Recent advances in artificial intelligence have intensified concerns not only about accuracy, alignment, or safety, but about the scope of legitimate participation of artificial systems in human decision-making. While the theory of Governed Cognition establishes the right to reason as a conditional and enforceable constraint on artificial intelligence, it leaves open a critical structural question: where is an artificial system permitted to participate at all? This paper introduces Cognitive Jurisdiction, a formal framework that defines territorially bounded domains of legitimate artificial intelligence participation. Cognitive jurisdiction separates domains of permitted reasoning, shared assistance, and absolute prohibition, independent of system capability, accuracy, user consent, or safeguards. The framework formalizes jurisdictional boundaries, jurisdictional overreach, and mandatory abstention as first-class governance constructs. We argue that many contemporary AI risks—including authority simulation, responsibility displacement, and existential fear narratives—arise not from insufficient alignment or control, but from ungoverned jurisdictional participation. By denying artificial systems the right to enter human-exclusive decision domains, Cognitive Jurisdiction renders entire classes of feared AI behaviors structurally impossible rather than merely undesirable. This work extends Governed Cognition by providing a jurisdictional layer that governs where cognition may occur, complementing prior constraints on whether and how reasoning may proceed. The result is a complete, auditable model of authority-aware artificial intelligence suitable for high-consequence and regulated environments.

title: LLM-Modulo Planning Agents with External Plan Verification and Iterative Self-Repair
authors: Tyler Ward; Yan Zhou; Stephanie Gray
venue: Journal of Information Systems and Business Technology
abstract: Large language models can translate natural-language goals into action sequences, but an action sequence is not a plan unless every precondition holds and the final state satisfies the goal. This study evaluates a modulo-style planning agent that assigns proposal generation to an LLM and delegates correctness to an external symbolic verifier. The evaluation used the PlanBench repository artifacts for Blocksworld: every stored GPT-4 candidate in four domain-size conditions and five prompt forms (6,000 direct plans), together with all 50 verifier-feedback trajectories containing 286 sequential candidates. Each candidate was parsed into PDDL actions and independently checked with VAL against the corresponding domain and problem file. Across the direct corpus, 934 of 6,000 candidates were valid (15.57%). Validity reached 27.53% in standard Blocksworld but only 3.60% after semantic obfuscation. State-tracking prompts were strongest in both conditions, while PDDL-form prompts did not compensate for weak state-transition reasoning. On the matched 50-instance repair set, direct execution completed 4 tasks (8%) and would have executed 46 invalid plans. A verifier gate preserved the same 8% completion while reducing invalid execution to zero through abstention. Iterative verifier-feedback repair completed 41 tasks (82%), repaired 37 of 46 initially invalid plans (80.43%), accepted no invalid plan, and required 5.72 candidate generations on average. Completion saturated after the ninth candidate; the paired gain was 74 percentage points with a 62-86 point bootstrap interval and exact McNemar p = 1.46 x 10^-11. The results establish a clear division of labor: formal verification supplies sound acceptance, while bounded feedback-driven regeneration converts safe rejection into high task completion.

title: Agentic Treasury Accounts: Synthetic Data, Research Software and D01–D03 Evaluation Records
