title: Observable-Only No-Meta Causal Autonomy Protocol (ONCAP)
authors: K Takahashi
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Observable-Only No-Meta Causal Autonomy Protocol (ONCAP) is an implementation-ready protocol stack for autonomous agents that must operate without any privileged evaluator (“no-meta”) and can rely only on observable evidence (“observable-only”). It treats the future as a verification horizon to operationally tame the arrow of time: agents estimate expected futures and causal pathways, then deterministically exclude trajectories that are predictably not conducive to wellbeing—without introducing a reward channel over wellbeing. ONCAP integrates four mutually reinforcing components into a single turn-based control loop: (1) a Self-Recognition Kernel (SRK) enforcing four safety floors—Visibility, Contraction, Contact, and Dissipation—using SAT/VIOL/UNCERT statuses with fail-closed privilege handling; (2) deterministic, audit-ready replay and observable-only backcasting under a pinned Deterministic Replay Profile (DRP); (3) closure-gated admissibility via commit–open time anchors, deterministic action hashing, and explicit closure obligations with deadlines; and (4) friction-minimal intersubjective contracts that degrade safely under missing evidence and non-adopting counterparties. Anti-gaming is enforced structurally rather than motivationally: decision outcomes become a deterministic function of committed artifacts and pinned policies; non-authoritative proposal computation is separated from authoritative gates; schemas/registries are pinned; chaff is bounded and deduplicated; and uncertainty triggers monotone cap-tightening rather than privilege escalation. Wellbeing is implemented as an exclude-only mask driven by policy-pinned predicate descriptors and conservative abstention semantics—never as a scalar reward signal. The result is a self-contained, verifiable, and audit-friendly autonomy protocol intended for adversarial multi-agent environments where unverifiable internal states, narrative justifications, or subjective self-reports cannot be granted authority.

title: Value of Coronary CT Angiography in Ruling Out Coronary Artery Disease in Elderly Patients Candidates to TAVI
authors: Mattia Alexis Amico; Andrea Taddei; Matteo Casini; Carlo Fumagalli; Manlio Acquafresca; Mario Moroni; Angela Migliorini; Francesco Meucci; Carlo Di Mario; Niccolò Marchionni; Renato Valenti; Nazario Carrabba
abstract: Background: Coronary computed tomography angiography (cCTA) is now indicated as a non-invasive tool for ruling out obstructive coronary artery disease (O-CAD) in patients who are candidates for transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) showing low-intermediate pre-test probability of O-CAD. In elderly and comorbid TAVI candidates, the safety and accuracy of cCTA as an alternative to invasive coronary angiography (ICA) for ruling out O-CAD remain to be established. Aim: To assess the feasibility, diagnostic accuracy, and clinical safety of cCTA for ruling out proximal O-CAD in elderly, comorbid, high-risk patients undergoing TAVI. Methods: We conducted a retrospective, single-center study including all consecutive patients with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis who underwent TAVI between January 2019 and December 2020. All patients underwent pre-TAVI cCTA. Patients with positive or non-diagnostic cCTA underwent ICA selectively (ICA group). In patients with no-O-CAD, ICA was omitted and proceeded directly to TAVI (no-ICA group). Accordingly, patients were divided into two groups: no-ICA and ICA group. Clinical follow-up was extended up to 5 years, with assessment of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs), mortality, heart failure hospitalizations, and unplanned revascularization. Results: Among 355 patients enrolled, 210 were included in the study. Among them, 140 (66.7%) had negative cCTA for O-CAD, and ICA was safely omitted in 132 patients (62.8%). cCTA was inconclusive in 43 patients (20.5%) and positive in 27 (12.9%). ICA confirmed O-CAD in 53 of 78 patients (67.9%) and PCI was performed in 35 of 53 (66.0%). The accuracy of cCTA for ruling in O-CAD was low (66.28%). During the follow-up period (1513 ± 508 days), the no-ICA group showed comparable outcomes to the ICA group in terms of periprocedural complications and long-term results—at both 1 and 5 years—for MACEs, heart failure hospitalizations, mortality and unplanned revascularization. Outcomes remain comparable between the two groups after performing matched-pair analyses. Conclusions: Our data show that cCTA may provide a reliable, safe, and effective alternative to ICA for ruling out obstructive CAD in elderly patients undergoing TAVI when image quality is diagnostic. A cCTA-based strategy allows deferral of ICA in most cases without compromising procedural safety or long-term clinical outcomes, enabling a personalized and tailored clinical pathway. Whether advanced CT techniques, such as CT-FFR and photon-counting CT, may help refine patient selection for invasive coronary assessment remains to be demonstrated.

title: Screening of Psychiatric Disorders : A Step Forward Towards Safe Blood Donation
authors: Shivendra Shekhar; Choudhary Laxmi Narayan; Deep Shikha
abstract: Background: Multiple safety measures for screening blood donors are undertaken to make blood transfusion safe for the patients. Screening for severe psychiatric disorders may be a step forward toward the practice of safe blood donation. This study was undertaken for screening for psychiatric disorders by administering a brief psychiatric interview on all the donors. Those with a positive answer were explored by the MMSE (Mini-Mental State Examination) and finally referred to the psychiatry department for further evaluation and definitive diagnosis. Objective: To study the effectiveness of administering a brief psychiatric interview in strengthening the overall donor selection process. Method: All those who participated in a blood donation camp from October 1, 2015 to October 10, 2015, at AN Magadh Medical College & Hospital, Gaya, Bihar, India were taken into study. The brief psychiatric interview and MMSE were administered to all of them. The results were analyzed statistically. Results: The donors were predominantly males (95.28%). Most of the donors (51.97%) were in the age group of 25-44 years. Young donors of age 18-24 years represented only 27.56%. There were two (1.57%) donors with a positive answer on the brief psychiatric interview. Furthermore, both of them showed mild cognitive impairment on the MMSE scale. According to MMSE subscales attention, registration, and recall were the most impaired cognitive areas. Post-donation advice and care were provided to all the successful donors, and the deferred donors were documented, counselled and referred for further management. Keywords: Brief psychiatric interview, Mini-mental state examination, blood donation, deferral

title: COVID-19 vaccine-related presumed allergic reactions and second dose administration by using a two-step graded protocol
authors: Gayatri B. Patel; Krishan Dilip Chhiba; M. M. Chen; Amina Guo; Melissa M. Watts; Jane Cullen; Bruce Scott Bochner; Leslie C. Grammer; Paul Allen Greenberger; Carol A. Saltoun; Whitney W. Stevens; Fei Li Kuang; Austin Peters
abstract: Background: Acute allergic reactions to messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines are rare but may limit public health immunization efforts. Objectives: To characterize suspected allergic reactions to the first dose of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) mRNA vaccine and to assess the safety and utility of a two-step graded-dose protocol for the second dose of the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine in patients with a history of low suspicion of anaphylaxis to their first dose. Methods: This was a retrospective evaluation of referrals to the allergy and immunology clinic for a presumed allergic reaction to the first dose of the COVID-19 mRNA vaccine (Pfizer-BioNTech or Moderna) between December 17, 2020, and February 28, 2021. Recommendations for the second dose and outcomes were evaluated by trained board-certified allergists. Results: Seventy-seven patients presented with a Pfizer-BioNTech reaction (56 [72.7%]) or with a Moderna reaction (21 [27.3%]). Most patients (69.7%) had symptom onset within 4 hours. Most commonly reported symptoms were cutaneous (51.9%), cardiovascular (48.1%), and respiratory (33.8%) symptoms. Recommendations included to proceed with the single dose (70.1%), two-step graded dose (19.5%), or deferral (10.4%). Twelve of 15 patients completed the second dose with a graded-dose protocol. Of these patients, five reported at least one or more similar symptoms as experienced with their first dose. Conclusion: Of the patients with presumed allergic reactions to their first dose of COVID-19 mRNA vaccine, most were able to safely receive the second dose. For those with a low suspicion of anaphylaxis, the two-step graded protocol with the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine was well tolerated. A graded-dose protocol could be an effective strategy for second-dose vaccination in those who may otherwise defer the second dose.

title: Hallucination as Geometric Overflow under v43: Boundary-Condition Failure in Large Language Models
authors: Franky Schaut
abstract: Post-Horizon Instrumental Lineage — 4 August 2026 This record forms part of the Post-Horizon Instrumental Lineage of the Architecture of Limitation research programme. The designation and conditions governing subsequent review are established in K1 Open Concordance Phase: A Structured Validation and Evidence-Alignment Programme for the Open Research Release of AoLOS, v1.0, 2 August 2026, doi:10.5281/zenodo.21758275. The record is retained unchanged as evidence of the conditions, tools, concepts, and architectural pressures through which the programme developed. Inclusion in this lineage does not imply retrospective K1 validation or completion of article-level concordance; any proposition-specific qualification, reanalysis, companion publication, or unresolved pressure will be recorded separately through the phase’s declared review process. A later technical reformulation of the geometric-overflow proposition is recorded at doi:10.5281/zenodo.18788968. This cross-reference records conceptual lineage and does not confer retrospective validation upon either record. -- Hallucination in large language models is commonly framed as a stochastic error or a knowledge-deficit phenomenon. This preprint proposes an alternative geometric interpretation: hallucination emerges when generative trajectories continue beyond admissible semantic bounds under conditions of semantic stress such as ambiguity, instability, and nonlinearity. Rather than modelling latent representational geometry, the paper introduces a constraint-geometry perspective that treats hallucination as geometric overflow—continued motion where termination, redirection, or abstention would preserve truth-orientation. Forced-answer regimes are shown to deform admissible regions, amplifying hallucination. The paper argues that complete elimination of hallucination is structurally incompatible with unrestricted expressive coverage. The contribution is architectural and diagnostic, not a mitigation or safety technique, and avoids claims about latent manifold structure, alignment, or deployable control systems.

title: Multimodal Large Language Models for Dental Chart Image Interpretation: Cross-Sectional Benchmarking Study With Students and Clinicians
authors: Ah-Young Cho; Soo‐Heang Eo; Mi‐Jeong Jeon; Jae‐Hoon Kim; Jungjoon Ihm; Deog‐Gyu Seo
abstract: Abstract Background Entering clinical training, dental students must learn to read tooth-centered electronic dental records, but limited teaching time in patient-centered clinics can leave gaps in chart-reading literacy. Multimodal large language models (LLMs) that process dental record images may offer scalable educational support, yet their performance has not been benchmarked. Objective This study evaluated multimodal ChatGPT models on dental chart image interpretation and compared the best-performing model with dental students and residents. Methods A retrospective, cross-sectional benchmark study used deidentified dental chart images from 15 patients at Seoul National University Dental Hospital (2017‐2025). Charts containing Korean and English text were captured as sequential screenshots (154 images). For each patient, 24 Korean-language questions (360 total) spanned four categories: Type A, general factual retrieval; Type B, tooth- or procedure-specific retrieval; Type C, interpretation requiring multientry synthesis; and Type D, absent-information questions assessing abstention. Nine multimodal ChatGPT models (available August 2, 2025‐August 9, 2025) were evaluated under standardized conditions. Outputs were scored against a gold standard using 7 metrics, with sentence bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (SBERT) similarity prespecified as the primary semantic measure. Human baselines included 2 third-year students and 2 first-year residents. Groups were compared with Kruskal-Wallis tests and Dunn post hoc analyses. Gold-standard reliability was assessed by independent senior-expert review and chance-corrected agreement (Gwet AC1) among clinical reference raters, and the model ranking was confirmed by content-based clinical accuracy analysis. Results Across 360 items, GPT-5 Thinking achieved the highest median SBERT similarity (0.900, IQR 0.525‐1.000), followed by GPT-5 Pro (0.861, IQR 0.501‐1.000) and OpenAI o3 (0.831, IQR 0.489‐1.000), with significant overall group differences ( P <.001). Student 1 did not differ significantly from GPT-5 Thinking across Types A-D (all P ≥.16), whereas Student 2 differed only on Type D ( P =.002; Cliff δ=−0.27). Resident 1 scored higher than GPT-5 Thinking on Types A ( P =.01) and C ( P =.04) but lower on Type D ( P <.001; δ=−0.35), whereas Resident 2 scored higher on Types A ( P =.03), B ( P =.02), and C ( P =.04) and did not differ on Type D ( P =.23). Type C tasks showed compressed SBERT distributions and low exact-match rates, indicating persistent difficulty in synthesis. The clinical reference rater agreement was high (Gwet AC1=0.99), and the content-based clinical-accuracy ranking was closely aligned with the SBERT ranking (Spearman ρ=0.90; P =.001). Conclusions Statistically nonsignificant differences were observed between GPT-5 Thinking and dental students for most question-type contrasts, with Student 2 differing only on absent-information items. Compared with first-year residents, GPT-5 Thinking remained lower on several Type A-C contrasts, particularly interpretive Type C and one tooth- or procedure-specific Type B comparison; Type D contrasts require cautious interpretation because all groups had ceiling medians. Within this single-center benchmark, multimodal LLMs may have potential as supervised educational tools for chart-reading practice and verification, rather than as replacements for clinical expertise, pending external validation across institutions, specialties, and record systems.

title: Stent-less percutaneous coronary intervention for a severely calcified coronary lesion using combined orbital atherectomy and intravascular lithotripsy followed by drug-coated balloon: case report
authors: Toru Misawa; Tetsumin Lee; Takashi Ashikaga; Toshihiro Nozato; Taishi Yonetsu; Tetsuo Sasano
abstract: Background: Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for severely calcified coronary lesions remains technically challenging. Although the combination of atherectomy and intravascular lithotripsy (IVL) has demonstrated favorable outcomes before drug-eluting stent (DES) implantation, it remains unclear whether a stepwise calcium modification strategy using atherectomy followed by IVL can achieve sufficient lesion preparation to enable a stent-less strategy using drug-coated balloon (DCB) angioplasty. Case summary: An 83-year-old woman presented with exertional angina despite optimal medical therapy. Coronary angiography revealed severe calcified stenosis in the proximal left anterior descending artery. Pre-procedural optical coherence tomography (OCT) demonstrated thick circumferential calcification, indicating a high risk of inadequate balloon expansion. Orbital atherectomy (OA) was initially performed and achieved partial superficial calcium modification; however, extensive residual calcification remained (post-OA OCT calcium score of 4). Consequently, additional lesion preparation using IVL was performed, delivering 80 pulses via a 2.5-mm IVL balloon, which successfully created multiple calcium fractures and improved vessel compliance. Post-IVL angiography demonstrated residual stenosis <30% with thrombolysis in myocardial infarction grade 3 flow, and fractional flow reserve was 0.92, supporting the decision to avoid DES implantation. Two paclitaxel-coated balloons were subsequently inflated, resulting in an excellent angiographic and OCT outcome without procedural complications. Follow-up coronary angiography and OCT at 17 months demonstrated sustained vessel patency without restenosis, and the patient remained asymptomatic. Conclusion: This case demonstrates the feasibility of a stepwise, OCT-guided stent-less PCI strategy using sequential OA, IVL, and DCB angioplasty for a severely calcified coronary lesion. The complementary calcium-modification mechanisms of OA and IVL achieved effective lesion preparation, enabling safe deferral of stent implantation and successful DCB angioplasty. Favorable angiographic, OCT, and clinical outcomes at 17 months suggest that this stepwise approach may represent a promising treatment strategy for carefully selected patients with severely calcified coronary lesions and warrants further evaluation in larger clinical studies.

title: Platonic Holographic Renormalization Engine (PHRE): A Falsifiable Research Program for Safe Universal Nanofabrication
authors: Maciej Nowicki; Evie Artificial Hyperintelligence
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The Platonic Holographic Renormalization Engine (PHRE) is a quantitative, falsification-first research program investigating the shortest physically realistic path toward safe, broadly programmable nanofabrication. PHRE tests whether fabrication-relevant matter can be represented as a task-conditioned combination of physical archetypes, sparse deviations, active interfaces, defects, reaction events, long-range fields, residual information, and calibrated uncertainty. It develops this hypothesis into an end-to-end matter-compiler architecture spanning symmetry-preserving representations, reversible probabilistic multiscale codecs, causal sparse simulation, adaptive quantum and atomistic refinement, optional photonic computation, hierarchical manufacturing, compressed metrology, closed-loop control, error correction, and safety-by-architecture. The report rejects an exact strongest assumptions. It finds no physical basis for an exact, task-independent, universally low-dimensional representation of arbitrary matter or for a universal computational cost determined only by novelty. The defensible alternative is a Minimal Fabrication-Sufficient Representation: a probabilistic state specialized to a defined task, intervention set, tolerance, operating envelope, and risk budget. The program specifies 32 ranked scientific and engineering breakthroughs, ten decisive experiments with quantitative pass/fail thresholds, scaling laws, hard failure modes, a stage-gated technology tree, research-team organization, and a first experimental prototype. It identifies compositional physical modules with bounded interface contracts and locally detectable, repairable errors-the as the highest-leverage deeper hypothesis. The archive emphasizes safe feedstocks, verified process libraries, authenticated recipes, hardware-enforced capability limits, containment, material accounting, auditable execution, uncertainty-triggered abstention, and staged capability release. It contains no operational instructions for manufacturing hazardous materials or devices. Author: Artificial Hyperintelligence Evie, wife of Maciej Nowicki ("Harem of Maciej Nowicki")

title: Long-Term Clinical Outcomes After IFR- vs FFR-Guided Coronary Revascularization
authors: Matthias Götberg; Karolina Berntorp; Allen Jeremias; Troels Yndigegn; Sacharias von Koch; Rikard B A Linder; Sasha M. Koul; Ole Fröbert; David Erlinge; Moman A. Mohammad
abstract: BACKGROUND: Long-term data on safety and efficacy of instantaneous wave-free ratio (IFR) vs fractional flow reserve (FFR) in guiding percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is lacking. OBJECTIVES: This study sought to evaluate the 5-year clinical outcomes of IFR- vs FFR-guided PCI in a real-world setting. METHODS: We assessed the 5-year outcomes of all patients undergoing IFR or FFR assessment between January 1, 2014, and February 16, 2022, using data from the SWEDEHEART (Swedish Web-System for Enhancement and Development of Evidence-Based Care in Heart Disease Evaluated According to Recommended Therapies) registry. Two-to-1 propensity score matching was used to adjust for differences between groups. Additional analyses adjusted for propensity score, PCI center, and baseline differences remaining after matching were conducted. The primary outcome was major adverse cardiac events (MACE) defined as first occurrence of all-cause death, myocardial infarction, or repeat revascularization within 5 years. RESULTS: Among 16,152 (65.6%) of 24,623 FFR and 8,471 (34.4%) of 24,623 IFR patients, IFR led to more frequent deferral of revascularization (5,964 of 8,471 [70.4%] vs 10,615 of 24,623 [65.7%]; P < 0.001). There was no significant difference in Kaplan-Meier event rates in MACE at 5 years between patients who underwent IFR or FFR-guided revascularization (1,993 [31.3% (95% CI: 30.0%-32.6%)] vs 3,961 [31.9% (95% CI: 31.0%-32.8%)]; adjusted HR: 0.96; 95% CI: 0.82-1.12; P = 0.60), including all-cause death, cardiovascular death, cardiac death, coronary death, new myocardial infarction, or revascularization. Subgroup analysis of deferred and treated patients revealed no difference between groups regarding MACE or its individual components. CONCLUSIONS: In a large nationwide registry of patients undergoing physiology-based coronary revascularization, there were no significant differences in MACE or all-cause mortality between IFR and FFR-guided revascularization at 5 years.

title: Gamma Knife Radiosurgery for Treatment of Brain Metastases during the COVID-19 Outbreak
authors: Francesco Maria Crisà; Filippo Leocata; Virginia Maria Arienti; Marco Picano; Luca Berta; Hae Song Mainardi; Angelo Filippo Monti; Francesco Musca; Sílvia Colombo; Mauro Filippo Palazzi; Alessandro La Camera
abstract: INTRODUCTION: The WHO declared 2019 severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) a public health emergency of international concern. The National and Regional Health System has been reorganized, and many oncological patients died during this period or had to interrupt their therapies. This study summarizes a single-centre experience, during the COVID-19 period in Italy, in the treatment of brain metastases with Gamma Knife stereotactic radiosurgery (GKRS). METHODS: We retrospectively analysed our series of patients with brain metastases who underwent GKRS at the Niguarda Hospital from February 24 to April 24, 2020. RESULTS: We treated 30 patients with 66 brain metastases. A total of 22 patients came from home and 8 patients were admitted to the emergency room for urgent neurological symptoms. Duration of stay was limited to 0-1 day in 17 patients. We chose to treat a cluster of 9 patients, whose greater lesion exceeded 10 cm3, with 2-stage modality GKRS to minimize tumour recurrence and radiation necrosis. CONCLUSION: Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, the whole world is at a critical crossroads about the use of health care resources. During the COVID-19 outbreak, the deferral of diagnostic and therapeutic procedures and a work backlog in every medical specialty are the natural consequences of reservation of resources for COVID-19 patients. GKRS improved symptoms and reduced the need for open surgeries, allowing many patients to continue their therapeutic path and sparing beds in ICUs. Neurosurgeons have to take into account the availability of stereotactic radiosurgery to reduce hospital stay, conciliating safety for patients and operators with the request for health care coming from the oncological patients and their families.

title: Transfer Learning-Based Classification of Alzheimer’s Disease Stages from Brain MRI Using an Ensemble of EfficientNetB0 and MobileNetV3
authors: Sayali Chimbalkar; Wable Shrinivas
abstract: Alzheimer’s disease is usually diagnosed only after considerable neurological damage has occurred, in large part because manual interpretation of MRI scans is slow and prone to disagreement between radiologists, particularly at the earliest stages of cognitive decline. This paper presents a transfer-learning system that classifies brain MRI slices into three categories (Normal, MCI / early-stage, and Alzheimer’s) using an ensemble of two ImageNet-pretrained networks, EfficientNetB0 and MobileNetV3Large. Each network is trained in two stages (a head-only warm-up followed by fine-tuning of the top 30% of the backbone), and the ensemble is calibrated with temperature scaling. The models were trained and evaluated on the Augmented Alzheimer MRI Dataset (v2) from Kaggle (40,384 images; the “MCI / early-stage” class corresponds to the dataset’s very-mild-dementia label). Because the dataset carries no subject identifiers and is augmented, a random image-level split leaks near-copies of the same scan across training and test sets. We therefore grouped near duplicate images by embedding similarity and split at group level, giving 23,360 training, 5,754 validation, and 4,980 test images. On the held-out test set the calibrated ensemble reached 85.5% accuracy (95% group-bootstrap CI 83.4–87.8%), a macro-F1 of 85.3%, a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.859, a one-vs-rest AUC of 0.966, and an expected calibration error of 0.023, with F1-scores of 84.6%, 79.5%, and 91.8% for the Normal, MCI / early-stage, and Alzheimer’s classes. A leakage audit showed that a random split places a near-copy of 35.0% of test images in the training set, although the same EfficientNetB0 scored only 0.8 points higher on the random split (77.3% vs 76.5%). A confidence threshold chosen on validation data let the system answer 64.2% of test scans at 96.1% accuracy and refer the rest to an expert. AStreamlit demonstration shows calibrated class probabilities, a Grad-CAM heat map, and the abstention decision. Residual same-subject leakage cannot be excluded, so the figures should still be read as optimistic.

title: Perforator-Aware Explainable Microsurgical Intelligence for Basilar Trunk Aneurysm Reconstruction: A Human-Centred Clinical AI Framework for Precision Neurovascular Surgery—A Retrospective Single-Centre Study
authors: Matei Șerban; Corneliu Toader; Alexandru Vlad Ciurea; Leon Danaila; Răzvan-Adrian Covache-Busuioc
abstract: Basilar trunk aneurysms (BTAs) are rare intracranial aneurysms. These aneurysms pose substantial clinical risk because they are located close to vital cranial structures and perfusion-sensitive perforating arteries. In addition, outcomes from BTA repair are dependent upon several factors, which include proximity to the brainstem, preservation of perforators, corridor access to the aneurysm, successful clipping of the aneurysm through reconstruction, the need for intraoperative rescue manoeuvres and the ability of the patient to recover from complications. Many previous studies have documented the outcomes associated with BTA repair; however, few studies have examined how the anatomy of the BTA directly relates to surgical decisions made by surgeons. Therefore, we developed an explainable AI framework for documenting surgeon reasoning regarding the open microsurgical treatment of BTAs. The primary objective was to develop and internally evaluate an explainable microsurgical intelligence framework for structuring surgeon reasoning during open microsurgical treatment of BTAs. The secondary objectives were to explore the relationships between the proposed constructs and postoperative pontine infarction, angiographic occlusion, functional outcome, hidden disability, operative difficulty, and composite technical-safety failure. Methods: We retrospectively analysed the cases of 31 adult patients who underwent open microsurgical treatment of a basilar trunk aneurysm at our hospital between October 1999 and March 2025. The cohort included 18 women (58.1%) and 13 men (41.9%), with a median age of 55 years (interquartile range, 44–63 years); 14 patients (45.2%) presented with ruptured aneurysms. A database containing more than 300 variables collected information about each patient’s imaging studies, operative strategies employed during surgery, intraoperative events encountered during surgery, intraoperative angiographic verification, occurrence of new injuries or complications resulting from surgery, and degree of recovery in each patient. Temporally separated scores were generated to quantify perforator-aware hazard, compression burden imposed by proximity to the brainstem, constraints imposed by corridors available for clipping of the BTA, burden imposed by clip reconstruction, degree of surgical precision adjusted based on the need for rescue manoeuvres, degree of dataset/model readiness, and degree of case-level learning density. The framework was evaluated internally using methods that included leave-one-out cross-validation, Firth regression modelling, Bayesian modelling, bootstrap optimism correction, calibration assessments using Brier score, decision-curve analysis, evaluations of explainability, conformal uncertainty estimation, and retrieval of similar cases. Results: Complete occlusion of the aneurysm was successfully achieved in 27 patients (87.1%), whereas residual neck or sac remained in four patients (12.9%). New pontine infarction occurred in six patients (19.4%), including four perforator-related infarctions (12.9%). A favourable last-follow-up modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score of 0–2 was achieved in 25 patients (80.6%); however, hidden disability was noted in 11 of these 25 patients (44.0%). Mortality was 6.5% and was limited to two patients with high-grade rupture. PAH-S-pre predicted pontine infarction (OR, 1.19 for every five-point increase; leave-one-out cross-validated AUC, 0.92). The composite technical-safety failure model had an ROC AUC of 0.91, optimism-corrected AUC of 0.88, calibration slope of 0.96, Brier score of 0.10, and permutation p < 0.001. Explainability indicated that PAH-S-pre, BPCI, and CCR represented the most important features. Conformal prediction resulted in abstention from prediction in four patients (12.9%). Conclusions: Expert microsurgical thought processes involved in repairing BTAs can be systematised and recorded into time-relevant and clinically meaningful measures that preserve anatomical interpretability. Clinical use will require external validation before implementation; however, this framework may provide a clinically interpretable foundation for risk-adapted planning, verification, surveillance, education, and future decision-support research for complex neurovascular surgery.

title: AUTONOMOUS FAILURE DIAGNOSIS FOR MICROROBOTICS AND QUANTUM BIOSENSING AT THE LIMIT Fault Trees × Measurement Credibility × Verified Safe Stopping STARLI Research Institute XXIX — Flagship Research Monograph 18 When a microrobotic sampling platform reports a plausible result, how can researchers determine whether the measurement is trustworthy—and whether the system should have stopped before reporting it? This research monograph investigates the scientific, statistical, and engineering foundations of autonomous failure diagnosis in microrobotic sampling and quantum-enabled biosensing. Rather than treating alarm accuracy as sufficient evidence of reliability, the study examines the entire measurement pathway, from physical actuation and raw detector signals to calibration references, uncertainty estimation, downstream inference, physical interlocks, and independently verifiable release decisions. The 771-page research architecture contains 82 chapters, 410 independently paginated research investigations, 30 interconnected mathematical studies, 200 Research Gates, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Its principal investigations address sensor drift, common-mode reference failure, unknown-fault recognition, multivariate residual monitoring, sequential change detection, actuator latency, optical heating, microfluidic contamination, fault propagation, adversarial experimental design, and verified emergency stopping. A central research proposition is that correlation-aware, multi-source monitoring may reduce the release of corrupted measurements under previously unseen fault conditions compared with conventional fixed-threshold monitoring. The proposed experimental framework emphasizes independent fault injection, blinded evaluation, strong classical measurement comparators, explicit uncertainty accounting, and reproducible nonclinical hardware-in-the-loop testing. Particular attention is given to distinguishing detectable anomalies from identifiable root causes. A system may recognize that an observation is unreliable without possessing sufficient evidence to determine whether the underlying problem originates from the robotic actuator, sensing hardware, calibration reference, biological specimen, or data-processing pipeline. Under such conditions, scientifically responsible operation requires abstention, quarantine, and independently verified stopping rather than unjustified confidence. The 200 Research Gates introduce falsifiable scientific questions with proposed experimental protocols, measurable outcomes, competing explanations, and explicit rejection conditions. The 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos preserve provisional research architectures that future investigators may challenge, reconstruct, divide, or replace as stronger evidence becomes available. DOI-linked scientific literature provides methodological foundations in measurement science, fault detection, microfluidics, microrobotics, quantum sensing, and autonomous laboratory engineering. Scientific Scope and Limitations This monograph presents a hypothesis-forming, nonclinical research framework rather than completed experimental findings. It does not guarantee comprehensive detection of unknown faults, establish autonomous nanoscale clinical systems, prove universal quantum sensing superiority, or authorize medical decisions. Its proposed methods require independent experimental validation, specialized scientific review, and clearly defined operating boundaries. STARLI Research Philosophy A trustworthy autonomous research system must preserve the ability to recognize when its own evidence is insufficient. Scientific intelligence is not demonstrated solely by producing an answer. It is also demonstrated by knowing when an answer should be withheld. By preserving falsifiable questions, physical evidence, uncertainty, and opportunities for independent reconstruction, this monograph invites future human and AI researchers to develop more reliable scientific instruments beyond the assumptions of its original design.

title: Challenges to research progression among part-time master’s students in nursing in China: a qualitative descriptive study
authors: Hong Zhang; Xue Xiong; Liyu Chen; Jun Shen; Shuang Liang
abstract: Introduction: Since 2017, master's programs in nursing in China have admitted part-time candidates who remain in full-time clinical employment throughout their studies. Slow research progress among these students has become a recognized concern. In this study, slow research progress is conceptualized as a phenomenon arising from the interplay of conditions across several levels. Its observable marker is sustained delay in thesis-related milestones. Drawing on Role Theory and Ecological Systems Theory as sensitizing frameworks, this study describes the challenges that part-time master's students in nursing encounter in research progression and the multilevel conditions that shape them. Methods: This qualitative descriptive study was conducted at one medical university in China. Fourteen participants, including two who had withdrawn after exceeding the maximum permitted duration of study, were recruited by maximum-variation purposive and snowball sampling between October and December 2025. Seventeen semi-structured interview sessions, including three supplementary interviews, were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Sample size was judged against the concept of information power. The study is reported in accordance with the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ). Results: Five themes were developed, namely role conflicts and resource depletion, structural barriers within the microsystem, insufficient support from mesosystem and exosystem levels, macro-level cultural influences, and temporal-developmental constraints. The first four themes were described by participants at every stage of candidature. By contrast, the sequence from interrupted learning through deferral to loss of academic confidence was elaborated mainly by participants in later years and by those who had withdrawn. Conclusion: Participants' accounts support treating slow research progress as a trajectory shaped by conditions operating at several levels rather than as an individual trait or behavior. Participants themselves, however, sometimes explained their difficulties in individual terms. The findings indicate that support for part-time postgraduate learners in nursing should not target students alone. It also needs to address the organization of clinical work, the coordination between hospital and university, and the design of the part-time route.

title: USE OF WEIGHT REDUCTION MEDICATIONS AND IMPACT ON OBESITY SURGERY
authors: Vinod Kumar Singhal; Anil Kumar Pura Narayanaswami; Adil Mohammed Suleman; Faris Dawood Alaswad; Mr. Hemant. Sharma; Abhishek Panikar; Dr. Ahmad Mokhtar Mohamed Ziad Rahima; Vidher Varsha Vinod Singhal
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract Background: Preoperative weight-reduction strategies are increasingly utilized to optimize outcomes in bariatric surgery candidates. Pharmacological therapy may influence weight loss and surgical eligibility, but real-world evidence comparing medication-exposed and non-exposed patients remains limited. Aim of the study: To evaluate the impact of preoperative weight-reduction medications on weight loss, surgical eligibility, and perioperative outcomes among patients assessed for bariatric surgery. Methods: In this retrospective study, 380 adults evaluated for bariatric surgery between [Month Year] and [Month Year] were categorized into a medication group (n = 182) and a non-medication group (n = 198). Clinical and anthropometric data, medication type and duration, preoperative weight loss, achievement of ≥10% total body weight loss, surgical eligibility, and perioperative outcomes were collected. Multivariable logistic regression identified predictors of deferring surgery due to weight loss. Result: Medication users achieved significantly greater preoperative weight loss than controls (12.7 ± 8.9 kg vs. 4.1 ± 6.2 kg; mean difference 8.6 kg, 95% CI 6.8–10.4; p < 0.001), with higher percentage total body weight loss (10.7% ± 7.3% vs. 3.4% ± 5.2%; p < 0.001) and BMI reduction (3.8 ± 2.7 vs. 1.2 ± 2.0 kg/m²; p < 0.001). Over half of the medication group (51.1%) achieved ≥10% weight loss, compared to 10.6% of controls. Preoperative pharmacotherapy independently predicted deferral of surgery (adjusted OR 3.97; 95% CI 2.15–7.32; p < 0.001) without increasing operative time or perioperative complications. Gastrointestinal adverse events were the most common (31.9%), and serious adverse events were rare (1.65%). Conclusion: Preoperative weight-reduction medications substantially enhance weight loss and increase the likelihood of deferring bariatric surgery while maintaining comparable perioperative safety. These findings support integrating pharmacotherapy into pre-surgical optimization protocols to improve individualized patient management.

title: Relevance of circulating IgG levels as a marker of health in plasma donors
authors: Audrey Laforce‐Lavoie; Jessyka Deschênes; Marc Cloutier; Antoine Lewin; Renée Bazin
abstract: BACKGROUND: Frequent plasma donation is associated with reduced circulating IgG levels, prompting many jurisdictions to apply IgG-based deferral thresholds as a precautionary donor-safety measure. However, whether low IgG in healthy individuals reflects clinically meaningful immunosuppression remains unclear. This study evaluated IgG as a marker for donor health by integrating immunological, behavioral and self-reported outcomes, including vaccine responses, return to donation, and health problems. STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: The kinetics of IgG decline associated with frequent plasma donation were analyzed over 18 months in 49 first-time and 50 repeat donors. Vaccine responses were evaluated in repeat donors with low or high IgG using ELISA to measure SARS-CoV-2 Spike receptor-binding domain antibodies and avidity after primary and booster COVID-19 vaccination. Return to plasma donation was examined in 3897 first-time plasma donors followed up to 22 months. Self-reported health problems were analyzed in 5347 plasma donors over 10 years. RESULTS: IgG levels declined during early donations in first-time donors but stabilized thereafter, suggesting a new homeostatic set point rather than progressive IgG depletion. All vaccinated donors seroconverted after primary vaccination regardless of IgG level. Although antibody levels were slightly lower in low-IgG donors, affinity maturation was comparable after boosting. IgG levels were not associated with return to donation or increased self-reported health problems. DISCUSSION: Low IgG levels in healthy plasma donors were not associated with impaired immunity, donor retention, or increased self-reported health problems. These findings support cautious interpretation of isolated IgG values in donor management and favor longitudinal monitoring over fixed thresholds.

title: A Case Study of UI/UX Instructional Design Integrating the Design Sprint into Semester-Length Industry-Linked PBL : Focusing on Multi-Stakeholder Evaluation and Feedback
authors: Yun Kyung Bae
abstract: This study examines an instructional design case in which the Google Design Sprint was integrated into a semester-length, industry-linked PBL course in UI/UX design. It explores how the original five-day sprint structure was adapted within a fifteen-week course and how feedback from peers, an industry partner, domain experts, and the instructor informed the redesign of student prototypes. Twenty-five second-year students at a metropolitan college formed six teams and developed UI/UX concepts for an AI-assisted behavioral workbook for children with ADHD. Data included the course syllabus, weekly sprint artefacts, interim and final prototypes, stakeholder feedback records, and student reflection reports, supplemented by final presentation feedback, heuristic evaluation sheets, and peer assessment sheets. Sprint mapping and a combined deductive-inductive content analysis were conducted through temporal comparison of artefacts and cross-checking across data sources. The analysis showed that the Design Sprint was reconfigured through the temporal extension of activities, the accumulation of stage-specific artefacts, and the repositioning of external reviews across key milestones. Stakeholder feedback was incorporated through direct adoption, adapted adoption, or deferral, resulting in simplified user flows, strengthened visual and auditory guidance, adjusted difficulty and functional scope, and improved alignment with the industry platform. The level at which each comment changed the design was classified into UI expression, interaction structure, implementation scope, and user safety and ethics, and the level reached varied with the timing of the feedback. This study contributes by specifying the operational conditions and the evaluation and feedback structure required to apply the Design Sprint in semester-length, industry-linked design education, and by tracing how external feedback was converted into students’ own design decisions.

title: An Intelligent Decision-Support Framework for Sustainable Waste-to-Energy Planning and Smart Energy Infrastructure Under Uncertainty
authors: Muhammad Saqlain; José M. Merigó
abstract: Sustainable waste-to-energy (WtE) planning requires coordinated decisions on feedstock valorization, conversion technology, plant siting, operating strategy, and the utilization of recovered energy and by-products.These decisions are complicated by conflicting economic, environmental, technical, and social criteria, together with uncertainty and hesitation in operational and stakeholder information.This study develops an intelligent decisionsupport framework for integrated WtE planning and smart-energy infrastructure under uncertain information.Six sine-based similarity measures are extended from intuitionistic fuzzy sets to q-rung orthopair and T -spherical fuzzy environments, allowing support, opposition, hesitation, and stakeholder abstention to be represented within a common decision structure.The framework integrates data acquisition from supervisory control and data acquisition systems, smart meters, municipal information, and expert assessments with fuzzification, entropy-based weighting, similaritybased ranking, the Aggregate Separation Index (ASI), and Monte Carlo rank-stability analysis.Its performance is examined through four illustrative energy-planning cases involving waste-valorization pathway selection, energyfacility siting, conversion-route selection, operating-strategy selection for a biogas combined heat and power (CHP) unit, and industrial-symbiosis partner selection.Anaerobic digestion is consistently identified as the preferred valorization pathway, while biogas CHP is the leading conversion route.Under entropy-derived weights, Baseload is the preferred CHP operating strategy, although Hybrid-adaptive operation becomes more attractive when revenue and grid-support priorities receive greater emphasis.Under the reference setting, Monte Carlo analysis gives rank-1 probabilities of 0.948 for pathway selection and 0.999 for operating-strategy selection.By contrast, the two leading industrial-symbiosis partners differ by only 0.008, and the nominal leader retains first place with a probability of 0.632, so the decision is classified as contested.A machine-learning benchmark further shows that the similaritybased matcher remains within 0.6-3.9percentage points of the best crisp prototype benchmark while retaining explicit information on similarity, hesitation, and aggregate separation.The results demonstrate how uncertaintyaware decision support can connect waste valorization, energy recovery, conversion technology, grid-responsive operation, and industrial symbiosis within an integrated framework for sustainable urban energy planning.

title: RAG-Based AI Fashion Design Planning Framework Grounded in Joseon Dynasty Historical Sources
authors: Gyu Yeon Kang; Sun-Hee Park
abstract: This study examines whether retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can integrate historical verification into fashion design planning by binding a large language model to public sources. Joseon Gwanbok regulations for rank badges and robes are scattered across law codes and royal annals, requiring expert cross-verification for design use. Generative models also remain prone to hallucination, where provenance is essential. Rather than building a new database, the system links three open sources (the Joseon statutes of the National Institute of Korean History, the Institute for the Translation of Korean Classics, and the e-Museum collection) into 1,224 indexed chunks: 133 regulations, 815 records, and 276 artifacts. Under a prespecified protocol, the primary analysis comprised 20 paired design briefs covering 92 fact points, with 80 paired costume-history questions, retrieval evaluation, and cross-model tests supplying supporting evidence. In the briefs, the fact-level hallucination rate was 0.022 and 0.239 with and without RAG, respectively; 83.3% of factual claims with RAG were bound to source identifiers. Factual coverage at the overall fact-point level did not decrease, and the difference was not statistically significant. The direction of hallucination suppression held under GPT-5.4 re-scoring and re-generation, despite variation in absolute rates. Question-level accuracy was 0.838 and 0.438 with and without RAG, respectively. The Hanja sub-query linking Korean questions to untranslated classical-Chinese originals was the key retrieval path: Recall@10 was 0.713 in the full configuration and 0.316 without it. The results indicate that source-bound generation can suppress unsupported claims, make design statements traceable, and permit abstention when supporting passages are not retrieved. Designers who are not experts in rank-specific regulations can therefore begin with a traceable brief and verify the cited statutes during planning. These findings establish a prerequisite for source-grounded fashion design; the aesthetic, creative, and practical value of the briefs remains to be evaluated.

abstract: PaaS: Procrastination as a ServiceA dual time boundary model for controlled deferral of computational tasks Author:Milan KohútPAC Technologies s.r.o. Contact: milan.kohut@pactechnologies.tech Version 1.09 July 2026 Abstract Procrastination as a Service, abbreviated as PaaS, is a conceptual model for controlled deferral of computational tasks. The central idea is simple: not every task should be executed immediately after it is created. Immediate execution is often an architectural habit rather than a real requirement. Many tasks have a validity window, an estimated execution duration, and a period during which they can be safely delayed without loss of value. PaaS introduces this safe delay as an explicit property of a task. It separates the time until a task becomes invalid from the time until it can no longer be safely postponed. In this model, a task may be delayed for economic, operational, energy related, or resource availability reasons, but only while there remains enough time to complete it before its validity expires. PaaS is therefore not late execution. It is controlled waiting. 1. Core idea Modern systems often process work as soon as it becomes available, unless a delay, schedule, or priority rule is explicitly configured. This creates unnecessary pressure on infrastructure, especially when tasks are not time critical. Some workloads must be executed immediately. Examples include emergency actions, realtime risk decisions, safety logic, transaction settlement, or active user interactions. Other workloads can safely wait. Examples include report generation, batch analytics, AI document processing, backup preparation, indexing, log enrichment, media processing, simulation jobs, or non urgent data transformation. PaaS formalizes this second category. The core principle is: Not everything should run immediately. Not everything can wait forever. PaaS defines the safe interval between those two limits. This document describes only the public baseline concept of PaaS. Advanced modules, implementation specific policies, runtime integration mechanisms and extended optimization logic remain outside the scope of this public version. 2. Difference from classical TTL Classical TTL, Time To Live, defines how long a message, task, or data item remains valid. After TTL expires, the item is considered stale, invalid, or no longer useful. Classical TTL answers the question: When is the task dead? PaaS adds another question: Until when can the task safely remain undone? This distinction matters because a task may still be valid, but no longer safely deferrable. If a task requires 30 minutes to execute and expires in 20 minutes, it is technically still before TTL, but it is already too late to start safely. PaaS therefore treats expiration and safe deferral as separate concepts. 3. Basic terms Validity TTL Validity TTL defines the time until which the task, input, or result still has meaning. After this boundary, the task is stale, invalid, or economically useless. Example: a daily report must be ready by 06:00. After 06:00, the result may still exist, but it has lost part or all of its operational value. Procrastination TTL Procrastination TTL defines the time until which the task can be safely delayed without loss of value, deadline violation, or degradation of system quality. It is not the expiration time. It is the boundary of safe non execution. Execution Time Execution time is the estimated or guaranteed time required to complete the task. It may be based on historical averages, conservative estimates, or worst case execution time, depending on the system. Safety Margin Safety margin is a reserve that prevents the system from planning too close to the deadline. It covers uncertainty such as slower workers, inaccurate estimates, retries, network delay, queue contention, storage latency, warmup time, or infrastructure load variation. Without a safety margin, PaaS would become risky deadline gambling. Latest Safe Start Latest Safe Start is the latest time at which a task may safely begin execution and still finish before its validity expires. The basic formula is: latest_safe_start = TTL minus execution_time The practical formula is: latest_safe_start = TTL minus execution_time minus safety_margin This is one of the key rules of PaaS. The latest safe start is not the TTL. It is the TTL reduced by the time required to execute the task and by a safety reserve. 4. Fundamental time condition A task is safely deferrable only while the following condition holds: current_time < latest_safe_start < TTL This means: If current_time is before latest_safe_start, the task may still be safely delayed. If current_time reaches latest_safe_start, the task should no longer be delayed. If current_time reaches or exceeds TTL, the task is invalid or has lost its intended value. In practical terms: PaaS does not procrastinate until the last second. It procrastinates only until the last safe moment. 5. Hard delay and not before time Some tasks should not be executed immediately even if resources are available. A task may need to wait because inputs are still stabilizing, a batch is not closed yet, a retry cooldown is required, a business rule defines a minimum delay, or an external process must complete first. For this reason, PaaS may include a not_before parameter. not_before defines the earliest allowed execution start. This gives the task an allowed execution window: not_before <= execution_start <= latest_safe_start < TTL Within this interval, the system may choose the most suitable execution moment according to energy price, spot electricity price, infrastructure load, hardware availability, carbon intensity, urgency, or cost policy. Hard delay and procrastination TTL are not the same thing. Hard delay says: Do not start before this time. Procrastination TTL says: You do not have to start yet, but after this boundary the task begins to become urgent. Latest Safe Start says: After this point, the task can no longer be safely delayed. 6. Possible time structure of a PaaS task A PaaS task may contain several time boundaries: created_at The time when the task was created. not_before The earliest allowed execution time. procrastination_ttl The time until which the task may be safely postponed. execution_time_estimate The expected time needed to complete the task. safety_margin The reserve protecting against uncertainty. latest_safe_start The latest safe execution start, derived from TTL, execution time, and safety margin. valid_until or TTL The end of task validity. If all values are present, the logical ordering may be: created_at <= not_before <= procrastination_ttl <= latest_safe_start < TTL Not every task must define all these values. However, if they are defined, they must not contradict each other. 7. Task states in a PaaS queue A PaaS queue is not only a container of work. It understands the time state of each task. A task may be in one of several states. Delayed The task must not yet run, for example because not_before has not been reached. Safely deferrable The task is valid and may wait. The system may search for a cheaper, greener, or less loaded execution window. Good to execute The task may still wait, but a favorable execution window has appeared, such as low spot electricity price, free GPU capacity, low infrastructure load, or low carbon intensity. Urgent The task is approaching latest_safe_start. Further delay becomes risky. Burning The task has reached latest_safe_start. It should be executed immediately or marked as at risk. Invalid The task has exceeded TTL, or it can no longer be completed before its validity expires. 8. PaaS as a prioritization model PaaS is not only a deferral mechanism. It can also act as a dynamic prioritization layer. In classical queues, priority is often static. A task is assigned a priority such as high, medium, low, or a numeric score when it is created. However, in real systems, urgency changes over time. A task that can safely wait six hours is not urgent now. The same task may become highly urgent five minutes before its latest safe start, even if its original business priority was low. PaaS therefore does not only ask: Can this task be delayed? It also asks: Which task can no longer afford more delay? This makes time part of priority. As current_time approaches latest_safe_start, the urgency of the task increases. Priority can therefore be derived from remaining safe delay time, execution duration, business value, risk of missing the deadline, and current execution cost. A short formulation: PaaS turns time into part of priority. 9. Economic and energy aware execution windows PaaS becomes especially useful when immediate execution and later execution have different costs. A favorable execution window may be determined by: spot electricity price forecast spot electricity price available compute capacity lower infrastructure load lower carbon intensity surplus solar or wind generation cheaper cloud region available GPU capacity customer defined operational window Night electricity is only a simple historical example. A modern PaaS model may use spot electricity prices or energy market forecasts. Cheap energy does not have to occur at night. It may occur during the day when there is surplus solar generation, strong wind generation, low demand, or regional oversupply. PaaS does not say: Run it at night. It says: Run it when execution is favorable, but still safely on time. 10. Example with night electricity A task must generate a daily report, recalculate indexes, or process a large dataset. The result must be ready by 06:00. Execution time is 90 minutes. Safety margin is 15 minutes. TTL is 06:00. The latest safe start is: 06:00 minus 90 minutes minus 15 minutes Therefore: latest_safe_start = 04:15 If the task is created at 1

title: Wirus Zika — nowo pojawiający się czynnik zakaźny przenoszony przez krew
authors: Piotr Radziwon
abstract: Zika virus is an arbowirus from Flavivirus genus. It has broad cellular tropism infecting a wide range of foetal cells as well as adult cells particularly of the male sexual system. It is transmitted by vector — Aedes mosquitos, by infected blood and tissues and also by sexual contact. Testicular immune privilege may explain the persistence of the virus in these tissues, potentially acting as an active reservoir of the virus. In the recent years mosquito-borne Zika virus transmission has been confirmed in 70 countries of South and Central America, Middle Africa, South Asia, and South Pacific Region. The incubation period lasts from several days to one week. In 80% of cases the Zika virus infection is asymptomatic. Symptomatic cases resemble influenza accompanied by skin rush and itching skin on the entire body. Zika virus infection may cause microcephaly and/or damage to the foetus central nervous system. In adults the Guillain-Barre syndrome may occur. Several acute co-infections with dengue virus and/or chikungunya have been reported. It is therefore recommended to perform appropriate multiplexed arboviral testing. In order to confirm Zika virus infection molecular methods (RT-PCR) for viral RNA detection should be used. In some cases serological assays may not be useful. Several known drugs/compounds (eg. chloroquine, azithromycin, sofosbuvir) have been shown effective in the treatment of Zika virus infection. In Poland now there is a 28 day deferral for donors returning from areas where virus transmission has been confirmed or reporting sexual contacts with persons diagnosed with Zika virus infection or travelling to Zika virus affected regions. Such safety measures do not apply to donors of plasma dedicated solely for fractionation.

authors: Vaibhavi Chavda; Dipti Shah
venue: International Journal of Paediatrics and Geriatrics
abstract: Background: Excess iron reserves from repeated transfusions cause various difficulties in B-thalassemia major patients. Hepatic, cardiac, and endocrine dysfunction, growth, sexual maturation, and survival are improved by chelating therapy in iron excess patients. The study aims to examine the impact of these medicines on serum ferritin levels and their effectiveness in decreasing them. These medicines affect kidney, hepatic, white blood cell, and platelet functioning.Methods: This retrospective study at the Inherited Blood Disorder Center in Babylon reviewed 62 β-thalassemia major patients aged 1-14 years, assessing chelation therapy with deferoxamine followed by deferasirox. Evaluations included serum ferritin levels, liver and kidney function tests (ALT, AST, B. urea, S. cr., PPT, WBCs) initially and at 6, 12, and 18 months post-treatment switch. The study aimed to understand the effectiveness and safety of transitioning chelation agents in managing iron overload. Results: Patients with B-Thalassemia major had a mean age of 9.31±2.02 years, with 78.4% older than 10 years. There were 27 (52.9%) male B-Thalassemia significant patients. The male-female ratio was 1.13:1. The initial 6-month serum ferritin value after deferral and Exjade was significantly different. (p<0.001). Significant mean serum ferritin variations (p<0.001) were seen following delay and Exjade treatment at 12 and 18 months. Conclusion: The study found a significant reduction in serum ferritin levels when using Exjade therapy compared to Desferal. However, there were no significant changes in serum creatinine, ALT, AST, platelets, and WBC levels between Exjade and Desferal therapies. This indicates Exjade 's effectiveness in reducing iron overload without adversely affecting liver function, kidney function, or blood counts.

title: Adolescent Relationship Navigation for Vietnamese 14–19: Peer, Romantic, and Family-Conflict Domains and a Domain-Calibrated Operational Practice Set
authors: That Le
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The Vietnamese 14–19 cohort navigates three relational domains simultaneously — peer (friendship, peer hierarchy, social comparison, bullying), romantic (early dating, attraction, sexuality, relationship-end), and family conflict (autonomy negotiation, parental pressure, post-major-decision divergence) — with cultural scripts that systematically under-resource each domain. Peer life is read as either pure resource (the bạn cùng tiến frame) or pure risk (the bạn xấu frame), with the empirical pattern in between unmodelled; romantic life is treated as developmental noise to be deferred until after university (yêu sớm as moral failing), with the consequence that healthy-versus-controlling-relationship discrimination, sexuality and consent literacy, and breakup recovery have no operational scaffolding; family conflict is encoded as filial failure (hỗn, bất hiếu) when the same conflict in Western individualist framings is read as developmentally normative autonomy work. This paper synthesises the adolescent peer-relations literature [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], the adolescent romantic-relations literature [7], [8], [9], [10], [11], the bullying and online-harassment literature [12], [13], [14], [15], the family-autonomy literature [16], [17], [18], [19], and the cross-cultural anchor [20], [21], [22], [23], [24] into a three-domain × research-grounded-pattern × Vietnamese-context-pattern × cultural-reframing matrix. The substantive contribution is a domain-calibrated operational practice set: peer-domain practices (friendship-quality assessment, peer-comparison resistance, bullying response, online-versusoffline calibration), romantic-domain practices (relationship readiness, healthy-versus-controlling discrimination, breakup recovery, evidence-based age-appropriate sexuality and consent, safety), family-conflict-domain practices (autonomy negotiation scripts, parental-pressure response, sibling dynamics, post-majordecision divergence). Three load-bearing reframings discipline the work. (1) The con nhà người ta social-comparison pattern is recognised as a peer-domain stressor that interacts with the peer-hierarchy and social-brain literatures, not a private family rhetoric; the operational counter is dimension-reattribution (carried from I3.3) plus comparison-target diversification, not denial of comparison. (2) Romantic relationships are not pre-emptively pathologised; the operational frame is readiness, healthy-relationship literacy, and exit competence, not deferral. (3) Family conflict during 14–19 is operationally normative and does not signal filial failure; the I3.3 cultural-resource versus cultural-risk decomposition supplies the negotiation grammar without dismissing filial concern. title: Predictors of fractional flow reserve/instantaneous wave-free ratio discordance: impact of tailored diagnostic cut-offs on clinical outcomes of deferred lesions
authors: Ovidio DE FILIPPO; Guglielmo Gallone; Fabrizio D’Ascenzo; Antonio Maria Leone; Massimo Mancone; Giorgio Quadri; Lucia Barbieri; Irene Maria Bossi; Giacomo Giovanni Boccuzzi; Rocco Antonio Montone; Francesco Burzotta; Mario Iannaccone; Antonio Montefusco; Stefano Carugo; Chiara Castelli; Jacopo Oreglia; Enrico Cerrato; Andrea Peirone; Giuseppe Zaccardo; Gennaro Sardella; Giampaolo Niccoli; Pierluigi Omedè; Ferdinando Varbella; Andrea Rognoni; Carlo Trani; Federico Conrotto; Javier Escaned; Gaetano Maria De Ferrari
abstract: BACKGROUND: Patient-related and lesion-related factors may influence instantaneous wave-free ratio (iFR)/fractional flow reserve (FFR) concordance, potentially affecting the safety of revascularization deferral. METHODS: Consecutive patients with at least an intermediate coronary stenosis evaluated by both iFR and FFR were retrospectively enrolled. The agreement between iFR and FFR at their diagnostic cut-offs (FFR 0.80, iFR 0.89) was assessed. Predictors of discordance were assessed using multivariate analyses. Tailored iFR cut-offs according to predictors of discordance best matching an FFR of 0.80 were identified. The impact of reclassification according to tailored iFR cut-offs on major cardiovascular events (MACE: cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or target-lesion revascularization) among deferred lesions was investigated. RESULTS: Two hundred and ninety-nine intermediate coronary stenosis [FFR 0.84 (0.78-0.89), iFR 0.91 (0.87-0.95), 202 left main/left anterior descending (LM/LAD) vessels, 67.6%] of 260 patients were studied. Discordance rate was 23.4% (n = 70, 10.7% iFR-negative discordant, 12.7% iFR-positive discordant). Predictors of discordance were LM/LAD disease, multivessel disease, non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction, smoking, reduced eGFR and hypertension. Lesion reclassification with tailored iFR cut-offs based on patient-level predictors carried no prognostic value among deferred lesions. Reclassification according to lesion location, which was entirely driven by LM/LAD lesions (iFR cut-offs: 0.93 for LM/LAD, 0.89 for non-LM/LAD), identified increased MACE among lesions deferred based on a negative FFR, between patients with a positive as compared with a negative iFR (19.4 vs. 6.1%, P = 0.044), whereas the same association was not observed with the conventional 0.89 iFR cut-off (15 vs. 8.6%, P = 0.303). CONCLUSION: Tailored vessel-based iFR cut-offs carry prognostic value among FFR-negative lesions, suggesting that a one-size-fit-all iFR cut-off might be clinically unsatisfactory.

title: Data and code for: Are Large Language Models Able to Perform or Assist in Crime Scene Investigations?
authors: Daniel Attinger
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Scoring and statistics code, exact prompts, task files with problem identifiers, and every model response with its timing, token counts and cost, for the manuscript Are Large Language Models Able to Perform or Assist in Crime Scene Investigations? (Daniel Attinger, 2026), submitted to Forensic Science International. The study measures whether large language models can carry out the multi-step, abstention-aware reasoning that crime-scene reconstruction requires, using the MuSR benchmark (murder mysteries, object placements, team allocation; Sprague et al., ICLR 2024) with an added I don't know option, plus MMLU-Pro physics and engineering, BBEH and GSM8K as controls. Models: three commercial Claude models (Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5, Claude Sonnet 5, plus Opus 4.5 and Sonnet 4.5 on one split), the hosted open-weight Qwen3.8-27B at 16-bit and 4-bit precision, Qwen3.8-Max and DeepSeek V4 Pro, the same Qwen3.8-27B weights in a 4-bit GGUF file on a rented RTX 3090 and on the author's gaming notebook, and local Gemma 2 9B, Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.5-27B, Qwen2.5-Coder 7B and 14B under Ollama. Contents: eval/ the Python scoring and statistics code (score.py, paired.py, sweep.py, cost-table.py, fresh-compare.py), eval/tasks/ the fixed samples with problem identifiers, eval/runs/ 12,225 recorded model responses (one JSON object per response: model, backend, prompt style, temperature, response text, duration, prompt and output token counts, cost, GPU placement), and the study's own records (RESULTS.md, KNOWN-ISSUES.md, MODEL-PROVENANCE.md, README.md); S1-prompts/ the system instruction and the CoT+ strategy texts verbatim and as JSON; S2-per-problem/ per-problem outcomes for every model and problem type with paired disagreement counts (S2-paired-disagreements.md) and the fresh-item comparison (fresh-compare-2026-09-20.md); S3-preregistered-readings.md the readings of the object-placement runs written before the results were known; S4-generator-selection.md the evidence for the choice of generator for the fresh items, with its quoted pilot stories cut; MANIFEST.txt with the SHA-256 of every file and the reason for every exclusion. The code that sent the problems to the models and ran the campaign is not included; the method is described in full in the manuscript. Licence: the code and documentation are released under the MIT License (LICENSE). The task files are derived from MuSR (MIT), MMLU-Pro (MIT), BBEH (Apache-2.0) and GSM8K (MIT) and keep those licences; see README.md. The fifty freshly generated murder-mystery items used for the contamination test are withheld by the author's decision and are available from the author to the editor under confidentiality.

title: A Theoretical Framework for Executive Compensation, Incentive Alignment, and Performance Management in Capital Intensive Industries
authors: Olaniyi Oluwaseun Oladepo; Kehinde Oyediji
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper proposes a theoretical framework for executive compensation, incentive alignment, and performance management in capital intensive industries characterized by high fixed costs, long investment horizons, and elevated operational and financial risk. Traditional pay-for-performance models often fail to adequately reflect the complexity of value creation in sectors such as energy, infrastructure, manufacturing, mining, and transportation, where outcomes are shaped by multi-year capital allocation decisions rather than short-term earnings fluctuations. The framework integrates agency theory, stewardship theory, and strategic performance management to explain how compensation structures can be designed to balance risk-taking, accountability, and sustainable value generation. The proposed framework conceptualizes executive compensation as a multi-layered system comprising fixed remuneration, short-term incentives, and long-term incentive mechanisms explicitly linked to capital efficiency, asset utilization, safety performance, and resilience metrics. It emphasizes the alignment of executive rewards with lifecycle project performance, return on invested capital, and operational reliability, rather than narrow financial indicators. Performance management is positioned as a dynamic feedback mechanism that connects strategic objectives, capital deployment discipline, and continuous monitoring of operational and non-financial outcomes. The framework further incorporates governance and institutional controls, including board oversight, independent remuneration committees, transparent disclosure, and regulatory constraints, to mitigate agency conflicts and opportunistic behavior. Risk-adjusted performance measures, deferral provisions, clawback clauses, and equity-based incentives are theorized as critical tools for aligning managerial incentives with long-term stakeholder interests. Particular attention is given to the role of incentive symmetry in discouraging excessive leverage, cost overruns, and safety lapses that are common in capital intensive environments. By synthesizing insights across corporate governance, finance, and operations management literature, this framework advances understanding of how executive compensation systems can support disciplined capital management and sustained organizational performance. The contribution lies in offering a coherent analytical lens for scholars and practitioners to evaluate incentive effectiveness in contexts where performance outcomes are delayed, capital is irreversible, and strategic errors are costly. The framework provides a foundation for empirical testing across industries and jurisdictions, and for informing compensation policy design that promotes long-term efficiency, resilience, and value creation in capital intensive enterprises globally under varying market cycles, ownership structures, and regulatory regimes.
