title: A Digital Twin Framework for Multimodal Operator-Centered Human–Cobot Collaboration in Assembly Tasks
authors: David Alfaro-Viquez; Mauricio-Andrés Zamora-Hernández; Michael Fernandez-Vega; David Ortiz-Pérez; José García‐Rodríguez; Jorge Azorín-López
abstract: Current digital twin frameworks focused on human–robot collaboration rarely take into account the sensory degradation of real industrial environments, nor do they integrate the operator as an active agent within the system. This research presents a multimodal digital twin framework for a dual-arm collaborative robot at an assembly station; the system was developed using ROS 2 Jazzy and CoppeliaSim as the simulator. The architecture integrates three main components: the first is a perception layer that captures voice commands using Whisper ASR and the state of the workspace using a hybrid YOLO + ViT visual pipeline, both with per-channel metadata; the second consists of a Confidence-Weighted Late Fusion engine that dynamically adjusts the weight of each modality based on real-time signal quality, so that each fusion decision can be reconstructed from the signals that generated it; and the third component is a Reference Resolver that grounds linguistic intent within the visual context of the scene and in the fusion weights, using a local instance of Llama 3.1 8B that does not transmit audio, transcripts, or images outside the system. The framework was evaluated using 210 iterations distributed across seven degradation conditions of increasing severity, comparing adaptive fusion against a baseline of fixed weights (0.5/0.5). Under clean conditions and under visual degradation of any severity, both configurations achieved 100% accuracy. Under severe auditory degradation (SNR 0 dB), adaptive fusion activated the safety gate and refrained from executing most commands (13.3% accuracy), while the fixed-weight baseline executed more commands (60% accuracy) but made three incorrect object selections; under severe dual degradation, the pattern repeated (13.3% vs. 40%, with five incorrect selections in the baseline). The adaptive system made no grounding errors in the 210 executions, compared to eight in the baseline, substituting incorrect execution with conservative abstention when no modality provided a reliable signal. The implementation, featuring a versioned degradation protocol and a fixed seed, provides a reproducible benchmark for evaluating multimodal fusion strategies in human–cobot interaction.

title: Intraoperative FLIP to guide revisional hiatal hernia repair: early experience and outcomes
authors: Paul Symansky; Connor Caputo; Hemasat Alkhatib; Ramiro Cadena Semanate; Voranaddha Vacharathit; Kevin M El-Hayek
abstract: BACKGROUND: Revisional hiatal hernia repair (rHHR) represents a challenge in foregut surgery, given scarring, distorted anatomy, and high risk of morbidity. Traditional methods of intraoperative assessment, such as bougie calibration and endoscopic inspection, are subjective and lack physiologic correlation. The functional luminal imaging probe (FLIP) offers objective, real-time assessment of esophagogastric junction (EGJ) diameter, distensibility, and cross-sectional area. This study evaluates the utility of intraoperative FLIP to guide surgical decision-making and assess outcomes in a cohort of complex patients undergoing rHHR. METHODS: A retrospective review was conducted evaluating patients who underwent FLIP-guided rHHR from 2020 to 2025 at an urban safety-net hospital. Intraoperative FLIP measurements, specifically the diameter (D) and distensibility index (DI), were used to tailor surgical management, including decisions to take down, preserve, or alter the fundoplication. Longitudinal follow-up assessed symptom resolution and quality of life (QOL) using the GERD-Health-Related Quality of Life (GERD-HRQL) questionnaire. RESULTS: A total of 17 patients undergoing 18 revisional operations were analyzed (mean age 47.5 years; 88% female). Intraoperative FLIP values prompted a change in surgical management in 61% (11/18) of cases. Modifications included preservation of prior fundoplication (36%), tightening an existing fundoplication (27%), deferral of fundoplication (27%), and changing fundoplication type (9%). At a mean follow-up of 24.9 months, GERD-HRQL scores improved from 26.7 ± 8.5 preoperatively to 16.5 ± 12.9 postoperatively (p = 0.034). At long-term follow-up (mean 38.8 months), persistent symptoms were noted, including reflux requiring medication (70.6%) and dysphagia (35.3%), though 64.7% of symptomatic patients were managed nonoperatively. CONCLUSIONS: FLIP-guided revisional HHR facilitates a tailored surgical approach, prompting alterations in management based on objective physiologic data. While clinically meaningful improvements in quality of life were observed, the persistence of symptoms in this high-risk population highlights the intrinsic complexity of revisional foregut surgery and the need for future prospective studies.

title: A real-world experience of palbociclib-induced adverse events in women with HR-positive/Her2-negative metastatic breast cancer.
authors: Geoffrey Alan Watson; Oana M. Deac; Razia Aslam; Richard O’Dwyer; Sue Sukor; Michael John Kennedy
abstract: e13061 Background: Palbociclib is a novel small molecule inhibitor of cyclin dependant kinases 4 and 6, and has been shown to improve progression free survival in HR positive metastatic breast cancer patients when used in conjunction other endocrine therapies, with a manageable safety profile. The aim of our study was to provide a real world experience of the adverse events (AEs) reported on this treatment. Methods: We performed a retrospective, single centre audit of HR positive metastatic breast cancer patients treated with Palbociclib over a six month period in an Irish tertiary hospital. Results: 64 patients were included in the analysis. Median age was 62.5 years. Palbociclib was most commonly used in combination with Letrozole (n = 40). 10 patients received Palbociclib as 1st line treatment. The median number of cycles completed was 5 (range 1-9). 28 patients (44%) had treatment deferrals due to neutropenia, with a median time to first deferral of 4 weeks. Only one patient developed febrile neutropenia. 16 patients (25%) required dose reductions, however there was no association with an increased risk of progressive disease (p = 0.56). Only 3 patients discontinued treatment due to poor tolerance. AEs reported included fatigue (n = 28), gastrointestinal complaints (n = 17), infection (n = 11), thrombocytopenia (n = 7), anaemia (n = 7), alopecia (n = 3), deranged liver function tests (n = 3) and decreased appetite (n = 2). Of note 7 thromboembolic events (TEs) were recorded, with one patient suffering from a saddle pulmonary embolus. Conclusions: To our knowledge this is the largest real world analysis of the AEs associated with Palbociclib therapy. While a significant proportion may experience neutropenia, this is often uncomplicated. If dose reductions due to neutropenia are warranted this is not associated with an increased likelihood of progression. While the PALOMA III trial reported a 2% incidence of TEs, we observed a 9% incidence rate. It is difficult to ascertain whether these events were palbociclib related or disease related, thus clinical suspicion and awareness are paramount and further studies are recommended to determine if prophylactic anticoagulation may benefit these patients.

title: When Blood Remembers Its Sex: Toward Truly Personalized Transfusion Medicine
authors: Sotirios P. Fortis; Styliani I. Kokoris; Pavlos Kelepousidis; Georgios Dryllis; Maria-Aspasia Kosma; Theodoros Pittaras; Anastasios G. Kriebardis; Serena I. Valsami
abstract: Background: Biological sex differences are well-recognized as non-negligible factors in implementing precision medicine practice. Sex chromosomes influence protein expression and signaling, and thus cellular pathways are often regulated differently. Additionally, the importance of sex as a biological variable has gained significant traction in biomedical research, including transfusion medicine. Regarding transfusion medicine, several studies reveal the role of gender in blood transfusion, blood donors’ behavior towards donation, blood products’ composition and storage, transfusion therapy, and possibly post-transfusion patient outcomes. Methods: In this review, the role of sex and gender in the whole transfusion chain (from the blood donor to the blood product and the patient) is assessed and summarized using data from observational studies, registry analyses, and randomized trials. Results: Female donors face higher deferral rates due to biological factors (iron deficiency, low hemoglobin, pregnancy) and sociocultural factors (caregiving responsibilities, misinformation). However, women are more likely to donate based on empathy, moral duty, or community responsibility and are more consistent in sustaining voluntary donation during crises. Men donate more frequently, typically driven by external motivators, and provide red blood cell (RBC) products with higher hemoglobin content, whereas RBCs from female donors exhibit greater metabolic stability and reduced hemolysis during storage. Plasma from multiparous women possibly contains alloantibodies associated with adverse transfusion reactions, namely transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI). Platelet function also varies by sex, though its possible clinical impact is still unknown. Although observational studies suggest sex-mismatched transfusions are associated with increased morbidity and mortality—particularly in transfusions from female donors to male recipients—large registries and randomized controlled trials show inconsistent or negligible effect on survival. Conclusions: Donor and recipient sex are emerging variables of possible clinical importance in transfusion practice. Incorporating sex-informed insights into donor recruitment, blood product handling and transfusion policies may improve safety while advancing precision medicine. Further large-scale trials are needed to elucidate the impact of sex in transfusion, identify and eliminate possible risks, and bridge the gap between biological insights and clinical practice.

title: Glycemic Thresholds for Hair Transplantation: An Evidence-Informed Framework for Follicular Unit Excision
authors: Richard Moleno
venue: International Society of Hair Restoration Surgery
abstract: ABSTRACT Introduction: Follicular unit excision (FUE) hair transplantation entails the creation of hundreds to several thousand puncture wounds in a vascularized scalp tissue bed, producing a wound environment physiologically susceptible to the impaired healing mechanisms of diabetes mellitus. Despite the clinical relevance of preoperative glycemic control to graft survival, no specialty-specific guidance exists on acceptable preoperative glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) levels for FUE candidates with diabetes. Methods: A narrative review of published guidelines, consensus statements, and peer-reviewed literature from 2018–2025 was conducted across perioperative medicine, anesthesiology, dermatologic surgery, wound care, and plastic surgery. Databases searched included PubMed/MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar using the search terms; the full search strategy is provided in the Methods section. Guideline bodies reviewed included the American Diabetes Association (ADA), the UK Centre for Perioperative Care (CPOC), the Society for Ambulatory Anesthesia (SAMBA), the American Society of Plastic Surgeons (ASPS), the Wound Healing Society (WHS), and the European Society of Cardiology (ESC). Results: Across the specialties reviewed, preoperative HbA1c thresholds consistently cluster between 7.0%–8.5%, with both CPOC and ESC carrying recommendations for referral or deferral at or above 8.5% and the majority of plastic surgery and dermatologic surgery practitioners targeting values at or below 7.5%–8.0%. Meta-analytic data from elective abdominal surgery demonstrate a statistically significant increase in wound infection risk at HbA1c values exceeding 7%, with risk escalating continuously rather than at a single cutoff. Conclusion: To date, the author is not aware of any studies that have directly evaluated HbA1c as a predictor of graft survival in FUE. A tiered, risk-stratified HbA1c framework is offered for community consideration in FUE patient selection: proceed with standard precautions below 7.0%; proceed with optimization and multidisciplinary coordination between 7.0%–7.9%; exercise caution with documented shared decision-making between 8.0%–8.4%; defer for glycemic optimization between 8.5%–9.4%; treat values at or above 9.5% as a relative contraindication. Consideration for adoption of this framework by hair transplant surgeons supports consistent patient selection, informed consent, and patient safety.

title: Active Information Acquisition & Value of Information: When Should an Intelligent System Ask, Search, Retrieve, Measure, Experiment, Use a Tool — or Stop?
authors: Mark Lamont
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Intelligent systems increasingly choose not only what action to take, but whether to acquire additional information before acting. The relevant information action may be a search, retrieval, measurement, experiment, human clarification, feature acquisition, sensor observation, tool invocation, expert consultation or additional internal computation. R145 asks when such active inquiry adds incremental value after the complete cost and consequence of acquisition are counted. The study uses a comprehensive, adversarial and claim-centred evidence method with an evidence cut-off of 1 October 2026. The frozen research corpus contains 133 candidate works, of which 127 are conservatively eligible substantive sources after publication-class and duplicate-manifestation controls. Fifteen material propositions were audited for independent evidence, counter-evidence, freshness and prior art before the evidence state was frozen. The evidence supports a distinction between information quantity and decision value. Information gain is a legitimate objective where knowledge itself is terminal utility, but in consequential decision problems the value of an observation depends on what it can change in the downstream decision. The practically important quantity is therefore net acquisition value after monetary, computational, latency, interruption, privacy, reliability, side-effect and opportunity costs are considered. Across active learning, feature acquisition, Bayesian experimental design, bandits, active sensing, metareasoning, clarification, retrieval and selective prediction, two recurrent failure modes emerge: under-acquisition, where a system acts without information that would materially change the result, and over-acquisition, where it expends resources obtaining redundant, low-value or distracting information. Calibration is an important upstream dependency, while strong counter-evidence shows that sophisticated active-acquisition mechanisms do not universally outperform simpler, greedy, passive or lightweight alternatives. The thesis therefore develops a decision-relevant acquisition synthesis rather than a new fundamental law. An intelligent system should compare the expected net value of acquiring additional information with the value of acting, stopping, abstaining, deferring or escalating under the same state. The acquisition controller itself must earn its complexity against strong simpler comparators. A twelve-experiment falsification programme is specified to test the resulting propositions. R145 is Thesis 05 in an eighteen-thesis independent research programme derived from the Mazikeen research agenda. It is a research thesis and does not constitute a Mazikeen implementation or governance decision.

title: Static Arabic Sign Language Glove Corpus and Signer-Independent Evaluation Code
authors: mohamed aktham; Ammar F Abbas; Ahmed S. Abdullah; Z.T. Al-Qaysi; Omar Adel Labeb
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: corpus of 9,400 recordings of 94 static Arabic Sign Language signs, together with the code that reproduces the signer-independent analyses reported in the accompanying article. The vocabulary comprises 19 numerals, 28 alphabet letters and 47 one-handed word signs selected from the Unified Arabic Sign Language Dictionary for the Deaf (Part II, 2007). Ten volunteers each performed every sign ten times with the right hand, giving exactly 100 samples per class. Every execution was checked against the dictionary reference by a sign-language expert from the session video, and trials with execution errors were repeated. Each record is one settled hand posture described by twelve sensor channels: wrist orientation from an MPU-9250 inertial measurement unit, finger flexion from five resistive flex sensors, and four binary inter-finger contact states from FSR402 sensors. Acquisition used an ESP-WROOM-32 module with a 12-bit converter. The corpus contains no time series. The deposit includes the dataset, a data dictionary, the class list, the result files underlying every table and figure of the article, and code that reproduces the representation comparison, the signer-identification probe, the few-shot calibration curve, the selective-prediction analysis, the permutation-importance analysis, the angular-offset analysis and the class-pair separability analysis under leave-one-signer-out cross-validation. Three properties of the corpus are documented for users: session and class are perfectly nested, so no analysis of these data can separate a session effect from a sign effect; the recorded yaw carries a participant-specific offset of 25 to 79 degrees within a session; and 49 of 47,000 flex readings lie at the converter limits and are handled inside training folds by the supplied code. The corpus does not support claims about dynamic signing, continuous signing, coarticulation, non-manual grammatical marking or two-handed signs, none of which it contains. Ethics approval: Research Ethics Committee of the College of Computer Science and Mathematics, Tikrit University, Approval No. 103, 14 October 2025. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants, including consent for public release of the anonymised sensor recordings

title: Ethical practices in the area of blood transfusion
authors: Kanchan Bhardwaj; Rajni Bassi
venue: GMC PATIALA Journal of research and medical education
abstract: National Blood Policy and Drug & Cosmetic Act aims to curb unethical transfusion practices in India. These are related to donors, patients, blood establishments and clinicians. Ethical practices relating to Donors - Blood donation is a gift, so should be based on voluntary, non-remunerated repeat blood-donation. These have low prevalence of transfusion transmissible infections. No one should be forced to donate for family, economic or any other reason. Blood safety depends partly on the information provided by the donor. Unethical practices involve wilfully concealing information about high risk behaviour or medical history. Predonation counselling plays a pivotal role in sensitizing donors for self-deferral. Donor confidentiality, notification and consent are important ethical issues. Donor consent for donation of blood/its components and to the subsequent use of the blood by the blood establishment; regarding acceptance to the risk associated with donation procedure; for testing; for notification about abnormal results and for plasma fractionation for derivation of plasma products & their usage in any hospital is must. Ethical practices related to Patients - Unethical practices relating to patients are more common in our country. Patients do not have access to safe blood, free of charge, or need for replacement or the option of giving informed consent for transfusion after explaining the known risks and benefits of blood transfusion and/or alternative therapies or the right to accept or refuse the transfusion. They should be informed, if harmed and given due compensation. Ethical practices relating to Blood establishments - It is unethical to have a profit motive by the blood establishments. Wastage should be avoided to safeguard the interest of all potential donors &recipients. Ethical practices relating to Clinicians - There are no national guidelines for safe transfusion which leads to unethical/inappropriate transfusions. Rational use of blood helps to cater 4 different patients from single unit of whole blood. This ensures appropriate dosage of the required component and saves from adverse effects of unwanted component transfusion.

title: Predictors of fractional flow reserve/instantaneous wave-free ratio discordance documented during functional coronary stenosis assessment: impact of tailored diagnostic cut-offs on long-term outcomes
authors: Ovidio DE FILIPPO; Guglielmo Gallone; F. D’Ascenzo; Andrea Peirone; C Castelli; Antonio Maria Leone; Massimo Mancone; Enrico Cerrato; Giampaolo Niccoli; Antonio Rognoni; Ferdinando Varbella; Pierluigi Omedè; Federico Conrotto; Javier Escaned; Gaetano Maria De Ferrari
abstract: Abstract Background Patient- and lesion-related factors may influence concordance between instantaneous wave-free ratio (iFR) and fractional flow reserve (FFR), potentially affecting safety of revascularization deferral. Methods Consecutive patients with at least an intermediate coronary stenosis evaluated by both iFR and FFR were retrospectively enrolled. Revascularization was at physician's discretion. The agreement between IFR and FFR at their diagnostic cut-offs (FFR 0.80, iFR 0.89) according to patient- and lesion-level characteristics was assessed. Multivariate analyses were carried to identify the independent predictors of discordance. Tailored iFR cut-offs according to predictors of discordance best matching an FFR of 0.80 were identified by receiver-operating characteristic (ROC) curves. The impact of reclassification according to tailored iFR cut-offs on major cardiovascular events (MACE: cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or target lesion revascularization) among deferred lesions was investigated. Results 299 coronary stenosis (diameter stenosis 54±14%, FFR 0.84 [0.78–0.89], iFR 0.91 [0.87–0.95], left main/left anterior descending [LM/LAD] vessel 67.6%) of 260 patients were studied, and 46.5% were revascularized. Discordance rate was 23.4% (10.7% iFR-negative discordant, 12.7% iFR-positive discordant). Independent predictors of discordance were LM/LAD disease, multivessel disease, non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction presentation, smoking, reduced glomerular filtration rate and hypertension. Lesion reclassification with tailored iFR-cut-offs based on patient-level predictors carried no prognostic value among deferred lesions. Reclassification according to lesion location, which was entirely driven by LM/LAD lesions (iFR-cut-offs: 0.93 for LM/LAD, 0.89 for non-LM/LAD), identified increased MACE among lesions deferred based on a negative FFR, between patients with a positive as compared to a negative iFR (19.4% vs. 6.1%, p=0.044), while the same association was not observed with the conventional 0.89 iFR cut-off (15.0% vs 8.6%, p=0.303). Conclusion Tailored vessel-based iFR cut-offs carry prognostic value among FFR negative lesions, suggesting that iFR may more safely defer revascularization of LM/LAD lesions than FFR and that a single iFR cut-off might be clinically unsatisfactory. title: Knowing When to Defer: Trustworthy Multimodal AI for BI-RADS-Derived Management Using Paired Mammography and Ultrasound
authors: Muhammad Nouman; Ryo Haraguchi
abstract: Background: Breast imaging ends in a management decision, from routine return to biopsy, yet most models are evaluated by accuracy alone and say nothing about when they may be wrong. We present a trust-aware multimodal model that reads paired mammography and ultrasound, recommends one of three BI-RADS-derived management actions, and returns to the radiologist the cases it cannot call. Methods: Two foundation encoders are adapted with low-rank adapters and combined by a mask-aware fusion head. A trustworthiness layer adds calibration, conformal prediction sets, selective deferral, and an atypicality flag. We evaluated our method on the Breast Cancer Multimodal Imaging Dataset (BCMID), comprising 332 cases from 323 patients at a single centre. The reference standard is a three-class management grouping we derive from the reporting radiologist’s BI-RADS assessment, so performance is in concordance with that derived label rather than with pathology, observed patient management or longitudinal clinical outcome. Results: Macro AUROC was 0.759 and balanced accuracy was 0.556. Isotonic calibration reduced calibration error from 0.088 to 0.052, and prediction sets reached an empirical coverage of 0.934 at a mean set size of 2.32. Deferring the least confident 30% by a retrospective ranking of the pooled cohort raised balanced accuracy to 0.631. Two of 63 positive-management cases were under-triaged and 15 routed to additional imaging, with a recall of 0.730; freezing the encoders left macro AUROC at 0.756 but raised the under-triage count to twelve. Conclusions: Error rate and error direction are separable properties, and neither accuracy nor macro AUROC records the direction. The system therefore pairs each recommendation with calibrated probabilities, a conformal set of plausible actions and an explicit defer option, so uncertain cases return to the radiologist. These results establish an internally validated operating profile for radiologist-facing support; clinical safety, deployment readiness and benefit to patients still require external and prospective evaluation.

title: Optimizing Computational Economics : A Framework for LLM SLM Hybrid Orchestration and Semantic Routing
authors: Anteneh Tessema
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper, titled "Optimizing Computational Economics: A Framework for LLM-SLM Hybrid Orchestration and Semantic Routing" by Anteneh Tessema, introduces an architectural solution to reduce the high costs and latency associated with modern enterprise AI systems. Here is a breakdown of the paper's core components: The Core Problem: Computational Over-Provisioning. The author argues that current enterprise AI systems are inefficient because they are "model-centric rather than workload-aware". Organizations typically send all tasks to massive, frontier Large Language Models (LLMs), regardless of how simple the task is. Because industry data suggests that 70-90% of enterprise requests are relatively simple tasks (like formatting or data extraction), using a massive LLM for everything wastes money and slows down response times—a problem the paper formalizes as "Technometric Inefficiency". The Proposed Solution: The Hybrid Inference Pipeline (HIP). To solve this, the paper proposes a new architecture that shifts from a single massive model to a routed "model cascade". The system works in three steps: Semantic Routing: An intelligent routing layer evaluates incoming prompts based on their structural complexity, task domain, and historical failure data. SLM-First Execution: The system first attempts to process the prompt using a much cheaper, faster Small Language Model (SLM). Calibrated Abstention (Escalation): A verification mechanism checks the confidence of the SLM's draft. If the confidence meets a certain threshold, the answer is served. If the confidence is too low, the system abstains and automatically escalates the task to the heavy-duty LLM. Validation and Key Findings The author modeled this approach using Llama-3-8B as the SLM and GPT-4o as the LLM across standard industry benchmarks. Massive Savings on Simple Tasks: For data extraction workloads, the hybrid model successfully resolved 84% of queries at the SLM level, resulting in an 83% cost reduction and a latency improvement of over 60% compared to using the LLM alone. Diminishing Returns on Complex Tasks: For complex reasoning tasks, the SLM failed frequently, meaning 58% of queries had to be escalated. The paper notes that these highly complex tasks are better off bypassing the SLM entirely to avoid sequential latency penalties. Finally, the paper outlines critical failure modes engineers must watch out for when building these systems, such as "silent misrouting" (when an SLM confidently hallucinates an answer) and "calibration drift" (when shifting data causes the routing thresholds to fail)

title: Therapy of allergic rhinitis in routine care: evidence-based benefit assessment of freely combined use of various active ingredients
authors: Ludger Klimek; Ingrid Casper; Karl‐Christian Bergmann; Tilo Biedermann; Jean J. Bousquet; Peter William Hellings; Kirsten Jung; Hans Friedrich Merk; Heidi Olze; Ralph Mösges; Wolfgang W. Schlenter; Moritz Gröger; Johannes Ring; Adam M. Chaker; Oliver Pfaar; Wolfgang Wehrmann; Torsten Zuberbier; Sven Becker
abstract: Abstract Background Allergic rhinitis (AR) continues to increase in incidence and is the most common allergic disease. If abstention of the allergen triggering substances is not possible, allergen-specific immunotherapy (AIT) as causal treatment or a drug therapy with mast cell stabilizers, antihistamines (AHs), glucocorticoids (GCs), leukotriene (LT) receptor antagonists and decongestants is indicated. Despite these diverse therapeutic options, studies on the real-life care situation of patients with AR regularly show that a considerable proportion of patients do not feel adequately treated with monotherapy of the usual drugs and therefore use several preparations with different active ingredients simultaneously and in various combinations. However, such parallel applications of several active ingredients are normally not tested in approval studies and therefore carry a potential risk of side effects or lack of efficacy. Methods For the present publication, a focused literature search in PubMed, Livivo and on the World Wide Web for the previous 20 years (period 01/1999 to 01/2020) was carried out. This literature search included original and review articles in German or English. A further analysis of current publications was also conducted for German-language journals that are not available in international literature databases. Results AHs and nasal GCs represent the therapeutic standard in AR. Their efficacy is well documented for several preparations. The evidence for combination therapies is documented very well for a fixed combination of azelastine and fluticasone (MP29-02). For the simultaneous use of non-fixed combined monopreparations, only a few efficacy and safety studies based on modern evidence criteria exist. Conclusion The free combination therapies of mast cell stabilizers, decongestants, AHs and nasal GCs, frequently used in the routine care of patients with AR, cannot be recommended because they are not evidence-based. Due to the fact that over-the-counter antiallergic drugs are not reimbursable in Germany, there is no medical supervision of the therapy. In addition, there are doubts about appropriate treatment, especially of patients with persistent rhinitis with severe symptoms, as these patients often use several preparations at the same time to alleviate their symptoms.

title: Malaria Disease Recommendations for Solid Organ Transplant Recipients and Donors
authors: Lígia Câmera Pierrotti; Marilyn E. Levi; Sílvia Maria Di Santi; Aluísio Augusto Cotrim Segurado; Eskild Petersen
abstract: INTRODUCTION AND EPIDEMIOLOGY Malaria is an acute febrile infection caused by 5 species of Plasmodium (P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, and P. knowlesi). A life-threatening illness, malaria is regarded as the most important human parasitic disease. Over 40% of the world's population lives in tropical areas of sub-Saharan Africa, Asia, Oceania, and Latin America where malaria is transmitted. Globally, 214 million new cases of malaria were estimated in 2015 with 438 000 deaths,1 with Latin America accounting for about 10% of total malaria cases.2 About 90% of malaria cases in the Americas occur in the Amazon basin shared by Brazil, Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, French Guiana, Peru, Suriname, and Venezuela, whereas the other 10% occur outside Amazon regions, mainly along the coastal areas and lowland Andean valleys, as well as in some North and Central American countries, from Mexico to Panama2 (Figure 1). Brazil is responsible for 60% of the cases and for half of the deaths due to malaria in the region.2 Since 2000, substantial decreases in malaria incidence have been observed in the World Health Organization (WHO) Region of the Americas, and several countries are in preelimination and elimination phases, including Argentina, Belize, Costa Rica, Ecuador, El Salvador, Mexico, and Paraguay.1FIGURE 1: Confirmed malaria cases per 1000 population, 2013. Source: WHO Malaria Report 2014.3Although only about 8% of estimated global cases are due to P. vivax infections,3 in Latin American countries, this plasmodial species accounts for about 75% of malaria cases; the remaining 25% are caused by P. falciparum, and less than 0.1% by P. malariae.2 Malaria is typically transmitted to humans by the bite of infected Anopheles mosquitoes. Less commonly, malaria may also be acquired by blood transfusions, sharing contaminated needles and syringes, by means of mother-to-child transmission, or after solid-organ transplantation (SOT).4 Posttransplant malaria has been rarely reported in the literature even in endemic areas.5,6 One potential reason for this uncommon complication among SOT recipients is that areas of malaria risk generally have very low transplant activity. Brazil, for instance, is the country that accounts for the second largest absolute number of kidney and liver transplant procedures in the world.7 Amazon basin, where 99.8% of Brazilian malaria cases occur, was, however, responsible for less than 2% of the national supply of organs and transplant procedures in 2015.7 In the reported malaria infections associated with transplants, the source of infection has not always been possible to define. The infection can be a consequence of a donor-derived infection (DDI), or a reactivation of previous infection in the recipient (related to relapses in the case of P. vivax and P. ovale because of the reactivation of dormant hypnozoites in the liver or recrudescence because of persistent parasite in the blood despite immune response or treatment), or de novo posttransplant infection by the bite of Anopheles spp mosquitoes in endemic settings. DDI has been reported through transfusion of blood and blood products, through red blood cells (RBCs) within the transplanted organ, and through the transplanted liver from donors who were infected by P. vivax and P. ovale, because of the persistence of hypnozoites within hepatocytes when infection is due to either of these plasmodial species.4 Most malaria cases reported among SOT recipients have been described after kidney transplant. The potential of DDI of malaria are summarized in Table 1.TABLE 1: Malaria cases reported in SOT recipients probably through infected graft or blood transfusions posttransplantCLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS The malaria parasite life cycle involves 2 hosts and is illustrated in Figure 2.8 When the infected female of Anopheles mosquito takes a blood meal to enable the maturation of the eggs, sporozoites are injected to the dermis and start a human cycle. After remaining for up to 6 hours in the dermis, some of the sporozoites cross the capillary endothelium, reach the bloodstream, and infect hepatocytes. Inside liver cells, asexual reproduction begins, named schizogony, which results in the formation of liver schizonts, that release the merozoite to the bloodstream.FIGURE 2: Biological cycle of the parasite in human malaria. Source from Zhang et al.8At the end of the initial asexual replication in the liver (the preerythrocytic phase), thousands of unicelular parasitic forms, the merozoites, are released to the bloodstream, thus initiating the erytrhocyte cycle. P. vivax and P. ovale can generate dormant stage parasites (hypnozoites) that persist in the hepatocytes and may resume the replication after a variable period (weeks, or even years later). The hypozoites reactivation accounts for the reappearance of symptoms in relapses. In the blood, the released merozoites infect RBCs and initiate a new asexual schizogonic reproduction (erythrocytic cycle). The ring stage trophozoites mature into schizonts, rupture RBCs, and release merozoites that invade other erytrhocytes. Some parasites differentiate into sexual erytrhocytic stages (gametocytes), which are the forms that will infect the anopheline vector (vector cycle). It is important to highlight that the preerythrocytic cycle is asymptomatic and that clinical disease starts after infected RBCs periodically release merozoites and induce fever. Symptoms of uncomplicated malaria are nonspecific and indistinguishable from viral, bacterial, and other parasitic infections, including fever, chills, malaise, myalgia, arthralgia, and headache. Malaria symptoms appear 7 to 30 days after the mosquito bite.9 The duration of hepatic schizogony determines variation in the incubation period of malaria; shorter periods are observed with P. falciparum and P. vivax and the longer periods with P. malariae. However, longer incubation periods up to 3 months from possible exposure may occur and should be investigated immediately to permit prompt treatment. Prophylaxis with antimalarial drugs can delay the appearance of malaria symptoms by weeks or even months after the traveler has left endemic areas.9 If untreated, the disease can lead to severe complications and death. The severity of the disease is related to the type of transplantation, Plasmodium species, intensity of parasitemia, immunosuppression status, and delays in diagnosis and in onset of antimalarial therapy.10-12P. falciparum and P. knowlesi release a higher number of merozoites from the liver. Therefore, they are able to infect a large number of RBCs and can cause rapidly progressive severe illness, with the highest rates of complications and mortality; whereas P. vivax, P. ovale, and P. malariae, are associated with lower parasitemia and are less likely to cause severe manifestations. Severe disease is characterized by 1 or more of the following clinical and laboratory criteria: impaired consciousness or coma, severe normocytic anemia (hemoglobin, < 7 g/dL), thrombocytopenia, renal failure, acute respiratory distress syndrome, hypotension, disseminated intravascular coagulation, spontaneous bleeding, acidosis (elevated lactate), hemoglobinuria, jaundice, repetead generalized seizures, and/or level of parasitemia according to the patient immune response. A parasitemia of 2% or more of the RBC in nonimmune individuals and 5% or more RBC in semi-immunes are classified as severe malaria.13 Posttransplant malaria has not been necessarily associated with poor outcomes when compared with infections in the general population.12 Immunossupression, however, may be associated with fatality. A previous case of of P. malariae infection was reported in an asplenic patient from Brazil who acquired the parasite from blood transfusion during surgery, even though P. malariae is usually characterized by a benign disease in the general population.14 DIAGNOSIS Different diagnostic approaches should be taken into account for malaria: point-of-care diagnosis for symptomatic infections and the challenge of detecting parasites in asymptomatic infections, characterized by submicroscopic parasitemia. In the context of SOT, the focus must rely on sensitive techniques for pretransplant malaria screening aiming at the detection of low-level parasitemia. The Giemsa-stained thick blood smear microscopy remains the gold standard for malaria diagnosis, even though this technique is unchanged because it was introduced more than a hundred years ago. Conventional routine microscopy presents a limit of detection between 50 and 500 parasites/μL.15,16 Nonetheless, microscopy enables identification of individual species and developmental stages and provides a quantitative tool for monitoring response to treatment and detecting relapse. Detection of lower parasitemia (down to 5 parasites/μL) has been reported in some studies performed by very well-trained personnel.17,18 However, in individuals with low parasitemia or mixed infections, the accuracy of diagnosis can be challenging even to expert microscopists.19 Alternatively, rapid diagnostic test (RDT) is based on the identification of plasmodial antigens using immunochromatography. In some cases, detection is species-specific, such as P. falciparum histidine-rich protein (PfHRP) 2; in others, detection is based on pan-Plasmodium lactate dehydrogenase (pan-pLDH), P. vivax-specific and P. falciparum-specific pLDH or genus-specific aldolase (pan-aldolase).20 The specificity and sensitivity of these tests vary considerably according to the comercially available RDT used and the Plasmodium species (sensitivity is higher for P. falciparum and lower for all other species).21 However, among 200 RDTs products evaluated by the WHO, the limit of detection was 200 parasites/μL.22 Other disadvantages are that the test cannot quantify parasitemia; therefore, it is not useful to monitor therapy, exhibits cross-reactivity against human rheumatoid fator22 and false-negative results due to deletions of PfHRP2 and PfHRP3 genes.23 In addition, the higher reatogenicity and stability of HRP2 confer higher sensitivity to this test compared with lactate dehydrogenase and aldolase, but may yield false-positive results because of the persistence of PfHRP2 in the peripheral blood after treatment. Because of their performance and limitations, RDTs are considered useful in remote endemic areas where rapid diagnosis of malaria is needed but a skilled personnel to perform the gold standard microscopy may not be available.21 After the advent of molecular tools for malaria diagnosis, several protocols were reported, mainly targeting 18S ribosomal RNA gene sequences, detecting 0.05 to 5 parasites/μL.24 Snounou and colleagues25 developed a very sensitive nested PCR, able to differentiate between P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. malariae, and P. ovale. However, this technique is laborious and time-consuming. Genus-specific real-time PCR with limit of detection of 0.35 parasites/μL26 is an alternative for screening blood samples. Higher sensitivity can be achieved using larger volumes of blood, increasing the limit of detection to 0.022 arasites/μL of blood.27 The primers used for genomic molecular detecting tests can be common to all Plasmodium species (panspecific) or specie specific. Serologic tests are not suitable for the diagnosis of the malaria disease but rather measures past exposure, because antibodies can be detected even after cure, remaining in high titers even for years, particularly in patients repeatedly exposed to reinfections.28 RISK ASSESSMENT Donors and candidates who are at risk for malaria infection are divided into those who were born or raised in endemic areas and travelers.29 They may be apparently healthy and/or may also have been exposed to malaria in the distant past. The most important screening tool is therefore epidemiological; if history suggests that there is malaria risk or is unclear, laboratory confirmation should be obtained.30,31 Epidemiological History An epidemiological history relevant for malaria for both donor and candidate must be routinely investigated as outlined in Table 2.TABLE 2: Epidemiological history for malaria risk evaluation41,69,71Screening for Asymptomatic Parasitemia Residents of malarious areas are subjected to repeated exposures, resulting in a semi-immune status, often insufficient to achieve long-term or protective immunity.32 As a result, asymptomatic infections with low numbers of circulating parasites may develop.33 If they relocate to a nonendemic area they often resolve their infections, usually in 2 years for P. falciparum and in 3 years for P. vivax or P. ovale, whereas P. malariae infections persist indefinitely. Screening testing possibilities include thick blood smear (less sensitive), RDT for plasmodial antigens detection, NAT, nucleic acid testing (NAT) and antimalarial antibody detection.30 Screening for Plasmodium parasitemia with microscopy in individuals who have had previous malaria exposure is not sensitive enough, because donors who have transmitted the infection typically present with low-level parasitemias that may not be detected even by careful examination. Likewise, RDTs are not useful for detecting low parasitemia.15 Therefore, the best screening option in this scenario is the detection of Plasmodium DNA or RNA by the PCR, which is more sensitive and specific than microscopy, and has been used in donor blood screening.34 Those techniques allow detection of low parasitemia among donors even years after previous exposure because of the possibility of persistent asymptomatic infection.35 Serologic tests could also be used, but detection of antibodies does not necessarily indicate the presence of parasitemia but rather indicate exposure36 with the risk of organ exclusion of some donors with no parasitemia, as noted in European countries where serology testing was used to screen donors who have traveled to malarious areas.29,36 Serology testing, however, may be considered if the donor exposure history is unclear.6 The Role of Hypnozoites in Liver Transplantation The presence of a latent hepatic phase in P. vivax and P. ovale infections is a particular concern for donor screening before liver transplantation. After successful treatment of primary infection, parasites reside in hepatocytes in a dormant stage as hypnozoites, resulting in relapses after several months or even years.37,38 Pretransplant screening of blood smears will not identify hypnozoites, because these infect liver cells only. As a result, these 2 plasmodial species transmission through the tranplanted liver has been reported.6,39 The possibility of these 2 plasmodial species transmission through the SOT other than liver has also been reported5; authors point out that surgical stress can trigger malaria relapse. MANAGEMENT OF SYMPTOMATIC PARASITEMIA All potential donors with evidence of active infections are deferred from donation until diagnosed and treated. After treatment, the deferral period should follow local guidelines.30 Donor Deferral Recommendations The policies are largely based on local guidelines supported by malaria endemicity.40 Recommendations for donor deferral may be extrapolated from the blood donor literature with regional variations in policies, ranging from deferral based on epidemiological risk or a positive screening test. US guidelines require a 1-year deferral period for travelers and a 3-year deferral period for those who lived in an endemic area or who have had previous malaria infection.41 The rationale for the 3-year deferral is based on possible low-grade parasitemia that would either become symptomatic or resolve over time in the absence of reinfection.41 European guidelines defer the donor for 4 months for those who had epidemiological risk (donors who lived in a malarial area within the first 5 years of life or have a history of fever up to 6 months after a visit to an endemic area) but a negative serological or molecular screening test, and defer the donor for 3 years in the absence of a negative screening test. Moreover, the history of malaria determines a 3-year deferral after cessation of treatment and absence of symptoms, and the acceptance thereafter only if an immunological or molecular test is negative.42 In contrast, in nonendemic areas, the donor screening should be more discriminatory and use a shorter deferral period. The screening test in such areas is frequently the thick blood smear, not avoiding donors with previous exposure or infection but with negative parasitemia. In the current Brazilian guideline, for instance, donor deferral time and screening recommendations are based on the Annual Parasitemia Index43 of the area the donor has lived/visited. For endemic regions (Amazon basin), donors should be screened routinely for parasitemia. Additional exclusion criteria include malaria infection in the previous 12 months, fever in the previous 30 days, and having returned from a high Annual Parasitemia Index city in the previous 30 days. Outside the Amazon basin, individuals with history of malaria infection or having returned from a malaria risk area in the previous 30 days should be excluded, and from 30 days to 12 months should undergo screening tests to confirm negative parasitemia. Brazil also requires a permanent deferral for donors with a history of P. malariae infection.40 In the context of SOT, in contrast to the blood transfusion scenario, the donor screening policies should take into account the reduced availability of donors, the temporality to take the decision (there is no time to temporarily defer) and the endemicity. In addition, the epidemiological history of malaria exposure is sometimes impaired for deceased donors when information is obtained from relatives not necessarily aware about the real epidemiology risk of the donor. Recommendations about the deferral period for malaria risky donors vary among regions and countries, based on endemicity, availability of donor screening, and the level of risk of malaria transmission that is to avoided. Therefore, there are no uniform recommendations. A permanent deferral for donors with a history of P. malariae infection is recommended. All potential donors with evidence of active infections should be deferred from donation until diagnosed and treated. After treatment, the deferral period should follow local guidelines. POSTTRANSPLANT MANAGEMENT Malaria Reactivation and Recrudescence Loss of natural immunity due to immunosuppression in SOT recipients may lead to reactivation of latent P. vivax and P. ovale, or recrudescence of asymptomatic infection caused by other Plasmodium species.5,44,45 Cell-mediated immunity, particularly CD8+ T lymphocytes, is required to control the extracellular and intracellular life cycles of the malaria parasite.46 Malaria stimulates a robust T lymphocyte effector activity12 and induces malaria-specific memory T cells,47 which could be impaired with immunosuppression, leading to reactivation of the infection. Interestingly, though, some reports have described an antimalarial effect of calcineurin inhibitors, including cyclosporine and tacrolimus.48,49 In vitro studies have demonstrated that probably calcineurin inhibitors act on a number of parasites through T lymphocyte-binding proteins (cyclophilins and FK506 binding protein), which are structurally identified in a number of parasites, especially malaria and schistosomiasis. There are no reported data supporting whether the risk of activation is 100% or less. However, the immunossupression and stress conditions probably increase the risk of relapses in vivax malaria and of P. falciparum recrudescences in transplant recipientes as compared with the general population. In the general population, the risk of relapse is estimated to be around 25%,50 and the risk of P. falciparum recrudescences vary dramatically according to the geographic regions, treatment guideline, and prevalence of antimalarial drug resistance. Detection of parasitemia in patients after surgical stress has been described.51,52 Posttransplant Monitoring Screening donors based on epidemiological risk, even when it is complemented by laboratorial screening testing if positive for epidemiological risk, cannot completely prevent organ-donor transmission malaria. History information obtained from donors themselves or from their relatives in the case of deceased donors may be inaccurate, intentionally or unintentionally, because they misunderstand the question, or because they are unaware or have forgotten that they have had malaria. Taking this potential risk in to account, both donors and recipients from positive malaria risk donors should be prospectively monitored posttransplant, ideally for a period of 2 months. The reported data supporting the recommendation of posttransplant monitoring are, however, based on reported cases of transmission or recredescence of malaria after SOT.53 In the setting of a current or previous exposure, malaria should be considered as a cause of unexplained fever.54 Preemptive Treatment Preemptive treatment of malaria for transplant recipients has not been formally recommended.10 However, in case of high-risk DDI due to recent donor exposure or infection, treatment may be There are reports of treatment of asymptomatic SOT recipients from a donor who transmitted malaria to other In a of a diagnosis of DDI malaria in the liver transplant recipient parasitemia to be detected on thick blood smears and treatment of 2 recipients who had the and the kidney from the before In case a with acute who an peripheral blood transplant from was for malaria despite no malaria parasitemia by PCR, that P. vivax infection was diagnosed in the donor 1 after in this the recipient was with with no for because the DDI P. vivax transmission not the liver cycle. title: Early Versus Delayed Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator Implantation After Sustained Ventricular Arrhythmia in Suspected Myocarditis: A Systematic Review with Narrative Synthesis and a Resource-Adapted Decision Framework
authors: Thabit Mohamed; Omer Mamoun Mohamed; Awab Okasha; Ehab Ali; Mohammed Al-Shikh; Ezaldeen H. Omer; Yaslam Ba Srada; Bobakr Bawazir
abstract: This OSF registration documents a completed systematic review with narrative synthesis examining the clinical question of early versus delayed permanent implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) implantation after sustained ventricular tachycardia (VT) or ventricular fibrillation (VF) in patients with suspected myocarditis. The review addresses an important area of clinical uncertainty because ventricular arrhythmias occurring during acute myocarditis may resolve as myocardial inflammation improves, while some patients may retain a persistent arrhythmogenic substrate and remain at risk of recurrent malignant ventricular arrhythmias or sudden cardiac death. The review therefore focuses on determining which clinical, imaging, arrhythmic, and health-system factors may support early ICD implantation and under what circumstances protected deferral with reassessment may be appropriate. The population of interest includes adolescents and adults with suspected, clinically diagnosed, cardiac magnetic resonance-supported, or biopsy-confirmed myocarditis or inflammatory cardiomyopathy who experienced sustained VT, VF, aborted sudden cardiac death, or a closely related major ventricular-arrhythmic presentation. Outcomes of interest include recurrent VT/VF, appropriate ICD or wearable cardioverter-defibrillator therapy, sudden cardiac death, mortality, ventricular functional recovery, and prognostic features relevant to the timing of permanent ICD implantation. Eligible evidence includes clinical practice guidelines, consensus documents, observational cohorts, registries, and systematic reviews or meta-analyses. The review was conducted and reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020. The auditable search included MEDLINE/PubMed, relevant guideline repositories of the European Society of Cardiology, American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology, and Heart Rhythm Society, together with backward and forward citation searching. Searches covered the period from database inception to 21 August 2026. Search strategies were also developed for Embase, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and CENTRAL. Study selection involved title and abstract screening followed by full-text assessment. Data extracted included study design, myocarditis definition and subtype, arrhythmia phenotype, sample size, left ventricular ejection fraction, cardiac magnetic resonance and late gadolinium enhancement findings, ICD or wearable cardioverter-defibrillator use, follow-up duration, recurrent ventricular arrhythmias, appropriate device therapy, mortality, and factors relevant to device timing. Risk of bias was assessed using design-specific tools, including ROBINS-I for non-randomized studies, AMSTAR 2 for systematic reviews and meta-analyses, AGREE II for clinical practice guidelines, and the JBI checklist for expert consensus documents. Because no eligible study directly compared early permanent ICD implantation with delayed implantation with adequate adjustment for confounding, a meta-analysis was not considered appropriate. Instead, the evidence was organized into a structured narrative synthesis covering four major domains: risk of recurrent ventricular arrhythmia, prognostic markers, temporary bridging strategies, and health-system/resource capacity. These domains were used to develop a resource-adapted, hypothesis-generating clinical decision framework rather than a validated prediction model. The principal intended outcomes of the project are to clarify the strength and limitations of the evidence regarding ICD timing after myocarditis-related sustained ventricular arrhythmia; identify clinical characteristics that may support earlier ICD consideration; describe circumstances in which monitored deferral and reassessment may be reasonable; evaluate the potential role of wearable cardioverter-defibrillators and other temporary protection strategies; and examine how access to cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, rhythm monitoring, emergency services, follow-up, implantation expertise, and long-term device support may influence management decisions. The resulting framework is intended to support multidisciplinary, individualized decision-making rather than replace guideline recommendations or specialist clinical judgment. As this registration was created after completion of the review, it should be regarded as a retrospective OSF registration rather than a prospective protocol registration. The manuscript itself states that the review was not prospectively registered and that an internal protocol specified the population, timing strategies, outcomes, evidence domains, and resource-adaptation variables before full-text synthesis.

title: THE PRACTICE OF APPLICATION OF PENAL LIABILITY FOR THE OFFENCE OF RAPE COMMITTED BY TWO OR MORE PEOPLE: CONTROVERSIES AND SOLUTIONS: Sergiu BRÎNZA Universitatea de Stat din Moldova
authors: USM ADMIN
venue: Studia Universitatis Moldaviae Seria Stiinte Sociale
abstract: This study aims to analyze the various application of the provision set forth at lett.c) par.(2) art.171 PC RM and the errors admitted by practitioners that occur within the application of this provision. As a result of the conducted analysis, there are proposed solutions to these issues. It is established that rape is a complex offence. Therefore, in the case of rape, it is established that sequential co-authorship is possible. It is demonstrated that, in the context of the same offence, the same person cannot cumulate the qualities of accomplice and (co-) author both together. Not being specified in the provision of art.171 PC RM, the act of generating the victim's inability to defend him/herself or to indicate his/her will cannot form a part of the objective side of the offence of rape. An accomplice to the offence set forth at art.171 PC RM is to be considered that person, who contributed initially to the performance of sexual intercourse by someone else, generating the victim's inability to defend him/herself or to indicate his/her will. If there was a prior agreement between the perpetrators and the sexual intercourse is performed in turns, it is established that lett.c) par.(2) art.171 PC RM is applicable, regardless of whether at the place sexual intercourse happened, at the time the offence was committed, there was present only one of the perpetrators or all of whom participated in the prior agreement. In order for this qualification solution to be valid, the physical or psychological coercion must be performed – prior to the sexual intercourse or in parallel with the sexual intercourse – by one of the perpetrators or by all the perpetrators. Moreover, each of those who performed the sexual intercourse must realize that it was only possible because of the applied coercion. It is concluded that the abstention from the qualification under lett.c) par.(2) art.171 PC RM and art.208 PC RM does not contradict the impossibility of double sanctioning for the same act. This is because a rape committed by two or more people (among them the coerced minor) is a different act than that of influencing the victim to commit rape. Keywords: rape, two or more people, participation, co-authorship, accomplice, excessive authorship, competition of offences.

title: Demographic Status and Blood Group of Family Blood Donors with a Focus on Their Rejection
authors: Tashmim Farhana Dipta; Zakia Akter; Anamika Datta; Quamrun Nahar; Md Ashadul Islam
abstract: Background: The aim of donor selection should protect donors from any potential harm which may occur as a direct result of the donation process; secondly, shall protect recipients of blood transfusions from adverse effects, such as transmission of infectious diseases or other medical conditions and unwanted effects caused by any medications taken by the donor. Any reason for deferral, whether temporary or permanent, have been explained to the donor and recorded as per National Guideline and Blood Safety Law. Literature search showed there is dearth information on replacement blood donors in Bangladesh. So this study has been done to evaluate replacement family blood donors, exploring their demographic status, occupation, blood groups and why they were rejected during donor selection.Methods: This study was done to assess the demographic profile and blood group among family blood donors during donor selection. Age, weight, occupation, blood group and blood pressure have been explored among randomly selected two hundred ninety one blood donors attending Transfusion Medicine Department of BIRDEM as per Guideline.Results: Among them 261 (89.69%) were male and 30 (10.31%) were female with M±SD age 29±6 and 29±7 (yrs), respectively. Blood group of replacement family donors were, A positive (39.7%), B positive 90(32%), O positive 18 (6%), AB positive 39 (13%) majority (57.04%) were unmarried , 52.58% were doing business, while students were 29.90% and job holders were only 17.53%. Among nine deferred donors females were mainly rejected (89.28%) and the contributing factor was low blood pressure according to guideline. Finally 96.91% successful family blood donors donated blood for the patient party.Conclusion: Our study showed proper selection and following of blood donation guideline help to determine the eligibility to donate blood. Moreover, this pilot study may contribute in evaluation of Bangladeshi family blood donors those had positive blood group and negative serological markers as per WHO (World Health Organization) guideline for Bangladesh.Birdem Med J 2016; 6(2): 112-117

title: Coiled Tubing Deployed ESP Retrievable Completion Application in Algeria – A Success Story
authors: Tuna Eren; E. Ferraro; G. Franco; Abdelhalim Allal; Ruben Ortega Alfonzo; M. Norton; Steven Craig
venue: SPE/ICoTA Coiled Tubing and Well Intervention Conference and Exhibition
abstract: Abstract It is well known in the oil industry that on jointed tubing conveyed Electric Submersible Pump (ESP) completions there is always the likelihood of well re-completion either after the useful life or a premature failure of the ESP is reached. The re-completion becomes a significant downside versus conventional completion systems (naturally flowing wells). Most of these ESP replacement / re-interventions are usually associated with the need of a workover rig or snubbing unit and the related cost, logistics scheduling and operating time bound to it. In an attempt to evaluate a different cost-efficient alternative to address this ESP re-intervention work a Coiled Tubing Deployed ESP System / Project was initiated in Algeria to deploy the ESP systems via fit-for-purpose Coiled Tubing Deployed Retrievable ESP (CTDRESP) cable after the installation of the permanent downhole completion, with the intention to reduce the overall intervention cost, reduce the production deferment by: a) eliminating the need of having a rig on location, which have availability challenges re rig schedule) b) reducing the time required to connect the well back to production but not requiring the removal of flow lines and pipeline on the surrounding areas of the well), in a brown oil field located in an area where artificial lift systems are widely required for sustained production. This paper documents the first fit-for-purpose Coiled Tubing Deployed Retrievable ESP completion application in North Africa region, where +/-59m (194 ft) of BHA (Tail Pipe, Seal Stack and ESP assemblies) were deployed and run into the well using 1.5in Tubing Deployed Retrievable ESP (CTDRESP) system with a specialized sub-surface safety valve installed at landing nipple at +/- 64m (209ft) successfully. Oil production was successfully resumed after ESP installation with 99% oil ratio at surface, proving this practical and cost-efficient type of ESP deployment application in a well not capable to flow naturally. With the implementation of this technology the operating company in this region has enabled an alternative method to service its ESP wells, saved operating related costs, and reduced production deferral with a safe and cost-efficient alternative that also considers reduced personnel workforce and rigless approach (rather than full scale workover rig unit). This paper will review the project concepts, job planning, utilization of a sleeve style safety valve in the completion, well control and contingency considerations prior to reviewing the successful installation of the completion. Sharing the lessons learned will enable optimized future utilization of this technology.

title: STRATEGIC ASPECTS OF LABOR MARKET FORMATION AS A DRIVER OF THE COMPETITIVENESS OF THE UKRAINIAN ECONOMY
authors: Тетяна Стройко; Oleksander Bulavchenko; Alina Yeremeieva
abstract: The article considers the strategic aspects of the formation of the labor market as a driver of competitiveness of the Ukrainian economy. The situation on the labor market is also analyzed, namely: indicators of economically active population, including age groups in the period 2015 - 2019, unemployment rate and population outflow in the territorial - sectoral context in the period 2019 - 2020. The author investigated The main indicator that is characteristic of the labor market is the level of employment of the population by age groups on average to the corresponding group. The situation on the "black labor market" was also analyzed and labor market trends in coronavirus conditions were studied. It has been established which professions will be the most popular and are currently functioning. Strategic vectors of social and labor development have been formed, which in the future should form a qualitatively new socio-economic policy in Ukraine, use innovation-oriented mechanisms to overcome the deficit. It is proved that during the symbiosis of the financial crisis and the labor market crisis, the main tools that can mitigate the effects of coronavirus outbreaks should be: maintaining existing traditional jobs, creating new, virtual jobs, based on robotics, automation, artificial intelligence and IT -technologies; support for employment in general, and provide conditions for remote work for all who can switch to this form of work; protection of workers in the workplace; protection and prevention of workplaces to prevent or reduce the spread of infectious diseases; strengthening work to prevent discrimination against employees; taking into account the physiological and psychological needs of employees, raising their awareness, implementing occupational safety practices, investing in health care, sanitation and hygiene; development of skills and entrepreneurial activity; intensification of social dialogue; the introduction of temporary measures to apply tax benefits that would allow for the deferral of taxes, provided tax rebates to small businesses. Key words: labor market, competitiveness, coronavirus pandemic, innovations, professions, black market.

title: Timing of Systemic Therapy Initiation in Antepartum and Postpartum Pregnancy- Associated Breast Cancer: A National Claims-Based Analysis
authors: Shifa Kanjwal; Stephanie Rice; Yong Shan; Sharon Hermes Giordano; Yong‐Fang Kuo; David S. Lopez
abstract: Abstract Background Pregnancy-associated breast cancer (PABC) presents unique challenges in systemic therapy selection and treatment sequencing due to fetal safety considerations and pregnancy-specific therapeutic contraindications. While current guidelines outline recommended treatment approaches during pregnancy, real-world systemic therapy initiation patterns relative to delivery remain poorly characterized. Methods The Merative MarketScan Commercial Database was queried to identify patients with PABC, defined as breast cancer diagnosed during pregnancy or within 12 months following delivery. Patients were classified as antepartum (diagnosis within 280 days before delivery) or postpartum (diagnosis within 365 days after delivery). Claims for chemotherapy, HER2-directed therapy, and endocrine therapy were identified using pharmacy and procedure codes. Treatment initiation timing was calculated relative to delivery date (day 0) and categorized into predefined antepartum and postpartum intervals. Descriptive statistics were used to characterize treatment timing patterns. Results A total of 673 patients with PABC were identified, including 242 antepartum (36.0%) and 431 postpartum (64.0%) patients. Among antepartum patients, 94 (38.8%) initiated systemic therapy within the study windows. Median time from delivery to first systemic therapy initiation was − 43 days (IQR − 113 to 20). Chemotherapy was the most frequently initiated therapy, with substantial variability in timing; 56.7% initiated chemotherapy before delivery, while 43.3% deferred initiation until postpartum. HER2-directed and endocrine therapies were largely deferred until after delivery, consistent with current guideline recommendations. Among postpartum patients, 165 (38.3%) initiated systemic therapy during the study window, with a median time to initiation of 199 days after delivery (IQR 127–300). In this cohort, chemotherapy, HER2-directed therapy, and endocrine therapy initiation increased progressively with time from delivery. Conclusion Systemic therapy initiation patterns differ substantially between antepartum and postpartum PABC. Antepartum patients demonstrated expected deferral of HER2-directed and endocrine therapies, while chemotherapy timing remained highly variable, with many patients delaying treatment until after delivery. These findings highlight the complexity of treatment decision-making in PABC and underscore the need for multidisciplinary care models and further evaluation of drivers and outcomes of treatment timing decisions.

title: Auditing Coding-Agent Rule Updates under Selective Feedback
authors: Xulin Chen
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Persistent coding agents can compile corrections into rules, but selective feedback and changed policies complicate admission. We implement version-scoped finite-pool acceptance, rejection and deferral with executable retirement. Constructed studies show that historical certification need not cover future variants and useful conservative admission approaches a census: four selectors admit no eligible holdout candidate at 20 of 32 labels. Statistical finite-population alternatives preserve this cost. Small external-model studies diagnose stale controls and connect proposals to calibration without establishing superiority over textual memory. A fixed purposive corpus from ten public repositories contains 40 instruction-file transitions and 44 AI-assisted analysis groups, including two explicit local contract replacements; it does not estimate policy prevalence or deployed retirement. A separate pilot runs the real OpenAI Python SDK with two explicitly artificial cap faults. All twelve workers complete and restore the reference, while all four valid matcher proposals are rejected on an authored snippet census. Direct guards never fire and admitted guards never activate, so identical functional outcomes show no admission benefit. These results distinguish documented replacement, finite-pool compatibility and future task behavior. They support reproducible diagnoses, not recursive self-improvement, independent human policy judgments or a general safety guarantee. Exploratory working paper v0.8, first made public on GitHub on 8 October 2026. Not peer reviewed or accepted by a journal. The record mirrors the six files of the exact GitHub v0.8 release at commit 28435e716f8d6453662beb75a6c94e262cfd5f58. The supporting artifact includes constructed audits and model studies, a fixed purposive instruction-file corpus from ten repositories (40 file transitions, 44 AI-assisted analysis groups), and twelve repair workers on two explicitly artificial faults in one pinned real SDK. All four valid matcher proposals were rejected; direct guards never fired and admitted guards never activated. No admission benefit, deployed retirement, independent human policy judgments, multi-repository repair superiority, recursive self-improvement or general safety guarantee is established.
