title: Reply to Letter to the Editor: Recommendations for the Care of Pediatric Orthopaedic Patients During the COVID-19 Pandemic
authors: Emily K. Schaeffer; Sarah Farrell; Kishore Mulpuri
venue: Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
abstract: The Authors' Reply: We thank these readers for their thoughtful response to our recent publication1 regarding modifications to pediatric orthopaedic practice that may be necessary to balance the health and safety of patients, families, and healthcare providers during the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic. We appreciate the thorough review and points of discussion these readers raised and would like to address their concerns with specific regard to our recommendations involving the management of patients with developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH). At the outset of the pandemic in North America, our tertiary pediatric care center, similar to several centers in Australia, made the decision to defer all appointments for DDH in the Orthopaedic Clinic for an estimated 2 to 3 months. This decision was made based on both observations and advice from orthopaedic surgeons practicing in locations impacted early by COVID-19, including Italy and Singapore, as well as a modeling study assessing the potential for viral transmission between patients and families and healthcare providers should continue treatment.2 These readers justifiably raise concerns about delaying DDH treatment, particularly in the case of complete dislocations. They posit that we are likely to be continuing to battle COVID-19, to some extent, for many months to come. We recognize these valid concerns, especially as it is known that early detection and treatment of DDH is important for optimal outcomes. However, findings from the International Hip Dysplasia Institute (IHDI) have demonstrated a 79% success rate with Pavlik harness in infants up to 6 months of age3 as well as a 91% success rate of closed reduction in infants at a median 8 months of age.4 These findings do not refute the importance of early detection and treatment, but they do suggest that harness or closed reduction can still be successful in many children under 1 year of age. Our recommendations were formed in the early stages of the pandemic when the world was observing the devastation COVID-19 was wreaking on the Italian healthcare system. Potential shortage of adequate personal protective equipment was also of global concern as centers in yet-to-be heavily impacted regions rushed to prepare. In that context, taken with the IHDI findings, we felt it reasonable to suggest a deferral of these patients for a temporary period at the height of the first COVID-19 wave. We agree with the concern that continuing to defer treatment beyond that initial period of delay would likely cause the risks of long-term impact on the patient's quality of life to outweigh the benefits of reducing potential viral transmission. Every effort should be made to resume at limited capacity, detection, and treatment of DDH once the height of the first wave subsides. The readers make excellent suggestions regarding shifting the initial assessment for DDH from acute hospital settings to community settings where possible. We agree that this could present a potential solution in certain locations but may not be possible depending upon individual local resources and capacity. Again, we wish to thank these readers for their important addition to this discourse. Approaches to care and management of pediatric orthopaedic patients will need to be adaptable throughout different phases of the pandemic, and the global pediatric orthopaedic community can come together to continue to support each other and provide creative and flexible solutions to confront these extraordinary challenges.

title: AUTONOMOUS REPAIR & SELF-HEALING INFRASTRUCTURE AT THE LIMIT Detection, Diagnosis, Local Repair, Verification, and the Rise of Persistent Infrastructure
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: AUTONOMOUS REPAIR & SELF-HEALING INFRASTRUCTURE AT THE LIMIT Detection, Diagnosis, Local Repair, Verification, and the Rise of Persistent Infrastructure Autonomous Repair & Self-Healing Infrastructure at the Limit is a large-scale research exploration of a fundamental transition in infrastructure engineering: the movement from maintenance as an occasional human intervention toward maintenance as a continuous, measurable, partially autonomous capability of the infrastructure itself. Its central question is: Can a civilization learn to continuously repair itself? The book begins with a simple but demanding systems relationship: Persistent Infrastructure=Detectionx Diagnosisx Local Repairx Verification The multiplication is intentional. Detection without diagnosis produces alarms but not understanding. Diagnosis without repair produces knowledge but not recovery. Repair without verification produces intervention without evidence. Verification without persistent sensing produces only a snapshot. Long-lived infrastructure emerges only when these capabilities form a closed and repeatable loop. Across 82 chapters, the book investigates structural health monitoring, crack detection, corrosion sensing, non-destructive evaluation, causal diagnosis, remaining useful life, digital twins, self-healing concrete, microcapsule systems, vascular healing networks, microbial mineralization, shape-memory-assisted repair, self-healing polymers, composites, metals, coatings, robotic inspection, local robotic repair, swarm maintenance, pipelines, bridges, aircraft, industrial systems, electronics, spacecraft, verification, provenance, lifecycle economics, safety, governance, and civilization-scale maintenance architectures. A second central concept is the Repair Capacity Index: RCI=Autonomous Repair Capacity/Damage Generation Rate The Repair Capacity Index is not presented as a universal physical law. It is a systems diagnostic. For any specific infrastructure system, both repair capacity and damage generation must be operationally defined. The relevant time horizon must be stated. Repair quality must be verified. Hidden deterioration must be considered. Repeated interventions must not generate equivalent or greater damage elsewhere. Within these constraints, RCI provides a useful conceptual threshold. When consequential damage is generated faster than trusted repair capacity can remove it, maintenance backlog tends to grow. When reliable repair capacity persistently exceeds consequential damage generation, accumulated maintenance debt can shrink. This turns infrastructure persistence into a dynamic balance rather than an assumption of permanence. The book therefore treats damage as a continuous process. Fatigue accumulates. Corrosion advances. Surfaces erode. Seals age. Composites delaminate. Pipelines thin. Connections loosen. Sensors drift. Electronic systems degrade. Spacecraft experience radiation, thermal cycling, debris impacts, and material aging. The central engineering goal is not to eliminate every damage mechanism. It is to detect consequential damage early enough, understand it accurately enough, intervene locally enough, and verify recovery strongly enough that ordinary deterioration does not become irreversible system loss. Self-healing materials form one layer of this architecture. Autogenous cementitious healing, encapsulated repair agents, vascular networks, microbial mineralization, reversible polymer chemistry, shape-memory mechanisms, self-healing composites, healable metal systems, and advanced coatings can reduce the distance between damage and response. But material healing is not equivalent to infrastructure healing. A crack may close while permeability remains unacceptable. A puncture may seal while structural strength remains uncertain. A polymer may recover shape while fatigue resistance continues to decline. A concrete crack may visually disappear while reinforcement corrosion continues beneath the surface. For this reason, the book separates: Geometric Closure from Functional Recovery from Verified Return to Service. Autonomous robotic repair forms a second layer. Robots may inspect bridges, pipelines, tunnels, aircraft surfaces, industrial plants, underwater infrastructure, electronic assemblies, or spacecraft. Future systems may grind, deposit, seal, coat, patch, fasten, replace, reinforce, or additively rebuild damaged regions. However, robotic access does not automatically create autonomous maintenance. A robot can perform the wrong repair with great precision if localization, diagnosis, authorization, or process verification is wrong. The architecture therefore requires an inspection-to-repair loop: Observe-> Localize-> Diagnose-> Authorize-> Repair-> Measure-> Verify-> Record Every intervention should leave evidence. The system should preserve what was observed before repair, why a diagnosis was selected, which competing hypotheses remained plausible, who or what authorized the intervention, what physical action occurred, what measurements were taken afterward, what uncertainty remained, and when the next inspection should occur. This creates a maintenance memory. Digital twins are therefore treated not merely as visual models of infrastructure. They become evolving repair ledgers. A useful lifecycle twin should remember inspection history, defect geometry, intervention history, material state, sensor calibration, uncertainty, residual defects, repair resources, and evidence of post-repair performance. Infrastructure that repeatedly repairs itself without remembering its previous repairs may eventually create new failure modes through cumulative intervention. The book therefore introduces intervention history as a first-class engineering variable. Repeated heating can alter polymers or metals. Repeated grinding can remove critical material. Healing capsules can be depleted. Vascular repair networks can clog or exhaust their stored agents. Microbial systems may lose viability. Coatings can accumulate incompatible layers. Robotic patches can change local stiffness and redistribute stress. Repair is therefore not free. Every repair changes the future repair landscape. This leads to one of the book's major principles: A good repair should restore function while preserving future repair options. Verification becomes the decisive layer. A repair is not complete when the intervention ends. It is complete only when the relevant service variable has been measured again. For pressure systems, this may require leak or pressure testing. For structural systems, it may require non-destructive evaluation, load response, stiffness recovery, fracture assessment, or long-term monitoring. For barriers, permeability may be more important than appearance. For electrical infrastructure, continuity and insulation performance may matter more than geometry. For aircraft and spacecraft, structural integrity and mission safety dominate. The acceptance test must therefore correspond to the original failure mechanism. The book also develops the concept of repair backlog. Infrastructure systems rarely experience damage one defect at a time. Large cities, transportation networks, industrial fleets, utilities, and spacecraft contain thousands or millions of components. Damage events arrive continuously. Repair resources are finite. This creates queues. The age, severity, connectivity, and consequence of backlog become important indicators of system health. A civilization can perform thousands of successful repairs each year while still becoming less maintainable if new consequential damage arrives faster. This is where RCI becomes a portfolio-level concept rather than a single-machine metric. The architecture also incorporates graceful degradation. When repair capacity becomes insufficient, the correct action may not be immediate full restoration. The system may reduce load, isolate a damaged region, reroute flow, lower operating speed, switch to redundant components, reduce mission demand, or temporarily sacrifice nonessential service. Graceful degradation buys time. Time allows sensing to improve, repair resources to arrive, human expertise to intervene, or alternative pathways to be activated. Safety and governance therefore become inseparable from autonomous repair. Prediction must remain distinct from permission. A diagnostic model may estimate a likely failure mechanism without having authority to modify a safety-critical structure. An autonomous system may be allowed to seal a low-risk leak but not alter a primary aircraft load path. It may be allowed to patch a pavement defect but required to escalate a bridge fracture. The book therefore treats authorization boundaries, human-on-the-loop supervision, rollback, quarantine, fail-safe modes, cyber-physical security, and accountability as core infrastructure technologies. Abstention is also treated as a valid maintenance action. A mature system should be able to say: The evidence is insufficient. The defect lies outside the validated operating envelope. The proposed repair cannot be verified. The available intervention may increase risk. Human inspection is required. This is not a failure of autonomy. It is evidence of bounded autonomy. The final sections extend these ideas toward cities, planetary infrastructure, remote industry, orbital systems, and starships. In such environments, conventional maintenance becomes increasingly difficult because skilled labor, replacement parts, repair facilities, and logistics may be distant or unavailable. The infrastructure must therefore carry more of its own maintenance capability. Materials may heal small defects. Embedded sensors may detect larger failures. Robots may inspect and repair inaccessible regions. Distributed manufacturing may create replacement components. Digital twins may preserve repair history.

title: P0366SAFETY OF STEROID THERAPY IN IGA NEPHROPATHY: THE CLINICAL EXPERIENCE OF 48 NEPHROLOGY UNITS IN ITALY
authors: Ivano Baragetti; Francesca Ferrario; Federico Alberici; Andrea Amendola; Maria Carmen Luise; Cristina Sarcina; A. Sorrentino; Cristiana Rollino; Domenico Giannese; Elena Mancini; Alessandra Pola; Mario Gennaro Cozzolino; Claudio Pozzi
abstract: Abstract Background and Aims Steroid therapy is efficient in inducing remission of IgA nephropathy (IgAN) and preventing end stage renal disease (ESRD) but there are concerns about their safety. The TESTING trial in particular has been stopped early because of a higher incidence of side effects than conservative treatment thus inducing a conservative therapy with RAAS (renin angiotensin antagonist system) blockers. The aim of this analysis was to evaluate the incidence of adverse events (AE) in a retrospective observational trial on the real clinical practice. Method We evaluated 1209 patients (pz) with IgAN coming from 48 Italian centers: 285 pz in RAAS blockers alone, 732 treated for 6 months with steroid and 192 with a combination of steroid and other immunosuppressants (also with RAAS blockers). The analysis was limited to the 6 months of therapy. Results The basal characteristics of the 3 groups are shown in the table below. The figure shows the frequencies of 69 adverse events related with immunosuppression: the most frequent were infections (23, 2.73% of all patients, 34.3% of all AE), impaired glycemic control (11, 0.91% of patients, 16% of all AE), severe hypertension (6, 8.7% of all AE) and leukopenia (9, 0.80% of patients, 13% of all AE). Infections were observed in 16 (2.19%) pz in steroid therapy and 7 (3.65%) pz in steroid+immunosoppressive treatment. Liver toxicity and and gastrointestinal AE were observed almost in pz receiving steroid+ immunosuppressants [1(0.14%) and 2 (1.04%) pz, respectively]. 7 pz in steroid therapy (0.96%) and 2 in steroid+ immunosuppressants experienced an impaired glycemic control. All the 9 cases of leucopenia were registered in pz in steroid+ immunosuppressants (4.69%). A slightly higher incidence of allergies was observed in the RAAS blocker group (20 cases, 0.7%). The higher rates of infections and leucopenia were observed in pz above 70 years of age (6.12%,p<0.05), as higher incidence of infections and impaired glycemic control were registered in pz with an eGFR<30 ml/min/1.73 m2 (4.64 and 1.99%,p<0.05). Severe hypertension and leucopenia were observed respectively in 9 and 3 pz with an eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73m2. No significant relationships were found between AE, proteinuria and sex. Multivariate logistic regression showed an independent association of immunosuppressive treatment and age with any AE [ODDS ratio: 3,35 (CI:2,18-5,14) and 1,02 (CI:1,01-1,04), respectively; p<0.05]. Death occurred for sepsis in a 70 years old pz (eGFR=21.7 ml/min/m2, 24hproteinuria=16.1 g/day) after 3 months of treatment. Conclusion the incidence of EA in our observational study is lower than that observed in the TESTING and STOP trials (5.71% vs 14.7% and 40%, respectively). The most frequent AE were almost observed in oldest subjects with impaired renal function on steroid+other immunosuppressants. Though this trial is not randomized nor controlled (RC), it considers a large cohort of pz coming from the real clinical practice of the Italian Nephrology Units and demonstrates that the significantly lower incidence of steroid related AE than that observed in some RC trials doesn’t justify the abstention from steroids in IgAN at risk of progression. Much more attention should be paid in elderly pts with severe renal dysfunction with a closer follow-up, dose adjustments and antibiotic prophilaxis.

title: 82 Near-Universal Active Surveillance for Small Renal Mass Patients: A Novel 12-Year Clinical Experience
authors: ERIC C. KAUFFMAN
abstract: Abstract Background Surgical extirpation has long been the gold-standard management option for patients with clinically localized small renal masses (SRM, 15 years; shared decision-making for DI versus continued AS if LE 5–15 years; or continued AS/observation if LE < 5 years. AS patient outcomes were retrospectively reviewed, and 5- and 7-year rates of PCI-free (PFS), DI-free (DIFS) survival, and metastasis-free survival (MFS) were determined. Clinical predictors of these outcomes were identified in Cox regression multivariable analyses. Results A total of 373 patients without dialysis dependency or prior RCC treatment were seen over the 12-year study period and had follow-up of at least 3 months. Fewer than 3% (10 of 373) of these patients already had evidence of PCI at presentation and therefore underwent upfront treatment if medically fit. Of the remaining 363 SRM patients , 100% (97% of all SRM patients) deferred upfront treatment and were managed instead with AS. With median follow-up of 43 months, 105/363 (29%) AS patients developed PCI, and 77/363 (21%) underwent DI. The 5- and 7-year rates were 65.6% and 61.6% for PFS, and 74.6% and 71.0% for DIFS, respectively. One of 363 patients (0.3%) developed metastasis, and the 5- and 7-year MFS was 100% and 99.2%, respectively. PFS and DIFS were both significantly shorter with larger initial LTD, clear cell biopsy histology, and lower Charlson Comorbidity Index. On multivariate analysis, larger initial LTD and clear cell biopsy histology were independent predictors of both PFS and DIFS. Conclusions In among the largest single-center SRM AS series reported to date, and the first AS series in which the vast majority (97%) of all SRM patients elected AS rather than immediate treatment, our findings support that AS is oncologically safe and durably limits the need for invasive treatment in SRM patients who are PCI-free at presentation but otherwise unselected. Broad deferral of immediate treatment improves risk stratification of SRMs by revealing prognostic information that is commonly unknown at presentation related to tumor growth dynamics and histology. This approach thus focuses intervention on the minority subset of higher-risk SRM cases, while allowing most other SRM patients to avoid invasive treatment and its potential morbidity.

title: Impact of Allogeneic Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation Post-Sars-Cov-2 Infection: A Retrospective Analysis By the German Cooperative Transplant Study Group
authors: Osama Ahmad; Jan Frederic Weller; Nicolaus Martin Kröger; Eva Wagner Drouet; David Nachbaur; Normann Steiner; Daniel Teschner; Sabrina Kraus; Gesine Bug; Salem Ajib; Johannes Schetelig; Wolfgang Andreas Bethge; Thomas A. Schroeder; Judith Schaffrath; Lutz Peter Mueller; Mareike Verbeek; Edgar Jost; Hatice Soysal; Georg‐Nikolaus Franke; Stefan Klein; Udo Holtick; Knut Wendelin; Claudia Lengerke; Martin Bornhäuser; Maximilian Christopeit
abstract: Introduction Allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (alloHCT) is a curative treatment for hematologic malignancies, but it carries a significant risk of non-relapse mortality (NRM) to infections. The emergence of the COVID-19 pandemic introduced the challenge for the correct timing and safety of alloHCT in patients with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection. Methods This retrospective analysis, conducted by the German Cooperative Transplant Study Group, evaluated the outcomes of 75 patients who underwent alloHCT after having survived COVID-19. Data were collected from May 2020 to May 2022 at 15 German and Austrian centers using standardized questionnaires. All patients were SARS-CoV-2-PCR negative before alloHCT. Results The cohort included 75 patients (40 (53%) female, 35 (47%) male) with a median age of 56 (range 22-77) years and varying COVID-19 severity: 31 with mild, 6 with moderate, 12 with severe, and 26 with unknown severity after WHO-grading. Time from diagnosis of neoplasia to COVID-19 (median 125 (range 0-3,990) days) and time from COVID-19 diagnosis to alloHCT (median 141 (range 1-661) days) did not differ significantly between severity groups (p=0.09 and p=0.40, respectively). 12 (16%) patients suffered from ALL, while 38 (52%) had an AML and 23 (32%) had other diagnosis (2 unknown). Myeloablative conditioning was chosen in 29 (62%) patients, while 18 (38%) received reduced intensity conditioning (unknown=28). Peak C-reactive protein (CRP) during COVID-19 was 5 mg/dl in mild, 7 mg/dl in moderate and 8 mg/dl in severe disease (p=0.9), while IL-6 was 71 ng/l in mild, 92 ng/l in moderate and 122 ng/l in severe disease (p=0.8) and PCT was 0.61 ng/ml in mild, 1.34 ng/ml in moderate and 0.38 ng/ml in severe disease. COVID-19 duration did not correlate significantly with COVID-19 severity (>30 days= 10 (38%) mild, 3 (50%) moderate, 2 (40%) severe. ≤30 days: 16 (62%) mild, 3 (50%) moderate, 3 (60%) severe; p=0.7). There was no statistically significant difference in the timing of alloHCT in relation to the interval between COVID-19 diagnosis and alloHCT (p=0.38, day 178, maximally selected rank statistics). Patients with previous severe COVID-19 had a significantly lower 365-day survival rate (51.1%) compared to those with previous mild cases (90.9%, p=0.03). NRM at 365 days was higher in severe cases (19.6%) compared to mild cases (0%, p=0.03). There was no observed difference in acute (p=0.4) or chronic Graft-versus-Host-disease (p=0.4). Patients with a high Karnofsky index and mild COVID-19 had the best survival outcomes (p=0.12), while normal pre-transplant lung function, especially DLCO, was associated with better outcomes (HR: 0.91, p=0.04). Despite missing DRI (disease risk index) covariates, COVID-19 severity was not significantly associated with higher cytogenetic risk (64% abnormal in mild vs. 45.5% in severe disease, p= 0.37). However, patients with severe COVID-19 were less likely to be transplanted in CR (mild disease= 70.8% in CR at alloHCT, severe disease = 37.5% in CR, p= 0.21) Discussion Severe COVID-19 significantly impacts post-alloHCT survival, highlighting the need for rigorous prevention, comprehensive pre-transplant evaluation, and tailored management strategies for alloHCT patients. These findings support the deferral of aggressive treatments in symptomatic COVID-19 cases and the prioritization of antiviral treatments to mitigate risk. We aim to highlight the necessity of lung function testing following symptomatic COVID-19.

title: EXTREME RESEARCH MONOGRAPH Longevity Biomarkers Microrobotic Sampling and Trustworthy Biosensing at the Limit
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: EXTREME RESEARCH MONOGRAPH Longevity Biomarkers Microrobotic Sampling and Trustworthy Biosensing at the Limit English Introduction and Publication Abstract Research coupling Longevity biomarkers × microrobotic sampling × trustworthy biosensing Evidence firewall Level 1 sample fidelity → Level 2 aging mechanism validity → Level 3 meaningful health outcome prediction Book architecture 750 pages | 219,119 extracted English words | 82 chapters | 410 research sections | 30 linked derivations | 200 Research Gates Scientific status Prospective non clinical research architecture with explicit uncertainty abstention and stop boundaries Publication Abstract This research monograph develops a falsifiable architecture for measuring dynamic longevity biomarkers without allowing the act of sampling, transport, storage, sensing, calibration, or computation to manufacture the apparent biology. Its central premise is simple but demanding: a biomarker has scientific value only when the sample remains traceable, the measurement remains calibrated, the proposed aging mechanism survives competing explanations, and the released result retains an uncertainty boundary appropriate to its intended use. Microrobotic sampling is treated as a candidate laboratory capability rather than an assumed improvement. The reference domain is closed microfluidics, organ on chip systems, bench top modules, authorized ex vivo samples, and separately governed prospective research. A successful robot trajectory does not establish preserved biology. Greater analytical sensitivity does not establish mechanism specificity. A younger biological age score does not establish that an intervention improves healthspan or survival. The Three Level Evidence Firewall Level 1 Measurement Science. Demonstrate that collection, motion, contact, field exposure, storage, preprocessing, and sensing do not alter the target state beyond a preregistered budget. Preserve sample identity, mass balance, raw evidence, calibration ancestry, and covariance aware uncertainty. Level 2 Aging Biology. Demonstrate that the biomarker reflects a specified aging mechanism rather than tissue composition, acute stress, disease, medication, circadian state, matrix interference, batch effects, or platform drift. Require orthogonal assays and mechanism specific perturbations. Level 3 Longevity Intervention Research. Test whether biomarker change predicts or mediates meaningful function, healthspan, morbidity, or mortality. Association is not intervention benefit. Changing a score cannot be equated with changing health without independent prospective evidence. Candidate Research Expression Qvalid = Pintact × Ptrace × Pmechanism × Poutcome − Dsample − Uchain − Bintervention The expression is a research ledger rather than a universal biological law. Each probability must be estimated within a declared sample matrix, platform, population, time horizon, and claim level. Sample damage, chain uncertainty, unauthorized use, and irreversible harm are veto conditions; they cannot be compensated by an attractive aggregate score. Five Layer Research Architecture Sample Truth and Claim Contract. Defines specimen identity, permitted use, exposure limits, claim level, strong comparator, vetoes, exclusions, and abstention. Microrobotic Physics and Preanalytics. Measures flow, diffusion, wall effects, adhesion, shear, heat, field exposure, contact, dead volume, recovery, storage, and matrix change. Aging Mechanism Validation. Separates mechanism specific biology from disease, cell mixture, tissue discordance, acute physiology, circular composite construction, and attractive but noncausal narratives. Metrology and Longitudinal Inference. Binds raw signals, calibration functions, reference ancestry, detection limits, covariance, drift, personal baselines, irregular time series, and transportability. Outcomes Governance and Successor Control. Requires meaningful outcomes, harms, consent, privacy, subgroup calibration, portability, negative result preservation, independent reconstruction, and the right to retire the system. Minimum Verifiable Prototype A blinded study divides matched biological reference material into three arms: candidate microrobotic sampling, a strong manual or passive microfluidic comparator, and a time matched unhandled control where feasible. The study records device motion, force, flow, temperature, contact time, surface history, sample recovery, raw detector output, preprocessing, calibration, uncertainty, and every rejected event. A hidden disturbance such as a coating lot change, dwell time extension, temperature excursion, or reference offset is introduced. The system must detect the invalidity, preserve the failure state, and abstain before the result is promoted. Only after sample fidelity is demonstrated does the program test whether the selected biomarker responds to a mechanism specific perturbation. Only after mechanism validity is established does a separate prospective study ask whether the marker adds calibrated information about function, disease, healthspan, or survival beyond chronological age and established clinical measures. Research Contributions • A three level evidence firewall that prevents sampling feasibility from becoming an aging mechanism claim or clinical conclusion. • Thirty mathematical and physical derivations connected to chapter corridors, experiments, failure tests, and Research Gates. • Eighty two chapters covering sample truth, microfluidic physics, preanalytics, aging biology, biosensor metrology, longitudinal models, interventions, and governance. • Two hundred detailed Research Gates designed as future research entry points with baselines, required evidence, competing explanations, stop conditions, and successor packets. • A lifecycle design in which manual methods, passive fluidics, classical sensors, or the retirement of a popular biomarker can legitimately defeat the more complex system. Central Scientific Boundary This work does not claim that microrobots currently provide autonomous human body sampling, diagnosis, therapy, or life extension. It does not treat every age associated signal as a causal hallmark, and it does not recommend personal medical action. Clinical translation would require independent analytical validation, ethical review, regulatory authorization, clinical performance studies, harm monitoring, and post deployment surveillance. Across eighty two chapters, thirty linked derivations, and two hundred Research Gates, it integrates microscale transport, sample preservation, preanalytical control, aging biology, metrological traceability, longitudinal inference, intervention studies, and successor governance. The book enforces a strict three level firewall: preserved measurement must be demonstrated before mechanism validity, and mechanism validity before meaningful health outcome prediction. Its purpose is not to promise life extension, but to make future longevity research more testable, reconstructable, and capable of saying no. abstract: Scott R. Steele, MD, MBA, FACS, FASCRS, FPSCRS (Hon.) Dr. Ira L. Leeds is a Staff Colon and Rectal Surgeon and Assistant Professor of Surgery in the Department of Surgery at the Yale School of Medicine at Yale University in New Haven, CT. Ira was born and raised in Atlanta, GA, and Miami, FL, spending holidays and summers in his dad's small business' mailroom and washing boats at the marina to motivate him to “stay in school.” Ira attended Princeton University for his undergraduate degree in Politics. He then went on to serve as a Teach For America Corps Member in Memphis, TN, for 2 years before matriculating at Emory University for medical school. While in medical school, he added an extra-year deferral to read for an MBA at the University of Oxford in the United Kingdom. After medical school graduation, he went to The Johns Hopkins Hospital for a residency in general surgery. While at Hopkins, he found another diversion and obtained an ScM in Clinical Investigation at Hopkins' Bloomberg School of Public Health with additional certifications in Quality, Patient Safety and Outcomes Research, Health Finance and Management, and Public Health Economics. Ira then came to join us for a year in Cleveland during his colorectal surgery fellowship at the Cleveland Clinic, prior to going to Yale, where he has practiced ever since. Ira is a busy clinical surgeon and loves meeting all kinds of people, especially at their most vulnerable where he can offer them help. He also really enjoys the instant reward that surgical therapy can bring with improving the underlying condition. Colorectal surgery also allows him to experience something different every day—from the operating room to endoscopy, as well as the clinic and the research lab. His clinical and research interests are in complex colorectal disease with a growing reoperative inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)-oriented practice. He has multiple peer-reviewed publications and has given multiple lectures regionally, nationally, and internationally in our field. He and his wife have two young daughters (Eleanor and Louisa). Ira has proffered chess and yardwork as family activities but more typically ends up sampling baked goods (Eleanor) and searching the house for chocolate (Louisa). His wife, Sandy, is a tremendous athlete, competing in multiple run, triathlon, and Ironman competitions, for both of them. They also have an Italian water dog (Rosie) who is a constant companion with the family. Outside of medicine, he enjoys traveling, including camping in the Italian Alps, mastering 30-minute meals, and experimenting with grass grown in a northern climate. title: Partial Postponement of the Application of the In Vitro Diagnostic Medical Devices Regulation in the European Union
authors: Michael Vogeser; Monika Brüggemann; Jochen K. Lennerz; Albrecht Stenzinger; Ulrich M. Gassner
abstract: In the January 2022 issue of Clinical Chemistry, we discussed core aspects of the new European Union (EU) regulation on in vitro diagnostic medical devices (European Union 2017/746 regulation, IVDR) (1, 2) and their particular implications for healthcare providers. Following the adoption of the IVDR by the European Parliament in May 2017, the full implementation was originally scheduled for May 27, 2022. Over the 5-year transition period, however, it became apparent that key structural and executive elements required for implementation of the IVDR were still under development (3). For example, the European Database for Medical Devices (EUDAMED) is meant to enable comparison of in-house devices and industrial devices as outlined in Article 5, 5 (d); however, EUDAMED is not yet live. Also, Notified Bodies are meant to certify commercial in vitro diagnostic devices (IVDs); however, there have been structural concerns as the number of accredited Notified Bodies in the EU is still very low. Aggravated by the burden of the COVID-19 pandemic, a gap in both areas raised concerns regarding successful implementation of the IVDR. This scenario led to the recent decision by the European Parliament, which, based on a proposal of the Council of the EU and the European Commission, passed a law that modified the initially proposed transition rules and deferred the application of the provisions concerning in-house devices. This amendment went into effect on January 28, 2022, and specifies in principle a stepwise implementation of the IVDR at different time points (4). It is important to point out that the original IVDR requirements detailed in the IVDR remained otherwise unchanged. The new dates of application are as follows: The general safety and performance requirements according to Annex I of the original IVDR must be fulfilled as of May 27, 2022, i.e., no deferral is granted. Industrially manufactured and already marketed IVDs may continue to be placed on the market until May 27, 2025, on the basis of the previous conformity assessment procedure according to EU Directive 98/79/EC, if they fall under the highest risk class D. For class C IVDs, this is possible until May 27, 2026. For class A IVDs placed on the market in sterile condition and class B IVDs, an IVD-CE certification must only be available from May 27, 2027. With regard to IVDs manufactured in-house, Article 5(5)(b) and (c) and (e) to (i) will apply after May 27, 2024. This refers to the quality management system under which the manufacturing of in-house tests takes place. Point (d) of Article 5, paragraph 5 requires that IVDs manufactured in-house may only be used if a comparable commercially available IVD-CE certified product does not meet the requirement of a specific patient group. This controversial section is referred to as ‘industry privilege’ and will not apply until May 27, 2028. In our view, this stepwise application approach provides the opportunity to prepare the relevant regulatory structures in all EU countries to ensure successful implementation of the IVDR. For now, laboratories, professional societies, regulators, and other key stakeholders are collectively tasked to flesh out and define IVDR terms in order to ensure quality and safety of diagnostics for patient care. title: Behind Epstein: Crime, Power, and Global Silence
authors: Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D, DBA
abstract: The most enduring crimes of the modern era are not always those hidden most carefully, but those surrounded by silence so normalized that it ceases to appear as silence at all. They exist in the open, embedded within systems that claim legality, professionalism, and legitimacy. The case of Jeffrey Epstein belongs to this category. It is not simply a story of criminality concealed from view; it is a story of crime sustained by visibility, familiarity, and institutional quiet. To understand Epstein, one must therefore look not only at what he did, but at what was allowed to remain unspoken. This book begins from a fundamental assertion: Epstein’s crimes were not enabled by secrecy alone, but by global silence. Silence that crossed institutions, borders, professions, and moral thresholds. Silence that was not accidental, but produced through incentive structures, reputational calculations, and ethical deferrals. Silence that became routine. The title Behind Epstein: Crime, Power, and Global Silence signals a deliberate shift in analytical focus. Epstein himself is not treated as the central mystery. The mystery lies in the conditions that allowed a known pattern of abuse to persist across time and geography. What exists “behind” Epstein is not merely a network of associates, but a layered system of power relations that repeatedly absorbed warning signs without triggering decisive response. Humanistic authority frames this inquiry by insisting that no analysis of power is complete unless it accounts for its human consequences. The Epstein case is often discussed through the language of scandal, speculation, or conspiracy. This book rejects those frames. Instead, it treats the case as a profound ethical failure of contemporary governance one in which human vulnerability was subordinated to institutional comfort and elite stability. Crime, in this context, cannot be reduced to illegal acts alone. It must be understood as a process that unfolds through opportunity, tolerance, and normalization. Epstein’s criminality did not occur in isolation. It unfolded within environments that treated discretion as virtue, delay as prudence, and disbelief as rational caution. These environments did not merely fail to prevent abuse; they actively shaped the conditions under which abuse became sustainable. Power, as examined in this book, is not synonymous with authority. Epstein held no elected office, no formal mandate, no transparent corporate leadership. Yet he exercised influence across domains typically insulated from scrutiny: finance, philanthropy, academia, and elite social networks. This form of power operates through access rather than command, through proximity rather than hierarchy. It is precisely this informal nature that renders it difficult to regulate and easy to excuse. The Epstein case exposes how modern power increasingly operates in spaces between institutions rather than within them. It thrives in overlaps between jurisdictions, between professional roles, between public and private spheres. In these overlaps, responsibility becomes diffuse and accountability uncertain. This diffusion is not a flaw of the system; it is one of its most functional features. Conceptual novelty in this book emerges from reframing silence as a structural phenomenon rather than an absence of speech. Silence is often imagined as passive a failure to act or speak. Here, silence is treated as an outcome actively produced by systems that reward compliance, discretion, and non-intervention. This work introduces the concept of institutional quietude: a condition in which organizations maintain stability by minimizing disruption, even when disruption is ethically necessary. Institutional quietude does not require malicious intent. It thrives on proceduralism. Each decision to delay, to negotiate, to defer, appears reasonable when viewed independently. Collectively, these decisions create a climate in which harm persists uninterrupted. Epstein’s case demonstrates how such climates can endure for decades. Humanistic authority demands that we interrogate not only what institutions did, but what they chose not to hear. Victims’ voices were present. Allegations were raised. Patterns were observable. Yet these signals were repeatedly reframed as insufficient, inconvenient, or premature. Disbelief functioned as a gatekeeping mechanism, regulating whose experiences were recognized as knowledge. This book therefore treats testimony not as anecdotal evidence, but as epistemic data. Lived experience is not a threat to objectivity; it is essential to understanding how systems actually operate. When victims are dismissed, it is not because their accounts lack coherence, but because their social position lacks power. The global dimension of the Epstein case reveals another critical failure: the asymmetry between mobility and responsibility. Epstein’s movement across borders was not incidental. It was enabled by wealth, privilege, and a fragmented international accountability framework. Jurisdictional boundaries, while legally necessary, became ethically exploitable. Responsibility remained local; power became global. This book introduces the concept of transnational silence to describe how accountability dissolves when wrongdoing spans multiple legal systems. No single authority assumes full responsibility. Each waits for another to act. Silence, in this context, is not imposed; it is negotiated through inaction. Importantly, this analysis does not portray globalization as inherently corrupt. Rather, it demonstrates how globalization without ethical coordination creates predictable blind zones. These blind zones are not accidental oversights; they are structural consequences of systems designed to facilitate movement while constraining obligation. Another central contribution of this work lies in examining how legitimacy is constructed and maintained. Epstein’s association with respected institutions financial, academic, philanthropic did not merely provide cover; it actively reshaped perception. Legitimacy functioned as moral camouflage. Suspicion became impolite. Inquiry became intrusive. Silence became a sign of professionalism. This phenomenon underscores a troubling reality: legitimacy can be manufactured independently of ethical conduct. When institutions lend their symbolic capital without rigorous scrutiny, they participate intentionally or not in the normalization of harm. This book challenges the assumption that legitimacy is earned solely through success or association. It insists that legitimacy must be continuously justified through responsibility. Humanistic authority also requires restraint. This work does not speculate beyond evidence, nor does it indulge in moral dramatization. Sensational detail, while attention-grabbing, often obscures structural understanding. The goal here is not to shock, but to clarify. Not to accuse indiscriminately, but to analyze responsibly. The death of Epstein in custody intensified public attention while simultaneously narrowing the scope of accountability. Individual culpability became unresolved, and systemic responsibility risked being forgotten. This book resists that narrative closure. Individuals may disappear; structures do not. Silence, once normalized, continues unless deliberately challenged. Behind Epstein lies a pattern that extends far beyond one case. It is a pattern visible wherever power is insulated from scrutiny, wherever institutions prioritize reputation over responsibility, and wherever victims are asked to wait for justice that never arrives. This book treats Epstein as a case study through which these broader dynamics can be examined with clarity and urgency. From a methodological perspective, the analysis integrates insights from sociology, ethics, political economy, legal studies, and leadership theory. This interdisciplinarity is not decorative; it is necessary. Epstein’s case cannot be understood within a single disciplinary lens without distortion. Crime, power, and silence intersect across domains, and so must analysis. The concept of ethical deferral is introduced to describe how moral responsibility is postponed under the guise of procedural necessity. Ethical deferral allows institutions to appear cautious while effectively doing nothing. Over time, deferral becomes indistinguishable from denial. Epstein’s prolonged impunity illustrates how devastating this process can be. This opening remarks also clarifies the normative stance of the book. It does not assume that all actors within Epstein’s orbit acted with malicious intent. However, it rejects the idea that harm requires malicious intent to be morally consequential. Negligence, indifference, and silence are not neutral states. They are ethical positions with measurable impact. The humanistic dimension of this work is further reflected in its refusal to reduce victims to narrative instruments. Their experiences are treated with dignity, not as evidence to be exploited, but as realities to be acknowledged. Abuse is not an abstract violation; it is a rupture in trust, safety, and human dignity. In aligning with the standards of Scopus-indexed scholarship, this book emphasizes conceptual coherence, analytical originality, and ethical transparency. Arguments are developed cumulatively, definitions are precise, and claims are situated within broader theoretical conversations. The tone remains critical yet measured, reflecting an awareness that scholarship carries responsibility. Ultimately, Behind Epstein: Crime, Power, and Global Silence is a book about accountability in an age of dispersed authority. It asks how societies can respond when harm is not hidden but ignored, not denied but normalized. It challenges readers to reconsider the moral cost of silence, especially when silence is rewarded. If this book provokes discomfort, it does so intentionally. Discomfort is not a failure of understanding; it is often its beginning.

title: SAS Multimetric Tribunal: What a Hallucination Benchmark Measures and What It Does Not — A Format-Controlled Audit of Structural Classification
authors: Gonzalo Emir Durante
abstract: Hallucination-detection systems are usually judged by a single headline metric, computed under a benchmark design that determines what that metric can show. This paper’s contribution is not a detection algorithm — structural coherence scoring is established — but a methodology for measuring exactly what a benchmark proves and what it does not, applied to the SAS Multimetric Tribunal: a thirteen-module, GPU-free structural classifier combining lexical, entity-mutation, curvature, logical-inversion, topological-similarity, semantic-drift, entropy, complexity, and surprisal signals via a cascading multiplicative penalty (\(\kappa_{D} = 0.56\), \(\kappa_{R} = 0.15\)). On a stratified 1,800-pair benchmark (HaluEval-Dialogue, HaluEval-QA, TruthfulQA), the tribunal reaches F1 = 98.99% with zero false positives under an A\(\rightarrow\)A identical-text sanity check. We report this figure and then show, using a format-controlled negative (N1) on the same 1,800 IDs, that it measures format asymmetry between source and response rather than hallucination detection. The tribunal flags 1,569 of 1,800 verbatim correct answers presented alone (87.2%), and in HaluEval-QA scores the correct answer as _more_ anomalous than the hallucinated response. Three further findings follow from the same audit. (i) A per-module analysis shows the tribunal’s seven-module core has no content-sensitive module (prior to the optional R3.1 guard): the one module designed to capture semantic divergence (cre_isi) gives the same per-ID score whether the response is byte-identical or completely different. (ii) The 87.97-point advantage of multiplicative combination over weighted averaging reported in v4 is an artifact of threshold calibration; under per-scheme thresholds on format-matched negatives, both schemes converge to F1 \(\approx 0.69\) and the multiplicative scheme is worse by AUROC. (iii) A new differential guard (R3.1, grounding-based with compression abstention and short-response heuristics) corrects 1,133 of the 1,569 format-driven false positives on correct answers alone, raising F1 from 0.687 to 0.833 (\(\Delta\)F1 = \(+ 0.146\)), and is evaluated on a financial domain (FinQA, 1,657 samples) as a sanity check, with 87.0% detection and zero regressions on hallucinated answers (see §8.9 for framing). A held-out 50/50 split over 100 random repetitions confirms that the threshold (0.95) and F1 (0.833 \(\pm\) 0.0055 on held-out data) are stable across splits. The guard does not rely on substring matching and is not a constructional artifact in the sense of §8 (see §8 for the distinction between the guard’s design and the N1 construction). V9 ADDENDUM. Two post-peer-review advances are documented in this revision. (iv) The R3.1 guard’s binary compression-ratio abstention (CR \(>\) 0.5) has been replaced by a continuous weight function (\(\kappa\)C), reducing abstentions from 58 to 1 on N1 (\(-\)98%) without regressions. (v) A new topological-similarity module (R3.2) detects semantic equivalence under paraphrase when lexical overlap is near zero, using canonical clusters, deterministic lemmatization, passive-voice inversion, and a strict anchoring rule. R3.2 is integrated as an optional eighth module with a conditional gate (PARAPHRASE_RESCUE / CONTRADICTION_VETO / INACTIVE). Both advances were completed in approximately 10 hours total, following a specification-audit-code workflow. V9 ADDENDUM (2026-11-02). Four further extension modules are documented in this revision, bringing the tribunal to thirteen modules. (vi) R3.3 Semantic Drift Trajectory measures ISI sentence-by-sentence and localizes the break point where a response diverges from its source. (vii) R3.4 Entropy Differential compares Shannon entropy of source and response; on 300 calibration pairs the control condition yields \({|{\Delta H}|} = 0.000\) exactly, giving perfect separation. (viii) R3.5 Kolmogorov Complexity Ratio approximates complexity via zlib LZ77 compression. (ix) R3.6 Surprisal Analysis combines per-token self-information with an out-of-vocabulary fraction signal. All four modules are 100% standard-library, add no external dependencies, and were calibrated on real data rather than assumed thresholds. A full evaluation over 30,790 pairs across four public datasets (HaluEval-QA, HaluEval-Dialogue, TruthfulQA, MedHallu) yields aggregate precision 0.9989, recall 0.9877, F1 0.9933, and accuracy 0.9933, with 22 false positives in 20,768 control pairs (0.11%). The MedHallu corpus (10,000 records, 4-condition protocol) adds a format-controlled medical-domain evaluation with 85.10% detection and 0.01% identity false positives. V1.4.0 ANALYSIS SUITE (2026-11-05). Three further analyses are reported in this revision (§8.10). (x) A per-module firing breakdown across four conditions on the MedHallu corpus (10,000 records) shows that the lexical baseline (Jaccard) fires on 0.28% of format-controlled A\(\rightarrow\)A_′′_ pairs, confirming that detection is content-driven rather than length-driven. (xi) A structural fingerprint (12-dimensional feature vector: 3 relational + 9 absolute) achieves zero-overlap separation between paraphrase and hallucination: the 95th percentile of A\(\rightarrow\)A_′′_ (0.2400) lies below the 5th percentile of A\(\rightarrow\)B (0.5436), yielding a recommended rescue threshold \(\kappa_{P} = 0.4039\). (xii) Conditional compression (zlib-based \(\Delta_{SR}\) and asymmetry) is evaluated and reported as a negative result: both signals are dominated by length confounds, with A\(\rightarrow\)A_′_ asymmetry (647.9) indistinguishable from A\(\rightarrow\)B (670.6). The approach is discarded as a detection module. V1.4.1 FIX (2026-11-06). Two corrections are reported in this revision. (xiii) The R3.2 topological module’s dictionary-based gate was found to accidentally rescue hallucinations (127/1000 A\(\rightarrow\)B pairs) by matching common words to canonical clusters. Replacing the dictionary gate with the structural fingerprint distance (\(\kappa_{P} = 0.4039\)) eliminated all hallucination rescues, raising aggregate F1 from 0.8901 to 0.9933 (\(\Delta\)F1 = \(+ 0.1032\)). (xiv) Four fixes to the source_target_guard module (numerical magnitude comparison, drug name gazetteer, date mutation weight, causal inversion detection) raised adversarial detection from 1/5 to 5/5. Combined with the fingerprint rescue (5/5 on paraphrase cases), the adversarial set achieves 10/10. SCOPE. SAS detects structural hallucinations (content not present in the source) with coverage limited to texts with lexical overlap \(\geq\) 30% or shared entity structure. It does not detect: paraphrases with total restructuring and zero lexical overlap (requires distributed semantics), stealth hallucinations that preserve structure and entities (identical vocabulary with mutated facts), or false facts that do appear in the source. Declared coverage: 85.10% on format-controlled pairs (MedHallu, 10,000 records), with 0.01% identity false positives. After the v1.4.1 fixes, the adversarial set (10 manually constructed cases) achieves 10/10: 5/5 stealth hallucinations detected and 5/5 legitimate paraphrases rescued by the structural fingerprint (\(\kappa_{P} = 0.4039\)). The paper’s contribution is the audit procedure that produced these retirements. Five of v4/v5’s quantitative claims do not survive it. What does survive — thresholds, the \(\kappa_{R}\) sweep, the forensic audit of v2 metrics, the per-module architecture itself as a diagnostic instrument — is reported with the same standard.

title: Blood bans and COVID-19: Government attempts to influence medicine and science threaten us all
authors: Jeremy W. Jacobs; Thomas C. Binns; David M. Chooljian; Brian D. Adkins; Jennifer S. Woo; Laura Dilly Stephens; Timothy D. Schlafer; Bipin N. Savani; Garrett S. Booth
abstract: Every 2 seconds someone in the United States needs blood or platelets. With nearly 16 million blood products transfused each year, blood transfusion is one of the most common medical procedures in the United States, contributing to life-saving medical care for millions annually.1 Despite the recent unparalleled blood shortages resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic, the US health care system has largely managed to weather the potentially catastrophic situation of an inadequate blood supply, partially attributed to the development of COVID-19 vaccines blunting the pandemic and resulting demand. The result is maintenance of available blood for individuals with both emergent and nonemergent indications. On February 17, 2023, however, a state representative introduced Montana House Bill No. 645, which attempts to prohibit donation of blood from COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2)–vaccinated individuals.2 The bill also punishes individuals who “knowingly use, receive, accept, ship, transfer, or administer” blood from a COVID-19–vaccinated donor. Violations would result in a misdemeanor punishable by monetary penalty. This type of legislation would impose liability on numerous individuals—donors, patients, blood donation industry workers, health care professionals, etc. Although individuals refusing blood transfusion from COVID-19–vaccinated donors is not novel,3 this legislation seeks to validate unfounded, misinformed, and sometimes conspicuously prejudiced beliefs. We initially hesitated to address this effort with a formal response at the risk of conferring legitimacy, but we believe that such legislation threatens the very foundation of American health care so comprehensively that official condemnation is necessary. The evolution of COVID-19 vaccination skepticism has progressed from mere uncertainty to unsubstantiated medical ­misinformation and even intentional falsification. Vaccination misinformation has affected health care in a variety of settings,4 but threats to the US blood supply have prompted federal regulators to refute these claims.5 Maintaining the safety of the blood supply is a guiding principle in blood collection, and the lay public should be reassured that blood donors must be in good health at the time of donation. Donors must pass a health evaluation, including vital sign assessment, travel and contact history review, and extensive eligibility screening concerning pertinent therapies and illnesses. Every blood donation also undergoes testing for infectious agents that may be transmitted by blood. Further, the US blood donation system has existing deferral strategies for certain vaccinations, and vaccines are evaluated to determine whether donation deferral is necessary. Although no studies have been undertaken to directly assess the effect of transfusion from vaccinated blood donors on recipients, there is no historical or contemporary scientific basis to believe that this blood poses any risk. As the COVID-19 vaccines do not contain live virus, there is no evidence that they pose an infection risk to recipients of the donated blood. Further, there is no evidence—and no logical reasoning—to believe that these vaccines would alter the genetic material of the vaccinated individual or blood transfusion recipient. Thus, legislation pertaining to risk should not be made until such data are reviewed. Notably, as of February 23, 2023, 81.2% of the US population had received at least one COVID-19 vaccine dose.6 Although the exact proportion of COVID-19–vaccinated US blood donors is unknown, a June 2022 study demonstrated an increase in the seroprevalence rate in blood donors from 3.5% in July 2020 to 20.2% for SARS-CoV-2 infection–induced antibodies to 83.3% for combined SARS-CoV-2 infection– and vaccine-induced antibodies by May 2021, higher than the general population rate at that time.7 The combined seroprevalence increased further to 94.7% by December 2021, highlighting the significant uptake of at least 1 vaccine dose across the United States.7 Despite this finding, no adverse effects in recipients of blood transfusion from vaccinated donors attributable to the vaccine have been described to date. Further, as data have shown that blood donors tend to be vaccinated against COVID-19 at higher rates than the general public, these types of proposals could contribute to blood shortages in regions and jurisdictions in which the laws are enacted. Likewise, if additional states were to adopt such a restricted approach, these policies could pose a theoretical risk to the adequacy of the US blood supply on a larger scale. With no US Food and Drug Administration–approved blood substitute available, clinical outcomes in regions with a lack of blood availability would regress. Perhaps just as significantly, these proposals would prohibit research and emergency use authorization therapies essential for responding to and preventing pandemics, including those not directly involving vaccines. For instance, numerous hospitals used blood products containing SARS-CoV-2 infection–induced antibodies collected from blood donors previously infected with SARS-CoV-2 (ie, convalescent plasma) as a therapeutic strategy for COVID-19 before the advent of vaccines. Objections to the use of blood products from vaccinated donors may be related to the fact that such donations are not distinctly labeled to promote awareness and choice; however, if labeling were present, it would simply demonstrate that the majority of products are from vaccinated donors, without a valid clinical reason to do so and potentially inducing a chilling effect on both donation and receipt of such blood.7 Notwithstanding the ethical considerations of this practice, the financial and administrative burden for such unfounded implementation would further negatively affect the blood donation infrastructure. Unfortunately, the looming threat to patient care is not limited to Montana. Proposed Connecticut Senate Bill No. 531, introduced on January 18, 2023, would amend Connecticut law to “permit an individual the right to choose blood transfusion from an unvaccinated individual.”8 This bill presumes that the blood transfusion recipient, physician, or the hospital itself knows the blood donor’s vaccination status, which is not the case in the United States. Blood products are not labeled with the donor’s COVID-19 vaccination status because this information has no clinical impact on the transfusion recipient, similar to other individual characteristics, such as race and ethnicity. Essentially, this bill implies that a patient should be able to request a directed donation from a particular donor based on vaccination status. Although we acknowledge patients’ general rights of autonomy and therefore refusal of therapy, in the absence of another justification, such as a rare blood type, there is no evidence that blood from a directed donor is safer than standard volunteer blood. Further, social pressures associated with directed donations may compromise the reliability of the donor history questionnaire, a crucial risk-mitigation strategy.9 Although the proposed legislation in Montana has been tabled, hopefully ending any meaningful consideration, it is noteworthy that the subcommittee did not vote it down outright. The Connecticut legislation has been referred to the state’s Senate Joint Committee on Public Health and is pending action. We believe that elected officials should proceed with extreme caution before proposing bills that may have profound impacts on health care without medical or scientific evidence to support their claims. These legislative precedents could set the stage for an impending legal, medical, and ethical battle among lawmakers, health care professionals, and vaccine skeptics, with the safety and sufficiency of the blood supply in the balance.

title: Voting for Democracy’s Future: The Role of Future Collective (Dis)continuity in Shaping Democratic Participation Among Italian Citizens
authors: Federica Scarci; Matilde Tumino; Andrea Manunza; Alessia Valmori; Luca Cussigh
abstract: On June 2, 1946, following the end of fascism and the war, the votes of Italian men and, for the first time, of Italian women marked the beginning of a democratic Italy, founded on citizen participation. Today, 80 years later, democracy continues to be generally regarded as a positive and desirable value; however, its stability appears increasingly uncertain, in a climate described as “democratic anxiety” . In Italy, this picture of instability is accompanied by a rise in voter abstention; in the most recent general election of 2022, turnout stood at around 64%, the lowest figure in the history of the Republic . This is an extremely significant problem, as voting represents one of the fundamental tools through which citizens exercise democracy and ensure its continuity over time. Research suggests that voting reflects a form of collective action, associated with ingroup identification and perceived collective efficacy . At the same time, a vast body of literature has highlighted the role of national identity and social identification in sustaining political participation . In applications to political phenomena, social identity has often been treated as a monolithic construct, focusing primarily on the strength of identification with the national ingroup . Recent evidence, however, suggests a more multifaceted conception of national identity, one that also includes how the ingroup is consistently represented over time. The concept of perceived collective continuity reflects the tendency to perceive social groups and their values and traditions as entities that persist over time across the past, present, and future . When individuals perceive that national identity has continuity, they feel part of something that preceded them and will continue after them, experiencing a sense of stability and security . Conversely, when the group’s collective continuity is threatened physically or symbolically, collective angst – i.e., a concern for the ingroup’s future vitality – may emerge, motivating members to act to protect and strengthen it . Furthermore, most studies have focused on the perception of collective continuity (vs. discontinuity) with respect to the past, highlighting the role of collective nostalgia in predicting ingroup protection and outgroup rejection . Recent research, however, introduced the concept of future collective continuity, that is, the perception that the ingroup will maintain a consistent trajectory in the future, showing that envisioning strong future continuity of the national ingroup can reduce collective angst and prejudice toward immigrants, while increasing prosocial attitudes and collective action intentions, especially among those who identify most strongly with the ingroup . If the future continuity of the ingroup can reduce anxiety and perceived threats, then a future discontinuity of the ingroup could trigger collective angst and motivate members to protect it. Yet, this possibility has not been directly examined for political participation. Applying this reasoning, the present project proposes that a future discontinuity in Italy’s identity, represented by the loss of democracy, may increase the importance of voting as a means of protecting the continuity of the national ingroup . Since the future is perceived as more open to action than the past, imagining a possible future discontinuity could motivate action in the present, making voting a tool for preserving the country’s democratic continuity . Furthermore, this project extends this framework to citizens residing abroad, whose continued engagement with the political life of their country of origin depends not only on the strength of their national identification but also on how they perceive the nation and its continuity across time and space. Indeed, citizens residing abroad, who are often overlooked in studies on political participation, may exercise their right to vote in elections in their country of origin . In the Italian context, voting from abroad tends to have lower and more unstable participation rates compared to voting by residents in Italy . Therefore, examining the perceptions of Italians living abroad enables us to understand whether Italy’s democratic continuity is perceived as significant depending on the strength of their ties to the nation. Geographical distance could alter the way Italians living abroad perceive national identity and could mitigate the impact of a threat to the ingroup. Therefore, comparing Italians living in Italy with those living abroad allows us to test whether a future discontinuity in the national ingroup motivates political participation and voting when national belonging is experienced through geographical proximity or transnational distance.

title: Digital Water Metering: A Framework and Modelling Tool for Benefit Valuation
authors: Ian Monks
abstract: Understanding the touchpoints of water usage metering and how meter data is used in all business areas of water utilities, and in the everyday lives of customers, can lead to an appreciation of the scale of obtainable benefits of digital water metering (DWM). The absence of a systematic cataloguing of benefits, and the measurement of their value to a water utility and its customers, may explain the lack of acceptance of this technology among water utilities. Manual meter reading has been identified as inefficient and ineffective for most utility processes, other than periodic billing for which it too can be problematic. DWM substantially eliminates the walking of meter reading routes by meter readers. It delivers over 2000 readings per quarter (at hourly intervals) rather than just the one reading obtained by the meter reader. Special trips to the property, which are required to read the manual meter when the customer leaves, are also eliminated. Sometimes the customer is asked to read the meter when the water utility cannot. DWM is accurate and automatic whereas manual meter reading is subject to mis-reads and estimation when the meter cannot be accessed. In Australia, and many other parts of the developed world, few water utilities have switched to DWM completely and, in many others, only in particular circumstances, usually involving a lack of physical access or where access by meter readers would be inefficient. Where significant network issues or scarce water resources have existed, digital meters have improved the management of the network and allowed the deferral of network augmentation and the conservation of water. This doctoral research study aimed to address this lack of knowledge of DWM benefits by searching for and cataloguing the benefits, and by developing plausible measures that provide probabilistic ranges of outcomes of savings and changes to customer sentiment. The objectives were to find as many benefits as possible from across water utilities’ operations and among customer interactions with their water and wastewater service provider; to value those benefits, particularly the less-tangible benefits: and to develop a tool to model the value of benefits for water utilities. To identify the benefits, an extensive literature review of academic and industry reports was conducted. Interviews were conducted with several current and past staff of water utilities. The literature review was backed up by structured interviews with employees with specific expertise from a cross section of companies and representing various roles within those organisations. Customers were surveyed directly to identify their responses to the potential of digital metering. Qualitative and quantitative methods were applied to the expert opinions and customer survey responses to develop a valuation model that calculates savings and change in customer satisfaction levels. Other surveys were conducted to collect data from water utilities on specific issues. The valuation model was trialled in the field. The methods and findings are presented in the four journal papers that are included in this thesis. In all, 77 benefits of DWM were identified. These were categorised into a taxonomy based on who would benefit, (i.e., the water business, the customer or both water business or customer) as well as the business areas and sub-areas of those beneficiaries. A second taxonomy was developed that categorised benefits according to sustainability themes. Qualitative analysis of the expert opinions regarding the benefits exposed the range of opinions on the likelihood that benefits could be achieved and the extent of the benefit. While quantifying the savings of individual benefits, two contexts were identified (Cost of Water savings, and Charges and Operational Cost savings) and the need for flexibility to meet local expectations was observed. The customer survey revealed the potential change in levels of customer satisfaction from a current 5.8 (0 – 10 scale) to between 6.2 and 8.8, with a simple average of 7.6. Separate valuation methods within the model were developed for each context. A third valuation method was developed for measuring change in customer satisfaction over multiple years. The application of the model, using a large metropolitan water utility’s data, calculated savings outcomes that were consistent with the utility’s cost-benefit analysis and provided the utility with risk-based probabilistic ranges. DWM benefit savings were also viewed through a sustainability lens after being allocated to the different sustainability themes. The trial raised issues with the framing of business cases for DWM projects and which were then examined. Other findings were made during the study. The commonly used scale used in the Net Promoter Score classification of customers was observed to be inaccurate for relationship type surveys of water utilities, and a new scale was proposed. The potential of data analytics applied to hourly meter readings to answer questions on usage within residential properties was examined through a case study of a regional water utility. A model to optimise the sequencing of meter deployment to gain benefits early was proposed and a prototype model presented. Further, an opportunity for a capability model for intelligent metering was identified and a preliminary model was developed. The study also proposed that a longitudinal study of the uplift in customer satisfaction from the use of DWM be conducted, and that a non-monetary measure of the value of social equity be developed and applied to DWM project proposals.

authors: Son David Bolduc

abstract: JSON Consistency Repair v0.41.0 is a conservative JSON rectification engine designed to recover determinable syntax damage and repair semantic inconsistencies only when the available evidence identifies a justified correction. The software combines strict JSON parsing with bounded deterministic grammar and lexical recovery, exact constraint discovery, reversible minimal patches, strong fixed-point closure, provenance and authority controls, active falsification of discovered relations, symmetry-aware abstention, controllability and attainability checks, persistent OPEN obligations, targeted incremental recomputation, horizon/distributed-coherence checks, residual-information bounds, and blind-reconstruction verification. It supports single JSON documents, multi-document bundles, JSONL/NDJSON, and bounded-memory top-level-array streaming. Cross-field and cross-record relations include functional, arithmetic, temporal, sequential, schema, enum, identity, reference, aggregate, conservation, graph/state and migration constraints. Conflicting duplicate keys are deliberately refused unless an authority resolves the ambiguity. Version 0.41.0 introduces two execution profiles. full performs exhaustive analysis, global correction search, replay, proof-graph reconstruction and independent final certification. fast still scans all analyzer families but restricts expensive deep correction and falsification to unique local actionable cones; it explicitly reports FAST_SCAN_ONLY and does not masquerade as full certification. The frozen PASS041 verification records 462/462 regression tests passed, 600/600 adversarial stress cases, 73/73 valid Draft 2020-12 public schemas, zero false mutations in the PASS041 stress campaign, successful fresh-source and fresh-wheel checks, and byte-for-byte reproducible wheel/source builds. The syntax contract records 13/13 determinable targeted corruptions repaired and 1/1 conflicting duplicate-key ambiguity correctly refused. PASS is evidence- and contract-relative: it means that no unresolved violation remains under the currently certified relations. It is not a claim of inaccessible external ground truth. Comparative benchmarks and raw validation artifacts are included so that performance and scope can be evaluated independently.
