title: Update of recommendations for the management of COVID-19 in patients with haematological malignancies, haematopoietic cell transplantation and CAR T therapy, from the 2022 European Conference on Infections in Leukaemia (ECIL 9)
authors: Simone Cesaro; Małgorzata Mikulska; Hans Hellmuth Hirsch; Jan Styczyński; Sylvain Meylan; Catherine Cordonnier; David Navarro; Marie von Lilienfeld-Toal; Varun Mehra; Francesco Marchesi; Caroline Besson; Raul Cordoba Masculano; Gernot Beutel; Hermann Einsele; Johan A. Maertens; Rafael de la Cámara; ECIL 9; Marie von Lilienfeld-Toal; Rafael de la Cámara; Per T Ljungman; Livio Pagano
abstract: In 2022, the European Conference on Infections in Leukemia, 9th edition (ECIL-9), published the guidelines for the management of severe acute respiratory syndrome infection (SARS-CoV-2) and disease (COVID-19) in hematological malignancy (HM) and haematopoietic cell transplant (HCT) patients [ 1 ]. During the year 2022, the worldwide epidemiology, morbidity, and mortality changed for the better compared to the previous two years of the pandemic due to the positive effect of public health and social measures, the mass vaccination campaigns, availability of antiviral drugs and anti-spike monoclonal antibodies (MoAbs) [ 2 ]. The achievements were partly hampered by the continuous emergence of highly contagious variants of concern, escaping the immunity acquired by infection or vaccination. Considering these significant changes, an update of the SARS-CoV-2/COVID-19 recommendations was performed at ECIL-9 Conference held in Nice, France, on 14–15 September 2022 and published on the ECIL web page ( https://www.ecil-leukaemia.com/en/program ). Table 1 shows the updated recommendations on prevention, diagnosis, vaccination, and therapy. Table 1 Summary of ECIL-9 recommendations on prevention, diagnosis, vaccination and therapy for SARS-CoV-2/COVID-19 in adult and pediatric onco-hematological patients. Full size table In the prevention part, the added recommendations highlight the importance to personalize the decision to defer chemotherapy, HCT, chimeric-antigen-receptor-T (CAR-T) therapy, and other non-cellular therapies in asymptomatic patients or in patients with prolonged viral shedding, based on the individual risk/benefit ratio assessment. The deferral of treatment to avoid the risk of progression to severe COVID-19 is no longer considered mandatory but should weigh the urgency of the patient’s treatment, the effect of postponing therapy on the risk of relapse or progression of the underlying disease, the degree of immunocompromise, the remission status against the possibility to control viral replication by antivirals and/or MoAbs. In the diagnostic part, the new recommendations highlight the need for the surveillance and external quality assurance of the performance of nucleic acid tests and rapid antigen assays on newly emerging (sub)variants. While nucleic acid tests on nasopharyngeal specimen remain the reference, the use of less invasive samples such as oropharyngeal gargle or saliva can be a reliable alternative only for the symptomatic patient. Sampling of lower respiratory tract fluids is not needed for patients testing positive for SARS-CoV-2 RNA on upper respiratory tract specimens, but is recommended in case of a differential diagnosis with other clinical etiologies, of suspicion of coinfections (together with the appropriate diagnostic workup with blood and sputum cultures, fungal serum markers, urine antigens for pneumococci and Legionella) or if upper respiratory tract sampling is negative but SARS-CoV-2 is suspected. The prognostic significance of the qualitative and quantitative detection of SARS-CoV-2 RNAemia or N-antigenemia requires further investigation [ 3 ]. Testing for SARS-CoV-2 spike antibodies, whose levels correlate with serum neutralizing activity, is not recommended for clinical decision-making regarding vaccine boosters and administration of MoAbs [ 4 ]. Despite T-cell responses having a protective role after natural infection and vaccination, the use of SARS-CoV-2 T-cell assays is not recommended for clinical decision-making [ 5 ]. In the vaccine part, the recommended mRNA vaccine schedule for the vulnerable population of HM and HCT patients is adjourned to the three-dose primary schedule followed by an additional vaccine dose. A third dose improved the rate of seroconversion in patients who had not responded to two doses of mRNA vaccine [ 6 , 7 ] and a 4th dose was safe and could increase antibody titers [ 8 ]. It is highlighted that there are no safety issues in non-transplanted HM patients and that vaccination should not delay the treatment of the underlying disease. With the spread of the Omicron variant many patients with HMs and after HCT have now developed SARS-CoV-2 infections both before and after having received vaccinations. It is recommended that the interval between COVID-19 and subsequent boosters should be at least three and preferably four months. An important change in the recommendations is that also patients with expected poor or very poor responses, such as those receiving therapy with anti-CD20 antibodies or being 6–12 months after the last dose, those with profound hypogammaglobulinemia (<4 g/L), deep lymphopenia (<500/μL), receiving B-cell-maturation-antigen (BCMA) targeted bispecific therapy and patients starting induction chemotherapy for acute leukemia, might still benefit from vaccination also by inducing a T-cell response. Regarding patients after allogeneic HCT, several studies have shown that additional doses of vaccine can result in seroconversion of patients not having responded to the first two or three doses [ 9 ]. At the time of the meeting, the mRNA adapted bivalent vaccines targeting original strains and Omicron subvariants BA.4/5 had just been licensed, initially as booster dose and also for primary immunization in the following months. The of use of updated bivalent vaccines was supported in the guidelines even though it was recognized that there was no information regarding their efficacy in severely immunocompromised patients Although it is not a new recommendation, increasing evidence exists regarding the risk for the development or worsening of graft-versus-host disease after mRNA vaccination and this risk should be considered when planning vaccination schedule. It was noted that the transfer of donor-specific SARS-CoV-2 immunity has been documented but it is unknown if such transfer can be protective early after HCT or improve the vaccine response of the recipient. A new section of the recommendations deals specifically with patients having received CAR-T cell therapy. Various studies have shown that patients with B-cell aplasia are very unlikely to have an antibody response but T-cell responses can be seen in a majority of them [ 10 ]. As in other populations, the protective value of these responses remains, however, unknown. Also in CAR-T recipients additional doses resulted in improved vaccine responses. In the therapy part, the main changes concerned the loss or significant reduction of activity of all authorized MoAbs against the new VOCs, and the increased availability of three antivirals for early treatment of mild/moderate COVID-19 [ 11 ]. MoAbs had been previously shown effective in the prevention and treatment of mild/moderate COVID-19, and, in seronegative patients, of severe COVID-19. Their limitations included the need for intravenous administration and the risk of developing in-vivo resistance in immunocompromised patients due to prolonged viral shedding and ineffective viral clearance resulting from the lack of T-cell immunity. For pre-exposure prophylaxis with long-lasting antibodies, the increase of dose has been proposed to counteract the loss of efficacy against the BA.1 Omicron variant in February 2022, but even higher doses are currently not expected to be effective. Therefore, the recommendation is to use (probably new ones) MoAbs for prophylaxis and treatment in the HM population only if they are active against circulating VOCs. Antivirals are the cornerstone of therapy since their activity is not influenced by VOCs, and randomized trials demonstrated that, when administered within 5 or 7 days from symptom onset, they were effective in reducing the rate of hospitalization or death in unvaccinated outpatients with mild/moderate COVID-19 who had risk factors for severe COVID-19 [ 12 , 13 , 14 ]. Although few HM patients were included, this population is expected to gain maximum benefit from anti-viral treatment, as demonstrated in observational studies [ 15 ]. Oral nirmatrelvir/ritonavir or intravenous remdesivir are the first choices based on efficacy data. Drug-drug interactions limit the use of nirmatrelvir/ritonavir, but the careful reduction of immunosuppression or targeted therapy agents can allow its use in most HM patients. Molnupiravir use is limited by the lower efficacy in the randomized trial (relative risk reduction of 30%, compared to 87% of nirmatrelvir/ritonavir or remdesivir), the lack of European Medicine Agency (but not FDA) authorization and, therefore, the unavailability in some countries. The advantages of molnupiravir include absence of drug-drug interactions and the possibility to use in case of renal failure (ClCr <30 ml/min). The data available for high titer of convalescent plasma (CVP) does not support its role in the routine treatment of mild/moderate COVID-19. Considering the polyclonal protection given by CVP, less influenced by protein-S mutations which led to the loss of activity of MoAbs, CVP might be useful in immunocompromised patients, in addition to antivirals. In severe or critical COVID-19 in HM, remdesivir treatment is recommended together with steroid treatment and a second immunosuppressant (mainly an anti-IL-6 agent), if required. In the HM patients, when choosing the second immunomodulator, the recent hematological treatment should be also considered, especially if patients are already on ruxolitinib, which should not be discontinued in case of SARS-CoV-2 infection. No data suggest the need for different treatment in HM children compared to HM adults, although children have a much lower risk of severe COVID-19 and the data are more limited. The reason for providing early treatment to children could be hastening the cure from SARS-CoV-2 infection to allow continuing HM treatment program. In conclusion, the ECIL9 2022 provided the updated set of recommendations for the management of COVID-19 in HM and HCT patients. The advancements in knowledge on SARS-CoV-2/COVID-19 and massive economical investments in immunization and treatment led to improvement of morbidity and mortality figures although the pandemic is not declared over. Many areas of research are still open and include the role of a combination of antivirals and MoAbs, the evaluation of prolonged courses of antivirals, the management of the underlying disease/deferral of transplant in case of positivity, the role of recent high titer CVP, the use of T-cell therapies against SARS-CoV-2, and the risk of complications during HCT in patients with previous COVID-19.

title: Constraint-First Governance for Gemini-Class AI Systems
authors: Mark Anthony Brewer
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Constraint-First Governance for Gemini-Class AI Systems Classification: PUBLIC-SAFE(Architectural analysis only. No operational thresholds, enforcement logic, or proprietary mechanisms are disclosed.) Author: Mark Anthony BrewerContext: Gemini-class AI systems developed by GoogleStatus: Research & discussion draft PURPOSE, SCOPE, AND SAFETY STATEMENT 1. Purpose This paper documents how constraint-first governance patterns align naturally with Gemini-class AI systems, particularly those integrating search, long-context reasoning, and agentic workflows. The purpose is not to propose adoption, partnership, or implementation.The purpose is to make a governance abstraction legible that becomes increasingly necessary as Gemini-class systems scale in scope, persistence, and consequence. This document is public-safe and descriptive. 2. Scope This paper applies to AI systems that exhibit the following characteristics: integration of search and retrieval into reasoning long-context synthesis across heterogeneous sources persistence across sessions or workflows emerging agentic or tool-mediated behavior deployment across consumer, enterprise, and public-sector contexts These characteristics define Gemini-class systems in an architectural sense, not a branding sense. 3. Explicit Safety Boundary This paper intentionally does not include: implementation instructions enforcement thresholds convergence metrics memory architectures agent control logic reconstruction or validation pipelines All references to governance mechanisms are abstract and non-procedural. 4. Why Governance Becomes Central for Gemini-Class Systems As Gemini-class systems mature, their value shifts from: isolated answersto sustained participation in knowledge creation, synthesis, and decision support. At this stage, the dominant risks are no longer: model error, or lack of capability. They are: escalation of exploratory reasoning into authority, loss of continuity across contexts, and drift between relevance and lawfulness. These risks are structural. 5. Key Design Premise Gemini-class systems do not fail because they are insufficiently intelligent.They fail when authority is not explicitly governed. Constraint-first governance addresses when outputs are allowed to persist, propagate, or act—independently of how they are generated. 6. Reader Guidance This paper should be read as: an architectural alignment note, a vocabulary for governance discussion, and a description of failure-prevention patterns. It is not a roadmap or a technical specification. WHY SEARCH-INTEGRATED INTELLIGENCE REQUIRES GOVERNANCE AT SCALE 7. Search Changes the Nature of Intelligence Search-integrated AI systems differ fundamentally from closed-corpus models. When search is integrated: the system reasons over live, heterogeneous sources, evidence is dynamically retrieved, and synthesis becomes continuous rather than episodic. This shifts the system from answering questions to shaping knowledge landscapes. At this point, search is no longer neutral. 8. Relevance Is Not the Same as Validity Search systems optimize for: relevance, recency, connectivity, and popularity. These properties correlate with usefulness, but they are not equivalent to constraint validity. As a result: frequently cited claims can overshadow lawful but less visible ones, correlated errors can reinforce each other, and repetition can masquerade as verification. Without governance, search becomes a drift amplifier. 9. Long-Context Reasoning Increases Both Power and Risk Gemini-class systems are capable of: synthesizing across long documents, maintaining extended reasoning chains, and integrating multiple perspectives simultaneously. This capability increases: depth of insight, speed of analysis, and apparent coherence. It also increases: confidence collapse, premature convergence, and difficulty distinguishing exploration from conclusion. The more context a system can hold, the more important it becomes to govern what that context is allowed to settle into. 10. Search-Driven Consensus Is Not Truth A common failure mode emerges when: search retrieves multiple sources, synthesis integrates them smoothly, and the resulting narrative appears “well supported.” In reality, the system may be observing: citation loops, shared assumptions, or inherited errors. This creates illusory consensus. Constraint-first governance treats consensus as evidence to be tested, not authority to be granted. 11. Why Human Review Alone Cannot Solve This Human oversight is necessary but insufficient when: search spaces are large, synthesis happens faster than review cycles, and outputs persist across sessions. By the time a human intervenes: the synthesis may already have propagated, downstream systems may have acted on it, and context for revision may be lost. Governance must operate before authority is granted, not after harm occurs. 12. Search as Exploration, Not Commitment In a governed Gemini-class system: search expands the hypothesis space, synthesis explores relationships, and conclusions remain provisional until constraints converge. This preserves: creativity, breadth, and discovery, while preventing: premature closure, overconfident assertions, and unsafe escalation. Search remains powerful, but authority is withheld. 13. Design Implication Any AI system that: tightly integrates search into reasoning, persists across contexts, or influences decisions, must treat search as: exploratory by default, bounded by constraints, and explicitly non-authoritative until governed. Without this separation, scale guarantees instability. AUTHORITY, TIME, AND THE SEPARATION OF EXPLORATION FROM COMMITMENT 14. Why Authority Must Be Explicit in Gemini-Class Systems Gemini-class systems operate with: high fluency, broad synthesis, and rapid response. These qualities create a subtle risk: outputs may be treated as authoritative simply because they are coherent and timely. In reality, authority is not a property of language quality.It is a permission state that must be explicitly granted. Constraint-first governance distinguishes: what can be generatedfrom what is allowed to settle or act. 15. Time as a Governance Dimension In many AI systems, time is implicit: an answer appears, and it persists until replaced. For Gemini-class systems, time must be treated as an explicit governance axis. Different activities require different temporal postures: rapid exploration, careful deliberation, and durable commitment. Conflating these modes increases risk without increasing insight. 16. Separation of Cognitive Phases Constraint-first governance introduces a phase distinction that mirrors real decision-making: Exploratory activityGenerates possibilities, tolerates contradiction, and remains reversible. Deliberative activityEvaluates consistency with constraints, context, and prior commitments. Authoritative activityProduces outputs that are permitted to persist, propagate, or influence action. This separation is conceptual, not procedural, and does not prescribe specific timing. 17. Why This Matters for Search and Agents In Gemini-class systems: search results inform synthesis, synthesis informs planning, and planning may inform action. Without explicit phase separation: exploratory reasoning can be mistaken for decisions, provisional insights can harden into commitments, and downstream systems may act on unstable conclusions. Governance prevents this collapse. 18. Authority Is Not Confidence Constraint-first governance rejects the idea that: confidence, eloquence, or consensuscan grant authority. Authority emerges only when: uncertainty has been acknowledged, constraints have been considered, and escalation is justified. Until then, outputs remain provisional—regardless of quality. 19. Making Commitment Visible A key governance goal is legibility. Users and downstream systems should be able to distinguish: exploratory synthesis, ongoing deliberation, and settled conclusions. This transparency: improves trust, supports auditability, and reduces misuse. It does not require exposing internal mechanisms. 20. Silence as a Temporal Outcome When deliberation does not converge: deferral, delay, or silenceare correct system behaviors. In Gemini-class systems, silence: preserves reversibility, prevents false certainty, and protects against escalation. Silence is a governance feature, not an error. 21. Design Implication For Gemini-class AI systems, responsible scaling requires: explicit separation between thinking and deciding, time-aware authority gating, and refusal to treat fluent output as commitment by default. These patterns enable powerful exploration without sacrificing safety or coherence. MEMORY, CONTINUITY, AND LONG-HORIZON COHERENCE 22. Why Memory Is the Hidden Scaling Risk As Gemini-class systems persist across: sessions, workflows, users, and domains, memory becomes the dominant determinant of system behavior. The primary risks are not memory loss, but: silent reinterpretation of prior conclusions, loss of context for why decisions were made, and drift between past commitments and present assertions. These are continuity failures, not storage failures.

title: Who Helps Me Be Alone?:The Digital Work of Digital Disconnection
authors: Christoffer Bagger
venue: Research at the University of Copenhagen (University of Copenhagen)
abstract: Disconnection requires work, and sometimes more work than is readily apparent. This paper will present an integrative framework for how digital disconnection - understood as the deliberate non-use of media - is made possible by the work and efforts of not just the disconnecting individual, but also the people surrounding them, as well as people with whom they otherwise have no interaction. Broadly speaking, I argue that digital disconnection is something which creates work along axes. It creates work for (1) the selves disconnecting, (2) their surroundings and for (3) strangers somewhere else producing the tools and services which facilitate – or wish to minimize - disconnection. Asking the central question “Who is digital disconnection creating work for?”, this framework will integrate several strands of disconnection research under the aegis of digital labor (Gandini, 2021; Jarrett, 2022) and digital work (Orlikowski & Scott, 2016). Thus far digital disconnection research has broadly been interested in either the the meaningfulness of disconnection to the individuals implicated (e.g. Bucher, 2022; Portwood-Stacer, 2013), on the communities and surroundings which do or do not make disconnection possible (Sutton, 2020; Fast, 2021), or on the technologies which make disconnection more or less impossible (Karppi, 2018). The focus on the labor and work which underlies this framework will unite these different concerns. Whether it is our selves, our partners (Lai, 2021) or workplaces (Fast, 2021), or people we have never met (Beattie, 2020), our disconnection is likely made possible by someone else’s labor. In considering this, we can ask vital questions about whether digital disconnection “reduces” or “shrinks” the amount of digital communication which underlies the digital economy (Gandini, 2021; Jarrett, 2022), or whether it merely displaces these activities on to other actors, as is the case in other aspects of the digital economy where work is ostensibly reduced or eliminated (Andrejevic, 2019; Munn, 2022). In this way, the paper will expand on the commonplace focus on individual struggles to disconnect, which are prevalent in both research and popular literature on disconnection (Syvertsen & Enli, 2020; Bagger, forthcoming; Portwood-Stacer, 2013). It will integrate this focus with the recent turn towards disconnection as something potentially facilitated by families, workplaces, or other formal organizations (Fast, 2021; Syvertsen, 2022; Lai, 2021), or made possible by third parties such as companies delivering services or producing apps or other products facilitating disconnection (Beattie, 2020; Karppi et al., 2021). In problematizing the common preconceptions of individualization in the emerging field (Enli & Syvertsen, 2021; Lomborg & Ytre-Arne, 2021), this paper will bring digital disconnection research into dialogue with broader discussions of the often-invisible labor and work inherent in the digital economy (Fuchs, 2014; Gandini, 2021; Munn, 2022; Jarrett, 2022). In addition to questions about the value or feasibility of digital disconnection (Bucher, 2020; Karppi, 2018), the framework presented in this paper presents a heuristic to inquire into the material effects of disconnection beyond the disconnecting individual themselves. title: 07 — Integration Architecture: Inputs, Outputs, Interfaces, and Failure Isolation
authors: Kenneth Lee Roberts
abstract: **07 — Integration Architecture: Interfaces, Dependencies, Accepted Outputs, and Failure Containment** This component defines the integration layer of the **Space Bioindustrial Architecture (SBA)**. Candidate systems do not become settlement capability merely by functioning internally. A focal organism, process, reactor, device, software system, robot, filter, power unit, or hybrid module becomes architecturally meaningful only when its complete capability package is connected to the declared settlement case through controlled inputs, outputs, interfaces, dependencies, utilities, validation pathways, accepting systems, maintenance provisions, failure controls, evidence, authority, and claim-state records. Integration makes a package **system-visible**. It does not make the package **Countable**. The governing distinctions are: > **Defined interfaces are not necessarily allocated, qualified, functioning, or maintained interfaces.** > **Physical transfer is not downstream acceptance.** > **Package integration is not settlement-wide integration.** > **Repair or restart is not restored countability.** > **Integration does not confer infrastructure credit.** The component distinguishes five levels of integration: 1. **Module-level integration** — the internal elements of the focal module operate together. 2. **Package-level integration** — the module is connected to the supporting, validating, accepting, maintaining, recovering, and governing elements required by the exact claim. 3. **Habitat integration** — the package connects to actual habitat utilities, controls, operations, maintenance access, safety systems, and downstream uses. 4. **Cross-domain integration** — resources, outputs, burdens, risks, and dependencies move among several settlement requirement domains. 5. **Settlement-portfolio integration** — shared infrastructure, competing resource demands, criticality, redundancy, comparators, authorized capabilities, and systemic gaps are governed across multiple packages and claims. Success at one level does not establish success at the next. A module may function while the package remains incomplete. A package may be complete in design while lacking actual habitat allocation. A habitat-connected package may remain unaccepted by the downstream system. A locally successful integration may remain unfavorable when evaluated across the settlement portfolio. The complete capability package is the primary integration object. It includes the focal module and every element required to operate, validate, accept, maintain, repair, recover, contain, govern, and retire the claimed contribution. Some elements may be dedicated to the package. Others may be shared settlement infrastructure, including: * power generation and storage; * thermal rejection; * gas and water handling; * sterile processing; * data and software services; * assay and calibration equipment; * maintenance workshops; * robotic servicing; * storage; * quarantine; * disposal; * and accepting authorities. Shared infrastructure is not treated as free, unlimited, or automatically available. Capacity, allocation, ownership, margin, competing demand, reserve, substitution, interruption consequences, and qualification state must remain explicit. The integration architecture also distinguishes: * the focal capability-package boundary; * shared settlement infrastructure; * external mission or terrestrial dependencies; * and downstream accepting systems. External dependencies remain part of the claim boundary even when they are physically located on Earth. These may include imported cultures, reagents, manufacturer-specific parts, remote software support, specialist expertise, launch services, external laboratories, or recurring terrestrial logistics. An accepting system is the system, user, controlled pathway, or authority that receives and authorizes an output for the declared use. A physical connection to another system does not prove that the output is acceptable, safe, useful, or authorized. The component establishes a controlled interface and integration record containing, as applicable: * package identity and configuration; * declared case and system boundary; * exact claim; * stage relevance and placement; * permitted role; * prohibited claims; * lifecycle state; * formal claim state; * complete-package elements; * shared infrastructure; * external dependencies; * accepting systems; * inputs and feedstocks; * outputs and co-products; * wastes and rejected outputs; * interface classes and states; * power and thermal profiles; * data and software relationships; * crew and robotic tasks; * validation points; * acceptance criteria; * maintenance and replacement pathways; * failure modes; * containment provisions; * bypass and substitution options; * degraded modes; * recovery requirements; * capability and assurance gaps; * responsible authorities; * decision history; * and requalification triggers. The architecture recognizes several interface classes: * gas; * liquid; * solid and bulk material; * biological; * data and software; * power and thermal; * mechanical and structural; * crew operation; * robotic operation; * validation and acceptance; * and assurance interfaces. Assurance interfaces connect evidence to claims, evidence to configurations, assumptions to decisions, validation results to accepting authorities, anomalies to claim effects, gap closure to requalification, and accountable authority to formal claim state. An assurance interface can fail even when the physical system continues to operate. Examples include expired calibration, evidence that no longer matches the installed configuration, an unreviewed software revision, a changed assumption, or the loss of an accepting authority. Interface maturity is controlled through the following progression: > proposed > → defined > → allocated > → qualified > → functioning in the exact configuration > → maintained under operational change Interfaces may subsequently become: * degraded; * unavailable; * quarantined; * or retired. The distinctions are material: > **Defined is not allocated.** > **Allocated is not qualified.** > **Qualified is not functioning in the exact package.** > **Functioning once is not maintained qualification.** A replacement interface, altered software system, new organism, changed accepting system, or substituted component may create a new configuration and require renewed qualification. Dependencies are classified as: * internal package dependencies; * shared settlement dependencies; * external mission dependencies; * terrestrial dependencies; * accepting-system dependencies; * validation dependencies; * and authority dependencies. Each dependency should identify its provider, owner, function, criticality, availability, allocation, reserve, substitute, interruption tolerance, consequence of failure, qualification state, and closure status. > **An unrecorded dependency is not an eliminated dependency.** The component applies the canonical contribution sequence: > theoretical output > → gross output > → validated output > → accepted output > → avoided import > → baseline displacement > → lifecycle-qualified contribution No stage may be skipped. Oxygen evolution does not become accepted atmospheric contribution until its composition, purity, routing, monitoring, atmospheric compatibility, receiving-system integration, and authority acceptance are established. Biomass does not become food contribution until its identity, safety, processing, nutritional value, palatability, storage, use class, and food-system acceptance are established. A locally produced material does not become repair capability until its use class, performance, safety, processing, inspection, storage, and accepting authority are established. A produced medical compound does not become medical capability until identity, purity, potency, sterility, dose, formulation, stability, storage, clinical authorization, and acceptance are established. Cross-domain integration may generate useful transfer, shared infrastructure, resource competition, contamination pathways, opportunity costs, or propagated failure. Outputs and burdens must therefore be allocated explicitly. A finite output divided among several uses cannot be credited beyond the validated and accepted total. Shared power, thermal support, maintenance, validation, storage, crew time, robotics, and infrastructure cannot disappear from the burden record merely because several domains benefit. > **Cross-domain integration may increase settlement value, but outputs, avoided imports, baseline displacement, and shared burdens must not be counted more than once.** The component also defines failure containment as governed, branched response logic rather than as a mandatory linear sequence. Cross-cutting controls include: * power, thermal, and utility continuity; * monitoring, data, configuration, and controlled records; * human and robotic operations and maintenance; * lifecycle sustainment and replacement; * and isolation, bypass, substitution, and recovery. An anomaly may trigger: * immediate claim-effect assessment; * isolation; * quarantine; * bypass; * substitution; * degraded operation; * safe shutdown; * preservation; * repair; * decontamination; * decommissioning; * or another bounded response. The architecture immediately determines whether the event requires: * suspension of accepted output; * restriction of use class; * removal from the authorized capability boundary; * assignment of Conditional status; * assignment of Quarantined status; * deferral; * refusal; * or retirement. Failure impact may be: * **local** — contained within one component or interface; * **domain-level** — affecting one requirement domain; * **cross-domain** — affecting several domains or shared infrastructure; * **settlement-systemic** — threatening

title: Anticoagulation in Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation for Trauma: Striking a Balance
authors: Richard A. Greendyk; Phillip E. Mason; Cara L. Agerstrand
abstract: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation in a venovenous configuration (VV-ECMO) is increasingly recognized as an important therapeutic option for patients with severe acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).1 Accumulating scientific evidence as well as experience garnered during both the 2009 influenza A (H1N1) and coronavirus 2019 (COVID-19) pandemics, have resulted in widespread adoption of VV-ECMO for patients with ARDS.2–5 In this context, ECMO centers have expanded the application of VV-ECMO to other indications, including severe respiratory failure due to traumatic injury.6–8 The article by Niles et al.9 offers an important contribution to the field of ECMO for respiratory support in traumatically injured patients. In this single-center, retrospective cohort study, 75 patients with trauma-related acute respiratory failure were managed with VV-ECMO over an 8 year period. Pulmonary contusion was the most common etiology of respiratory failure (49% of patients) with aspiration (15%) and transfusion-related acute lung injury (11%) as other leading causes. Thirty-two percent of the patients experienced cardiac arrest before initiation of VV-ECMO and approximately 50% of patients had traumatic brain injury (TBI). Overall survival to hospital discharge was 68%. Thirty-eight (51%) patients received no anticoagulation during ECMO. Of the 37 patients who received systemic anticoagulation, 27 (73%) had anticoagulation infusion held at some point during the ECMO run. In multivariable logistic regression, there was no association between exposure to anticoagulation and survival. Nearly half of the total cohort developed a hemorrhagic complication and 28% developed a thrombotic complication during ECMO, most commonly oxygenator thrombus requiring exchange. Notably, there was no significant difference in hemorrhagic or thrombotic events based on anticoagulation status. Nearly all patients were transfused packed red blood cells (pRBCs) during the first 72 hours of ECMO support regardless of exposure to anticoagulation. Patients receiving systemic anticoagulation required a significantly lower number of transfusions of pRBCs and other blood products than did patients not on anticoagulation. Survivors were less likely to require transfusions of pRBCs and other blood products than were nonsurvivors. Traumatically injured patients pose management challenges due to the risk of bleeding (related to the injury itself or from surgical sites) and thrombosis (due to the potential for a trauma-related coagulopathic state resulting from vascular injury and activation of pro-inflammatory cytokines). The use of ECMO introduces another level of complexity; systemic anticoagulation is recommended during ECMO to prevent circuit and systemic thrombosis, yet may not be advisable in trauma patients due to the nature of the injury or ongoing procedural interventions.10 In this study, Niles et al.9 demonstrate the safety and feasibility of withholding systemic anticoagulation in patients with trauma-related acute respiratory failure supported with VV-ECMO. Evidence supporting the deferral of anticoagulation during ECMO has been limited, although described in patients with TBI.11,12 Niles et al.9 report a high overall survival, which is similar to the survival reported in other cohorts of VV-ECMO for traumatic injury and for patients receiving VV-ECMO for acute respiratory failure for other indications.5,7 After adjusting for relevant variables, survival was not related to anticoagulation status. By using a low activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) target rather than full therapeutic anticoagulation, Niles et al.9 provide further support for this approach in VV-ECMO patients with traumatic injury and suggest it appropriately balances bleeding and thrombotic risk.13–15 Niles et al.9 report that patients who received anticoagulation required fewer transfusions than their counterparts who never received anticoagulation. Although patients receiving anticoagulation may have been less critically ill and less likely to suffer from ongoing bleeding (thus rendering them better candidates for ongoing anticoagulation at baseline), the case-by-case decision-making described by Niles et al.9 reflects the dilemma that ECMO practitioners often face at the bedside: what level of bleeding risk renders the initiation of systemic anticoagulation inappropriate? When should anticoagulation be held in the event of bleeding or coagulopathy? Niles et al.9 show that a personalized approach to decision-making based on individual risk assessment may offer a safe strategy for anticoagulation management during VV-ECMO for trauma-related acute respiratory failure. Furthermore, whereas the conclusions of the study should be extrapolated with caution in other populations before additional evaluation, the safety profile observed with holding anticoagulation in this cohort may offer guidance when considering the need to hold anticoagulation for patients receiving VV-ECMO for respiratory failure in the absence of traumatic injury. This study has several limitations including its single-center, retrospective design and the potential for unmeasured confounders that may have impacted patient outcomes. Furthermore, the authors note that their analysis only included thrombotic events occurring during the ECMO run. Prior studies have reported an incidence of cannula-associated deep vein thromboses (CaDVT) as high as 85%.16 In this population, it would be informative to measure thrombotic events following ECMO decannulation to assess if the incidence of CaDVT or systemic thromboembolism differed by anticoagulation status. Finally, the decision of whether to initiate ECMO and administer systemic anticoagulation may be affected by institutional experience in caring for both trauma and ECMO patients. Practice patterns may differ at other institutions and impact outcomes. Future studies may be informed by use of multi-institutional registry data or multicenter prospective analyses to minimize the risk of confounding and to broaden the generalizability of the results. Although prospective, randomized controlled trials of patients receiving ECMO come with many challenges, a clinical trial of anticoagulation during VV-ECMO for traumatic injury may best offer definitive guidance on the safest approach to managing these critically ill patients. In conclusion, this study suggests that anticoagulation can be safely held in patients with traumatic injury receiving VV-ECMO without increasing mortality, complications, or transfusion requirements. Niles et al.9 offer important insights and provide further evidence supporting the use of VV-ECMO in patients with severe respiratory failure caused by traumatic injury.

title: Pillar 1: GR-Razor Stress Tests: Independent Cosmological Falsification Series
authors: Charles Richard Walker (C. Rich)
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Cosmological Pangea This document establishes the GR-Razor Stress Test Series: an ongoing program of structured, quantitative falsifiability analysis applied to cosmological theories that propose to resolve current observational tensions from within general relativity and without the introduction of unobserved physical entities. The series is conducted by an independent researcher operating outside institutional structures, applying the same multi-axis guillotine-testing methodology developed and self-applied during the construction of Lava-Void Cosmology. This Foundation Document contains two parts. Part One introduces the researcher, the two intake metrics that define the series scope (general relativity and Occam’s Razor), and a full account of Lava-Void Cosmology (LVC): its core claims, its relationship to the two metrics, and the exhaustive internal stress-testing to which it was subjected before this outward series began. Part Two presents Pillar 1 of the series: a structured falsifiability analysis of the 2025 Tsagas proposal, which argues that a fully relativistic treatment of peculiar velocities within the standard FLRW framework can accelerate linear structure growth and resolve the JWST early galaxy excess without new physics. The Tsagas proposal satisfies both intake metrics and is subjected to five guillotine tests. It fails decisively on amplitude grounds. Each subsequent Pillar in this series will be deposited as its own Zenodo record with its own DOI, citing this Foundation Document as the methodological basis. This Foundation Document is the permanent reference point for the series framework, authorial context, and intake criteria. Framework ready for full Boltzmann validation. Pillar 1-10 Complete GR-Razor Series Capstone: Cosmological Pangaea Triumph The GR-Razor Stress Tests series delivers a paradigm-shifting verdict: Cosmological Pangaea, a GR-pure, non-singular cosmology, completely resolves all major cosmological tensions through internal physics alone. Sweeping victories achieved: Singularity eliminated Horizon problem solved Hubble tension resolved CMB acoustic peaks reproduced All 10+ guillotine tests passed decisively ΛCDM's foundational pillars fall: No inflation required No new fields/particles needed No action modifications No fine-tuned potentials No quantum gravity framework Final standing: The past half-century in theoretical physics has witnessed a profound deviation from the discipline's foundational ethos: the relentless pursuit of empirically grounded, falsifiable explanations of nature. What began as a triumphant era, marked by the consolidation of the Standard Model of particle physics and the widespread acceptance of General Relativity, devolved into what can only be described as an extended orgy of intellectual folly, self-aggrandizement, and institutional capture by career incentives and funding imperatives. Consider the trajectory since the mid-1970s. The Standard Model, completed in its essential form by the early 1980s, accounted for all observed particles and interactions with extraordinary precision. Yet, rather than accepting this as a provisional but robust framework and directing resources toward its experimental refinement or toward unresolved tensions (such as quantum gravity or cosmological anomalies), the field embarked on a speculative proliferation unmatched in prior scientific epochs. String theory, supersymmetry, grand unified theories, eternal inflation with its multiverse landscape, loop quantum gravity, and myriad variants of quantum foundations emerged not as responses to acute empirical crises but as mathematically seductive extensions pursued for their internal elegance and the promise of unification at arbitrarily high energies. These frameworks share a common pathology: they have failed to yield a single verifiable prediction that has withstood experimental scrutiny. Over four decades, string theory has generated no testable low-energy signatures; supersymmetry has evaded detection at ever-higher collider energies; inflationary models have multiplied into an uncountable array of parameter-tuned variants, each retrofitted to accommodate cosmic microwave background observations without falsifiable novelty. The multiverse hypothesis, often invoked to explain fine-tuning, renders itself empirically sterile by construction, untestable in principle, it serves primarily as a philosophical escape hatch rather than a scientific advance. This stagnation stands in stark contrast to the rigorous demands of what might be termed the GR-Razor: a protocol insisting on General Relativity primacy, thermodynamic closure at every scale, ontological parsimony, and end-to-end predictive traceability from axiomatic foundations to observable consequences. Under such a criterion, mainstream paradigms reveal their deficiencies. Theoretical physics has increasingly rewarded those who produce voluminous publications, secure large grants, deliver polished conference addresses, and cultivate networks within elite institutions. Careers are built not on decisive empirical confrontation but on the perpetual deferral of testability: "just beyond the reach of the next accelerator" or "at Planck-scale energies forever inaccessible." Self-congratulation abounds in review articles and popular expositions that celebrate mathematical beauty as proxy for truth, while genuine progress, measurable by novel, confirmed predictions, remains absent. The field has become a closed ecosystem of mutual reinforcement, where criticism is marginalized as unconstructive or philosophically naive, and where funding flows to those who perpetuate the dominant narrative rather than challenge its foundational assumptions. This is not mere incremental slowdown; it is a systemic failure of scientific method. True theories, historically, achieve closure: they are constructed from minimal axioms, derive observables end-to-end, and submit to decisive experimental arbitration. General Relativity itself exemplifies this: proposed in 1915, it yielded immediate predictions (perihelion precession, light deflection) confirmed within years. Quantum electrodynamics followed suit, with precision tests at the level of ten decimal places. In contrast, the post-1970s speculative edifice has produced no analogous triumphs. Instead, it has accumulated epicycles, extra dimensions, branes, swampland conjectures, anthropic selection effects, each layer added to salvage prior commitments rather than to confront observational discord. The cost is not merely intellectual. Vast resources, human talent, computational infrastructure, public funding, have been diverted into pursuits that, under rigorous audit, fail the test of necessity. A reset is overdue: one that restores empiricism as sovereign, demands thermodynamic integrity, and enforces GR as the irreducible substrate of cosmology and gravity. Only by excising the accretions of unchecked speculation and careerist inertia can physics reclaim its mandate as a disciplined inquiry into the architecture of reality. The alternative is continued stagnation, where theories multiply without resolution, and the discipline risks descending into elegant but ultimately barren mathematics. This body of work declares that the future of cosmology no longer lies in speculative proliferation but in structural reduction. title: Personal Health Twin OS: A Privacy-Preserving Edge-to-Cloud Framework for Causal Whole-Body Digital Twins
authors: Khan Tahsin Abrar
abstract: Personal Health Twin OS: A Privacy-Preserving Edge-to-Cloud Framework for Causal Whole-Body Digital Twins Author: Khan Tahsin AbrarIndependent Researcher, BangladeshKhan.tahsin.abar.kta@gmail.com Abstract Digital twin technology, virtual avatars continuously synchronized with real-world data, offers transformative potential for personalized medicine. Yet prevailing implementations remain constrained to single organs or discrete domains (e.g., metabolic health), lacking system-wide integration, robust privacy safeguards, and causal decision support. This theoretical study proposes the Personal Health Twin Operating System (PHTwin-OS), a modular architecture that unifies mechanistic physiology and AI-driven personalization into a whole-body digital twin deployable on edge devices with federated, blockchain-secured cloud support. PHTwin-OS embeds HL7 FHIR, OMOP CDM, and Open mHealth standards for interoperability; employs federated learning with differential privacy and homomorphic encryption; integrates causal twin graphs for counterfactual “what-if” planning; and leverages Bayesian uncertainty quantification to ensure safety. We detail the system design, formalize causal twin graph methodology, and outline a simulation-based evaluation strategy using synthetic and converted OMOP datasets. PHTwin-OS advances digital twin research by addressing interoperability, privacy, scalability, and clinical utility, charting a path toward equitable, precision medicine without requiring wet-lab resources.Keywords: digital twin, precision medicine, federated learning, causal inference, edge computing, privacyIntroduction Digital twins, digital replicas of physical systems updated in real time, have enabled predictive maintenance in industry (Grieves & Vickers, 2017) and are emerging in healthcare for personalized simulation, risk stratification, and decision support (Ringeval et al., 2025; Shen et al., 2024). Applications such as Twin Health’s metabolic twin demonstrate sustained type 2 diabetes remission through AI-guided nutrition and activity interventions, yielding mean HbA1c reductions of 1.8% and substantial medication elimination (Smith et al., 2024; Twin Health, 2024). Likewise, Dassault Systèmes’ Living Heart Project provides patient-specific cardiac simulations for device testing and procedural planning (Dassault Systèmes, 2025). However, these successes remain domain-limited, with key gaps in whole-body integration, multi-organ modeling, privacy-preserving data governance, and causal intervention planning (Katsoulakis et al., 2024; Ringeval et al., 2025).This study proposes PHTwin-OS, a theoretical yet implementable framework to overcome these limitations via a layered architecture that: (1) harmonizes heterogeneous data using HL7 FHIR, OMOP CDM, and Open mHealth standards; (2) distributes computation across edge and cloud; (3) composes hybrid mechanistic–AI organ models into whole-body twins; (4) embeds causal twin graphs for counterfactual reasoning; (5) secures data through federated learning, differential privacy, homomorphic encryption, and blockchain; and (6) ensures clinical safety via Bayesian uncertainty quantification. Our contributions include formal causal twin graph methodology, a privacy-by-design federated-blockchain learning stack, and an edge-first deployment strategy. The framework supports synthetic evaluation with open-source datasets and OMOP conversion protocols, enabling research and preprint publication without laboratory resources.Literature Review Digital Twin Clinical Outcomes Twin Health’s whole-body metabolic twin demonstrated significant clinical benefits in observational and randomized studies. In 1,853 participants, mean HbA1c decreased by 1.8% (SD = 1.7), 89% achieved medications, with concomitant weight loss (M = 12.3 kg) and improvements in cardiovascular risk factors (Smith et al., 2024; Twin Health, 2024; Jones & Patel, 2024). Living Heart Project models have undergone preclinical validation for device testing and secured regulatory feedback, illustrating the feasibility of patient-specific organ twins (Dassault Systèmes, 2025; Lee et al., 2025).Standards for Interoperability Interoperability underpins scalable digital twins. HL7 FHIR (v4/R5) provides RESTful APIs and resource profiles for clinical data exchange (HealthIT.gov, 2024). The OMOP Common Data Model standardizes multi-source observational data for analytics and cohort studies (Observational Health Data Sciences and Informatics, 2024). Open mHealth schemas normalize patient-generated data from wearables and mobile apps (Open mHealth, 2020). While these standards exist, their combined use in digital twin architectures remains underexplored (Ringeval et al., 2025).Privacy-Preserving Learning Federated learning enables distributed model training without centralizing raw data, reducing privacy risks (McMahan et al., 2017). Differential privacy adds statistical noise to guarantees ε-differential privacy (Dwork et al., 2006). Homomorphic encryption permits computation on encrypted data (Brakerski et al., 2012). Combining these techniques preserves confidentiality while allowing population-scale learning and updates (Smith et al., 2025; Zhang & Rivera, 2025).Causal Inference and Uncertainty Causal models support counterfactual “what-if” analysis essential for treatment planning (Pearl, 2009). Structural causal models over physiological variables enable personalized intervention simulation (Li et al., 2025). Bayesian uncertainty quantification methods, conformal prediction and Bayesian neural networks, calibrate model confidence, ensuring safety in clinical recommendations (Lechuga López et al., 2025).Proposed Framework: Personal Health Twin OS Architecture Overview PHTwin-OS comprises six layers:Data Semantics & Ingestion : Automated, schema-validated ETL pipelines ingest FHIR resources, convert to OMOP tables, and map wearable streams to Open mHealth Observations.Edge/Cloud Hybrid Computation : Edge modules perform anomaly detection and lightweight simulations with <1 s latency on consumer devices; the cloud aggregates encrypted model updates and runs cohort-scale analyses.Twin Modeling Core : Composable organ modules blending mechanistic models (e.g., cardiac electrophysiology) and AI personalization layers form a multi-scale, multi-organ twin graph.Causal Decision Engine : A formal causal twin graph G = (V, E, θ) encodes physiological variables (V), directed causal edges (E), and parameters (θ) learned from data to support do-operator interventions.Privacy & Governance : Federated learning coordinates model updates; differential privacy ensures ε-private aggregation; homomorphic encryption secures edge–cloud computations; blockchain smart contracts manage consent and provenance.Uncertainty & Safety : Bayesian UQ modules quantify predictive confidence and trigger clinician review or abstention for high-risk recommendations.Methods Data Harmonization ETL pipelines use FHIR profiles (R4/Post-US Core) to extract EHR data, then apply OHDSI’s ETL tools to populate OMOP CDM v6 tables, and utilize Open mHealth JSON schemas for streaming data. Validation employs JSON Schema and SQL integrity checks (Observational Health Data Sciences and Informatics, 2024; Open mHealth, 2020).Edge & Cloud Implementation Edge inference engines run TensorFlow Lite or PyTorch Mobile models for anomaly detection and vital sign simulation. Cloud services use Kubernetes clusters for federated aggregation with TensorFlow Federated and Microsoft SEAL for homomorphic encryption (Brakerski et al., 2012).Causal Twin Graph Formalism Build structural causal graphs using domain knowledge and data-driven discovery (e.g., PC algorithm). Simulate interventions via Pearl’s do-calculus, estimating p(Y|do(X=x)) for variables X and outcomes Y (Pearl, 2009).Privacy Stack Federated learning rounds use secure aggregation; differential privacy budgets ε∈[0.1,1.0] per round; CKKS homomorphic encryption secures weight aggregation with 80-bit security (Brakerski et al., 2012).Uncertainty Quantification Implement MC dropout ensembles and deep Gaussian processes. Calibration assessed via prediction interval coverage probabilities and Brier scores on synthetic benchmarks (Lechuga López et al., 2025).Evaluation Plan Use Synthea-generated populations transformed to OMOP by ETL scripts for synthetic validation. Tasks: anomaly detection (accuracy, latency), causal inference (RMSE of counterfactual estimates), privacy-utility trade-offs (privacy loss vs. AUC), uncertainty calibration (coverage vs. interval width). Performance measured on Raspberry Pi 4 (4 GB RAM) and AWS GPU instances.Discussion PHTwin-OS unifies standards, privacy, causal reasoning, and multi-scale modeling into a cohesive framework, extending current organ-specific twins to whole-body applications. By leveraging open standards and synthetic evaluation, it empowers academic researchers without lab funding to prototype and publish preprints.Clinical Implications A fully realized PHTwin-OS could transform chronic disease management (e.g., diabetes, hypertension) by providing real-time, personalized recommendations and enabling in silico clinical trials, reducing time and cost for new therapies.Limitations Theoretical evaluation relies on synthetic data; real-world EHR variability and device heterogeneity may challenge ETL and model generalization. Future work requires clinical pilots and regulatory collaboration.Conclusion This paper presents PHTwin-OS, a comprehensive, privacy-preserving, edge-to-cloud architecture for whole-body digital twins. By integrating standards, federated-blockchain privacy, causal decision support, and uncertainty-aware safety, it offers a blueprint for the next generation of personalized, equitable digital medicine, publishable on preprint servers and ready for prototype development by resource-constrained academic teams.References Brakerski, Z., Gentry, C., & Vaikuntanathan, V.
