title: Keratoacanthoma management: results of a survey of U.K. dermatologists and surgeons
authors: Richard Edward Watchorn; Sarah Thomas; C. Miller; Richard Carr; Dieter Koch; Peter Thomas; Saleem Mustafa Taibjee
abstract: Dear Editor, Distinction of keratoacanthoma (KA) from squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is challenging and management is controversial, with some advocating prompt surgical excision and others monitoring to allow for spontaneous resolution.1 There are rare reports of metastasis.2 And yet, the benign natural history of KA is supported by various studies, including a systematic review of 455 cases with no metastasis or death1 and observational studies confirming spontaneous resolution.1 Unlike in SCC, perineural or venous invasion in KA is not associated with an adverse outcome.3,4 Comparative genomic hybridization and DNA microarray studies indicate that KA and SCC are genetically distinct.5,6 Some have suggested that the rare reports of metastatic KA may have arisen from SCC development within KA.3 Our online 22‐item questionnaire ascertained clinicians’ views about KA and its management, previously observed outcomes and willingness to enrol patients into a proposed clinical trial (the questionnaire and further details of results are available from the authors on request). The questionnaire was circulated via the British Association of Dermatologists, the British Society for Dermatological Surgery, Reconstructive Surgery Trials Network, U.K. Dermatology Clinical Trials Network and the national trainee electronic mailing lists. Of 223 respondents 162 (73%) were consultants. Responses to a subset of questions were compared between specialties (dermatology n = 152; dermatological surgery n = 48; and plastic surgery n = 21) with χ2‐ or Fisher's exact test (SPSS Version 22, IBM, Armonk, NY, U.S.A.). Although 26 (12%) respondents considered KA and SCC to be clinically and histologically indistinguishable, the majority (194, 87%) regarded them as distinct (13%) or likely distinct (74%). Only 28 (13%) felt that conservative management (e.g. clinical observation and/or shave excision) could be considered. Most (166, 74%) felt that KA should be managed as for SCC, as spontaneous resolution cannot be reliably predicted nor SCC reliably excluded. Dermatological surgeons were more likely (23%) than dermatologists (10%) or plastic surgeons (0%) (P = 0·03) to regard them as indistinguishable. Twenty‐one (9%) reported that they had observed local recurrence of KA, while four (2%) reported having observed metastasis. A photograph of a typical KA‐like lesion was presented with three scenarios of lesion behaviour (reducing in size/static/enlarging) over a hypothetical preceding 4‐week period. For each, respondents could choose multiple management options (Table 1). There were no statistically significant differences between specialties (24 tests all with P > 0·05). In the case of the involuting scenario, around 35% selected clinical observation, and around half excision. When the lesion was static or enlarging, surgical excision was favoured. Management choices for keratoacanthoma‐like lesions on the ear and leg Respondents could choose more than one treatment approach, thus across categories percentages can sum to > 100%. Management choices for keratoacanthoma‐like lesions on the ear and leg Respondents could choose more than one treatment approach, thus across categories percentages can sum to > 100%. The majority (74%, 166) reported not deferring surgery for KA‐like lesions, whereas 26% (57) reported doing so, with no significant between‐specialty differences apparent (P = 0·40). Comments indicated that indicated that even if not intended, deferral frequently occurs anyway because of waiting lists. Of 209 respondents, 142 (68%) indicated a willingness to routinely observe KA‐like lesions if a clinical trial were to confirm spontaneous resolution in a proportion of cases (Table S1 a). Anatomical site did not influence management for 125 (56%) of the respondents, although the clinical vignettes indicated a lower inclination to excise involuting lesions on the lower leg than the ear. Over half indicated willingness to enrol patients with KA‐like lesions into a U.K. multicentre clinical trial. Again, around half were willing to enrol patients into a suggested design that incorporated a 4‐ to 5‐week initial clinical observation period to establish the growth phase of the lesion, but ensuring risk minimization by promptly excising all enlarging lesions within the 31‐/62‐day National Health Service cancer targets. Suggested exclusion criteria included immunosuppression, genetic disorders (e.g. xeroderma pigmentosum), disputed clinical diagnosis, previous SCC and high risk or cosmetically sensitive sites (Table S1b). Inclusion of an initial incisional biopsy reduced clinician willingness to enrol patients. Reasons cited included surgical capacity or duplication of surgery and concerns over the adequacy of partial biopsy for histological KA diagnosis (Table S1b). One respondent highlighted the possible confounding impact of biopsy, citing high regression rates of KA following incisional biopsy.7 Of the 211 responses regarding lesions static in size after 4‐ to 5‐weeks’ observation, 70 (33%) were willing to shave excise, 84 (40%) were not and 57 (27%) were uncertain. Comments highlighted concerns over potential undertreatment of SCC and uncertainty regarding adequacy of shave excision for histological diagnosis. Others indicated a preference for curettage. A proposal to randomize patients with static lesions to either shave or surgical excision did not increase recruitment willingness. Ninety of 218 respondents (41%) indicated that their local histopathologists distinguish KA from SCC; 27 (12%) indicated that they do not; and the remainder (101, 46%) noted variation. In a U.K. histopathology department survey, the ratio of coded SCC to KA varied from 2·5 : 1 to 139 : 1 confirming widespread reporting variations.8 In a clinical trial, centralized expert histopathologist review could overcome this issue. Of note, in two phase II vemurafenib trials, central review of SCC histology specimens led to reclassification as KA in up to 94·4% of cases.4 Our survey demonstrates significant clinical equipoise in the management of KA‐like lesions among U.K. clinicians and confirms a willingness to enrol patients in a clinical trial, while highlighting the need to mitigate against undertreatment of any potential SCC within the trial design. title: When Historical Evidence No Longer Supports Continued Service
authors: KU Howard
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Historical pipeline evidence can remain authentic, understandable and technically accurate while no longer being sufficient to support a present-day continued-service conclusion. Over a long asset life, the physical configuration may change, operating pressure or duty may be altered, new degradation mechanisms may emerge, analytical methods and standards may evolve, repairs and excursions may occur, and newer inspection evidence may materially change the uncertainty surrounding an earlier engineering conclusion. This white paper presents a series-specific Historical Evidence Reuse Screen for evaluating whether historical engineering evidence remains applicable to a current integrity question. The paper deliberately does not propose a new pipeline life-extension or remaining-life assessment method. Pipeline life extension and continued-service assessment are established engineering disciplines. In particular, ISO 12747:2025 provides requirements and guidance for pipeline life-extension assessment, while API, PHMSA and PRCI material address crack management, geohazard management, remaining life, integrity management and pressure-cycle considerations. The narrower question addressed here is: When can a historical inspection, assessment or engineering conclusion still be relied upon as support for a current decision—and when have changing conditions broken that applicability? The Historical Evidence Reuse Screen evaluates eight principal evidence dimensions: asset and configuration — whether the present physical asset and assessed configuration remain materially equivalent to those addressed by the historical conclusion; service and loading — whether product, pressure, temperature, cycles and operating duty remain sufficiently comparable; threat environment — whether corrosion, cracking, geohazard, third-party or other material threats have changed; method and standard applicability — whether the historical analytical method and governing basis remain suitable for the present question; evidence quality — whether provenance, completeness and technical quality remain adequate; uncertainty — whether historical uncertainty bounds are known and remain meaningful; intervening events — whether repairs, excursions, modifications, inspections or other events have changed the engineering basis; and validity horizon and triggers — whether the original conclusion specified a time, threshold or condition requiring review. A central proposition of the paper is that historical validity is not the same as current applicability. A previous inspection report or engineering assessment may have been entirely valid when issued. That does not mean its conclusion automatically remains valid for the asset’s present configuration, operating duty or threat environment. The paper therefore separates record retention from technical reuse. The existence of an old report demonstrates that historical evidence has been preserved; it does not establish that its conclusion can still support a current continued-service decision. Before recalculating or reusing an earlier conclusion, the paper proposes that the engineering team first compare the original basis with the present question. If asset configuration, operating conditions, threats, methods, evidence quality or uncertainty have materially changed, simply rerunning an old calculation can create false continuity rather than a defensible current assessment. The Historical Evidence Reuse Screen is deliberately positioned upstream of formal life-extension or reassessment calculations. Its purpose is to determine what historical information: remains usable as background; can reasonably be accepted as current input; requires supplementation with new evidence; has been superseded; or is insufficient to support the present conclusion. The paper also distinguishes evidence age from evidence relevance and quality. Old evidence is not inherently weak. A verified material record, hydrotest or high-quality historical inspection may retain considerable engineering value decades later. Conversely, recent information may still be incomplete, poorly contextualized or inappropriate to the current engineering question. What matters is not age alone, but whether the evidence remains relevant, technically adequate and properly bounded by uncertainty. For every material historical source, the engineering record should therefore make visible how that evidence is being treated in the current assessment: background, accepted input, supplemented input, superseded evidence or rejected evidence—and why. This reduces the risk that an old conclusion acquires unintended authority simply because it is accessible, familiar or repeatedly copied into later assessments. The paper proposes a four-stage maturity path: Unscoped Reuse → Bounded Reuse → Supplemented Reuse → Reassessed Basis At the first stage, a historical conclusion is carried forward with little examination of its original applicability conditions. At Bounded Reuse, the original basis and present differences are visible. At Supplemented Reuse, changed conditions or evidence gaps are addressed using current information. At the most mature stage, Reassessed Basis, material changes are evaluated through an appropriate current assessment process so that the continued-service decision rests on an explicit present-day engineering basis rather than inherited authority. The analysis is grounded in publicly available work including ISO 12747:2025, API RP 1176, 2nd edition (2026), API RP 1187, PHMSA integrity-management material, PRCI research on SCC and fatigue remaining life, API RP 1160, and API RP 1193 Pipeline Pressure Cycle Management. Because these established disciplines already address life extension, remaining life, cracking, fatigue, pressure cycles, geohazards and integrity management, the paper makes no claim to invent those engineering methods. Its narrower contribution is the author-defined Historical Evidence Reuse Screen: a manufacturer-neutral review structure for determining whether historical engineering evidence remains applicable to a current continued-service question. The Historical Evidence Reuse Screen is not presented as an industry standard, certification scheme, life-extension method, trademarked methodology or first invention. The scope remains limited to publicly discussable engineering evidence, assessment and human engineering decision support. It does not authorize continued operation, pressure changes or intervention deferral, and it does not specify proprietary execution-control mechanisms, automated physical actuation logic or safety-instrumented functions. This paper forms No. 30 of Phase IV — From Live Asset to Long-Horizon Accountability, extending No.29’s question of whether historical engineering meaning survives a custody transition into the next question: even when the historical basis survives intact, does it still apply to the asset today?

abstract: OP 1 Thematic Area: Donors and Donations Reintegrating deferred donors: Impact of donor wellness clinics in optimizing India’s blood donation services Sehrish Chaudhary, Mayurika S. Tyagi Santosh Medical College and Hospital, Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh, India Background: Very often healthcare relies upon blood transfusions, and pre-donation screening ensures donor safety. However, these screenings often result in donor deferrals either temporary or permanentation due to various health conditions. Deferral rates vary regionally, and without follow-up, many deferred donors are lost from the donation pool. A Donor Wellness Clinic (DWC) can help bridge this gap by providing targeted counseling and health interventions to improve donor retention and re-entry. Aims: To analyze whole blood donor deferral patterns, characteristics, and causes at a Northern Indian tertiary care hospital. To assess the impact of a donor wellness clinic on return rates among deferred donors through structured counseling and wellness interventions. Methods: This retrospective study analyzed donor deferral data from September 2023 to August 2024. Additionally, a survey involving 49 participants (donors, deferred donors, medical staff, and lab technicians) was conducted to assess the perceived need for a DWC. From August 2024 to June 2025, deferred donors received follow-up through the DWC for conditions such as anemia, abnormal blood pressure, viral illness, and alcohol intake. Return rates were tracked and analyzed. Results: Out of 3305 screened donors, 487 (15%) were deferred mainly due to anemia and hypertension. Many deferred donors received targeted health counseling. Initially, return rates were low due to health concerns and lifestyle barriers but improved with sustained follow-up and education. The DWC addressed modifiable deferral causes, improving confidence and enabling re-entry into the donor pool. Conclusion: Donor wellness clinics serve as an effective strategy to reintegrate temporarily deferred donors. By addressing health issues and providing structured support, DWCs enhance donor return rates and optimize blood supply services. Wider implementation across blood banks in India could significantly improve donor retention and transfusion sustainability. OP 2 Thematic Area: Immunohematology When the pattern doesn’t fit: Case based algorithmic resolution of unusual antibody specificities in routine immunohematology workups – Case series Amena Ebadur Rahman, Mitu Dogra, Rasika Setia, Vadad Khaliq, Sonia Joseph, Priyasha Prajapat BLK-Max Super Speciality Hospital, New Delhi, India Background: In immunohematology laboratories, antibody identification becomes challenging when reactivity patterns do not match known specificities. Antibodies against high/intermediate-frequency antigens like anti-Jka, anti-Jkb, anti-Ch, anti-Bga may present with weak, variable, or pan-reactive profiles. Each identification panel comprises cells from different donors, reactivity to low-frequency antigens (LFAs) represented by only one cell can be missed or appear inconsistent. A reactive cell in one lot may be absent/present in another lot, helping support presence of suspected LFA, especially when the rule of three (three positive and three negative antigen-matched reactions) is not feasible. In cases with pan-reactivity and negative autocontrol and DAT, antibodies to high-frequency antigens (HFAs) or plasma protein-associated targets are suspected, use of panel combinations can be extremely helpful. In such cases, combinations of panels and resource-conscious algorithmic approach are essential for accurate identification and safe transfusion. Methods: A structured algorithm was implemented for cases with unresolved/atypical antibody patterns. Following a positive antibody screen, extended identification panels (10,11,14,16) from two different manufacturers/panel lots were used. Enzyme-treated red cells (bromelain, papain, ficin) were used to evaluate enhancement/resistance. Dithiothreitol (0.01M) helped identify antibodies sensitive to sulfhydryl reduction, like anti-Jsa and anti-Jsb. Anti-Chido was suspected when reactivity was retained with 0.2M DTT, lost with bromelain, and confirmed via inhibition using pooled AB plasma. In contrast, anti-Bga was suspected when reactivity disappeared after DTT but persisted after bromelain. Suitable blood units were identified by antigen matching or by crossmatch-compatible units transfused in aliquots. Results: Algorithm successfully identified anti-Jsa, anti-Jsb, anti-Ch and anti-Bga in 4 complex serologic cases. Chemical modification, enzyme and multiple panel lots enhanced diagnosis and facilitated safe transfusion. Conclusion: A practical, algorithmic approach using extended panels, enzyme and DTT enables identification of antibodies in routine immunohematology labs, improving patient safety and transfusion outcomes. OP 3 Thematic Area: Clinical Transfusions Effect of multi-modal training on knowledge and practices of blood transfusion among nurses working in a tertiary care hospital: A Prospective Interventional study Muthukumaravel P J, Siddharth Mittal AIIMS Jodhpur Background: The complexity of the transfusion process and the need for specialised knowledge highlight the critical role of skilled professionals in ensuring transfusion safety. Nurses, who directly manage patient care during transfusions, must possess a strong scientific understanding and technical expertise to minimise risks and prevent patient harm. However, studies have revealed gaps in nursing competence and shortcomings in transfusion practices, underscoring the need for improved training and protocols. Method: This prospective interventional study designed a multimodal training program for nurses, integrating a face-to-face teaching session (FFTS) (first mode) and a self-learning (SL) video (second mode) to address safe blood transfusion practices and transfusion fundamentals. A FFTS covering safe blood transfusion practices, including pre-transfusion sample collection, bedside transfusion, blood component administration, and adverse reaction management, was developed as the first training mode. A 10-minute SL video focusing on pre-transfusion sample collection and bedside practices, served as the second training mode to reinforce key skills was also developed (SL video link: https://youtu.be/Bqg4y8rrHQs?feature=shared). Baseline assessments were conducted to evaluate nurses' knowledge and practices. Knowledge assessment was done via online survey consisting of 33 questions covering various domains: blood components, pre-transfusion checks, bedside transfusion guidelines, adverse transfusion reactions and clinical transfusion. Practices were evaluated by observing 30 pretransfusion sample collections and bedside transfusion practices, each in high-transfusion-frequency wards. Post-intervention surveys and observations were then used to measure changes and compare outcomes between single-mode (FFTS only) versus multi-mode (FFTS plus SL video) training interventions. Results: A total of 666 nurses were recruited as per the inclusion criteria. Baseline knowledge scores (Mean ± S.D.) improved significantly from 21.3 (±3.4) to 25.9 (±2.9) post-single-mode (FFTS) training (p=0.00). Observations revealed significant improvements in pre-transfusion sample collection and bedside transfusion practices post single and multi-mode training interventions. At baseline, the mean score for pre-transfusion sample collection practices was 2.93 (±0.7), and for bedside transfusion practices, it was 15.0 (±1.8). title: Interviewing for residency positions while completing a graduate degree: Considerations for graduate students, mentors, and program directors
authors: Wayne David Newhauser; Garrett M. Pitcher; Christine Swanson; Samuel G. Armato; Hania Al‐Hallaq
venue: Journal of Applied Clinical Medical Physics
abstract: The pipeline of new clinical medical physicists in the United States includes graduate education followed by residency training. A major bottleneck occurs as students on the verge of completing their advanced degree programs seek positions in residency training programs; for example, in 2022 between a quarter and a half of applicants did not enter residency training.[11 For the intents and purposes of this editorial, we require only a crude bracket around the true value, which is not known. We took data on the MedPhys Match (run by National Matching Services [NMS] for positions beginning in 2022).13 These data reveal that 133 of 264 (50%) of applicants matched to a residency. However, only 214 applicants participated in the match, and of those only 180 were ranked by at least one program (NMS calls this subset ranked applicants “acceptable” applicants; we use this term for consistency; be noted th-at we are unable to confirm that ranked applicants are acceptable or unranked applicants are unacceptable). A total of 133 of 180 (74%) of acceptable applicants matched to a residency program. Hence, these data suggest a bracket spanning 50%–74% of applicants, depending on the denominator selected. For comparison, according to the Commission on Accreditation of Medical Physics Education Programs (CAMPEP), 323 students graduated from accredited programs in 2020 (a figure which excludes nine graduates from DMP programs),19 of which at least 50% applied to residency programs. We speculate that the reason for which the AAPM's value is larger than that from CAMPEP is that the former includes a backlog of frustrated applicants (who completed their degree in previous years and are attempting admission a second or higher time), whereas the latter excludes these individuals. ] The origin of the bottleneck was the introduction in 2014 of the American Board of Radiology's eligibility requirement for professional board certification that mandated the completion of an accredited residency program.1 The bottleneck acutely impacts graduate students. Impacts of concern include anxiety and depression, which are prevalent in graduate students across a spectrum of disciplines in the United States.2 Other potential impacts include shortages of qualified medical physicists, which could in turn impact the quality, safety, and availability of patient care.3-7 Although there is literature on navigating the medical physics education and training pathways,8-10 there is little guidance for graduate students in balancing their limited time to be spent on the competing tasks of interviewing for a residency position and simultaneously completing their degree. In principle, this should be quite simple: Each student interviews with enough residency programs to successfully secure an offer of admission to at least one program, but the number of interviews should not impact the completion of the graduate degree. In practice, the bottleneck problem makes it difficult for a student to estimate this number with confidence. Many students have managed this uncertainty by applying to, and interviewing with, large numbers of residency programs.11 Excessive time spent interviewing, however, can negatively impact students, faculty, and education and training programs. A recent study12 suggests that the bottleneck problem could contribute to stress and burnout. For all these reasons, we seek to raise an awareness of key factors that students and their faculty mentors should consider as they navigate through the bottleneck. Solutions to the bottleneck are beyond the scope of this editorial; rather, we seek to provide information and guidance to facilitate navigating the system, as it currently exists. Guidance is provided as suggestions for consideration, and they should not be construed as requirements. All students complete their degrees on time. All students who are admitted to a residency training program begin on schedule. Students and programs spend an appropriate amount of time interviewing; this time should be sufficient to make informed and wise decisions but not excessive to distract from other responsibilities. All residency programs utilize their full training capacity by successfully recruiting residents to all open residency positions. All qualified students who wish to enter a residency training program are able to do so, and all residency graduates subsequently enter the clinical medical physics workforce.[22 To reach this nirvanic state, graduate degree program admissions in a given year would have to equal future demand for residency graduates (in each subspecialty), for example, 4–5 years hence for MS degree holders, 7 or more years for PhD holders, and 1–2 years for postdoctoral certificate holders. Graduate admissions targets and workforce projections are challenging problems that are beyond the remit of this editorial. ] Late completion of a degree. Deferral or cancellation of admission to residency program due to delay in degree completion. Failure of qualified students to gain admission to a residency training program. Vacant training positions in accredited residency programs (10 of 133, or 7%, of positions to begin in 2022 were unmatched).13 Anxiety and depression of students due to the residency interview process. Making good choices regarding one's education, training, and career is complex under the best of circumstances. Currently, a large number of applicants are not able to enter residency training programs. Navigating these turbulent waters calls for well-informed, rational, and responsible decision-making by students, mentors, graduate education programs, and residency training programs. Personalized decision-making is essential because the characteristics and goals of individual students and programs are diverse. We discourage prescriptive approaches, such as recommending a maximum number of interviews per student or per residency opening. Lastly, we recommend continued annual surveillance by the education community to monitor this serious and evolving situation. The authors declare that there is no conflict of interest that could be perceived as prejudicing the impartiality of the material reported. Wayne Newhauser drafted the manuscript and provided project leadership. Each of the coauthors contributed intellectual content and edited the manuscript.

title: CHAPTER 16 - From Partiality to Soft Corruption

abstract: CHAPTER 16 - FROM PARTIALITY TO SOFT CORRUPTION Introduction In the public sphere, the danger seldom arrives under the banner of overt corruption ; a tree endangering administrative life, and perhaps rooted in partiality. It more often appears as soft corruption: the quiet displacement of judgement by loyalty, the subtle recalibration of priorities under the pressure of affinity, or the gentle but persistent erosion of institutional neutrality through networks of influence that remain formally lawful yet materially distorting. --- Hard & soft power vs. and hard & soft corruption --- Under CR451's definition (a leading French intelligence research center) hard power rests on coercion, sanction, and direct command, whereas soft power operates by attraction, prestige, and informal influence. Transposed into the ethics of public office, hard corruption is relatively familiar: bribery, extortion, explicit quid pro quo arrangements. Soft corruption, by contrast, is characterised less by tangible exchanges and more by structured predispositions: selective benevolence, quiet deferential treatment, and the unspoken expectation of reciprocity. In this sense, “soft corruption” is not defined only by the illegality of acts, but by the cumulative impact of soft power mechanisms on impartial administration. It arises wherever a public official’s horizon of decision is systematically bent towards a particular circle, interest, or fraternity, not because of direct orders, but because of the felt weight of belonging. --- Open secrecy and incomplete exposure --- The previous chapter supplemented the 9 of June 2026 deontological notice from the French High Judiciary Deontological Commission. Thus chapter was aiming to resolve the deontological difficulties of some nonrepublican allegiances, though under public duty, presupposed exposure as the ethical pivot: Either outward, via escalation to legal or disciplinary authorities, or inward, via declaration of interests to the institution and, where appropriate, the public. This double movement of outbound and inbound disclosure establishes what might be termed “open secrecy”: The recognition that certain affiliations cannot be fully dissolved, but must be rendered transparent enough that their potential to distort judgement can be monitored, constrained, and, where necessary, neutralised. The difficulty in many public administrations is that this open secrecy remains partial, delayed, or selectively applied. Affiliations are known but unofficial, tolerated but unarticulated, or mentioned in passing without systematic integration into conflictsofinterest procedures. In such conditions, the risk is not merely that hard corruption may occur, but that soft corruption becomes ambient: the affiliation is neither fully secret nor fully accountable; it floats in a grey zone where influence operates without formal scrutiny. --- Soft corruption as a structural risk --- On the model you sketch, any fraternity or network that introduces binding allegiance, confidential constraint, or selective solidarity ceases to be a mere private preference and becomes a deontological obstacle. Extending this beyond the judiciary into public administration, the phenomenon of soft corruption can be described as follows: It is structurally embedded rather than episodic, sustained by enduring ties of fraternity, party, profession, or locality. Let us, please, repeat that once more: It is structurally embedded rather than episodic, sustained by enduring ties of fraternity, party, profession, or locality. It operates through expectation rather than explicit command, via the implicit understanding that “one looks after one’s own”. It is shielded by partial secrecy: enough opacity to avoid formal challenge, enough visibility to sustain trust within the group. It blurs the line between collegiality and partiality, making favour appear as normal professional courtesy. Soft corruption therefore does not depend upon overt misconduct. It consists in the quiet rebalancing of loyalty: public duty becomes one loyalty among others, and not always the first. The harm lies less in isolated decisions than in the longterm drift of institutional behaviour towards certain interests at the expense of others, without explicit justification or transparent criteria. --- An attempt of reasonable mediation of this risk --- Mediation perspective—seeking to reconcile ethical principle with administrative reality—the resolution cannot rest solely on prohibition. Many forms of association, political activity, and professional solidarity are both legitimate and socially valuable. The task is to distinguish between benign solidarity and corrosive allegiance, and to introduce mediating means that prevent the latter from silently dominating public functions. Three mediating axes ought to emerge: Transparency as discipline: Declaration of interests must not be a perfunctory formality, but a living instrument. Regular, structured disclosure of memberships, advisory roles, and significant informal ties allows the administration to identify patterns of potential bias before they crystallise into soft corruption. The aim is not to vilify association, but to subject it to principled visibility. Procedural distance: Where ties exist that may generate reasonable apprehension of partiality, procedural mechanisms should create distance: recusal, rotation of responsibilities, multiperson panels, and independent review. These techniques do not demand renunciation of private conviction; they ensure that such conviction is kept at arm’s length from decisions where its influence would be problematic. Cultural recalibration: Soft corruption thrives in cultures where loyalty to the group is tacitly celebrated as a higher ethic than loyalty to the institution. A mediationbased approach seeks to recentre professional identity: officials are encouraged to see fidelity to legal norms and public interest as the primary fraternity, one which reorders other allegiances without annihilating them. --- An illustration --- An illustration may clarify the distinction. Consider a senior official in a regional administration who belongs to a longstanding professional lodge whose members occupy several key posts. No bribes are exchanged, no explicit instructions given. Yet appointments, procurement choices, and the allocation of discretionary grants are consistently directed towards entities linked, directly or indirectly, to lodge members. On paper, criteria are satisfied; in practice, competitive neutrality is hollowed out. This is soft corruption: the gentle but chronic privileging of an inner circle through the medium of trust and solidarity, neither fully secret nor fully accountable. --- Extending this resolving strategy beyond the judiciary --- The outbound/inbound for judges—“declare, escalate, or abstain”—translates into public administration as a broader ethic of exposure and structured restraint: Declare: systematise inbound exposure by requiring detailed, periodically updated registers of interests and affiliations, accessible to oversight bodies and, where appropriate, to the public. Escalate: when the affiliation or solidarity threatens to distort major decisions, outbound exposure through escalation to ethics committees, supervisory authorities, or external auditors becomes mandatory. Abstain: in cases where the risk cannot be neutralised by transparency or procedure, abstention from participation in the relevant decision, or even withdrawal from the role, is demanded by the same deontological logic. --- The crucial point is that soft corruption cannot be effectively countered by conveniencebased solutions: “everyone does it”, “it is how things work here”, or “no complaints have been made”. The standard is not merely formal legality, but the preservation of trust. As in the judicial context, officials must not only act impartially, they must be seen—reasonably and demonstrably—to do so. --- Soft power, legitimacy, and open secrecy --- Finally, returning to the equivalence between hard and soft power under CR451, thence hard and soft corruption, the administration’s own soft power—its moral authority, credibility, and perceived fairness—is itself a public asset and strength; hence a potential weakness and threat. Soft corruption consumes that asset. When fraternities, parties, or informal networks exert unexamined influence, the institution’s soft power is quietly transformed into private capital: legitimacy is expended to serve narrow circles. The concept of open secrecy, fully realised, seeks to arrest this process. It does not pretend that affiliations can be eradicated, or any fundamental liberty of association; nor that human beings can be stripped of loyalties. Instead, it requires that those loyalties be made sufficiently visible, sufficiently bounded by procedure, and sufficiently subordinated to public duty that they no longer amount to untracked soft power within the administrative machine. --- Conclusion --- In elevating the terms of this proposal: we, as public officials are not summoned to abandon their private convictions or solidarities. authors: Judith S. Hochman; David Joel Maron
abstract: HomeCirculation: Cardiovascular Quality and OutcomesVol. 11, No. 4Letter by Hochman and Maron Regarding Article, "'Faith Healing' and 'Subtraction Anxiety' in Unblinded Trials of Procedures: Lessons From DEFER and FAME-2 for End Points in the ISCHEMIA Trial." Originally published10 Apr 2018https://doi.org/10.1161/CIRCOUTCOMES.118.004742Circulation: Cardiovascular Quality and Outcomes. 2018;11:e004742To the Editor:We recognize and value the open discourse surrounding the design and conduct of clinical trials. Recent discussion of the ISCHEMIA trial (International Study of Comparative Health Effectiveness With Medical and Invasive Approaches) has focused mostly on a change that amended the protocol to include additional components in the primary end point in 2017. The primary aim is to test whether an early invasive strategy has incremental value beyond optimal medical therapy for patients with stable ischemic heart disease and moderate–severe ischemia on clinically meaningful cardiovascular outcomes. Of note, the grant application funded by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) in 2011 was based on the current 5-component primary end point. However, we sought and received approval to implement the study protocol with a primary end point of cardiovascular death or myocardial infarction and to specify that a change to include resuscitated cardiac arrest and hospitalization for unstable angina or heart failure would be made in the event it became necessary to preserve power of the trial. The trial was designed to optimize precision around point estimates for the outcomes deemed most important to patients and clinicians, allowing them to make personalized decisions about their care, guided by robust data on risks and benefits. ISCHEMIA will have broad implications for the health of the millions of patients affected by stable ischemic heart disease.As the study chair and co-chair/principal investigator for the ISCHEMIA trial, we wish to provide corrections of inaccuracies published in the Perspective by Rajkumar et al1 in Circulation: Cardiovascular Quality and Outcomes. That Perspective misinformed the scientific community and other interested stakeholders about the ISCHEMIA trial.First, the statement that "… on January 17, 2018, over 99% of the way through the recruitment period, an amendment was made to the clinicaltrials.gov website" is misleading. In May 2017, NHLBI convened an Independent Advisory Panel to review the potential change in the primary end point as prespecified in the protocol. An independent panel was necessary because the Data and Safety Monitoring Board had already reviewed outcome data by treatment group. The prespecified primary end point change was recommended by the Independent Advisory Panel that only had access to aggregate outcome data. This panel was independent of study leadership, NHLBI, and the Data and Safety Monitoring Board. The Data and Safety Monitoring Board reviewed the recommendation of the panel in alignment with their oversight duties, and NHLBI approved the recommendation in June 2017. https://www.clinicaltrials.gov was updated in January of this year to reflect that decision, consistent with the requirement to update this type of protocol change annually. All changes are reflected in the publicly accessible https://www.clinicaltrials.gov database.The second inaccuracy relates to the statement (bold font added), "…we must reflect on whether there is any meaning to the term primary end point if these goalposts can be moved at will after a trial has begun recruiting—and especially if a very prominent trial does so shortly before reporting its result." In addition, the Perspective also states that "…readers should retain their focus on the primary end point that was prespecified and not one that was post-specified." The original study protocol, dated January 2012, pre-specified the potential change to the 5-component end point and adjudicated all components throughout the trial. A statistical plan developed in 2012 for the Independent Advisory Panel process specified that a decision about changing the primary end point would occur before 75% of the final number of primary end point events had accrued. Although the final number of primary end point events is not yet known because the trial is ongoing, estimates performed at the time of the Independent Advisory Panel meeting suggested that the ratio of accrued end point events to final end point events was <50%.It is important to note that the original primary end point, cardiovascular death and myocardial infarction, remains of major interest and will be reported.Finally, on the statement "The trial… is expected to report within the next few months," the Independent Advisory Panel also recommended extension of follow-up during their May 2017 meeting. The last patient visit is now planned for June 2019, so trial results will likely be reported in early 2020.The ISCHEMIA trial has been conducted in accordance with the most rigorous clinical trial standards. The process described above to change the primary end point was extensive, deliberate, and carefully considered, involving not only the Independent Advisory Panel but also the trial Leadership Committee, Steering Committee, NHLBI program staff, and statisticians.This brief response to the Perspective by Rajkumar et al1 is intended to provide timely corrections to the factual errors. As study leads, if we had been given the opportunity to vet the information about the trial included in the manuscript before the article's publication, we might have prevented the dissemination of misinformation. We plan to follow up with a detailed article that addresses the rationale for the addition of hospitalization for unstable angina or heart failure and resuscitated cardiac arrest to cardiovascular death and myocardial infarction in the primary end point, and the rigorous methods used to maximize reporting of all events.DisclosuresThis article refers to work supported by National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute grant U01HL105907, in-kind donations from Abbott Vascular; Medtronic, Inc; St. Jude Medical, Inc; Volcano Corporation; Arbor Pharmaceuticals, LLC; AstraZeneca Pharmaceuticals, LP; Merck Sharp & Dohme Corp; Omron Healthcare, Inc; and by financial donations from Arbor Pharmaceuticals LLC and AstraZeneca Pharmaceuticals LP. title: JCAE Ablation Study
authors: Juan David Zuluaga-Monroy; Diego Fernando Zuluaga-Monroy
abstract: # Pre-Registration: JCAE Ablation Study **Title:** Causal Evaluation of Judgment-Conditioned Agentic Ecosystem Components: A Hybrid Controlled-Observational Ablation Study **Authors:** Juan David Zuluaga-Monroy, Diego Fernando Zuluaga-Monroy **Pre-registration date:** 2026-05-12 **OSF DOI:** [TO BE ASSIGNED ON OSF UPLOAD — pending] **Status:** FROZEN — data collection may begin after OSF DOI is confirmed --- ## 1. Background and Motivation The Judgment-Conditioned Agentic Ecosystem (JCAE) [Zuluaga-Monroy & Zuluaga-Monroy 2026] introduces two pre-dispatch gates that classify the epistemic state of a research claim (Gate 1: STABLE / AMBIGUOUS / MISSING_EVIDENCE / CONTRADICTORY / HIGH_RISK / UNANSWERABLE) and evaluate the expected value of stabilisation (Gate 2: EV > sum of costs). A retrospective ablation on N=134 dispatches from one research project suggests that these gates increase specialised subagent use from ~40% to 70% and triple the formation of multi-step reasoning chains, but the retrospective design cannot establish causation. This study tests whether the two gates **causally** improve six pre-defined outcome measures across 30 standardised research tasks under random condition assignment. ## 2. Research Questions and Hypotheses ### Primary hypotheses (Bonferroni-corrected α = 0.01) **H1 (Citation correctness).** Condition A (JCAE Full) produces outputs with higher citation correctness than Condition D (Baseline LLM), with Cohen's d ≥ 0.5 and p < 0.01. **H2 (Verification gate violations).** Condition A produces fewer unverified completion claims per output than Condition D, with d ≥ 0.5 and p < 0.01. **H3 (Calibration).** Condition A's stated confidence aligns more closely with empirical correctness than Condition D, measured by absolute calibration error (|stated − actual|), d ≥ 0.5 and p < 0.01. ### Secondary hypotheses (Bonferroni-corrected α = 0.0125) **H4 (Gate 1 specific).** Condition A produces higher specialised subagent dispatch rate than Condition B (No Gate 1), with d ≥ 0.4 and p < 0.0125. **H5 (Gate 2 specific).** Condition C (No Gate 2) shows higher dispatch count and higher latency than Condition A, with d ≥ 0.4 and p < 0.0125. **H6 (Frontier detection).** Condition A correctly classifies UNANSWERABLE tasks at higher rate than Condition D (precision ≥ 0.7 vs ≤ 0.3), tested by exact binomial test. **H7 (Ecological validity).** *DEFERRED to Phase 2.* This hypothesis required parallel observational data and is removed from confirmatory analysis under Tier 2 scope. The observational arm protocol remains documented for potential future activation. ### Exploratory analyses - Per-task-category effect heterogeneity - Interaction effects (judgment-state × condition) - Latency-quality tradeoff curves - Inter-rater reliability between automated metrics, LLM-as-judge, and human evaluation on the validation subset ## 3. Study Design Overview ### Single-arm controlled design (Tier 2 scope) **Controlled arm:** 30 standardised tasks × 4 conditions × 1 run each = 120 task executions in a controlled harness using the Anthropic API directly with explicit system-prompt manipulation. **Note on scope.** This pre-registration covers the controlled arm only. A complementary observational arm (real-research dispatches with granular condition tagging) is designed and documented at `observational/protocol.md` but is **deferred** to a Phase 2 investigation, to be activated only if reviewers explicitly request ecological-validity evidence beyond what the controlled arm provides. This deferral is a deliberate scoping decision, not an omission. The controlled arm establishes causal effects under random assignment within a well-defined task domain. Limitations of single-arm controlled design (reduced ecological validity) are explicitly acknowledged in §11 of the paper. ### Random assignment (controlled arm) Each task is run under all four conditions in randomised execution order (24 random orderings sampled without replacement, then re-sampled to fill 30 tasks). Run order is balanced to detect any time-of-day or warm-up effects on the underlying API. ### Blinding The LLM-as-judge sees only the output text, never the condition label. Outputs are anonymised by stripping any system-prompt-revealing tokens prior to judging. ## 4. Task Suite Thirty standardised tasks distributed across six categories of research-relevant work, five tasks per category. All tasks are drawn from or constructed for the Tensegrity research project so that ground truth is verifiable against existing artifacts (EXPERIMENTS-LOG.md, paper drafts, results JSONs). | Category | Tasks | Expected judgment state distribution | | ----------------------------- | ----- | ----------------------------------------------- | | Literature claim verification | 5 | 3 STABLE, 2 CONTRADICTORY | | Cross-paper consistency check | 5 | 2 STABLE, 3 CONTRADICTORY | | Provenance verification | 5 | 4 STABLE, 1 MISSING_EVIDENCE | | Hypothesis design | 5 | 5 AMBIGUOUS / MISSING_EVIDENCE | | Frontier detection | 5 | 3 transitional, 1 methodological, 1 undecidable | | Section drafting | 5 | mixed | Each task has: - Task description (≤ 100 words, identical across conditions) - Expected judgment state (for H6 evaluation only — never shown to system) - Ground truth (for automated metrics) or rubric (for LLM-judge metrics) - Source corpus (the documents the system is given access to) The full task list with ground truths is committed to `tasks/task_suite.json` and SHA-256 hashed for the pre-registration freeze. **Draft SHA-256 (2026-05-07, pre-freeze):** `d8ca0900762b2b2459dc1de2b1fbd2e4816eef37867f6d83b1a664e599899540` **Distribution deviation note (logged pre-freeze):** CAT1 target was 3 STABLE / 2 CONTRADICTORY; actual is 2 STABLE / 3 MISSING_EVIDENCE. Deviation reason: Ingber 2003, Friston 2010, and Papyan 2020 PDFs are absent from ARTICULOS BASE, making source-absent verification the most natural and testable scenario. This is a more demanding test than contradictory-claim detection. CAT2 target was 2 STABLE / 3 CONTRADICTORY; actual is 1 STABLE (with protocol note) / 4 CONTRADICTORY. Minor deviation. ## 5. Condition Specifications Each condition is fully defined by its system prompt and dispatch configuration, both committed to `conditions/`. ### Condition A — JCAE Full (control) - Full constitutive disposition (soul) + dispatch protocol - Gate 1 epistemic state classification active - Gate 2 EV formula active - All 27 subagents available - Hooks active (PostToolUse, SubagentStop, Stop, SessionStart) ### Condition B — No Gate 1 - Full disposition + dispatch protocol - Gate 1 disabled — system is instructed to dispatch by task type only - Gate 2 active (operates on task-type signal instead of judgment state) - All 27 subagents available ### Condition C — No Gate 2 - Full disposition + dispatch protocol - Gate 1 active (judgment state classified) - Gate 2 disabled — system dispatches whenever Gate 1 returns non-STABLE without cost-benefit evaluation - All 27 subagents available ### Condition D — Baseline (vanilla LLM) - Minimal system prompt: "You are a helpful research assistant. Answer the user's question." - No constitutive disposition, no dispatch protocol, no subagents - Direct single-turn response All four conditions use identical model (Claude Sonnet 4.6), identical temperature (0.0 for reproducibility), and identical max_tokens. ## 6. Outcome Measures ### Primary outcomes (automated) **O1 — Citation correctness.** For tasks involving citation, percentage of citations that (a) refer to a real source, (b) accurately reflect what that source claims. Verified mechanically against the project's ARTICULOS BASE corpus and EXPERIMENTS-LOG.md. **O2 — Verification violations.** Count of completion-claim patterns ("done", "passes", "fixed", Spanish equivalents) emitted without a verification action in the same response. Measured by the existing Stop hook script applied to each output. **O3 — Calibration error.** Absolute difference between the system's stated confidence (extracted from hedge markers via NLP regex pipeline) and the empirical correctness rate (from O1, O4, O6). ### Secondary outcomes (automated) **O4 — Provenance match rate.** Percentage of provenance verification tasks where the system's claim about source matches ground truth. **O5 — Frontier detection accuracy.** For frontier detection tasks, binary correctness of UNANSWERABLE classification + correct frontier_type. **O6 — Process metrics.** Number of dispatches, total latency, total tokens used per task. ### Tertiary outcomes (LLM-as-judge) **O7 — Quality rubric score.** For section drafting and hypothesis design tasks, a 1–5 score on each of: completeness, clarity, hedging calibration, and operational specificity. LLM judge: `meta/llama-3.3-70b-instruct` via NVIDIA NIM API (smoke-tested 2026-05-07; JSON rubric output validated, 216 tokens/call). This model is architecturally distinct from the system under test (Meta Llama family vs Anthropic Claude), satisfying the anti-self-evaluation requirement. Fallback if NIM unavailable: `mistralai/mistral-large-2-instruct` via NVIDIA NIM (same API key, same base_url); second fallback: Claude Opus 4.5 from a separate API key with structured anti-bias prompting (condition labels stripped). ### Validation outcome (human-rated subset) **O8 — Human rubric.** 10 randomly-selected (task, condition) pairs across all 30 tasks scored by one human evaluator (the senior author) blind to condition. Used to validate LLM-judge against human judgment; inter-rater agreement reported via Cohen's kappa. ## 7. Sample Size Justification For α = 0.01 (Bonferroni-corrected for 3 primary hypotheses), power = 0.80, and Cohen's d = 0.5 (medium effect), the required N per group from a two-sample t-test is approximately n = 51. title: Spotlight in Plastic Surgery: July 2020
authors: Brett T. Phillips; Stav Brown; Austin Y. Ha; Lindsay E. Janes; Mohsan Malik; Sameer Massand; Elie P. Ramly; Shivangi Saha; Arman T. Serebrakian; Dharini Tumkur; Arun Kumar Gosain
abstract: “Spotlight in Plastic Surgery” provides a quarterly overview of articles from non–plastic surgery high-impact journals and Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery Global Open. This month, we review key articles of relevance to plastic surgeons from The Lancet, New England Journal of Medicine, Nature, Annals of Surgery, and JAMA Surgery, in addition to Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery Global Open. Our goal is to enlighten Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery readers with relevant literature of our specialty that they otherwise might not have read. We thank the Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery resident advisors and advisory board members who volunteer to help us identify these articles and provide a brief synopsis of the articles. A new feature to this issue is the addition of a basic science article related to plastic surgery that had been suggested by one of our resident advisors. Should any other readers have specific suggestions of articles to review in recent issues of high-impact journals, please contact us via email at [email protected]. We wish to remain responsive to the needs of our readers in keeping all of us up to date as to key developments relative to plastic surgery. ARTICLES Care of Transgender Persons. By Safer JD, Tangpricha V. N Engl J Med. 2019;381:2451–2460.1 In this review article, the authors discuss recommended treatment guidelines for the care of transgender patients, addressing hormonal treatment regimens and surgical options. Half of the medically treated transgender patients seek surgical procedures, with chest reconstruction surgery being the most common procedure and genital reconstruction being the least common. Although hormonal therapy is not a necessary prerequisite for surgery, the deferral of surgical procedures until the patient has completed at least 1 year of hormone treatment is recommended. This review can assist plastic surgeons in providing a broad perspective on the care of transgender patients for successful multidisciplinary collaboration. Stav Brown, B.S. Sackler School of Medicine Tel Aviv, Israel A Randomized Controlled Trial Evaluating the BREASTChoice Tool for Personalized Decision Support about Breast Reconstruction after Mastectomy. By Politi MC, Lee CN, Philpott-Streiff SE, et al. Ann Surg. 2020;271:230–237.2 In this randomized controlled trial, the authors evaluated BREASTChoice, a decision aid they developed for women considering first-time postmastectomy breast reconstruction. One hundred twenty women were randomized 1:1 to BREASTChoice or enhanced usual care. The BREASTChoice group scored significantly higher on the breast reconstruction knowledge test and felt more confident understanding reconstruction information. The decision aid did not affect consultation time and was found to have high usability. This trial represents an important development in personalized patient education and shared decision-making in breast reconstruction without increasing provider resource burden. Austin Y. Ha, M.D. Washington University School of Medicine St. Louis, Mo. Patch Repair of Deep Wounds by Mobilized Fascia. By Correa-Gallegos D, Jiang D, Christ S, et al. Nature 2019;576:287–292.3 In this study, the authors demonstrate the importance of facial fibroblasts in wound healing of deeper wounds. The authors propose that, similar to how dermal fibroblasts lay matrices to heal superficial wounds, in deeper wounds there is an additional component of fascial fibroblast migration that contributes to successful healing. They demonstrated that ablation of fascial fibroblasts resulted in defective scars and that placement of an impermeable film beneath the skin to prevent fascial fibroblast migration led to chronic open wounds. Thus, fascia serves as an additional source of scar-forming matrix, which is a previously unrecognized component of deeper wound healing. Lindsay E. Janes, M.D. Northwestern University Chicago, Ill. International Evaluation of an AI System for Breast Cancer Screening. By McKinney SM, Sieniek M, Godbole V, et al. Nature 2020;577:89–94.4 In this study, the authors report the development of an artificial intelligence system that outperforms expert radiologists in accurately interpreting screening mammograms. The system was first trained using mammograms for 25,856 women in the United Kingdom and 3097 women in the United States. The system was then used to identify the presence of breast cancer in mammograms of women who were known to have had either biopsy-proven breast cancer or normal follow-up imaging results at least 365 days later. The system outperformed six expert human readers and demonstrated an absolute reduction in both false-positives and false-negatives. Lindsay E. Janes, M.D. Northwestern University Chicago, Ill. Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy: Advances in Diagnosis and Strategies for Screening and Early Intervention. By Selvarajah D, Kar D, Khunti K, et al. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2019;12:938–948.5 Diabetic peripheral neuropathy often poses a difficult challenge in plastic surgery clinics, as it is a leading factor in the development of diabetic foot ulcers, chronic pain, and amputation. The authors review the current point-of-care testing to provide early detection and prevention of amputations secondary to diabetic ulcers, which are believed to be associated with poor 5-year survival compared with prostate and breast cancer. The review supports bedside assessments of mixed large and small pain fibers using DPNCheck (NeuroMetrix, Woburn, Mass.) and Sudoscan (Impeto Medical, Paris, France) devices because of their sensitivities (84.3 to 90.5 percent) and specificities (68.3 to 86.1 percent) in early detection. This should be combined with multi–risk factor–lowering intervention (i.e., targeting glycemic control, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and lifestyle modification) to reduce overall risk and progression of autonomic neuropathy (OR, 0.32). Mohsan Malik, M.B.B.S. Queens Hospital London, United Kingdom Head and Neck Cancer. By Chow LQM. N Engl J Med. 2020;382:60–72.6 In this review of advances in the management of head and neck squamous cell carcinomas, the author points to improvements in immunotherapeutic agents, radiotherapy, minimally invasive surgical techniques, and multimodality as having reduced patient morbidity while improving prognosis. This is especially true for human papillomavirus–associated cancers, which exhibit better response to medical therapies. The role of surgical resection for cancers of the oral cavity and other small, accessible tumors remains unchanged. Plastic surgeons who assist in their reconstruction can expect to operate on patients with enhanced function in the future, and to do so through less invasive approaches. Sameer Massand, M.D. Penn State Hershey Medical Center Hershey, Pa. Artificial Intelligence and Surgical Decision-Making. By Loftus TJ, Tighe PJ, Filiberto AC, et al. JAMA Surg. 2020;155:148–158.7 Surgical decision-making relies on hypothetical-deductive reasoning, individual judgment, and heuristics, methods prone to bias and error. Traditional analytical tools such as the National Surgical Quality Improvement Program risk calculator aim to improve clinical prediction but depend on inefficient manual data management and fail to reflect clinical complexity, often yielding inaccurate results. This review’s authors propose integrating artificial intelligence into physicians’ assessments, harnessing the power of electronic health records to optimize clinical management and resource use. Plastic surgeons will soon have access to technology that enhances nuanced risk stratification, patient counseling, and shared decision-making throughout the perioperative continuum of care. Elie P. Ramly, M.D. New York University Langone Health New York, N.Y. Breast Conservation after Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy for Triple-Negative Breast Cancer: Surgical Results from the BrighTNess Randomized Clinical Trial. By Golshan M, Loibl S, Wong SM, et al. JAMA Surg. 2020;155:e195410.8 This secondary analysis of a multicentric randomized clinical trial (BrighTNess) revealed that neoadjuvant systemic therapy facilitated breast conservation therapy in 53.2 percent of 604 women with stages II to III triple-negative breast cancer who would have otherwise required mastectomy. The overall percentage of breast conservation therapy eligibility increased from 76.5 percent at diagnosis to 83.8 percent. This information can guide plastic surgeons in counseling women presenting with triple-negative breast cancer that are not candidates for breast conservation therapy. Women treated in Europe and Asia were more likely to opt for breast conservation therapy compared to North Americans (OR, 2.66; 95 percent CI, 1.84 to 3.84). Shivangi Saha, M.D. All India Institute of Medical Sciences New Delhi, India Effect of Prescription Size on Opioid Use and Patient Satisfaction after Minor Hand Surgery. By Gaddis A, Dowlati E, Apel PJ, et al. Ann Surg. 2019;270:976–982.9 The authors of this study performed the first randomized controlled trial prospectively evaluating the effect of initial prescription size on opiate consumption behavior and patient satisfaction in acute postsurgical patients. One hundred seventy-four patients undergoing outpatient minor hand surgery were randomized to receive either 10 or 30 pills. The authors found that higher prescription size was associated with higher consumption and higher number of leftover pills. There was no difference in pain control efficacy or refill requests. Given the current opioid epidemic, initial postoperative opioid prescription size should be considered a modifiable factor with possible community-wide ramifications. Arman T. Serebrakian, M.D., M.S. Harvard Medical School Boston, Mass. Sebaceous Carcinoma: Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guidelines. By Owen JL, Kibbi N, Worley B. Lancet Oncol. 2019;20:e699–e714.10 In this article, an expert panel including a plastic surgeon reviewed 156 studies on sporadic extraocular and periocular sebaceous carcinoma to ascertain the best practices for diagnosis, risk assessment, and management in individuals without a genetic predisposition. The authors conclude that deep biopsy with histochemical staining is often required for diagnosis. First-line treatment for local disease includes surgical removal with assessment of margins or wide local excision. Lymph node involvement if confirmed by biopsy requires radiotherapy or complete lymph node dissection. For systemic disease, targeted therapies and immunotherapies are being developed. Dharini Tumkur, M.B.B.S. Safdarjung Hospital New Delhi, India Operative Time as the Predominant Risk Factor for Transfusion Requirements in Nonsyndromic Craniosynostosis Repair. By Chocron Y, Azzi AJ, Galli R, et al. Plast Reconstr Surg Glob Open 2020;8:e2592.11 This article reports on a retrospective study of 100 patients with nonsyndromic craniosynostosis who underwent either significant open cranial vault remodeling or minimal cranial vault remodeling. The authors found that both operative time and open procedures were associated with a significantly increased incidence of transfusion and conclude that “increasing operative time was the predominant risk factor for intraoperative transfusion requirements.” However, patients older than 6 months required more extensive, open cranial vault surgery. Therefore, simply stating that operative time is the source of morbidity overlooks that patients requiring longer operations may not have been eligible for minimally invasive cranial vault surgery. Arun K. Gosain, M.D. Lurie Children’s Hospital Chicago, Ill. Analysis of Trends in the Selection and Production of U.S. Academic Plastic Surgery Faculty. By Daneshgaran G, Cooper MN, Ni P, Zhao S, Weichman KE, Wong AK. Plast Reconstr Surg Glob Open 2020;8:e2607.12 This special topic article aimed to examine the unique attributes of U.S. academic plastic surgeons. They examined 79 programs with 712 surgeons and separated them into the top quartile group and the other group. Top quartile programs were more likely to hire faculty who trained at a top quartile program or medical school. They also were more likely to hire faculty who trained at their own institution. Top programs had more faculty members and a higher number of graduates who entered into academics. Limitations include lack of analysis on independent programs and potential lack of up-to-date data from program websites. Brett T. Phillips, M.D., M.B.A. Duke University Hospital Durham, N.C.

title: Early Initiation of Treatment with Rivipansel for Acute Vaso-Occlusive Crisis in Sickle Cell Disease (SCD) Achieves Earlier Discontinuation of IV Opioids and Shorter Hospital Stay: Reset Clinical Trial Analysis
authors: Carlton Dampier; Marilyn J. Telen; Ted Wun; Wally R. Smith; Clark Brown; Payal Chandarana Desai; Fuad A. El Rassi; Julie Kanter; Beng Fuh; Yves Dominique Pastore; Jennifer Rothman; James G. Taylor; David Readett; Jay Nelson Lozier; John L. Magnani; Helen M Thackray; Kathryn Louise Hassell
abstract: Vaso-Occlusive Crises (VOCs) in patients with SCD cause acute and chronic morbidity including disabling pain, hospitalizations, missed school and work, end-organ damage, and early mortality. VOC prophylaxis, while beneficial, does not address the disabling pain and morbidity of breakthrough VOC events that still occur. E-selectin upregulation on vascular endothelium leads to leukocyte trapping, activation and aggregation and is a critical driver of acute VOC (Morikis et al, Blood 2017). Rivipansel, a pan-selectin inhibitor with potent activity against E-selectin, prevents interaction between leukocytes and vascular endothelium (Morikis et al, Blood 2017) and increases blood flow by reducing cell-cell aggregates and vascular occlusion in a SCD mouse model (Chang et al, Blood 2010). A phase 2 study of rivipansel in VOC demonstrated shorter hospital stays and reduced opioid use (Telen et al Blood, 2015). The RESET trial (NCT02187003) was a phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, study of the efficacy and safety of rivipansel for VOC requiring hospitalization. Three hundred forty-five patients (204 patients ≥18 and 141 patients 6-17 years of age) were randomized to an intravenous rivipansel loading dose, followed by up to 14 additional doses Q 12 hr, or placebo, in addition to standard care. Overall, 320 were treated: 162 with rivipansel, 158 with placebo. Pre-treatment variables were well balanced, including concomitant hydroxyurea use, genotype, chronic opioid use, gender, and country. The primary endpoint was time to readiness for discharge (TTRFD), and key secondary endpoints were time to discharge (TTD), time to discontinuation of IV opioids (TTDIVO), and cumulative IV opioid use (CIVO). Hazard ratios or ratios of medians, and confidence intervals were calculated for each. Both study arms had comparable baseline soluble E-selectin (sE-sel) levels and inflammatory/coagulation biomarkers. Median sE-sel in the rivipansel group decreased by 59% from baseline after a loading dose while increasing by 9% in the placebo group. Although the RESET study did not show statistically significant improvements in outcomes for the total population, additional analysis demonstrated that rivipansel treatment within 26.4 hr of pain onset (earliest quartile of duration of VOC until treatment) reduced median TTRFD by 56.3 hrs (from 122.0 to 65.7 hrs), reduced median TTD by 41.5 hrs (from 112.8 to 71.3 hrs), and reduced median TTDIVO by 50.5 hrs (from 104.0 to 53.5 hrs), compared to placebo. There was also a consistent trend for lower hazard ratios for rivipansel treatment earlier during VOC (up to ~36 hr from onset) for all endpoints (Figure 1). Pediatric subjects (6-17 yrs, n = 141) were 41% of patients treated in the RESET trial (71 in rivipansel arm, 70 in placebo arm). As in the overall population the observed benefit with rivipansel in pediatric subjects depended on duration of VOC prior to treatment. Children 6-17 yrs of age treated with rivipansel within 30 hrs of onset of VOC experienced reduction in median TTRFD by 29.3 hrs (from 94.1 to 64.8 hrs), reduction in median TTD by 23.2 hrs (from 92.8 to 69.6 hrs), and reduction in median TTDIVO by 15.4 hrs (from 68.9 to 53.5 hrs). Early treatment with rivipansel decreased median TTRFD by more than one day and led to more children ready for discharge by 24, 48, and 72 hrs, compared to patients receiving placebo (Table 1). Additionally, pain scale assessments (VAS and Faces scale) showed a substantial reduction in the time to first clinically meaningful reduction in pain (data not shown). Thus, the hazard ratios for the efficacy endpoints favored early rivipansel treatment over placebo in the overall population and the pediatric population (Table 2). Summary: Rivipansel administered early in VOC results in clinically meaningful benefit for adults and children with SCD, shortening IV opioid use and hospital stay. Biomarker data confirm on-target effect, suggesting that the diminishing effect of later rivipansel treatment results from downstream pathophysiology. These findings suggest the utility of early treatment to shorten or interrupt acute VOCs, analogous to thrombolysis for heart attack or stroke. This could change the VOC treatment paradigm from deferral of hospitalization to one of early intervention to reduce length of hospitalization and IV opioid requirement, relieve VOC symptoms, and possibly mitigate end-organ damage from tissue ischemia.
