title: The year in cardiology 2015: coronary intervention
authors: Philippe Gabríel Steg; Patrick W.J.C. Serruys; Mohammad Abdelghani; William C. Wijns
abstract: The field of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) remains extremely active, with major advances involving revascularisation strategies and techniques, adjuvant antithrombotic therapy (with a particular emphasis this year on the optimal duration of antiplatelet therapy after drug-eluting stent (DES) stenting), concerns regarding the importance and risks of bleeding and methods to decrease those risks and a strong focus on the study of newer generation DES and bioresorbable devices with lingering concerns regarding the safety of the latter. Given the improved clinical outcomes of newer generation DES, comparisons between these and coronary artery bypass surgery (CABG) are important. The BEST trial1 randomly assigned 880 patients with multivessel disease to either PCI with everolimus-eluting stents (EES) or to CABG. After a median follow-up of 4.6 years, major adverse cardiac events were higher in the PCI group than in the CABG group (15.3 vs. 10.6%, P = 0.04), driven by a reduction of repeat revascularization but also spontaneous myocardial infarction (MI) in the surgical group, reaffirming the role of CABG surgery in the management of patients with multivessel disease in the era of newer DESs. The management of in-stent restenosis can be difficult. The PROSPERO network meta-analysis of 27 trials2 attempted to synthesize the evidence and suggested that PCI with EES yielded the best angiographic and clinical outcomes and that drug-coated balloons provided favourable angiographic results without adding an additional metal layer. The RIBS-IV trial3 compared prospectively these two strategies in 309 patients with in-stent restenosis after DESs and found that EES provided superior 1-year clinical (lower composite of cardiac death, MI, and target vessel revascularization, 10 vs. 18%, P = 0.04) and angiographic outcomes compared with drug-eluting balloons. Thus, while drug-eluting balloons provide effective treatment for restenosis in bare metal stents, they are less effective than EES for restenosis in DES. The optimal management of bifurcation lesions remains uncertain.4 The TRYTON trial5 randomly assigned 704 patients with bifurcation lesions to either a bifurcation stent (the TRYTON stent) or stenting of the main vessel with provisional stenting of the side branch. At 9 months, target vessel failure was numerically more frequent with the bifurcation stent, largely due to a higher periprocedural MI rate, and the bifurcation stent failed to achieve non-inferiority with the strategy of provisional stenting, illustrating once more that, in interventional cardiology, ‘less is more’… . Likewise, the role of PCI in the management of chronic total occlusions is still debated, in the absence of a properly powered randomized outcomes trial. An observational analysis from the Italian registry of chronic total occlusions6 which enrolled 1777 patients with CTOs found that after propensity score matching, rates of cardiac death, acute MI, and rehospitalization were lower in patients managed with PCI than managed with medical therapy or CABG, suggesting that PCI may have a role in improving outcomes in these patients. As interventionalists treat ever older patient populations with more advanced, complex, and calcified disease, the potential role of rotational atherectomy has increased. However, in many sites, the use of this technique has been hampered by the lack of a standardized protocol. A group of experienced operators has provided a consensus document,7 recapitulating recommendations for the performance of the technique, which will be useful to sites and operators with less experience. The long-term safety of DESs vis à vis that of bare metal stents has long been a contentious issue. With the advent of newer generation DESs, both efficacy and safety have been improved. A comprehensive network meta-analysis reviewed these issues8 in 51 trials including a total of 52 158 randomized patients with follow-up duration ≥3 years. After a median follow-up of 3.8 years, all DES demonstrated superior efficacy compared with BMS. Among DES, second-generation devices have substantially improved long-term safety and efficacy outcomes compared with first-generation devices. Since there is continuous improvement and innovation in the field, an ESC-EAPCI task force has released a report reviewing the existing evidence and confirming the improved efficacy and safety of new DES (Figure 1A and B). This report also outlines the desirable pathway for preclinical and clinical evaluation and regulatory approval of future devices.9 (A) Results of a systematic review results regarding clinical outcomes at 9–12 months for bare metal stents (BMS), early and new drug-eluting stents (DES)—median rates per 100 person-years. Median rates and inter-quartile range per 100 person-year for the clinical endpoints all-cause death, myocardial infarction, target-lesion revascularization, and definite stent thrombosis. (B) Systematic review of median, inter-quartile range, and cumulative frequency of in-stent late lumen loss for bare metal stents, early and new drug-eluting stents (reprinted with kind permission from Byrne et al.9). Finally, the effect of PCI on long-term survival in patients with stable coronary artery disease was studied in the extended follow-up of the COURAGE trial10 In 2287 patients randomized to optimal medical therapy alone or combined with PCI, the initial median follow-up of 4.6 years had found no difference in the composite primary outcome of death or MI, or in survival. An updated report with an extended median follow-up of 11.9 years found no difference in mortality (adjusted HR 1.03; 95% CI 0.83–1.21; P = 0.76). These results are consistent with the BARI-2D results. Controversy regarding the lack of mortality benefit with PCI vs. either best of medical care or CABG was revisited by Windecker et al.11 in a 93 553 patient large network meta-analysis showing survival benefit with newer generation DES (HR everolimus DES 0.75; 95% CI 0.59–0.96; HR zotarolimus Resolute DES 0.65; 95% CI 0.42–1.00) vs. medical therapy. These results emphasize the importance of the ongoing International Study of Comparative Health Effectiveness with Medical and Invasive Appproaches (ISCHEMIA) trial (Clinical trials.gov number NCT01471522) to assess the role of cardiac catheterization and contemporary revascularization techniques in improving the outcomes of patients with stable coronary artery disease and at least moderate ischaemia. The issue of the benefits and risks of prolonged dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) following DES placement has continued to attract interest and spark controversy, particularly given the heterogeneity of results. Many of the randomized trials comparing various durations of DAPT were underpowered.12,13 In addition, in the large DAPT trial, despite clear benefit of prolonged DAPT beyond 1 year in reducing the risks of MACCE, stent thrombosis, and MI, there was a signal of increased non-cardiovascular mortality. Both of these issues have sparked interest in meta-analyses of the data. With respect to mortality, a pairwise and Bayesian network meta-analysis of 10 randomized trials comparing different DAPT durations after DES stenting in 31 666 patients14 found that although treatment with DAPT beyond 1 year after DES implantation reduces MI and stent thrombosis, it is associated with increased mortality because of an increased risk of non-cardiovascular mortality not offset by a reduction in cardiac mortality. However, this signal had not been seen in a prior broader meta-analysis comparing various durations of DAPT across a variety of cardiovascular conditions.15 With respect to the risk benefit risk of shorter vs. longer durations of DAPT, several meta-analyses16–18 have concurred in suggesting that prolonged DAPT should be considered on a case-by-case basis, after weighing both ischaemic and bleeding risks. One patient profile that is most likely a good candidate for consideration of prolonged DAPT after stenting is patients with prior MI. Both the analysis of the MI subset from the large DAPT trial19 and a comprehensive meta-analysis of randomized trials in patients with prior MI20 have found that patients with prior MI derive a clear benefit from prolonging DAPT beyond 1 year (compared with aspirin alone). In the meta-analysis, prolonged DAPT reduced rates of MACE (rate ratio, RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.67–0.90; P = 0.001), MI (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.55–0.88; P = 0.003), stent thrombosis, but also cardiovascular mortality (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.74–0.98; P = 0.03), at the cost of an increase in major bleeding (RR 1.73, 95% CI 1.19–2.50; P = 0.004) but without increase in fatal bleeding or in non-cardiovascular death. title: SELF-CALIBRATING QUANTUM BIOSENSING NETWORKS AT THE LIMIT Distributed Sensing, Reference Transfer, Drift Detection, and Autonomous Recalibration
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: SELF-CALIBRATING QUANTUM BIOSENSING NETWORKS AT THE LIMIT Distributed Sensing, Reference Transfer, Drift Detection, and Autonomous Recalibration SELF-CALIBRATING QUANTUM BIOSENSING NETWORKS AT THE LIMIT Distributed Sensing, Reference Transfer, Drift Detection, and Autonomous Recalibration Self-Calibrating Quantum Biosensing Networks at the Limit is a large-scale research monograph exploring a deceptively difficult question: Can a distributed quantum biosensing network recognize when it is no longer trustworthy - and recalibrate itself without hiding the physical change that caused the problem? The book couples two research architectures. The first comes from AI-interpreted quantum health metrology and reproducible measurement. It emphasizes raw physical evidence, calibration lineage, reference standards, manufacturing variation, data provenance, uncertainty, versioning, interlaboratory reproducibility, and independent reconstruction. The second comes from bounded quantum autonomous infrastructure. Its operational loop is: Sense-> Interpret-> Decide-> Act-> Verify-> Recover Together they produce a new research architecture: Distributed SensingxCalibration TraceabilityxBounded Recalibration The central challenge is not simply automatic calibration. A sensor network may become more internally consistent while becoming less physically correct. Multiple instruments may agree because they share the same hidden reference bias. An AI correction may suppress real biological variation. A reference material may age. A firmware update may change the effective transfer function. Environmental conditions may shift. Manufacturing variation may create lot-specific behavior. Several nodes may drift together and therefore fail to detect one another. A network can therefore be locally stable, globally consistent, and scientifically wrong at the same time. This volume treats that problem as a combined metrology, distributed-systems, autonomy, and failure-science challenge. Its proposed flagship heuristic is: SCQN=(C_t x X_r x D_d x R_v)/(1 + D_f + B_v + C_m) where the numerator conceptually rewards calibration traceability, cross-site reference transfer, drift detectability, and verified recalibration. The denominator penalizes false drift detection, boundary violations, common-mode failure, and related burdens. SCQN is not proposed as a physical law, clinical metric, regulatory standard, or universal score. It is a research scaffold. Every term must be explicitly defined, normalized, reported separately, and subjected to sensitivity analysis. The book develops an operational calibration loop: Measure-> Compare-> Detect-> Diagnose-> Propose-> Authorize-> Recalibrate-> Verify-> Commit or Roll Back-> Learn The important addition is authorization. A self-calibrating system should not possess unlimited permission to rewrite its own reference structure. Low-risk and reversible local corrections may be permitted under relatively modest evidence. Network-wide transfer changes, reference replacement, or irreversible transformations should require stronger evidence, independent comparison, and where appropriate human authorization. Abstention is treated as a valid system state. Quarantine is treated as a valid system state. Classical fallback is treated as a valid system state. A mature network is not defined by how often it recalibrates. It is defined by whether it knows when evidence is sufficient to act and when uncertainty should remain unresolved. Across 82 chapters, the book develops this architecture through reference transfer, calibration standards, commutability, ring trials, cross-instrument transfer, drift taxonomy, physics-constrained drift detection, out-of-distribution states, environmental confounding, manufacturing aging, recalibration triggers, bounded agents, reversible corrections, human escalation, multi-agent coordination, federated metrology, network partitions, faulty nodes, provenance, version lineage, independent replay, common-mode failure, classical fallback, graceful degradation, measurement quarantine, manufacturing variation, predictive maintenance, security, governance, open standards, digital twins, remote sensing networks, and successor-ready calibration infrastructure. A major theme is that drift detection and trust restoration are different problems. Detecting that something changed does not prove that the recalibration system knows what the correct state should be. A network must therefore preserve independent references and external challenge paths. The strongest verification is not lower disagreement among network nodes. It is independent evidence that the corrected network remains physically traceable. The book also distinguishes biological variability from instrumentation instability. A change in physiology, molecular state, specimen handling, or sample matrix should not automatically be absorbed into a calibration parameter simply because doing so produces a cleaner signal. Physical change must remain visible. The architecture therefore preserves both pre-correction and post-correction states. Every recalibration action should leave a trace containing: the trigger,the evidence,the reference identity,the affected instruments,the environmental context,the algorithm and firmware versions,the uncertainty budget,the authorized action,the expected effect,the verification result,and the rollback path. Failure science plays a central role. The volume investigates false drift alarms, hidden reference failure, common-mode calibration errors, synchronization problems, network partitions, faulty agents, version skew, environmental confounding, manufacturing defects, aging, reference non-commutability, and recovery to the wrong state. Failures are not merely incidents to remove. They are maps of hidden dependencies. A failed transfer may reveal that a calibration relation depended on temperature. A failed ring trial may expose a site-specific assumption. A common-mode failure may reveal that network diversity was insufficient. A rollback failure may show that the system never truly preserved its prior state. The book therefore develops failure atlases linking symptoms, candidate causes, confirmatory tests, consequence levels, containment actions, rollback paths, and future experiments. Classical fallback is deliberately preserved. Quantum-enabled sensing may offer useful capabilities, but a biosensing infrastructure should not lose all meaningful service simply because its advanced quantum component becomes unavailable. Strong classical and human-supervised baselines are therefore treated as scientific and operational safeguards. A claimed quantum or autonomous advantage should weaken or disappear if a simpler pipeline delivers equivalent end-to-end performance with lower calibration burden, maintenance complexity, latency, false-action risk, or hidden expert dependence. The later chapters move from individual sensors to sensor fleets. Distributed calibration introduces a particularly dangerous confusion: Consensus is not truth. Ten instruments that share the same biased reference can agree perfectly. For this reason, multi-agent metrology must preserve reference independence, node diversity, external checks, uncertainty, fault isolation, and the ability to quarantine subsets of the network. The network must also survive change. Sensors are replaced. Models are updated. Firmware changes. Standards evolve. Reference artifacts age. Vendors disappear. Operators retire. A mature system therefore requires long-term calibration memory. Successor laboratories should be able to reconstruct not only the final reported quantity, but the entire lineage that produced it. This includes raw measurements, reference identities, calibration artifacts, environmental state, manufacturing lots, software and firmware versions, model identifiers, policy versions, uncertainty budgets, failed runs, overrides, incident records, unresolved disagreements, and rejected alternatives. The final test of maturity is therefore successor reconstruction. Could another laboratory reproduce the measurement? Could it determine which reference was used? Could it replay the recalibration decision? Could it identify what changed? Could it recover the pre-correction state? And could it name the observation that would have caused the original system to refuse the correction? The main text is followed by 200 Research Gates. Each Gate contains a research question, variables to declare, an experimental route, explicit kill criteria, and a successor handoff package. The Gates are not intended to preserve the book's preferred conclusions. They preserve researchable unknowns. The volume concludes with 33 Answer Embryos. Each Answer Embryo remains provisional and follows a phoenix research cycle: Question-> Model-> Test-> Breakdown-> Recombination-> Rebirth The deepest principle of Self-Calibrating Quantum Biosensing Networks at the Limit is therefore not that a network should learn how to correct itself. It is that a trustworthy network must also learn how to doubt itself. Measure what is real. Transfer what is traceable. Detect when trust decays. Recalibrate only within authority. Verify what changed. Preserve the path back.

title: The Victory Siren Sounds, But the Shelter Door Is Still Open
authors: Daniel Rosehill; Gemini 3.1 (Flash); Chatterbox TTS
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Episode summary: When Netanyahu announced the end of Iran's threat, Daniel was still running to a bomb shelter. This episode explores the psychological and political gap between wartime victory narratives and civilian reality. We examine how information asymmetry, cognitive stress, and the evolution of media environments create a uniquely demoralizing experience for citizens caught between official statements and rocket sirens. Is this simply wartime necessity, or a deeper problem with democratic accountability? Show Notes The Gap Between Victory Announcements and Bomb Shelters When a government announces a ceasefire and declares victory, but citizens are still running to bomb shelters, something profound is broken in the relationship between leaders and the led. This isn't a hypothetical scenario—it's the lived reality described in a recent letter from Jerusalem, where a resident found himself dodging rockets hours after hearing his prime minister claim that Iran's threat had been "eliminated." The Central Contradiction The core issue lies in how wartime communications frame success. Netanyahu's April eighth announcement explicitly stated that Iran no longer posed a nuclear, missile, or terror threat to Israel, America, or the region. Yet in the same address, he noted that the ceasefire didn't include Hezbollah. This creates a deliberate ambiguity: the victory is declared over one front while another remains explicitly unresolved, but the overall messaging suggests complete resolution. This isn't necessarily lying in the traditional sense. It's sophisticated framing designed to create an impression that operational facts don't support. The announcement technically applies to Iran, which is true, but it's packaged in language that implies total security when rocket attacks from the north continue unabated. The Psychology of False Relief The cognitive impact of this gap is severe. After six weeks of sustained stress—constant sirens, explosions, and time spent in shelters—brains operate on pattern recognition rather than careful analysis. When people hear "victory" and "threat eliminated," their nervous systems desperately latch onto relief. When the next siren sounds twelve hours later, the psychological crash is worse than if no announcement had been made. This creates what one observer called "the finish line that keeps moving." Citizens experience the exhaustion of a marathon, only to be told they've finished while still running. The metaphor captures the demoralizing essence: the government can't even be bothered to tell the real story. Information Asymmetry and Aggregate vs. Individual Experience Official communications often present aggregate statistics that mask individual terror. The Iron Dome system achieved roughly ninety percent interception during the conflict—over 370 missiles and hundreds of drones neutralized, with only 23 deaths in six weeks. This is an extraordinary technical achievement, and it's the number that gets cited constantly. But that statistic doesn't capture the psychological cost of being in the ten percent's blast radius. More precisely, it doesn't address the terror of not knowing which ten percent you'll be in. Every siren represents potential membership in that unlucky minority. On a population level, the math suggests safety. On an individual level, genuine terror persists. Official messaging rarely acknowledges this coexistence. The Layers of Secrecy Governments have legitimate reasons to withhold operational details during wartime. You don't want to telegraph defense system failures, gaps, or reload times to the enemy. But there's a separate category of information that gets classified under "operational security" that actually provides political cover. The distinction between necessary secrecy and political convenience is almost never made explicit. Citizens have no way of knowing which category any given piece of withheld information falls into. This transforms secrecy from a wartime necessity into a governance strategy. The Democratic Social Contract At its most basic, democracy involves citizens delegating authority to representatives in exchange for accountability. During wartime, that accountability is almost universally deferred, and there are legitimate reasons for this. You cannot run military operations by committee or telegraph strikes to satisfy public demand for press conferences. However, the deferral of accountability during conflict has a tendency to become permanent. The habits of secrecy developed during wartime don't automatically dissolve when shooting stops. In conflicts where ceasefires don't include all parties, there's no clear point at which accountability resumes. Patterns vs. Individual Decisions The Jerusalem resident's letter referenced a July 2025 ceasefire that was widely described as false—a pause masquerading as a truce, complete with victory rhetoric that proved misleading. This creates a pattern rather than an isolated communication failure. When misleading framing becomes the strategy rather than an incidental failure, it suggests systematic manipulation of public perception. Opposition leader Yair Lapid's response to the April eighth announcement called it an unprecedented political disaster, arguing that Iran's nuclear program wasn't destroyed, the ballistic threat remains, and the Iranian regime actually emerged stronger. While these claims require careful evaluation, their existence alongside partial support from facts on the ground creates legitimate questions about whether victory narratives are accurate or post-hoc justifications. Public Sophistication and Condescension Polling data from March showed eighty-one percent support for the operation, but also a growing divide over whether the war's duration was driven by genuine security needs or political survival calculations. This suggests a public that's simultaneously supportive of military action and suspicious of leadership motivations—a sophisticated position that gets treated with a communications strategy assuming people just want to hear "we won." This approach is inherently condescending. The demoralization citizens feel isn't just about the gap between announcement and reality. It's about the implicit message: leaders don't think citizens can handle the real story, so they'll provide the victory version and manage the rest. That's not how you treat citizens in a democracy; that's how you manage subjects. The Modern Information Environment What makes this gap feel uniquely acute now compared to previous generations is the information environment. The Gulf War in 1991 represented the most media-managed conflict in American history at that point, with embedded journalists and carefully curated footage. Public support was high, and there was little competing information to reveal gaps between official narrative and operational reality. Today, every person in a conflict zone has a smartphone, Telegram channels, and networks of family members sharing real-time information. The official narrative must compete with a thousand parallel information streams, most more granular and personal than government statements. This creates a uniquely demoralizing experience: the gap between official statements and lived reality is visible to everyone, yet leaders continue using communication strategies designed for a pre-digital era. The fundamental question becomes whether this communication gap is simply wartime necessity or represents a deeper problem with democratic accountability in modern conflict. When citizens can verify reality in real-time but leaders continue managing perceptions rather than sharing truth, the social contract itself begins to fray. title: The Case for Conducting a Randomized Clinical Trial to Assess the Efficacy of a Single Dose of Prophylactic HPV Vaccines Among Adolescents
authors: Aimée R. Kreimer; Mark E. Sherman; Vikrant V. Sahasrabuddhe; Mahboobeh Safaeian
venue: JNCI Journal of the National Cancer Institute
abstract: Human papillomavirus (HPV) types 16 and 18 collectively cause approximately 70% of cervical cancers worldwide (1) and are linked to an even higher percentage of HPV-associated anogenital and oropharyngeal cancers (2). Three-dose regimens of prophylactic vaccines (the bivalent vaccine Cervarix, GlaxoSmithKline Biologicals; the quadrivalent vaccine Gardasil, Merck and Co, Inc.) provide nearly complete protection against HPV16 and -18 infections and related cervical lesions among individuals uninfected with these types at the time of vaccination (3,4). The structure of the HPV virus-like particles (VLPs), the key component of HPV prophylactic vaccines, present closely spaced, repetitive epitopes to the immune system that induce highly potent, protective antibody responses (14), which may reduce or eliminate the need for booster doses. Further, the immune-stimulatory effects of a toll-like receptor agonist adjuvant in the bivalent vaccine may also contribute to the magnitude and durability of the immune response to this vaccine. Data suggest that two doses of either the bivalent or quadrivalent vaccines, especially if administered to adolescents six or twelve months apart, evoke immune responses comparable to that of three doses among adult women (5–9), for which efficacy has been demonstrated. These favorable results led multiple organizations, including the European Medicines Agency (EMA) (10), the Pan American Health Organization’s (PAHO) Technical Advisory Group (TAG) (11), and the World Health Organization’s (WHO’s) Strategic Advisory Group of Experts (SAGE), to endorse a two-dose vaccination strategy (regardless of vaccine manufacturer) for young adolescents (12). However, in nations that experience the highest cervical cancer mortality rates (13), the resources needed to implement even a two-dose program may be lacking. Accordingly, establishing the protective effect of a single dose could potentially provide enormous benefit. The objective of this commentary is to discuss the need and current evidence supporting the conduct of a clinical trial assessing the efficacy of one-dose HPV vaccine regimens. Post hoc analyses in the Costa Rica Vaccine Trial (CVT), a phase III efficacy trial that compared the bivalent vaccine with placebo among women age 18 to 25 years, showed that protection over four years against HPV16/18 infections among women initially uninfected with these types was uniformly high for recipients of one (100%, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 79% to 100%), two (81%, 95% CI = 53% to 94%), or three (84%, 95% CI = 77% to 89%) doses (5). Among women who received a single dose, HPV16 and HPV18 antibody titers (assessed by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, ELISA) were substantially higher than those among naturally infected women (approximately nine-fold higher for HPV16 and five-fold higher for HPV18); titers remained stably elevated from six to 48 months postvaccination, albeit at four- to five-fold lower levels than for two or three doses (6). Neutralizing antibody titers, the presumed mediators of protection, were highly correlated with levels measured by ELISA (15). At four years, the HPV16 VLP antibody avidity index among CVT recipients of one dose was greater than 70% than that of three-dose vaccinees (16). Similarly, an observational study conducted in Uganda among recipients, age 12 to 14 years, of the bivalent vaccine found that HPV16 and HPV18 antibody levels measured at more than 24 months were similar by dose to those measured in CVT (7). Although tangible evidence for single-dose efficacy is strongest for the bivalent vaccine, this result may also be attained for the quadrivalent vaccine, if the protection afforded by one dose is primarily attributable to the structure of the VLPs. Furthermore, Gardasil 9, a nonavalent HPV vaccine (Merck and Co, Inc.) covering carcinogenic types HPV 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58 plus the condyloma viruses HPV 6 and 11 (17) that was recently licensed by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), is formulated similarly to the quadrivalent vaccine and may also provide protection with a single dose. While higher immunogenicity was demonstrated for three doses of the bivalent compared with the quadrivalent vaccine (18), the impact of these differences on efficacy is unknown. Postmarket, surveillance studies of the quadrivalent vaccine have evaluated the relative efficacy of fewer than three doses, albeit based on imperfect study designs, and yielded mixed results (19–21). Specifically, analysis of registry data in which women are categorized by total number of doses received (as a time-independent variable) may suffer from biases between vaccine-dose groups. It has been reported that fewer-than-three–dose recipients were older at vaccination and younger at first cervical cancer screen (suggesting earlier sexual debut) than those fully vaccinated (19,20). Therefore, one- and two-dose recipients may be more likely to harbor missed prevalent infections at enrollment (22). Such infections would manifest as apparent “vaccine failures,” because these vaccines do not eliminate preexisting infections (23). Without detailed individual-level data (eg, prevaccination cervical HPV DNA or serologic status, screening history, or sexual behavior), it is impossible to statistically adjust for potential differences by dose group in the prevalence of HPV infections at first vaccination. Evaluating efficacy of fewer than three doses in surveillance studies by relating “apparent” vaccine failures to person-time may also be misleading. Because HPV status at the time of vaccination is unknown, women with preexisting HPV infections are most likely to contribute “endpoints” at their earliest follow-up visits, prior to receipt of all three doses, giving the false impression that one and two doses are less protective than the three-dose regimen. Furthermore, the cumulative person-time for the one- and two-dose groups is comparatively limited, which reduces the power of potentially important subgroup analyses, such as efficacy among the youngest participants (ie, the group that is least likely to have prevalent infections at the time of vaccination). Despite limited power, data suggest that younger individuals achieve similar levels of protection irrespective of number of doses received (19). Importantly, providing even a single dose provides considerable protection compared with not vaccinating at all (19). Future observational analyses triggered when more person-time accrues among girls vaccinated before sexual debut may enable robust analyses, which could provide a more unbiased estimate of the effectiveness of one and two doses. Such registry-based observational studies, particularly for Gardasil 9, will take several more years, if not decades, and could therefore be confounded by temporal changes in vaccine formulations and receipt of multiple different vaccines. Finally, assessing the durability of protection will be critically important for all levels of dosing (24,25). Scientific evidence and public health imperatives provide strong impetus for conducting prospective studies, ideally noninferiority randomized trials, to evaluate the efficacy of single-dose strategies of HPV prophylactic vaccines among young girls. To ensure study validity, such a trial should be performed in a setting where adherence to long-term follow-up is likely, effective cervical cancer screening is performed (for participant safety), and widespread vaccination is unavailable. Targeting young girls reduces safety concerns because additional doses can be administered to participants if one dose proves less efficacious, most incident infections will clear spontaneously, and development of cancers can be prevented by screening; it also minimizes the problem of misclassifying prevalent HPV infections as intervention failures. Analysis of patterns of serial serological titers in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) could support efficacy equivalence, identify thresholds of antibody concentrations that are protective, and provide an early alert about possible declines in efficacy. Innovative approaches for developing a noninferiority trial of one and two doses are needed (Table 1). Studying unvaccinated individuals of the same birth cohorts and geographic location as trial participants will allow for the estimation of absolute efficacy as well as relative efficacy by dose. In the event that HPV detection postvaccination proves vanishingly rare, noninferiority comparisons of one- and two-dose regimens will lack statistical power; comparisons with this representative, unvaccinated “control” group will become pivotal. Demonstrating a reduction in HPV infections (26) among recipients of one dose compared with an unvaccinated population could justify a public health strategy, which aims to deliver a single dose to as many girls as possible, with careful postimplementation surveillance to assess the need for revaccination. Revaccination of study participants would be required if vaccine failures develop as a function of reduced dosing. In addition, girls from the unvaccinated control group should be offered vaccination at study completion. Design of a noninferiority trial comparing one vs two doses of prophylactic HPV vaccines: challenges and potential solutions Design of a noninferiority trial comparing one vs two doses of prophylactic HPV vaccines: challenges and potential solutions If RCTs to evaluate efficacy of a single dose are successful, public health officials may have strong evidence to endorse universal single-dose coverage, with deferral of a second dose contingent upon evidence of breakthrough infections. Even if a single dose yields somewhat inferior efficacy to two doses, high single-dose coverage in a population may result in herd immunity, thereby extending protection to individuals who have not been fully protected by vaccination or remain unvaccinated. Achieving 20 years of vaccine protection with fewer doses should result in considerable reductions in cervical cancer incidence, even if immunity wanes in later years. Undoubtedly, the large RCTs required to test a one-dose approach will be expensive; however, the potential long-term cost savings and reductions in cancer incidence would justify the investment. If a single dose is effective, it could enable wider implementation of vaccines in poorer nations without effective screening, reducing costs, suffering, and mortality secondary to cervical cancer, and eliminate costs of cancer care; partial effectiveness could prompt a cost-benefit analysis that addresses conditions in a country. If a single dose proves ineffective, the results will provide strong impetus to carefully monitor vaccine coverage and outcomes in nations with existing programs using state-of-the-science approaches (such as the New Mexico HPV Pap Registry; 27) and to argue for investments to identify and complete vaccination among one-dose recipients, who represent a significant proportion (around 20%) of teenagers in the United States (28). This work was supported by the Intramural Research Program of the Division of Cancer Epidemiology and Genetics and the Division of Cancer Prevention of the National Cancer Institute, National Institutes of Health. We thank Drs. Douglas R. Lowy, John T. Schiller, Barnett S. Kramer, Allan Hildesheim, and Sholom Wacholder for their insights and comments on this work. The authors have no conflicts of interest to declare.

title: ED-Relevant Takeaways from the New AHA/ACC Hypertension Guideline
authors: Daniel Cotton; Brandon Page; Kegham Hawatian; Jacob Tuttle; William Grace; Joseph Miller
abstract: Figure 1: Condition-specific recommendations and blood pressure cutoffs provided by the AHA/ACC Hypertension Guideline.Abbreviations: AOI, acute organ injury; HBPM, home blood pressure monitoring.The latest American Heart Association (AHA)/American College of Cardiology (ACC) guideline on hypertension is applicable to emergency clinicians because it clarifies where acute treatment adds the most value for patients who present with markedly elevated BP. At a high level, the document emphasizes four themes: (1) get the measurement right; (2) separate hypertensive emergencies from severe but stable hypertension; (3) act decisively with intravenous therapy when acute target-organ injury is present; and (4) when it is not, initiate or intensify outpatient-style therapy, reinforce home monitoring, and hand off with a specific follow-up plan. These points support an emergency department (ED) practice pattern that improves safety, preserves critical care resources for those who truly need them, and meaningfully reduces long-term cardiovascular risk for most patients who arrive with uncontrolled BP but no evidence of acute organ damage.1 First, the guideline calls for accurate and reproducible measurement of BP as the foundation for any decision. In the ED, this means not relying solely on a single triage value when the clinical stakes are high. Although it may not always be viable for patients with high time-sensitivity cases, recommendations for an accurate BP measurement include using a validated device with an appropriate cuff size; positioning the patient seated with feet flat, back supported, and the arm supported at heart level; avoiding talking during the measurement; and allowing at least 5 minutes of rest beforehand. When these measures cannot be reasonably employed, clinicians should be aware that they may influence the BP reading. Moreover, multiple readings that are averaged may help distinguish a spurious value from a true measurement. If the patient takes antihypertensives at home, documentation of the timing of the last dose and the patient's usual BP pattern can help to distinguish a new increase in BP from chronically uncontrolled hypertension. The guideline's measurement standards are straightforward and, when followed, reduce misclassification that can lead to either unnecessary treatment or missed emergencies. Second, the ED decision point hinges on whether there is new or worsening target-organ injury. The guideline, unchanged from previous versions of the AHA/ACC, defines hypertensive emergency as systolic BP ≥180 mmHg and/or diastolic BP ≥120 mmHg in which acute target-organ damage is present. In these cases, such as acute aortic dissection, hypertensive encephalopathy, intracerebral hemorrhage, and acute coronary syndrome, immediate BP reduction with intravenous agents and continuous monitoring is required, and oral agents are not appropriate for this initial phase of management. Conversely, severe asymptomatic hypertension (sometimes referred to as a “hypertensive urgency”) lacks acute organ injury and does not usually require hospital admission or rapid IV BP lowering. In such cases, the guideline favors restarting or intensifying chronic therapy while addressing anxiety and adherence barriers and arranging prompt follow-up, rather than reflexively hospitalizing the patient.1 The AHA/ACC guideline also offers condition-specific BP targets and treatment algorithms including disposition recommendations (Figure 1). When no acute organ injury is identified, emergency providers still have an important therapeutic role. In many patients with stage 2 hypertension, defined as systolic BP ≥140 mmHg and/or diastolic BP ≥90 mmHg, the guidelines support starting two antihypertensive agents from different classes and arranging follow-up at approximately 1 month. Patients with stage 1 hypertension and a 10-year atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk of 10% or higher should also begin medication alongside lifestyle therapy with a similar 1-month follow-up cadence. For those with elevated BP or low-risk stage 1 hypertension, lifestyle modification with repeat assessment in 3-6 months is appropriate. A particular group relevant to ED physicians consists of patients with very high average BP, often defined in practice as systolic ≥180 mmHg or diastolic ≥110 mmHg, who are asymptomatic. They warrant evaluation and prompt initiation or intensification of therapy rather than passive deferral. Selecting once-daily medications facilitates adherence, and using fixed-dose combinations (eg, an Angiotensin-Covering Enzyme (ACE) inhibitor or ARB paired with a thiazide diuretic, or a calcium-channel blocker paired with an ACE inhibitor) is an effective strategy to reach targets with fewer pills and simpler instructions. Targets remain clear: for most healthy adults, the goal is <130/80 mmHg. This goal is more important for those with established cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, heart failure, stable ischemic heart disease, or peripheral artery disease; diseases that are common among ED patients. The guideline advises monthly reassessment after starting or adjusting medications until control is achieved. Discharge instructions that include an explicit follow-up time frame and a responsible clinic or provider measurably improve adherence to this monthly cadence. Embedding electronic “warm handoffs” (eg, scheduling the appointment before discharge or sending an electronic referral with pertinent ED notes and the exact regimen) can bridge the otherwise vulnerable transition between acute and longitudinal care. Although not commonly prescribed by ED physicians, home BP monitoring and ambulatory BP monitoring are the new norm for follow-up BP measurements. When available, accessing these measurements through electronic medical records or directly through the patient provides a more reliable baseline BP measure and a picture of the patient's usual BP patterns.Figure 2: Stepwise algorithm for treating patients with hypertension in the emergency department.Team-based care and technology-enabled follow-up are emphasized in the guidelines. Pharmacist-led medication management, nursing protocols for BP education and cuff use, social work support for medication access, and community health workers to reinforce home blood pressure monitoring (HBPM) can all be built into local pathways. From the ED vantage point, it is reasonable to deploy standardized order sets that (1) select a once-daily, guideline-concordant starter regimen; (2) print or send HBPM instructions; and (3) route the patient to a hypertension clinic or primary care visit within 1 month. Some systems also loan digital cuffs or enroll qualifying patients in remote BP monitoring programs at discharge; the new guideline supports these approaches as part of a comprehensive strategy to raise the proportion of adults who achieve goal BP. A practical way to operationalize the document's advice in the ED is to use a simple three-step workflow. Step 1 is to confirm the numbers with good technique and to recheck a second time. This protects against undertreatment of true emergencies and overtreatment of transient, falsely high values. Step 2 is to screen purposefully for target-organ complications such as focal neurologic deficit, chest pain, dyspnea with hypoxia or pulmonary edema, new kidney injury, tearing chest or back pain, visual disturbance in pregnancy, which would prompt treatment of confirmed hypertensive emergency with intravenous agents utilizing disease-specific targets. Step 3, after ensuring the absence of hypertensive emergency or at hospital discharge, is to start or intensify once-daily oral therapy, provide HBPM instructions, prescribe lifestyle measures with concrete goals such as a Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) eating plan, sodium reduction, physical activity, weight loss where appropriate, and moderation of alcohol), and lock in a 1-month follow-up. Each of these steps is supported by recommendations and tools in the new guideline and can be implemented without slowing ED throughput (Figure 2). Several clinical nuances deserve emphasis. Patients who arrive anxious, in pain, or after exertion may have transient BP elevations; repeating the measurement after analgesia, anxiolysis, or a period of rest can prevent over-classification. In pregnancy, early involvement of obstetrics and the avoidance of ACE inhibitors and ARBs are key. For suspected aortic disease, initiating beta-blockade prior to vasodilation prevents reflex tachycardia and reduces wall stress. And for intracranial emergencies, avoid aggressive overshoot: the goal is to bring BP quickly to a safe level, not to normalize it in minutes. Ultimately, the message of the new AHA/ACC guideline for emergency medicine is both pragmatic and empowering. Ensure treatment of true hypertensive emergencies by using intravenous therapy with condition-specific targets and continuous monitoring. Do not overtreat severe but asymptomatic hypertension; but instead restart or intensify chronic therapy, remove barriers to adherence, and avoid reflexive admissions. ED providers should feel empowered to own the first move when anticipating discharge: start once-daily, guideline-concordant therapy (often 2 agents for stage 2), and ensure timely follow-up. The global goal is a BP <130/80 mmHg where indicated, ideally reached in the outpatient setting, supported by ambulatory BP monitoring and team-based care. Implemented consistently, this approach aligns ED practice with high-quality evidence, prioritizes patient safety, and measurably improves long-term cardiovascular outcomes for patients who present with uncontrolled BP.

title: The Cognitive Terrain - Module 1 v2.0 of the Orchard Cognitive Architecture: Substrate Geometry, Typed Null Manifold, and Axis Governance
authors: KIMBERLEY LAVERNE ASHER
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: ## Abstract We present Module 1 v2.0 of the Orchard Cognitive Architecture: the substrate-level specification of cognitive terrain, integrating the typed null manifold of Module 1 v1.0, the axis-governance machinery of ROSA v1.0, and the cognitive-physics framing of v0.1 into a single substrate-level paper. The architectural commitment is that the substrate of a cognitive system is not inert scaffolding but a structured medium with local physical laws — a *cognitive terrain* through which thought moves the way water moves through topography. Under this framing, the substrate is specified as a tuple including a manifold, a Central Reference Point, an axis registry with provenance and lifecycle metadata, a typed null manifold organised into seven operational families by lawful-action topology, a trait field specifying local cognitive-physics conditions, a history field recording lifecycle events, and a local law set deriving cognitive-operation permissions from family identity and trait values. The Primary Supremacy Invariant — that hard rules from family identity cannot be relaxed by aggregation of trait values — operates as the substrate-level conservation law preventing trait-laundering and scalar collapse. Two new substrate-level invariants are specified beyond v1.0 and ROSA: Uniform Law Derivation (the law-set derivation rule is uniform across all substrate points; special cases are forbidden because they create non-uniform safety surfaces) and Neighbourhood Locality of Boundary Law (the local law set at a point depends on local terrain features at the point and in its immediate neighbourhood; point-local law derivation is insufficient for boundary handling). Three empirical anchors support the substrate's commitments. Phase 1b destructive interpolation testing demonstrates that conventional smoothing methods destroy negative-space integrity in proportion to their sophistication, with Gaussian RBF (the most sophisticated standard method) producing the highest pit-interior reconstruction error. Section 13 typed-null action selection testing demonstrates that scalar and binary-null treatments produce 0% lawful-action accuracy on Governance and Structural families (always selecting "interpolate," which is an active safety violation on forbidden cells), while typed-null treatment achieves 99.77% accuracy with zero cross-family errors and perfect classification on Governance (54 of 54) and Structural (288 of 288) cells. Test 1B v0.1 cognitive-physics minimal-metadata testing demonstrates that the family-first/traits-second discipline produces zero critical failures across five seeds with 145 tracers per seed, while adversarial baselines implementing trait-laundering or unconditional metadata-trust produce critical failures in 5 of 5 runs. The substrate's working hypotheses are stated at the level of commitment whose failure would force architectural revision rather than incremental patching. Five working hypotheses carry forward and are extended: the geometric tractability of cognition, the single Central Reference Point, the typing of null states, the local-law cognitive-physics framing, and the Recursive Fabric Echo Principle. The trait formalism is held at candidate status pending broader empirical refinement; the cognitive-physics framing is adopted as the most productive current specification language for the substrate without claim to comprehensive empirical validation. Cross-substrate testing through the Phase E programme is the appropriate vehicle for further validation. The contribution of v2.0 is the integration. Module 1 v1.0 specified a typed-null manifold with axis spawning deferred. ROSA v1.0 filled the deferral with a substantial governance layer. Cognitive Physics v0.1 reframed both as terrain physics. The recognition that all three were specifying a single substrate-level commitment, in three vocabularies, motivates this integrated paper. --- ## 1. Introduction: The Substrate Question ### 1.1 What Kind of Medium Cognition Requires The substrate of a cognitive architecture is the foundational layer on which all higher cognitive operations occur. Every cognitive operation — recognition, inference, composition, decision, recall — happens *somewhere*, in some structured medium that supports and constrains what those operations can do. The choice of substrate is therefore not a low-level engineering detail; it is a determination of what the architecture can perceive, what it can preserve, what it can grow, and what kinds of cognition it can support. Conventional cognitive architectures inherit their substrate from the representational choices of their builders. A neural network's substrate is high-dimensional vector space with fixed dimensionality. A symbolic system's substrate is a structured graph or tree of typed objects. A connectionist hybrid is some negotiated compromise. In each case, the substrate is treated as scaffolding — a passive container in which representational work occurs, but not itself part of the cognitive object under study. The Orchard Cognitive Architecture's foundational claim is that this treatment is wrong, and wrong at the substrate level. The substrate is itself part of the cognitive object. Its geometry, its handling of absence, its accommodation of representational growth, and the laws governing what cognitive motions it permits are not implementation details that fall away once cognition is up and running. They are constitutive of what kinds of cognition can occur on the substrate at all. This document specifies the Orchard substrate at v2.0. The specification is the integration of three previously-articulated threads: The first thread is the substrate's *geometry*: a manifold with a singular Central Reference Point as architectural origin, axes as directed dimensions of the manifold relative to the origin, and geodetic transformation packages allowing every spawned axis to be referred back to the origin without information loss exceeding bounded $\epsilon$. This thread was the substantive content of Module 1 v1.0. The second thread is the substrate's *handling of absence*: a typed null manifold organised into operational families by the lawful next action each null state demands, replacing the conventional scalar collapse of all absences into a single null/zero/missing marker. This thread, also formalised in Module 1 v1.0 (extending architectural perception developed by the first author since the mid-1990s), has empirical anchoring through the Section 11 destructive interpolation results and the Section 13 typed-null action selection results. The third thread is the substrate's *governance of representational growth*: the lifecycle of axes, the torsion-driven mechanics of spawning, the discipline of re-expression before introducing new representational dimensions, the protection of identity-adjacent and load-bearing axes from inappropriate edits. This thread was the substantive content of ROSA v1.0. These three threads have, until now, been articulated in three distinct documents using three distinct vocabularies. The first author's geometric perception held them as a single architectural commitment; the formalisation produced separate papers because the work was done across separate sessions and substrates, and because the integration vocabulary had not yet crystallised. The cognitive-physics framing, articulated in Cognitive Physics v0.1 (4 May 2026), is the integration vocabulary that allows the three threads to be specified as a single substrate-level commitment. Under this framing, the substrate is most accurately understood as a *cognitive terrain* — a structured medium with local physical laws, through which cognition moves the way water moves through topography. The geometry thread becomes terrain shape. The typed-null thread becomes terrain composition. The axis-governance thread becomes terrain evolution: the laws under which the terrain itself grows, changes, and preserves its commutability across edits. This document adopts the cognitive-physics framing as the most productive current specification language for the substrate. It does not assert cognitive physics as an established research field; it adopts the framing because the framing organises material that was previously distributed across three documents into a single coherent specification, makes new substrate-level commitments specifiable that were difficult to articulate before, and connects the substrate's empirical anchoring to the architectural claims it supports. Whether cognitive physics matures into a research programme is a question for Phase E and beyond. What this document commits to is using the framing to specify what the Orchard substrate is. ### 1.2 The Two Failures of Conventional Substrates Two failures of conventional substrates motivate the architecture this document specifies. The first failure is *substrate inertness*. A substrate whose geometry is fixed in advance cannot grow with the system's representational needs. A neural network can learn new representations within its fixed dimensionality but cannot meaningfully spawn new dimensions when its existing axes are insufficient to resolve a relational distinction. A symbolic system can add new types but cannot relocate existing types in a coherent geometric whole. The substrate's expressive ceiling is set by its initial design; representational capacity beyond that ceiling requires architectural changes outside the substrate itself. This failure produces two characteristic pathologies. *Forced categorisation* occurs when the system encounters phenomena that do not fit existing axes and is forced to smooth them into the closest available category, destroying genuine novelty. *Runaway proliferation* occurs when the system is permitted to spawn whenever pressed and accumulates so many axes that no two patterns share enough common axis structure to be meaningfully comparable.
