title: Impasses of the Nation: The Practical Political Philosophy of Marcel Mauss
authors: Rosalind C. Morris
abstract: The nation is an enigmatic phenomenon, explains Marcel Mauss in his draft notes for the never-completed book, La Nation.1 It is a rare and recently emergent political form, he asserts, but it is preceded by the experience of nationality and the practices of international— or, as he prefers to term them, intersocial (and perhaps more properly named intersocietal) relations. It is a medium for administering a nationalized economy but something other than the state. It is a product of integration, but it is also defined by a tendency to individuation, separation, and even isolation. It is characterized by the recession of intermediary political institutions such as the clan and the tribe, but also by the generalization of an increasingly totalizing technical mediation, one that exceeds the nation while conditioning its possibility. As a corollary, the nation is a form in which individuals are linked to each other as subjects in an apparently immediate relation to a self-consciously apprehended object. It is also distinguished by a tendency among its members to mischaracterize as origin what is co-emergent with its own appearance. It is an agency of warfare and the medium of its suspension. It is more than an ethnos, other than the state, at once emergent and still to come.The objective historical contradictions of the nation proliferate in seeming proportion to its function as regulative ideal. Such is the enigma of the nation for Marcel Mauss. That the book in which these propositions were made was never completed may be a result of the impasses to which his reflections repeatedly led, and which, in the end, he could only resolve in a displaced mode, by an analysis not of the modern nation but of the “archaic” institution of the gift. The impasses were also practical and political, and they can be understood in terms of the context in which he wrote: the immediate post-World War I era, in which the attempt to generate an apparatus of international peace and reconciliation—via reparations and principles administered by international legal institutions—floundered as working-class nationalism and cosmopolitan capitalism allied against the more equitable ambitions of the radical socialist and cooperativist movements to which Mauss was himself deeply committed. In the opening (and earliest written) sections of La Nation, Mauss outlines his project in relatively simple terms. He commences by acknowledging that the problems of individualism and the antinomy between the nation and the state have been well analyzed by political theorists, and practically resolved in the overthrow of tyrannies and the establishment of civil society. This leaves the matter of relations between antagonistic groups within and among nations, the analysis of which Mauss hoped could enable an avoidance of war and especially of the total sort exemplified by World War I. Finally, there is the aspiration to realize the potential of the nation, in particular the French nation. Here, Mauss proposes to consider socializing and nationalizing tendencies through which nations could become in practice what they are in ideality: “masters of their economy” comprised of “natural title: In Search of Bunny Burgess, or Down the Rabbit Hole: Anecdotes, Secret Histories, and The Great Gatsby
authors: Sarah Churchwell
abstract: Anecdote: Something yet unpublished; secret history. – Samuel Johnson, A Dictionary of the English Language WhenThe Great Gatsbywaspublished in 1925, H. L. Mencken famously declared that it was ‘in form no more than a glorified anecdote’.1 This story is obviously unimportant … What ails it, fundamentally, is the plain fact that it is simply a story. … The story, for all its basic triviality, has a fine texture, a careful and brilliant finish. … ‘The Great Gatsby’, [is] a far inferior story at bottom … Fitzgerald, the stylist, arises to challenge Fitzgerald, the social historian, but I doubt that the latter ever quite succumbs to the former. The thing that chiefly interests the basic Fitzgerald is still the florid show of modern American life – and especially the devil’s dance that goes on at the top. … Their idiotic pursuit of sensation, their almost incredible stupidity and triviality, their glittering swinishness – these are the things that go into his notebook.2 What makes Gatsby an anecdote, for Mencken, is that it is ‘simply a story’, a ‘story [that] is obviously unimportant’, a story of ‘basic triviality’, ‘a far inferior story’. This repetitive assertion is not a definition, of course, but a tautology. The charge of anecdotalism also implicitly relates, for Mencken, to the novel’s function as social history, a contemporary record of ‘the devil’s dance’ of the jazz-age rich on Long Island. The triviality of the (real) people being evoked converges in Mencken’s judgement with the triviality of the story depicting them. He does not mention the novel’s brevity, only what he sees as its flimsiness: this is what makes it no more than an anecdote. But Mencken also suggests that its anecdotalism bears a tacit relation to notebooks, although whether he is calling Gatsby itself a notebook or merely supposing that it transcribes Fitzgerald’s own notebook documenting what he saw around him is unclear. Either way, the charge of anecdotalism is related to the idea of reportage, to a cultural hierarchy that values (what it recognises as legitimate) aesthetic forms over historiographical notebooks. The anecdote sits uncertainly somewhere between gossip and story, between history and art, its potential for meaning still contested. The question of what exactly distinguishes an anecdote from a story ‘proper’ remains an open one, with definitions tending to conflate qualitative and quantitative distinctions, so that an anecdote’s brevity is related to its insubstantiality, but also to its lack of immanent or transferable meaning.3 For Dr Johnson, an anecdote was first something ‘yet unpublished’, and second a ‘secret history’. The OED gives priority to this meaning (‘1. pl. Secret, private, or hitherto unpublished narratives or details of history’) before offering a more familiar definition: ‘2.a. The narrative of a detached incident, or of a single event, told as being in itself interesting or striking. (At first, an item of gossip.)’ Detachment as discontinuity is what differentiates the anecdote from other types of storytelling: the more attached or continuous it becomes, the less it is anecdotal. Anecdotalism is thus relative, not categorical; and its history associates it with gossip. This essay follows the trail of an anecdote that intersects with the formation of The Great Gatsby, the (re)construction of which may provide some insight into the role gossip and anecdote played in that formation. The story here traced is an anecdote in the Johnsonian sense of an unpublished, secret history, a hunt for a forgotten story to which Fitzgerald returned again and again in his memories of the production of Gatsby, an anecdote that refers to a man called Bunny Burgess. Pursuing the traces of this lost anecdote creates a trail that shows where problems of form converge with problems of intention, which is also where the textual comes up against the biographical. In the case of a novel like Gatsby, pursuing an anecdote associated with its origins invokes not only its social-historical meanings, but also its formal choices: brevity as a conscious withholding, resistance to epistemological certainty, elusiveness and fragmentation, refusal of plenitude, and deferral of meaning. Fitzgerald wrote to Mencken the day after his review appeared, explicitly defending his novel’s form against charges of anecdotalism: ‘the influence on [Gatsby] has been the masculine one of The Brothers Karamazov, a thing of incomparable form, rather than the feminine one of The Portrait of a Lady. If it seems trivial or “anecdotal” it is because of an aesthetic fault, a failure in one very important episode and not a frailty in the theme’.4 Having invoked the strong ‘masculinity’ of a fictive work of ‘incomparable form’ to defend his novel against charges of anecdotal ‘frailty’, Fitzgerald went on to write a much more exasperated letter to his friend Edmund Wilson, also invoking Karamazov to complain that no one, including Mencken, understood the actual meanings of Gatsby: Without making any invidious comparisons between Class A and Class C, if my novel is an anecdote so is The Brothers Karamazov. From one angle the latter could be reduced into a detective story. … Of all the reviews, even the most enthusiastic, not one had the slightest idea what the book was about.5 For Fitzgerald, the difference between art and anecdote is qualitative: if his novel seemed trivial, it was because of an aesthetic failure, not because its theme was ‘frail’. title: News and Community Behind Barbed Wire: The Topaz Times and Japanese American Incarceration in Utah
authors: Glen Feighery
abstract: On a Thursday in March 1943, Masaomi Yano sat at a table, head bowed as he made a stencil for a mimeograph machine. The twenty-five-year-old California native was translating English-language articles into Japanese for the bilingual newspaper he worked for. Like a typical small-town paper, it included items about a new golf course, sewing classes, and a bridge tournament, as well as a funeral announcement. The newspaper's readers didn't live in a typical community, however. They were confined at the Central Utah Relocation Project, better known as the Topaz internment (incarceration) camp, during World War II.Topaz was one of ten such camps, with others in California, Arizona, Idaho, Wyoming, Colorado, and Arkansas. They held 120,000 people of Japanese descent who had been removed from the West Coast after the attack on Pearl Harbor. Facing political and military pressure, President Franklin Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066, authorizing the mass evacuation of people—two-thirds of them US citizens—who had violated no laws. Between March and May 1942, Japanese immigrants (Issei) and second-generation Japanese Americans (Nisei) were forced from their homes and placed in crude temporary “assembly centers,” often fairgrounds or racetracks. Between May and October 1942, evacuees were moved to the ten semi-permanent relocation camps, where most remained throughout the war.1The Topaz camp occupied one square mile in the Sevier Desert of Millard County, sixteen miles northwest of Delta, near the tiny settlement of Abraham.2 Topaz was divided into dozens of blocks with military-style barracks, latrines, mess halls, and laundries. Living accommodations were spartan: Each barrack was divided into small “apartments,” bare rooms with a window, wood stove, and light bulb suspended from the ceiling. At its peak, the camp held 8,130 people, who worked as cooks, teachers, nurses, and firefighters and did most other jobs of running the community. People also attended church, played in sports leagues, gave music recitals, and read their local newspaper, the Topaz Times. This population was Utah's fifth-largest city at the time, a city behind barbed wire and watched by Army guards.3At the eightieth anniversary of Topaz's closure, this essay focuses on the intersection of Utah history and journalism history. It shows that Topaz functioned as a community in part because of the Topaz Times. Journalism historian David Paul Nord, who studied the connections between newspapers and the people they served, defined community as “common experience and sympathy, and a deep sense of interdependence,” as well as an “organized, common frame of reference” so people could “share a vision of social reality.”4 Newspapers accomplished this in two ways, Nord believed. They provided information to establish an “authority of facts” and served as a forum for debate and civic participation.5 Debate implied disagreement, which Nord portrayed as a hallmark of American democracy, because “to argue about the state was to be a member of the nation.”6This essay examines how the Times reported and commented on five episodes: setting up camp, the so-called loyalty oath, the killing of a resident by a guard, the military draft, and closing the camp. Through its coverage, the paper helped readers to identify as members of a discrete community, not just people thrown together by circumstance. It provided information, reflected Topaz's variety of voices, and bore witness to trauma. Also, as a Utah newspaper that published 438 issues between September 17, 1942, and August 31, 1945, the Times is worth consideration in its own right as a noteworthy publication in the history of the state.7In telling this history, it is important to consider language. Historian Roger Daniels objected to terms such as “internment” and “relocation,” calling them government euphemisms intended to obscure the lack of legal process. He noted that “incarcerated people themselves sometimes used the term concentration camp while they were in confinement.” Others agreed.8 Author Yoshiko Uchida concluded that “the ‘relocation centers’ are properly called concentration camps. The term is used not to imply any similarity to the Nazi death camps, but to indicate [their] true nature.”9 Utah historian Sandra C. Taylor argued that Topaz was “an armed concentration camp,” or at best, “a concentration camp with a human face.”10 However, many historians have adopted terms closer to those employed by the National Park Service and the Commission on Wartime Relocation and Internment of Civilians, using words such as “incarceration” and “prison camp” synonymously with “internment” and “relocation camp.”11 This essay follows a similar practice.Japanese American internment has been the subject of vast study. Daniels was the preeminent historian, portraying relocation as the result of racism and virulent nationalism fueled by resentment of Japanese Americans’ economic success. Like the other camps, Topaz was constructed in a remote location “where no one had lived before and no one has lived since,” Daniels observed. “The barbed-wire fences, the guards, and the surrounding wasteland were always there to remind the detainees that they were exiled, incarcerated Americans.”12 Authors Audrie Girdner and Anne Loftis also emphasized racial motivations. “In the West Coast hysteria that led to the evacuation, the Japanese, both aliens and citizens, were lumped together in a general racial indictment.”13 As will be seen, citizenship figured prominently in events the Topaz Times covered.Numerous historians have documented internment in Utah, beginning with Leonard J. Arrington. His comprehensive overview mentioned the harshness of the Topaz site, especially “the wind” and “seldom interrupted whirl of dust,” which turned to “gummy muck” after rain or snow. Arrington portrayed the Topaz Times as integral to community life, as it was “produced by evacuee staffs with a minimum of supervision and no overt exercise of censorship.”14 Uchida, who was incarcerated at Topaz with her parents and sister, described “an artificial government-spawned community on the periphery of the real world.” The alkaline dust was daunting, and she did not appreciate a Times item that told new arrivals they were “Residents, not Evacuees,” who should adopt a healthy “Mental Climate”—exhortations she found “patronizing.”15 A history of Millard County also dubbed Topaz an “artificial community” and remarked that Army recruitment was a “cause of serious unrest among the evacuees.”16 Allan Kent Powell situated Topaz in the context of Utah's role during World War II. The state was critical strategically and logistically, and importing more than eight thousand Japanese Americans added to racial tensions.17Taylor, a University of Utah historian, depicted the makeshift conditions, including that the camp was unfinished as people arrived. Built from pine boards and tar paper, structures had no insulation and “some barracks even lacked roofs,” she noted. Most people at Topaz were from Northern California, and “to people whose homes had been in the moist, green Bay Area, central Utah was a shock,” Taylor wrote.18 Social relations were also disrupted. “The breakdown in family life and the virtual disappearance of the individual home was devastating to women,” she found.19 As people were released, those settling in Utah were often unwelcome, even though the state lay well outside the West Coast exclusion zone.20 Taylor constructed her narratives from the extensive archives of the War Relocation Authority (WRA), oral history interviews with former residents, and issues of the Topaz Times. Taylor was somewhat dubious of the Times, asserting that it “cheerfully recorded” routine events but lacked a strong editorial voice. Still, she said, the newspaper was an “important institution in camp.”21Historians Linda L. Ivey and Kevin W. Kaatz also found that the Topaz Times was important to community life. News articles “detailed housing issues . . . and noted that it was particularly difficult to provide shelter and bedding for the new arrivals.”22 Topaz Museum founder Jane Beckwith explained the connections between Delta and Topaz. Her grandfather Frank A. Beckwith had close ties to the camp. He contributed articles to the Topaz literary journal TREK, and he hosted visiting Topaz Times staffers at the Millard County Chronicle. Beckwith's father hired a young man from the camp to help produce the Chronicle, which often reprinted news from the Times.23Topaz is often mentioned in internment histories because of the prominent people who were there, and curator Kenneth Hartvigsen chronicled the work of perhaps the most famous, artist Miné Okubo. Drawing from her 1946 graphic memoir Citizen 13660, Hartvigsen explored how Okubo used her art to “create a sense of control through creative action.” Internment was a “complicated and sometimes contradictory reality,” and she responded with “a truly radical text” that explored “the complex experience of trauma.”24 Okubo also created illustrations for the Topaz Times during its early life.25Much of the historical record about Topaz has been preserved in personal memoirs, oral histories, and the WRA archives. The Topaz Times is another primary source, often incorporated into secondary research. Histories of camp journalism have emphasized the lack of press freedom because the papers were published under WRA control.26 The most prolific scholar of camp newspapers, Takeya Mizuno, concluded title: Task-free continual learning with expansion-based granular CNN: Gradual partitioning of manifolds in image stream classification
authors: Leite, Daniel
abstract: This paper introduces an Expansion-based Granular Convolutional Neural Network (EG-CNN) framework for task-free continual learning in both domain-incremental (Domain-IL) and class-incremental (Class-IL) classification of image streams. EG-CNN comprises three components – a feature extractor, a refiner, and a granular classifier – each capable of independent adaptation over time. Unlike replay-based, regularization-based, or task-specific expansion methods that rely on task identifiers, multiple classifier heads, or episodic memory buffers, EG-CNN evolves a single classifier from scratch throughout lifelong learning, with no access to task boundaries or stored images. This design directly targets severe nonstationarity by addressing concept drift, class emergence, and inter-class interference through structural evolution rather than memory or task supervision. Guided dimensionality reduction is performed through geodesic and spectral refiners based on variants of Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) and direct incremental Linear Discriminant Analysis (iLDA), informed by a Levina-Bickel maximum likelihood estimator of intrinsic manifold dimensionality. These refiners generate latent bottleneck representations, allowing a compact and interpretable Evolving Granular Neural Network classifier (EGNN-C 2 +) to be incrementally built at the CNN top. The framework supports gradual partitioning of the sufficient manifold, dynamic information fusion, dynamic deferral for uncertainty handling, and structural plasticity without catastrophic forgetting. Experiments in three streaming scenarios – nonstationary object recognition with CIFAR-10 (Domain-IL), scene recognition with missing classes in Intel-6 (Class-IL under stream-induced drift), and large-scale scene understanding with SUN-397 (Class-IL under compounded domain drift with 397 classes) – demonstrate stable structural evolution and sustained accuracy under increasing levels of novelty and nonstationarity. © 2026 The Author(s)

title: MS-UA-Swin: An Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Scale Swin Transformer for Reliable Skin Cancer Detection
authors: Sumon, Salauddin Ahammed; Rahman, Md. Mahbubur; Hasan, Mahbub; Robin, Tanvir Islam; Ahmed, Toukir; Rahaman, Md Atikqur; Bepery, Chinmay; Amaline, Azrul; Rahman, Maksudor
venue: 2026 International Conference on Power, Electronics, Communications, Computing, and Intelligent Infrastructure, PECCII 2026
abstract: Skin cancer screening necessitates not only exceptional diagnostic accuracy but also robust confidence estimations that can facilitate the deferral of ambiguous cases. We introduce MS-UA-Swin, a multi-scale Swin Transformer that is attuned to uncertainty for the binary classification of skin cancer (malignant versus benign). This methodology integrates hierarchical representations derived from four distinct Swin stages through attention-guided aggregation and assesses predictive uncertainty by employing Monte Carlo dropout alongside numerous stochastic forward passes. In the context of the ISIC 2019 dataset, MS-UA-Swin attains a test ROC-AUC of 0.9474 and an average precision of 0.9142. Through the implementation of uncertainty-based selective prediction, accuracy enhances from 0.8798 (without rejection) to 0.9300 upon the rejection of the 20% most uncertain cases, and further to 0.9527 with a 30% rejection rate. For the purpose of interpretability, we present gradient-based saliency maps and assess the faithfulness of explanations utilizing perturbation-based deletion tests. The findings suggest that multi-scale fusion coupled with uncertainty-aware decision support can significantly enhance both performance and reliability within clinical screening workflows. © 2026 IEEE.

title: RC-MDNet: Risk-Controlled Malicious Domain Detection for Open-World Network Security
authors: Jing, Yuning
abstract: Open-world Internet traffic routinely violates the i.i.d. assumption, causing malicious domain detectors to become overconfident on out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs and to incur costly false alarms or misses. We introduce RC-MDNet, a risk-controlled framework that couples (i) post-hoc probability calibration via temperature scaling, (ii) a dual-threshold uncertainty-aware selective predictor that trades coverage for reliability, and (iii) conformal prediction (overall and class-conditional) to furnish distribution-free risk guarantees. Using a lightweight character-level BiLSTM backbone, we evaluate across internal splits (Random, Apex, Cold-start, TLD-holdout) and external zero-shot corpora. RC-MDNet maintains high utility while reducing effective error through abstention, achieving near-target automatic accuracy (Auto-F1 ≥0.995) with tunable coverage and certified risk. Robustness studies under character-level perturbations (InsDel, CharRep, Homoglyph) show stable performance, and ablations confirm the importance of calibration and the double-threshold design, while class-conditional conformal control supports asymmetric cost preferences relevant to security operations. Overall, RC-MDNet delivers graceful degradation and interpretable, deployment-grade reliability under shift, offering a practical path to risk-aware DNS threat detection. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026.

title: Confidence-aware semantic–numerical fusion via selective prediction for mutual fund style classification
authors: Wang, Xu; Hu, Kehan; Peng, Jiamin; Xu, Sichuang; Chen, Junyang
abstract: Accurate mutual fund style classification is essential for portfolio analysis and investment decision-making. Existing methods mainly rely on numerical indicators and often overlook semantic information from stock-level analysis. We propose a confidence-aware semantic–numerical fusion framework that integrates a Large Language Model (LLM) with a Support Vector Machine (SVM) using quarterly top-ten holdings. The LLM generates structured stock-level descriptions of volatility, Beta, Average True Range, financial fluctuations, and stock type. These descriptions are encoded by BERT and combined with weight-normalized numerical features to form fund-quarter representations. Prediction fusion is formulated as a sample-wise selective prediction problem, in which a confidence-guided strategy adaptively selects between the LLM and SVM outputs. Theoretical analysis shows that reducing confidence-ordering errors enables the fused predictor to approach an oracle selector. Experiments on Chinese mutual fund data from 2023–2024 show that the framework consistently outperforms standalone LLMs and representative machine-learning baselines in weighted F1-score. Ablation studies and qualitative cases further demonstrate the complementary value of semantic and numerical information. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. All rights are reserved, including those for text and data mining, AI training, and similar technologies.

title: Joint prediction and classification within a single multitask architecture for early fault diagnosis in chemical processes
authors: Chrysler J., Djogap F.; Chioua, Moncef
abstract: Accurate and early fault diagnosis in chemical processes is critical to prevent abnormal situations from escalating, yet most data-driven fault detection and diagnosis (FDD) methods are inherently reactive: they require long sequences of post-fault data before a fault signature becomes identifiable. This paper proposes the Five-Stage Cascade (FSC), a single Transformer model that learns multistep process prediction and fault classification together, so that the prediction is trained to expose the deviations that distinguish the faults. Early diagnosis is measured with an onset protocol: each model sees only the first samples recorded after the fault. On the Tennessee Eastman Process, against nine baselines tuned with the same budget, the prediction branch improves the diagnosis at all tested detection times. One hour after the fault, it reduces confident wrong fault labels from eleven to one and false alarms from four to zero, converting unsafe misdiagnoses into safe deferrals in which an emerging fault is still labeled nominal. The internal prediction is more accurate than a persistence baseline at every horizon and, combined with a causal map of the process, gives early fault propagation paths that point to the physical root cause of each fault about half an hour before the measurements confirm it. A SHAP analysis shows that the gain comes from the representations shared between the two tasks rather than from the predicted values read as extra input. © 2026 The Authors. Published by Elsevier Ltd. This is an open access article under the CC BY-NC-ND license. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/

title: Uncertainty-Aware Selective Prediction of Neovascular Age-Related Macular Degeneration Recurrence Using Artificial Intelligence
authors: Yoon, Won Tae; Kim, Hun-Gyeom; Moon, Junhyung; Ngo, Dat; Kim, Jae Hui; Cho, Baek Hwan
abstract: Neovascular age-related macular degeneration (nAMD) is a progressive, sight-threatening disease predominantly affecting older adults and a leading cause of global vision loss projected to rise with aging populations. Although existing artificial intelligence (AI) studies have investigated nAMD recurrence detection, predictive modeling remains underexplored, with limited performance in a few studies relying on a single type of retinal image. Therefore, we aimed to comprehensively explore AI-based recurrence prediction incorporating multiple types of retinal images and clinical data. We collected retinal photographs and clinical data from 399 nAMD patients. The retinal photographs are six images, comprising fundus photographs and optical coherence tomography (OCT) horizontal/vertical scans taken both before and after treatment. The clinical data includes demographic information, such as age, sex and medication type. Using our collected dataset, we proposed an uncertainty-aware selective-prediction model for nAMD recurrence. The proposed model, built on popular CNN architectures, filters out highly uncertain predictions to enhance reliability of the recurrence prediction. Results showed that OCT horizontal post-treatment images achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.662, which increased to 0.836 with Monte Carlo (MC) dropout by excluding uncertain predictions, while the double-threshold method yielded an AUC of 0.744. Incorporating clinical parameters further improved performance, raising the AUC to 0.855, and drug-specific modeling produced particularly high predictive performance, with AUCs of 0.934 for ranibizumab and 0.978 for aflibercept. Our experimental results highlight the potential of AI-based multimodal modeling, selective prediction, and treatment-specific analysis in improving prognostic prediction and guiding therapeutic decision-making for patients with nAMD. © 2013 IEEE.

title: Evaluating and Mitigating Bias in Loan Approval Systems: A Multi-Model Empirical Study Using Fairness Metrics and Post-Processing Techniques
authors: Asif, Ashikur Rahman; Oitizzo, Homayra Zohor; Sharif, Shekh Tanjil; Hossain, Md. Raihan; Syed, Lamia; Rahman, Rakibur; Hasan, Md Rokibol
venue: 2026 IEEE 2nd International Conference on Quantum Photonics, Artificial Intelligence and Networking, QPAIN 2026
abstract: Though automated loan approval systems based on machine learning offer effective results, can turn up demographic bias inherent in historical data. This study is a fairness-aware evaluation framework which works for binary loan approval that examines predictive performance, algorithmic fairness, and model explainability. Four classifiers - Random Forest, XGBoost, Logistic Regression, and Support Vector Machine are used under a unified experimental system. Fairness is evaluated using Desperate Impact, Statistical Parity Difference, and Equal Opportunity Difference. Bias mitigation is analyzed through both in-processing and post-processing using Reject Option Classification. SHAP AND LIME provided interpretability. Experimental results show that model training can escalate bias, whereas post-processing with Reject Option Classification effectively improves fairness with a modest accuracy trade-off. The findings emphasize the importance of integrating fairness considerations into automated credit decision systems. © 2026 IEEE.

title: Causal evidence that language models use confidence to drive behaviour
authors: Kumaran, Dharshan; Daw, Nathaniel; Osindero, Simon; Veličković, Petar; Patraucean, Viorica
abstract: Metacognition—assessing the quality of one’s own cognitive performance—guides adaptive behaviour across species. Confidence signals can be extracted from language model outputs, yet a fundamental question remains: do models actually use these signals to decide whether to answer or abstain? Here we developed a four-phase paradigm. Phase 1 elicited baseline confidence without an abstention option. Phase 2 showed that large language models apply an implicit threshold to internal confidence when abstaining, with confidence effect sizes roughly an order of magnitude larger than alternative mechanisms. Phase 3 provided causal evidence via activation steering: boosting or suppressing confidence correspondingly decreased or increased abstention, with mediation analysis confirming confidence redistribution as the primary mechanism. Phase 4 instructed models to abstain at different confidence levels and showed they adjusted their behaviour accordingly, indicating they read out and act on confidence to set abstention policies. Critically, verbal confidence—an explicit self-evaluation from a separate forward pass—independently predicted abstention across all models despite being less discriminatory of correctness, and activation decoding showed both measures (that is, token log probabilities and verbal confidence) are lossy read-outs of a richer internal representation. Together, these results suggest that abstention is captured by the joint operation of a multidimensional internal confidence representation and threshold-based policies—consistent with structured metacognitive control in large language models—a capacity of growing importance as models transition to autonomous agents that must recognize their own uncertainty. © The Author(s) 2026.

title: On Condorcet’s Jury Theorem with Abstention
authors: Meir, Reshef; Ghalme, Ganesh
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
abstract: The well-known Condorcet Jury Theorem states that, under majority rule, the better of two alternatives is chosen with probability approaching one as the population grows. We study an asymmetric setting where voters face varying participation costs and share a possibly heuristic belief about their pivotality (ability to influence the outcome). In a costly voting setup where voters abstain if their participation cost is greater than their pivotality estimate, we identify a single property of the heuristic belief—weakly vanishing pivotality—that gives rise to multiple stable equilibria in which elections are nearly tied. In contrast, strongly vanishing pivotality (as in the standard Calculus of Voting model) yields a unique, trivial equilibrium where only zero-cost voters participate as the population grows. We then characterize when nontrivial equilibria satisfy a version of the Jury Theorem: below a sharp threshold, the majority-preferred candidate wins with probability approaching one; above it, both candidates either win with equal probability. © 2026, Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (www.aaai.org). All rights reserved.

title: InkGuard: A hallucination mitigation framework for Traditional Chinese Painting appreciation under uncertainty
authors: Li, Te; Ke, Junming; Zhu, Biao; Zhang, Wei; Xiao, Jun; Chen, Wei
abstract: Traditional Chinese Painting (TCP) appreciation poses a distinctive challenge for Vision-Language Models (VLMs), since the visual evidence is often stylized and sparse, while factual information such as authorship, title, and historical context may be ambiguous. Standard Supervised Fine-Tuned (SFT) VLMs can produce fluent appreciations that fill these gaps with unsupported assumptions. We propose InkGuard, a framework combining unknown-aware supervised refinement, factuality-oriented Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with threshold-based abstention. The evaluation distinguishes reference-answer alignment, factual correctness, and retrieval reliability. A TCP-oriented model achieves higher composite reference-alignment scores, and DPO improves scores on the evaluated MMHal-Bench subset. Furthermore, we investigate both the potential and the limits of training alignment and retrieval gating for TCP appreciation under uncertainty. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. All rights are reserved, including those for text and data mining, AI training, and similar technologies.

title: QEGuard: A python package for guarded precedent reuse in Quantum ESPRESSO simulation records
authors: Kim, Hyunseob; Kim, Husung; Han, Sunggeun; Lee, Jeongcheol
abstract: First-principles simulations often rely on information from previous calculations, but structural similarity alone does not determine whether prior parameters can be safely reused. QEGuard is a Python package for guarded reuse of Quantum ESPRESSO simulation records. It parses completed calculations into structured records, retrieves relevant prior cases, and evaluates transfer eligibility before proposing starting parameters. The decision procedure separates retrieval relevance from transfer approval by considering method compatibility, scientific objectives, requested accuracy, structural representation, workflow context, and calculation quality. Reproducible Quantum ESPRESSO calculations across five material systems evaluate the resulting policy under representation changes, objective- and accuracy-dependent convergence requirements, and predefined negative-control scenarios. In targeted negative-control tests, unsafe transfers occurred under unguarded reuse but were prevented by the strict QEGuard policy. The package returns full-transfer, partial-transfer, or abstention decisions with explicit exclusion reasons, providing an inspectable and reproducible layer for parameter reuse while retaining the need for property-specific convergence validation. © 2026 The Authors.

title: Conformal prediction for byte-level CPS traffic classification under adversarial attacks
authors: Karanam, Venkat Sai Suman Lamba; Ramamurthy, Byrav
abstract: AI-driven traffic classification is increasingly used in networked cyber–physical systems (CPS) (e.g., smart grids) to enable monitoring from packet-byte representations, without relying on protocol-specific parsing. However, recent work shows that learning-based traffic classifiers can be vulnerable to adaptive adversarial manipulation of observed packet bytes, leading to severe degradation and brittle decisioning at runtime. In this paper, we propose a security-oriented traffic classification framework that integrates adversarial robustness with calibrated uncertainty quantification for CPS networks. Our approach employs a byte-level representation that requires no protocol-specific feature engineering, evaluates robustness under adaptive Carlini–Wagner attacks, and incorporates conformal prediction to provide statistical risk control on predictions during inference. Across multiple CPS traffic datasets, we show that adversarial perturbations substantially reduce classification performance, while adversarial retraining improves robustness. Further, conformal prediction exposes low-confidence regimes and supports reliable operational handling of suspicious or adversarial traffic via selective prediction (accept/reject) with coverage guarantees. © 2026

title: Evidential Neural Networks for Uncertainty-Aware Alzheimer’s Disease Screening from Resting-State EEG
authors: Ujjain, Siddhant; Kagathara, Vaibhav; Singh, Pooja; Singh, Abhishek Kumar; Kumar, Sandeep; Gandhi, Tapan Kumar
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is a low-cost and non-invasive modality that may support accessible dementia screening, but clinical deployment requires both high discrimination performance and reliable uncertainty estimates. We propose an evidential neural network (ENN) for subject-level screening of Alzheimer’s disease and related dementia from resting-state EEG, using a CN versus AD+FTD patient-control formulation. Building on an EEGNet backbone, the model predicts non-negative evidence that induces a Dirichlet distribution over class probabilities, enabling computation of vacuity as an epistemic uncertainty measure in a single forward pass. We further introduce a temperature scaled classification objective with an uncertainty-aware regularizer (UMSE) to encourage low vacuity on correctly learned samples while maintaining high uncertainty for ambiguous cases. Experiments on OpenNeuro ds004504 (88 subjects; CN vs AD+FTD) use leakage-safe 5-fold stratified group cross-validation with subject-level aggregation. The proposed ENN achieves strong discrimination (AUROC 0.95) while improving calibration and uncertainty quality (lower ECE, Brier, and NLL) compared to softmax EEGNet, MC Dropout, and Deep Ensemble baselines, without increasing inference cost. These results suggest evidential modeling can improve reliability and enable selective prediction for safer EEG-based dementia screening. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

title: Risk-Aware Downlink Throughput Prediction in High-Density 5G Networks
authors: Sirhan, Najem N.; Alrousan, Riyad; Al-Saqqa, Samar; Hamad, Faten; Khrisat, Zaid
abstract: Accurate short-horizon downlink throughput prediction is essential for automation in high-density 5G deployments (e.g., stadiums and events), where user load, scheduling decisions, and interference conditions change rapidly and produce highly variable user-perceived rates. This paper benchmarks lightweight regression models for per-user throughput prediction from readily available radio access network (RAN) key performance indicators (KPIs) and studies a risk-aware extension that augments point forecasts with calibrated uncertainty and an abstention (deferral) rule. Experiments use a strictly time-ordered train/calibration/test protocol on the Liverpool 5G High-Density Demand (L5GHDD) dataset. The target is strongly zero-inflated (about 62% of samples at 0 Mbps) and heavy-tailed, creating regimes where average-error optimization can mask rare but operationally important bursts. In the point-prediction benchmark, the best model is a tuned two-stage support vector regressor with a mean absolute error (MAE) of (Formula presented.) Mbps, while the strongest single-stage model attains a weighted mean absolute percentage error (WMAPE) of (Formula presented.). For uncertainty quantification, we compare standard split conformal prediction against two input-adaptive alternatives. Constant-width split conformal attains (Formula presented.) marginal coverage for a nominal 90% target with an average interval width of (Formula presented.) Mbps, but width-based deferral is degenerate because all intervals have the same size. Variable-length conformal intervals preserve near-nominal coverage ( (Formula presented.) ) while producing informative width variation: normalized conformal reduces the average width to (Formula presented.) Mbps, and conformalized quantile regression reduces it to (Formula presented.) Mbps. At a deferral threshold of (Formula presented.) Mbps, constant-width conformal defers all samples, whereas normalized conformal still acts on (Formula presented.) of samples with selective MAE (Formula presented.) Mbps. These results show that input-adaptive uncertainty is necessary for meaningful selective prediction in heteroscedastic 5G throughput dynamics. © 2026 by the authors.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Deep Ensemble Anomaly Detection For Industrial IoT: Tiered Dynamic Thresholding With Online Concept Drift Adaptation
authors: Babayomi, Oluleke; Kim, Dong-Seong
abstract: Deep learning-based anomaly detection systems for Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) security lack mechanisms to quantify prediction confidence, limiting their operational deployment in critical infrastructure. Existing frameworks cannot exploit uncertainty information for model-agnostic improved anomaly detection performance. Furthermore, existing methods neither guarantee improvement over baseline performance nor achieve uncertainty-aware concept drift adaptation without model retraining. Therefore, this article proposes uncertainty-aware tiered dynamic thresholding, an uncertainty-aware tiered dynamic thresholding framework that leverages epistemic uncertainty to enable anomaly detection with lightweight online drift-adaptation in IIoT systems. Three contributions are proposed as follows. 1) Architecture-agnostic uncertainty pattern detection and exploitation for improved detection performance. 2) Uncertainty-stratified tiered partitioning of detected anomalies with guaranteed precision. 3) Dual-channel concept drift detection via Kullback–Leibler divergence monitoring and adaptation without ensemble retraining. Experimental validation is done with public benchmark datasets across six representative architectures (spanning forecasting, reconstruction, attention-based, and graph-based paradigms). Results demonstrate that the highest-confidence tier achieves up to 57.3% precision improvement over baseline detection, while routing up to 92% of false positives away from autonomous response for operator review or deferral. Under concept drift, the online adaptation recovers up to 27.79% of Tier 1+2 precision lost to stale calibration, while maintaining Tier 1 precision stability across all evaluated architectures. © 2005-2012 IEEE.

title: Robust Multi-label Classification via Preference Learning
authors: Nguyen, Vu-Linh; Hoang, Xuan-Truong; Destercke, Sébastien; de Campos, Cassio; Huynh, Van-Nam
abstract: In this paper, we explore how multi-label classification (MLC) tasks can be cast into order structure learning. Our motivation for doing so is to exploit the very rich structure of the orders to improve and robustify MLC learning. We describe formally how MLC can be transformed into an order structure learning and prediction task, and then proceed to study the problem of predicting Bayes-optimal order structures. We then perform some experiments in settings where the use of order structures can be very beneficial: robust MLC in the presence of noisy and imbalanced labels, and making MLC predictions with partial abstention. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

title: Development of a Cross-Modal AI-based Decision Support System using IoT Sensor Networks and Satellite Imagery for Precision Pest Management
authors: Walanjkar, Deepika Dattatraya; Thete, Sharda; Deshmukh, Monali; Sujithra, L.R.; Sajiv, G.; Nilekar, Prachi Makarand
venue: Proceedings of 7th International Conference on Smart Systems and Inventive Technology, ICSSIT 2026
abstract: This paper presents the development of an Al-based decision support system that integrates simulated Internet of Things (IoT) sensor networks with satellite imagery to enable precision pest management without hardware deployment. The framework fuses environmental telemetry (temperature, humidity, and trap-count proxies) with multispectral vegetation indices to predict pest pressure and recommend timely interventions. A modular pipeline - comprising data harmonization, feature engineering, spatiotemporal modelling, and rule-to-action translation - drives an interpretable risk score. In a software-only proof-of-concept using public Sentinel-2 scenes and synthetically generated IoT series aligned to local weather, the proposed model demonstrated competitive performance against literature baselines. Illustratively, on held-out fields, the unified model achieved Accuracy of 96.42%, macro-F1 96.31, and AUC 0.981 while cutting false alarms relative to image-only and IoT-only ablations. Decision latency per field tile was under 812 ms on a CPU-only runtime, and the system produced actionable recommendations (spray deferral, targeted scouting, or biological control) under explicit economic thresholds. Unlike prior IoT-only or remote-sensing-only systems, the proposed fusion improves robustness under cloud cover, sensor outages, and phenological shifts by learning cross-modal compensation. This software design is readily transferrable to field prototypes and serves as a reference implementation for research and extension deployments. © 2026 IEEE.

title: Beyond Accuracy: Reliability-Aware Machine Learning for Handwriting-Based Alzheimer’s Disease Detection
authors: Mitra, Uddalak; Ul Rehman, Shafiq
abstract: Reliable clinical decision support systems require not only high predictive accuracy but also trustworthy probability estimates and robust uncertainty quantification. However, most medical artificial intelligence (AI) studies primarily emphasize discrimination performance while overlooking systematic reliability evaluation. This study proposes a reliability-aware evaluation framework for Alzheimer’s disease detection that integrates discrimination analysis, statistical validation, probability calibration, uncertainty quantification, robustness assessment, and clinical decision analysis within a unified pipeline. Multiple machine learning classifiers and ensemble configurations were evaluated using repeated stratified cross-validation and assessed through discrimination and calibration metrics. Support Vector Machine achieved the highest ROC-AUC (0.955 ± 0.046), while Extra Trees obtained the highest Accuracy (0.878) and F1-score (0.887). Friedman analysis confirmed statistically significant differences among classifiers ((Formula presented.)). Platt scaling consistently improved probabilistic reliability, whereas Beta calibration demonstrated stable performance under noise, feature perturbation, and reduced-data scenarios. Uncertainty-aware selective prediction increased high-confidence diagnostic accuracy by up to 8.1%, and decision curve analysis demonstrated improved clinical utility. The reliability analysis identified calibration-aware stacking as the most reliable ensemble configuration. An independent cross-dataset evaluation on a heterogeneous Alzheimer’s disease clinical dataset with a substantially different feature space yielded stable discrimination (ROC-AUC = 0.858 ± 0.025) and calibration (ECE = 0.132 ± 0.019) after the STACK_CAL architecture was independently retrained from scratch. These findings provide evidence of the cross-dataset applicability of the proposed reliability-aware strategy across different clinical data modalities, while further prospective and independent validation remains necessary before real-world clinical deployment. © 2026 by the authors.

title: SOFS-Rice: Self-Organized Field-Session discovery and Risk-Aware domain generalization for robust rice disease diagnosis across benchmark and North-Indian fields
authors: Singh, Chatter; Singh, Amar; Dhelim, Sahraoui
abstract: Accurate rice disease diagnosis in real fields remains challenging because models trained on curated or benchmark datasets often degrade under deployment shifts in illumination, background clutter, device optics, and local agronomic context. We present SOFS-Rice, a practical framework for smart agriculture deployments that targets two operational gaps: (i) real-field datasets frequently lack reliable metadata for leakage-resistant evaluation, and (ii) decision support should withhold predictions when inputs are out-of-distribution or uncertain to reduce risky interventions. SOFS-Rice first constructs Self-Organized Field Sessions (SOFS) by clustering image embeddings and merging near-duplicates via perceptual hashes, enabling strict group-wise Train/Calibration/Test splits without manual metadata. We train a ConvNeXt-T teacher using a two-stage benchmark-to-field strategy: Stage 1 warm-up optionally leverages the publicly available Paddy doctor benchmark mapped to the four overlapping diseases, while Stage 2 fine-tunes on field data only to mitigate negative transfer. Domain generalization is encouraged through MixStyle with an epoch warm-up schedule. At inference, predictive uncertainty (MC-dropout) and energy-based OOD scoring are combined with split conformal set prediction to implement calibrated abstention. Finally, knowledge distillation produces a compact MobileNetV3 student evaluated under the same strict protocol, while MC-dropout inference cost is reported separately to avoid overstating real-time edge deployability. We position SOFS-Rice as a deployment-oriented evaluation and decision-support framework for small real-field datasets lacking reliable session metadata, rather than as a claim of universal cross-region generalization. On a 659-image North-Indian field dataset (four diseases), multi-seed evaluation confirms that random splits can substantially overestimate performance compared with SOFS group splits. The proposed risk-aware policy exposes explicit accuracy–coverage trade-offs and abstention reasons, enabling conservative decision support under realistic distribution shift without assuming consistent gains from the full pipeline. © 2026 The Author(s). Published by Elsevier B.V. This is an open access article under the CC BY license. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

title: Distributed decision-making in multi-session academic information seeking: a process model of interruption, deferral, and reconstruction
authors: Chen, Shih-Chuan
abstract: Purpose – This study reconceptualises scholarly information seeking in multi-session contexts as a temporally distributed process and examines how decision-making unfolds across time. Design/methodology/approach – A qualitative research design was adopted, combining a two-week diary study with semi-structured interviews involving 15 participants. Data were analysed using thematic analysis and process modelling to capture behavioural patterns and decision processes across search sessions. Findings – The findings show that interruption is a normal condition that segments search into multiple sessions. Deferral enables users to postpone evaluation and distribute decision-making across time, while re-entry requires reconstruction of the search context. Through the interaction of these mechanisms, decision formation emerges as a gradual and evolving process rather than a single-point judgement. Research limitations/implications – The qualitative sample limits generalisability. Future research could incorporate quantitative methods to examine the proposed model across broader contexts. Practical implications – The findings suggest that information systems should support re-entry, ongoing information management and context reconstruction to better accommodate long-term search processes. Originality/value – This study proposes a process model that shifts the analytical focus from session-based behaviour to cross-temporal dynamics. It advances information behaviour research by reframing decision-making as an ongoing process, highlighting discontinuity as a defining feature of search and identifying deferral as a key mechanism linking search episodes. © 2026, Emerald Publishing Limited

title: PC-Audit: A Decision-Reliability Framework for Auditing Validation-Based Machine-Learning Model Selection in Weak-Signal Financial Time Series
authors: Li, Songrun; Zhang, Weiran; Wang, Yichen; Lei, Qi
abstract: Featured Application: PC-Audit provides a reproducible decision-reliability record for validation-selected models in weak-signal financial time series. It distinguishes selection-time evidence from completed-period audit and next-cycle governance, helping risk and model-governance teams document when a numerical validation winner should be interpreted cautiously rather than treated as deployment authorization. Validation-based machine-learning selection can name a numerical winner in temporally dependent weak-signal data without establishing that the decision will remain reliable in a later period. We present PC-Audit (Prequential-Calibration Audit) as a decision-reliability architecture—not a new forecasting model or accuracy-enhancement method—that records the evidence surrounding a validation-selected candidate. It combines target-date partitioning, prequential non-negative calibration, Model Confidence Sets (MCS), transfer and refit diagnostics, dependence sensitivity, and forward-only governance records. In 45 walk-forward cases for nine Chinese index ETFs (2020–2024), signed-return validation ranking transfers weakly (mean rank correlation 0.090), PC-Select achieves the lowest test MAE in 15 of 45 cases, and the prequential MCS retains 4.80/5 candidates on average. L1 calibration sensitivity, alternative validation horizons, and dependence sensitivity do not support a strong signed-return selection claim. Base-model refitting adds ranking instability to already weak validation-to-future transfer. A frozen controlled simulation shows that the protocol is not mechanically abstention-only under clearly separable stationary oracle risk, while an unobserved future reversal remains a prospective limitation. Daily information-aligned econometric comparators and QLIKE analyses show that audit evidence is target- and loss-dependent: squared-return results can improve under QLIKE-aligned selection, whereas absolute-return and range-proxy results do not improve uniformly. Fallback uncertainty intervals cross zero. PC-Audit therefore supports transparent qualification of validation-selected candidates and completed-period audit/next-cycle governance, rather than deployment authorization or claimed predictive improvement. © 2026 by the authors.

title: When In Doubt, Abstain: The Impact of Abstention on Strategic Classification
authors: Alkarmi, Lina; Huang, Ziyuan; Liu, Mingyan
abstract: Algorithmic decision making is increasingly prevalent, but often vulnerable to strategic manipulation by agents seeking a favorable outcome. Prior research has shown that classifier abstention (allowing a classifier to decline making a decision due to insufficient confidence) can significantly increase classifier accuracy. This paper studies abstention within a strategic classification context, exploring how its introduction impacts strategic agents’ responses and how principals should optimally leverage it. We model this interaction as a Stackelberg game where a principal, acting as the classifier, first announces its decision policy, and then strategic agents, acting as followers, manipulate their features to receive a desired outcome. Here, we focus on binary classifiers where agents manipulate observable features rather than their true features, and show that optimal abstention ensures that the principal’s utility (or loss) is no worse than in a non-abstention setting, even in the presence of strategic agents. We also show that beyond improving accuracy, abstention can also serve as a deterrent to manipulation, making it costlier for agents, especially those less qualified, to manipulate to achieve a positive outcome when manipulation costs are significant enough to affect agent behavior. These results highlight abstention as a valuable tool for reducing the negative effects of strategic behavior in algorithmic decision making systems. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

title: Knowing When Not to Act: Toward Capability-Aware Healthcare AI
authors: Hoque Tania, Marzia
venue: Communications in Computer and Information Science
abstract: The growing adoption of AI in healthcare has increasingly shifted research from improving predictive performance toward ensuring trustworthy clinical deployment. Advances in uncertainty quantification, confidence calibration, out-of-distribution detection, selective prediction, and human–AI collaboration have substantially improved the ability to determine whether a prediction should be trusted. A complementary question, however, has received comparatively less attention: when should an AI system participate in clinical decision making? Addressing this question shifts the focus from evaluating prediction reliability to estimating the operational capability of an AI–clinical interaction. In this paper, a conceptual formulation based on four levels of abstraction–interaction, capability, competence, and operational admissibility–is developed to motivate the notion of an Operational Capability Set, representing the evolving domain over which AI participation is operationally admissible. This formulation provides a common perspective for interpreting uncertainty estimation, confidence calibration, out-of-distribution detection, selective prediction, and related approaches as complementary sources of evidence for capability estimation. It also highlights connections between trustworthy healthcare AI, computational metacognition, and meta-learning, providing a conceptual basis for future research on adaptive and trustworthy healthcare AI. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

title: Conflict Across Coarsenings: A Hierarchical DST Diagnostic for ATC Drug Normalization
authors: Nguyen, Thi-Mai; Nguyen, Dang-Hieu; Nguyen, Hoang-Thuc; Nguyen, Loan T.T
abstract: Standard Dempster–Shafer fusion computes the conflict mass K on a single fixed frame, returning one scalar per pair of sources. When the label space is a strict taxonomy such as the Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) classification, this collapse hides whether the sources disagree about the broad anatomical group or only about the fine-grained chemical substance. We introduce hierarchical conflict mass (HCM), a multi-resolution diagnostic obtained by lifting K through the chain of coarsenings induced by the taxonomy. We identify a coarsening-coherence condition under which conflict mass is preserved under exact refinement/coarsening, and show that the practical projected construction used by HCM produces an approximately monotone multi-level profile empirically. From the profile we derive two summaries: a depth-of-agreement statistic D η and a level-weighted abstention score u HCM . We evaluated HCM in a MIMIC-III subset with three heterogeneous evidence sources and an operationally disjoint NDC-based reference pipeline, comparing against five baselines. HCM improves error-detection AUROC over flat conflict mass at every ATC level—with the highest gain around +0.07 at level 1 but a smaller +0.021 at level 3—and reduces level-3 selective risk at 80% coverage from 0.074 to 0.067, a modest but statistically significant change (p=0.034). The level-resolved profile additionally enables a level-graceful abstention rule that flat conflict cannot support. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

title: GroundTrader: Multi-Agent Transition Supervision for LLM-Based Financial Trading
authors: Cui, Xinda; Liu, Yutong; Zhang, Shulei
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based financial agents use market information to generate trading actions together with textual reasoning. However, the resulting executable position transition may conflict with its supporting analysis, while the effect of intervening on that transition becomes observable only after the market evolves. We propose GroundTrader, a reliability-oriented multi-agent supervisory framework for LLM-based financial trading. GroundTrader coordinates market-state, coherence, and record analysts to assess market context, review action–reasoning consistency, and use previously settled interventions to regulate subsequent deferral proposals. GroundTrader supervises selected transitions through bounded one-period deferrals and counterfactually evaluates each proposed deferral after the subsequent market return becomes available. The resulting settlements update a recoverable budget that regulates later intervention strength. We evaluate GroundTrader on nine financial assets using fixed upstream action–reasoning trajectories. Experimental results show that GroundTrader supervision improves annualized return and Sharpe ratio and reduces maximum drawdown relative to direct execution of the fixed upstream trajectories across all nine evaluated assets. Ablation results further show that contextual record reflection, action–reasoning coherence review, and adaptive budget control all contribute to the supervisory process. © 2026 by the authors.

title: Marebito: citation matching interface for the digital library zbMATH open
authors: Deb, Madhurima; Beckenbach, Isabel; Meuschke, Norman; Teschke, Olaf; Schubotz, Moritz
abstract: zbMATH Open is a leading curated bibliographic database covering approximately five million publications in mathematics. This paper presents Marebito, a production citation-matching system developed for zbMATH Open, and documents its architecture, domain-adapted feature design, and operational performance at scale. Marebito combines bibliographic parsing with GROBID, candidate retrieval with Elasticsearch, and a supervised Random Forest trained on domain-specific string-similarity features. Evaluation on internal zbMATH Open datasets yields precision and recall exceeding 98% on modern DOI-indexed records. Evaluation across two bibliographically distinct subsets reveals that classifier performance is strongly conditioned on metadata completeness, particularly title and author string quality, rather than DOI availability alone, documenting a concrete challenge for citation matching in mathematical literature. A preliminary comparison with Crossref on a manually verified subset of 2,037 entries illustrates the limitations of general-purpose matchers on specialist mathematical bibliography. A neural reranking baseline confirms that Elasticsearch-derived hard negatives are essential for abstention. We also discuss downstream bibliometric applications within zbMATH Open. © The Author(s) 2026.

title: Reliability-Aware Retinal Encoder for Ordinal Diabetic Retinopathy Severity Modelling
authors: Gamage, Sameera
venue: Communications in Computer and Information Science
abstract: Retinal imaging is a useful non-invasive source of information because the retina has biological and vascular links with the brain. Most retinal AI studies focus on disease classification, but future multi-modal Neuro-AI systems also need outputs that are reliable, calibrated, and explainable. This paper presents a reliability-aware retinal neuro-oculomics encoder for diabetic retinopathy (DR) severity modelling with ordinal evaluation. DR grading is used as a supervised retinal disease-burden task with five ordered stages, where the model is trained using standard classification loss and evaluated using ordinal severity metrics. The encoder produces severity probabilities, Retinal Burden Score, uncertainty, reliability, calibration information, and explanation maps. Several backbones were evaluated using APTOS 2019 for internal testing and DDR for external validation. ConvNeXt-Tiny achieved the strongest internal result with 0.8273 accuracy, 0.8905 QWK, 0.9335 AUROC, and 0.9482 reliability. In external DDR validation, the fundus-preprocessed ConvNeXt-Tiny model achieved the best ordinal agreement with 0.6251 QWK and 0.9023 reliability. Calibration and selective prediction showed that reliability scores can help identify higher-quality predictions. Explainability analysis gave visual model-inspection support, but the maps were not treated as exact lesion segmentation. The method is not proposed as a neurological disease detector. Instead, it provides a retinal representation that can later be combined with other modalities in Neuro-AI research. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

title: Critical Analysis of Legal Framework and Market Structure for the Future of Virtual Power Plants Using Artificial Intelligence in India
authors: Chatterjee, Avishikta; Ganguly, Rajiv; Basu, Abhisikta
venue: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
abstract: The energy industry is the one area of our life where environmental degradation is currently pushing us for paying closer attention to the adverse impacts of fossil fuels. Our centralized, aging power grid lacks the resilience needed to resist the catastrophic weather-related occurrences that have become more frequent in recent years, as seen by the frequent scheduled and unplanned outages. Virtual power plants (VPPs) are leading creator of renewable energy initiatives. During moments of high demand and extreme weather, which are occurring more frequently, the conventional electricity grid is prone to failure. It is becoming more and more obvious that major infrastructure changes, including substation renovations, are needed for our electrical grid. As an alternative to such upgrades, VPPs have been effectively implemented, allowing for the deferral of some modifications while addressing others. Internationally, German business Sonnen produces a battery meant to meet 75% of a home's annual energy demand with energy from renewable sources while sharing the rest with the community at large in a VPP context. In the USA, Tesla debuted Powerwalls in 2015. With the capacity to scale up to 1,000 assets, Central schweizerische Kraftwerke AG (CKW) in Switzerland developed a sizable VPP with 110 assets. This paper proposes use of artificial intelligence for prediction and virtual power plants can offer users more economical power and a more affordable energy alternative and also proposes the legal and policy reform to build the infrastructure to promote competition in the market. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026.

title: TRACER: Obfuscation-Robust Cyber Threat Detection with Selective State-Space Modeling and Conformal Risk Control
authors: Xu, Yue
venue: 2026 6th International Conference on Computer Science and Blockchain, CCSB 2026
abstract: Cyber threat triage requires more than high label accuracy; it also requires calibrated uncertainty, robustness to obfuscation, and efficient processing of long textual reports. This paper presents TRACER, a compact framework that combines canonical indicator normalization, a selective state-space encoder, transport-based concept alignment, and evidential classification with split conformal prediction. The proposed design avoids dependence on entity extraction, external threat graphs, or large pretrained encoders while remaining linear in sequence length. Experiments on a long-tailed security corpus show that TRACER achieves competitive discrimination, substantially lower calibration error, and exact robustness to indicator obfuscation. The resulting prediction sets provide distribution-free coverage, making the system better suited to analyst-facing deployment where confidence and abstention are as important as accuracy. © 2026 IEEE.

title: Evolutionary dynamics of trust with voluntary participation and group-shared sanctions
authors: Liu, Yuyuan; Wang, Lichen; Guo, Ruqiang; Hua, Shijia; Liu, Linjie; Zhang, Liang; Chen, Xiaojie
abstract: How trust is established and maintained in a population of strategic agents is a topic of significant interest in contemporary discourse. Traditional trust game models often assume that individuals who are assigned as investors must choose to invest and cannot take some countermeasures against untrustworthy individuals, which seems too idealistic. In this paper, we introduce endogenous participation and collective sanctioning into the classical trust game and investigate how they collectively influence the evolutionary dynamics of trust. In this mathematical framework, investors probabilistically choose between investment and abstention, while participating investors collectively impose quadratic sanction costs on untrustworthy trustees. We show that individuals are willing to invest even though they may be defrauded and have to bear the sanction cost. Interestingly, we find that when the sanction strength is weak, the system exhibits evolutionary oscillatory dynamics, where the frequencies of investors and trustworthy trustees exhibit periodic evolution along a limit cycle. For substantial sanctions, the system converges to a stable equilibrium characterized by a high proportion of investors and trustworthy trustees. Moreover, we demonstrate that the income of investors and trustworthy trustees remains considerable under the group-shared sanctioning, facilitating the emergence of trust. © 2025 Elsevier Ltd. All rights are reserved, including those for text and data mining, AI training, and similar technologies.

title: Reducing Hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented LLM Question Answering for Indian Code-Mixed Queries
authors: Gaikwad, Sonali S.; Gaikwad, Jyotsna S.
venue: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance in question answering and dialogue systems; however, they remain susceptible to hallucinations, producing fluent yet unsupported responses, especially in knowledge-intensive domains. This issue is further exacerbated in multilingual environments, such as India, where users frequently issue code-mixed queries that combine English with regional languages. In this paper, we propose a hallucination-aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework for domain-specific question answering over Indian code-mixed queries. The framework incorporates lightweight code-mixed query normalization, multilingual document retrieval, and a Hallucination Control Layer (HCL) that constrains answer generation to retrieved evidence and enforces explicit abstention when supporting information is insufficient. We evaluate the proposed approach on a custom dataset comprising English, Hindi, and Hindi–English code-mixed queries over a curated domain corpus. Experimental results demonstrate a substantial reduction in hallucination rates compared to both direct LLM answering and standard RAG pipelines, while maintaining comparable answer quality. The improvements are most pronounced for code-mixed inputs, highlighting the effectiveness of evidence-constrained generation for reliable multilingual deployment of LLM-based question answering systems. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

title: Failure-mode-aware uncertainty intervention routing for large language models
authors: Yin, Shiyuan; Zhang, Ruizhi
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently produce incorrect outputs, yet the underlying causes of failure vary across queries and call for different interventions. We propose failure-mode-aware intervention routing, a framework that extracts a 12-dimensional behavioral uncertainty signature characterizing the type of uncertainty for each query, then trains a lightweight router to select the optimal intervention: commit, deliberate (majority voting), acquire (retrieval-augmented re-generation), or defer (abstain). The signature comprises base, semantic, and intervention-delta features that capture model behavior under different conditions. A TF-IDF control experiment confirms that the signature provides routing signal beyond text-only dataset cues (p<0.001). On 3043 samples, an XGBoost router achieves utility 0.725, significantly outperforming the best single-intervention strategy (+35.2%), MLP routers, confidence-based abstention, adaptive thresholds, and a LinUCB contextual bandit baseline. Leave-one-out feature ablation identifies intervention-delta features as the strongest routing signals. Cross-architecture experiments on three model families (Qwen3-14B, DeepSeek-V3.2, Llama-family 8B) demonstrate generalization, with routing gains inversely proportional to model capability. Cross-family retrieval experiments confirm robustness when retrieval corpus relevance degrades by 69%. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

title: Strategies for Non-myopic Users in EIP-1559
authors: Ding, Yiming; Qi, Qi; Wang, Bingzhe
abstract: This paper analyzes strategic transaction submission behavior in Ethereum’s EIP-1559, focusing on non-myopic users who optimize costs over finite horizons. While prior work assumes myopic users who schedule their transactions in the immediate block, we formalize the dynamic decision-making of non-myopic bidders facing stochastic base fee adjustments, variable block capacities, and transaction deferral risks. We model the evolving base fee and user interactions as a semi-Markov process (sMP) and frame the optimal bidding strategy as a finite-horizon optimal stopping problem. By establishing equivalence to a semi-Markov decision process (sMDP), we prove the existence of deterministic stationary optimal policies and characterize the value function as the minimal solution to a recursive optimality equation. A value iteration algorithm is proposed to compute ϵ-optimal stopping policies, with explicit convergence bounds dependent on the semi-Markov kernel’s properties. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026.

title: CALM-TS: Risk-Controlled LLM Labeling for Time-Series via Calibrated Selective Gating
authors: Xiao, Yifan; Li, Shijie; Huang, Yu
venue: Proceedings of the ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining
abstract: Labeling time-series events such as anomalies and system failures is expensive and subjective, and distribution drift makes label definitions evolve over time. Large language models can generate weak labels with natural-language rationales, but their error rates are unbounded and their failure modes opaque. We present CALM-TS, a risk-controlled weak-supervision pipeline that bounds the labeling error rate while maximizing coverage. CALM-TS introduces behavioral probing over prompt surface form, sampling temperature, and temporal context window to elicit disagreement signals; a lightweight calibrator converts them into risk-bounded acceptance with finite-sample guarantees. CALM-TS attains 77 - 81% cost reduction on MIMIC-III and Yahoo S5 at empirical risk ≤ a=0.05 in all 10 dataset-seed pairs. On the official PhysioNet Challenge 2015 binary alarm-verification task with gpt-4o-mini over five seeds, CALM-TS is the only method among nine LLM-as-weak-labeler baselines whose 5-seed mean risk strictly falls below the unfiltered LLM at non-trivial coverage, delivering a 15.0% relative reduction (0.400 → 0.340) at coverage 0.286. The framework yields auditable evidence chains and a coverage-based, label-free drift indicator. © 2026 Owner/Author.
