title: Evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning for Robotic Manipulation
authors: Rahman Bhuiyan, Mohammad Arifur; Mozaffari, Saeed; Alirezaee, Shahpour
venue: Canadian Conference on Electrical and Computer Engineering
abstract: This paper presents a controlled evaluation of three reasoning strategies for vision-guided robotic manipulation: YOLO-only rule-based heuristics, Large Language Model (LLM) symbolic planning, and a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) planner. All methods use the same perception and control pipeline, with YOLO for object detection and a Franka Panda robot for execution. This setup isolates the impact of reasoning. We evaluate the planners on fifteen structured test scenarios covering phrasing variation, constraint following, ambiguity, abstention, recovery, and edge cases, for 150 episodes per planner and 450 total execution episodes. The RAG-enhanced planner achieves 98 percent task success, full policy compliance, zero unsafe actions, and a 92 percent reduction in retries compared to the baseline. All planners produce identical symbolic policies, showing that performance gains come from more robust execution rather than changes in plan generation. These results demonstrate that retrieval-augmented reasoning improves the reliability of language-driven robotic manipulation. © 2026 IEEE.

title: ImageTrust: Multi-backbone Fusion for AI-Generated Image Detection with Calibrated Uncertainty
authors: Iancu, Andrei-Alexandru; Galiş, Darius; Stefaniga, Sebastian-Aurelian
venue: Lecture Notes on Data Engineering and Communications Technologies
abstract: This paper proposes ImageTrust, a detection system which addresses some of the shortcomings usually associated with AI media detection, namely, poor performance after recompression and the missing calibrated uncertainty estimates along with predictions. ImageTrust concatenates embeddings from ResNet-50 (2,048-d), EfficientNet-B0 (1,280-d) and ViT-B/16 (768-d) into a single 4,096-dimensional embedding, which is classified by both an XGBoost and MLP meta-classifier. We employ temperature scaling to decrease calibration error (ECE = 0.016 for XGBoost) and use conformal prediction to provide 95.2% coverage guarantees with explicit abstention when ImageTrust makes an unconfident prediction. Training on a cumulative dataset of 604,589 images across 4 compression variants (None, WhatsApp, Instagram, screenshot) resulted in ImageTrust experiencing less than a 0.3% decrease in AUC when images were recompressed with social media, when compared to degradations of 3–8% observed in prior detectors. Furthermore, our fusion approach does not increase absolute AUC over the best single-backbone baseline (96.3 vs. 96.4); however, it produces calibrated uncertainty estimates that no other detector provides. We benchmarked ImageTrust on images generated by 24 generator architectures to demonstrate that cross-generator transferability has yet to be solved. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

title: Real-World Deployment and Energy Consumption of Federated Learning in V2N Scenarios
authors: Sezgin, Selman; Mokrani, Kahina; Jacques, Julien; Allio, Sylvain
venue: 2026 IEEE International Symposium on Measurements in Networking and Communications, MNC 2026 - Symposium Proceedings
abstract: Connectivity and Artificial Intelligence (AI) are the cornerstones of future smart cities, with Connected Vehicles (CVs) playing a pivotal role. However, training AI models on massive vehicular data streams raises critical privacy concerns. Federated Learning (FL) offers a decentralized approach, yet its performance under realistic, dynamic network conditions remains under-explored. This paper proposes a practical deployment architecture for FL in a Vehicle-to-Network (V2N) environment using a real-world 5G public network. By conducting field tests in urban and suburban environments, we evaluate the impact of mobility and radio fluctuations on energy consumption. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of FL over mobile networks and reveal a linear correlation between local dataset size and computational energy. By identifying the impact of radio handovers - which increase transmission energy costs by up to 35% - we derive actionable levers for energy optimization. These findings highlight the need for network-aware FL strategies, such as transmission deferral and adaptive client selection, to optimize the energy-performance trade-off of FL in urban mobility scenarios. © 2026 IEEE.

title: MMAP-Net: Missing-aware multimodal fusion for multi-label retinal disease classification with score-calibrated deferral
authors: Kınalıoğlu, İsmail Hakkı
abstract: Background and Objective:Deployment-oriented retinal AI systems should explicitly account for incomplete clinical metadata, prediction uncertainty, and inputs acquired under conditions that differ from model development data. Many retinal classification pipelines, including most image-only baselines on the Brazilian Multilabel Ophthalmological Dataset (BRSET), do not evaluate these issues together. We present MMAP-Net, a multimodal retinal classification prototype evaluated on BRSET and complemented by a single external-device shift check on mBRSET. The contribution is framed as empirical characterization of a deployment-aware workflow, not as evidence of clinical translation readiness.Methods:MMAP-Net combines a Swin-V2 image encoder, an FT-Transformer metadata encoder that represents missing values with mask tokens and per-feature missingness indicators, and a Bidirectional Gated Cross-attention with Dual Aggregation (BiGCDA) fusion module with a learnable per-sample modality gate α. The canonical reported output space contains Head A (four primary binary labels) and Head B (five-class diabetic-retinopathy grading). A score-calibrated deferral rule is fitted on the validation split and applied unchanged to the held-out test split and to mBRSET; it is a selective-deferral heuristic rather than a method with formal coverage guarantees. Epistemic uncertainty is estimated with MC Dropout. Six ablation variants are evaluated on BRSET ((Formula presented) images, 8,524 patients), and mBRSET ((Formula presented) portable-camera images) is used only as a frozen-model external-device check without domain adaptation.Results:Under the canonical single-seed Protocol 1 setting ((Formula presented) MC Dropout, validation-selected seed 42), MMAP-Net achieves macro-AUROC 0.9673 and diabetic-retinopathy AUROC 0.9982 [95% CI: 0.9969–0.9992] on the held-out BRSET test split. The clearest architectural effect is task-specific: removing the learnable modality gate lowers optic-disc AUROC by 0.0831 (95% CI: 0.0679–0.0978) and image-quality AUROC by 0.0346 (95% CI: 0.0178–0.0512). Under the matched single-pass ablation protocol, MMAP-Net yields a higher aggregate macro-AUROC than the image-only model ((Formula presented) ). It also meets the predefined equivalence criterion relative to early fusion at the aggregate macro-AUROC level (TOST, ± 0.01 bound, (Formula presented) ). Under 30% simulated MCAR metadata removal, macro-AUROC changes by only (Formula presented), comparable to early fusion ((Formula presented) ); this result supports stability under controlled random metadata loss, not evidence of a verified MNAR advantage. The score-calibrated deferral rule defers 64.56% of mBRSET samples versus 10.17% of held-out BRSET test samples at the validation-locked 90% setting, showing a larger deferral rate under this single external-device shift. Raw probabilities are miscalibrated for several labels; validation-fitted label-specific isotonic calibration reduces macro-ECE to 0.019 on the held-out test split with no test-set information used during fitting. At validation-locked DR operating points, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, and referral burden are reported to characterize workload trade-offs.Conclusions:The evidence supports MMAP-Net as a deployment-aware research prototype with task-specific gate benefits, explicit missingness representation, validation-fitted probability calibration, and score-calibrated deferral behavior under one external-device shift check. It does not establish aggregate superiority over early fusion, performance under verified MNAR mechanisms, formal coverage guarantees, quantitative faithfulness of visual explanations, or broad multi-country external generalization. A matched retraining ablation shows that the exploratory auxiliary hypertension branch changes primary-task macro-AUROC by only (Formula presented) ; it is therefore reported only as a negative auxiliary-task result and is not part of the canonical MMAP-Net architecture or reported output space. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. title: MedSymmFlow: Bridging Generative Modeling and Classification in Medical Imaging Through Symmetrical Flow Matching
authors: Caetano, Francisco; Abdi, Lemar; Viviers, Christiaan; Valiuddin, Amaan; van der Sommen, Fons
abstract: Reliable medical image classification requires accurate predictions and well-calibrated uncertainty estimates, especially in high-stakes clinical settings. This work presents MedSymmFlow, a generative-discriminative hybrid model built on Symmetrical Flow Matching, designed to unify classification, generation, and uncertainty quantification in medical imaging. MedSymmFlow leverages a latent-space formulation that scales to high-resolution inputs and introduces a semantic mask conditioning mechanism to enhance diagnostic relevance. Unlike standard discriminative models, it naturally estimates uncertainty through its generative sampling process. The model is evaluated on four MedMNIST datasets, covering a range of modalities and pathologies. The results show that MedSymmFlow matches or exceeds the performance of established baselines in classification accuracy and AUC, while also delivering reliable uncertainty estimates validated by performance improvements under selective prediction. The code is available at github.com/caetas/MedSymmFlow. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

title: Knowing When to Trust Cheap Retrieval: A Calibration and Cost-Aware Decision Layer for Open-Vocabulary Temporal Change Retrieval
authors: Giannikos, Panagiotis; Tzouveli, Paraskevi
venue: EReL-MIR 2026 - Proceedings of the 2nd International Workshop on Efficient Representation Learning for Multimodal Information Retrieval
abstract: Multimodal information retrieval in remote sensing increasingly poses free-text questions about time: given co-registered image pairs (T1, T2) of one location at two acquisition times, the task is to retrieve the pairs in which a described change - for example, "low vegetation became bare ground"- has occurred. The efficient way to serve this is to keep a large vision-language model frozen, embed each pair once, cache the result, and answer queries by vector arithmetic. We study what such a cheap, training-free pipeline can and cannot deliver, and contribute the decision machinery that makes it deployable. Under a pre-registered protocol on a public bi-temporal benchmark, with queries posed as templated transitions over six land-cover classes, a frozen encoder carries genuine ranking signal: 18 of 22 supported change transitions are forward-reliable at a false-discovery rate of q ≤ 0.05. As a per-item decision, however, it only ties a base-rate predictor on a coverage-fair selective-risk metric. Across three frozen encoders it never beats that predictor: it ties on two and is significantly worse on the third - the one whose ranking map is the strongest - so ranking quality does not purchase per-item decision quality. Re-pricing the same decisions under asymmetric misclassification costs recovers an operating envelope in which acting on the cheap signal is cheaper than following prevalence, and this advantage appears only where the ranking signal is genuine. The contribution is a near-zero-compute calibration-and-cost decision layer, evaluated jointly for effectiveness and serving cost, that tells an operator when a frozen, cache-once retriever is worth trusting, rather than a new backbone or a leaderboard number. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

title: Fixed-Candidate Reliability Auditing for Closed-Set Binary Function Retrieval Under Known-Source Cross-Compilation Protocols
authors: An, Yiming; Yu, Yanshu; Li, Weidong; Kochan, Orest
abstract: Binary code similarity detection (BCSD) ranks candidates but does not quantify the reliability of an already selected Top-1 match. We study this post-retrieval problem in a known-source, closed-set protocol: the target Top-1 is frozen before same-source cross-compilation views are queried, so auxiliary evidence audits cannot replace it. A frozen 34-variable map feeds a low-capacity logistic model with project-grouped cross-fitting, Platt calibration, and training-side threshold selection. On 413 families from 16 projects, cross-view evidence improved discrimination over target score/margin features. GCC-O0 was a dominant-anchor regime: Full showed no statistically resolved ROC-AUC gain over Primary-anchor, whereas Clang-O0 benefited from complementary non-primary evidence. On 240 project-identity-disjoint families from 55 projects, the design-locked structural branch accepted 75/240 GCC and 99/240 Clang candidates (31.3%/41.3% coverage) with no observed family-level errors. Correspondence mismatch reduced discrimination toward chance. Corrected TF-IDF remained supportive because correction followed label access. The contribution of this paper is a versioned candidate-preserving audit interface with explicit evidence and deployment boundaries, but not a universal retrieval improvement or distribution-free guarantee. © 2026 by the authors.

title: Multimodal Biometric Authentication Using Lip Motion and Spoken Passphrases
authors: Govindaraju, Venu Siddapura; Marrone, Stefano; Sansone, Carlo
abstract: This work presents a dual-factor biometric authentication system developed for the BIOVID Challenge 2025, targeting open-set verification scenarios using synchronized audio-visual data. Each authentication attempt consists of an MP4 video containing a spoken passphrase and corresponding lip motion. Our system employs a dual-stream deep learning model leveraging i) a ResNet3D-18 network with a Bidirectional GRU to extract spatiotemporal visual features from lip motion and ii) a fine-tuned ECAPA-TDNN (Emphasized Channel Attention, Propagation, and Aggregation Time Delay Neural Network) model to generate robust audio embeddings from speech. These modality-specific representations are fused using a Gated Multimodal Unit (GMU), which outputs a 256-dimensional joint embedding used for both classification and embedding-based matching for identity verification. A composite loss function combining triplet loss (with semi-hard negative mining) and cross-entropy loss is used for training. The system is evaluated using 3-fold cross-validation, achieving an average accuracy of 71.36%, EER of 28.61%, APCER of 28.68%, and BPCER of 28.55%. To make our system able to operate under an open-set decision-making scenario, we propose a method using a threshold-based cosine similarity reject option. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

title: SEMTRA: Global Semantic Transition and Rough-Set Rules for Auditable Post-Hoc Explainability
authors: Radiuk, Pavlo; Barmak, Oleksander; Krak, Iurii
abstract: Deep learning architectures generate highly effective but difficult-to-audit latent representations, creating a practical gap between predictive performance and verifiable explanations. Existing post hoc techniques often produce fragmented local attributions rather than dataset-level rulebooks. In this work, we propose Global SEMantic TRAnsition (SEMTRA), a post hoc framework that maps frozen representation features into semantic attributes, discretizes those attributes, and induces rough-set production rules with explicit coverage, conflict, fidelity, and abstention reporting. Evaluated on the Animals with Attributes 2 (AwA2) Protocol A, the semantic transition achieved a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of (Formula presented.). The extracted rulebook covered 84.80% of test instances, yielding a covered accuracy of 39.73% and a covered fidelity to the base predictor of 40.48%. Under the Protocol B split, continuous semantic-prototype transfer reached an unseen-object accuracy of (Formula presented.) as a semantic-transfer validation. Cross-domain validations using SUN and Derm7pt demonstrated that the audit protocol is portable yet strongly dataset-dependent. In the controlled synthetic benchmark, SEMTRA achieved a macro-F1 score of 0.879 at zero semantic noise and degraded to 0.838 at the highest evaluated noise level. Ultimately, SEMTRA serves as a transparent audit layer to expose the verifiable logical subset of a model, rather than replacing the underlying predictor. © 2026 by the authors.

title: An AI Agent for Immune Receptor Fingerprint-Based Diagnosis of Infection of Unknown Origin
authors: Ma, Jiahao; Li, Hongzong; Hu, Ye-Fan; Huang, Jian-Dong
abstract: When routine tests fail to find a pathogen, diagnosing infections of unknown origin stalls. We instead read the patient’s immune response for AI-readable clues. We formalize a new machine learning task: inferring plausible epitopes directly from immune-receptor repertoires and localizing their pathogen sources. To address this problem, we introduce a Transformer-based multi-sequence novel representation-learning model that jointly models T-cell receptors, human leukocyte antigen, and antigenic peptides, and we pretrain it across six tasks; the model achieves best or second-best performance across all six tasks against strong baselines. Building on this, we develop an end-to-end, clinically oriented agent that operates in a perceive–plan–act loop, orchestrating epitope generation, HLA-personalized filtering, consistency checks, and retrieval, with clinician-in-the-loop threshold adaptation; when evidence conflicts, it performs calibrated abstention and logs an interpretable decision trace. End-to-end on clinical-style repertoires with diagnostic report generation, the agent outperforms discriminative-pairing and direct-retrieval baselines. All code, models, and pathogen indices under a research license, together with de-identified evaluation data are in https://github.com/Ascaris-Equi/VitalT. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

title: Generalizing Abstention for Noise-Robust Learning in Medical Image Segmentation
authors: Moustafa, Wesam; Elsafty, Hossam; Schneider, Helen; Sparrenberg, Lorenz; Sifa, Rafet
abstract: Label noise is a critical problem in medical image segmentation, often arising from the inherent difficulty of manual annotation. Models trained on noisy data are prone to overfitting, which degrades their generalization performance. While a number of methods and strategies have been proposed to mitigate noisy labels in the segmentation domain, this area remains largely under-explored. The abstention mechanism has proven effective in classification tasks by enhancing the capabilities of Cross Entropy, yet its potential in segmentation remains unverified. In this paper, we address this gap by introducing a universal and modular abstention framework capable of enhancing the noise-robustness of a diverse range of loss functions. Our framework improves upon prior work with two key components: an informed regularization term to guide abstention behaviour, and a more flexible power-law-based auto-tuning algorithm for the abstention penalty. We demonstrate the framework’s versatility by systematically integrating it with three distinct loss functions to create three novel, noise-robust variants: GAC, SAC, and ADS. Experiments on the CaDIS and DSAD medical datasets show our methods consistently and significantly outperform their non-abstaining baselines, especially under high noise levels. This work establishes that enabling models to selectively ignore corrupted samples is a powerful and generalizable strategy for building more reliable segmentation models. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/wemous/abstention-for-segmentation. © 2026 CC-BY 4.0, W. Moustafa, H. Elsafty, H. Schneider, L. Sparrenberg & R. Sifa.

title: Large Language Models for Radiology QA: Benchmarking and Error Taxonomy on RadQA
authors: Hamidi, Alaleh; Roberts, Kirk
venue: Proceedings - 2026 IEEE 14th International Conference on Healthcare Informatics, ICHI 2026
abstract: Radiology reports are a critical source of clinical information but are often lengthy, variable in structure, and difficult for non-radiologists to navigate. Question answering (QA) systems can help clinicians rapidly retrieve relevant findings, yet existing evaluations of extractive QA on radiology reports rely heavily on aggregate metrics such as exact match (EM) and F1, which obscure important failure modes. In this work, we benchmark modern open large language models (LLMs), such as LLaMA 3.1-8B, LLaMA 3.2-3B, and Mistral-Small-22B, on the RadQA dataset under zero-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuned settings. We report performance using EM, F1, and a sentence-level measure (SM), and introduce a structured error taxonomy that disaggregates incorrect predictions into eight categories, including hallucination, superset, subset, and abstention errors. Our results show that fine-tuning substantially outperforms in-context prompting, with LLaMA 3.1-8B achieving 61% EM, 77% F1, and 85% SM, surpassing previously reported baselines on RadQA. The taxonomy reveals that fine-tuning not only raises accuracy but also eliminates hallucinations and reduces false positive and false negative abstentions, concentrating residual errors in boundary-level categories such as superset and subset. These findings demonstrate the value of combining standard metrics with taxonomy-driven analysis to better understand model behavior and highlight future directions, including reasoning-oriented LLMs and hybrid extractive-generative approaches, for building reliable clinical QA systems. © 2026 IEEE.

title: Dynamic Tariff Design for Demand-Side Flexibility: A Regime-Switching Approach to Consumption Forecasting in Distribution Grids
authors: Brylle, Lucas; Madsen, Henrik
abstract: Dynamic tariffs require forecasts of how consumption responds to price signals not yet observed. We develop a Markov-Switching Seasonal Autoregressive model with Exogenous variables (MS-SARX) that endogenously identifies latent consumption regimes and estimates regime-dependent price elasticities via an L 2 -regularised Expectation-Maximisation algorithm. Evaluated on operational smart-meter data from Denmark’s largest distribution system operator across three case studies, MS-SARX reduces root mean square error by 6–22 % at the primary substation level relative to the strongest baseline per case, with the largest gains where consumption exhibits multimodal regime structure. Embedding these forecasts in a revenue-neutral tariff optimisation yields model-implied peak-load reductions of 9–49 % and potential infrastructure deferral savings of 0.7–47.7 million DKK. These tariff and economic outcomes are simulation-based and contingent on the stability of regime-specific price response under tariffs not yet observed; field validation remains necessary. While demonstrated on a Danish DSO, the framework transfers to other tariff regimes, countries, and customer mixes wherever operational smart-meter and price data are available. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

title: Adaptive Claim Level Hallucination Detection and Mitigation for BlackBox LLMs on Amazon Bedrock
authors: Katta, Mukunda Rao
venue: 2026 IEEE 5th World Conference on Applied Intelligence and Computing, AIC 2026
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed through managed cloud APIs are increasingly relied upon in settings where incorrect output carries real cost enterprise search, healthcare triage, financial advisory, and legal question answering among them. Hallucination mitigation in these black-box environments is hard for two reasons: strong detection methods typically depend on model internals that hosted APIs do not expose, and current mitigation pipelines apply retrieval and verification uniformly, adding latency and cost even when a response is already well-grounded. This article describes Claim Guard, a cloud-native pipeline that breaks each LLM response into atomic factual claims, retrieves targeted evidence for each claim, estimates a calibrated per-claim risk score from three signal sources retrieval support, verifier disagreement, and Amazon Bedrock Guardrail feedback and selects the cheapest mitigation action whose expected cost does not exceed the risk. Actions range from accepting the original answer to RAG regeneration, chain-of-verification, selective claim rewriting, and abstention. Built on Amazon Bedrock, Kendra, Lambda, S3, DynamoDB, and Bedrock Guardrails, ClaimGuard treats factuality, latency, and per-query cost as joint objectives. A dynamic evaluation protocol pairs standard benchmarks TruthfulQA, FEVER, HotpotQA, HaluEval, RAGTruth with adversarial evidence perturbation and temporal drift stress tests. Across all benchmarks ClaimGuard achieves a mean hallucination rate of 11.9%, against 37.1% for unmitigated generation and 18.0% for always on RAG, at a mean end to end latency of 1.02 s well below the 2.87 s of always on RAG. © 2026 IEEE.

title: Learning to Abstain: Reliable Medical Image Segmentation With Rejection Option
authors: Sanisoglu, Mirac Ayberk; Navab, Nassir; Kim, Seong Tae
abstract: Uncertainty estimation is an important area of research in the deep learning field by offering numerous potential applications. Selective prediction is one of the possible applications that focuses on rejecting less confident samples to enhance the overall performance and reliability of accepted samples. In the context of segmentation, selective segmentation aims to allow the model to abstain from assigning labels to uncertain pixels. While selective classification has received considerable attention, only a few studies have explored selective segmentation. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach that addresses this gap by incorporating uncertainty learning during model training. Specifically, we propose a new training scheme that encourages the model to identify and flag uncertain pixels in a real-time manner. Comparative experiments on three public medical segmentation datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. Our approach achieves higher Dice scores across multiple coverage levels, surpassing the performance of existing approaches in the field. © 2013 IEEE.

title: Uncertainty-aware music genre classification using evidential deep learning
authors: Sidharrth, V.; Jayan, Sarada; Alatas, Bilal
abstract: Music is known to play a primary role in stress reduction, thereby enhancing our mental well-being. Retrieval of musical category tailored to specific needs of an individual is gaining traction but remains challenging and quite cumbersome. This is because of hazy and ambiguous nature of music classification, due to human subjectivity and disagreement which necessitates effective methods of classification. In the proposed work, the open source GTZAN dataset for musical genre classification from Music Analysis, Retrieval and Synthesis for Audio Signals (MARSYAS) collection has been utilized. Models despite achieving higher accuracy may provide incorrect predictions when genres overlap. In order to overcome this issue, this study proposes an uncertainty quantification by Dirichlet based evidence modeling with hybrid convolutional neural network-long short term memory network (CNN-LSTM), where the incorrect predictions have been penalized via Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. The initial expected calibration error (ECE) of 0.1401 and the corresponding reliability diagram suggest the overconfidence of the model in incorrect predictions. The ECE of 0.0791 after temperature scaling suggests the alignment of predicted confidence and the accuracy. From selective prediction plots, it can be observed that top 20% confident samples before calibration achieve an accuracy of 93–94%. Upon calibration, a similar accuracy is achieved by top 50% samples, which is a significant improvement. The study underscores the need for insights of quantitative trust upon the model, which is a crucial need for deploying music recommendation systems. © Copyright 2026 Sidharrth et al. Distributed under Creative Commons CC-BY 4.0 http://www.creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

title: Confidence-Guided Stepwise Model Routing for Cost-Efficient Reasoni
authors: Lee, Sangmook; Kim, Dohyung; Koh, Hyukhun; Yang, Nakyeong; Jung, Kyomin
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs)-particularly model scaling and test-time techniques-have greatly enhanced the reasoning capabilities of language models at the expense of higher inference costs. To lower inference costs, prior works train router models or deferral mechanisms that allocate easy queries to a small, efficient model, while forwarding harder queries to larger, more expensive models. However, these trained router models often lack robustness under domain shifts and require expensive data synthesis techniques such as Monte Carlo rollouts to obtain sufficient ground-truth routing labels for training. In this work, we propose Confidence-Guided Stepwise Model Routing for Cost-Efficient Reasoning (STEER), a domain-agnostic framework that performs fine-grained, step-level routing between smaller and larger LLMs without utilizing external models. STEER leverages confidence scores from the smaller model’s log-its prior to generating a reasoning step, so that the large model is invoked only when necessary. Extensive evaluations using different LLMs on a diverse set of challenging benchmarks across multiple domains such as Mathematical Reasoning, Multi-Hop QA, and Planning tasks indicate that STEER achieves competitive or enhanced accuracy while reducing inference costs (up to +20% accuracy with 48% less FLOPs compared to solely using the larger model on AIME), outperforming baselines that rely on trained external modules. Our results establish model-internal confidence as a robust, domain-agnostic signal for model routing, offering a scalable pathway for efficient LLM deployment. © 2026, Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (www.aaai.org). All rights reserved.

title: Large language models, ChatGPT, and beyond: A new paradigm for condition monitoring and prognosis in power and energy systems
authors: Benbouzid, Mohamed
abstract: Large language models and related foundation models offer new capabilities for interpreting heterogeneous information, retrieving engineering knowledge, and supporting high-level decision processes in power and energy systems. This Perspective examines their role in condition monitoring and prognostics and health management, with particular emphasis on remaining useful life estimation. To support language and multimodal model interpretation of structured and validated estimates, we propose a digital twin-centric architecture comprising physics-guided hybrid estimation, digital twin synchronization, rule-governed semantic translation, foundation model reasoning, output validation, and human supervision. The specific contribution is threefold. First, the proposed layering principle distinguishes physically consistent estimation, system integration, and higher-level reasoning functions. Second, an auditable semantic interface is defined to encode health indicators, degradation states, remaining useful life distributions, uncertainty information, operating context, provenance, retrieved evidence, and permitted reasoning scope. Third, a deployment-oriented reliability framework relates physical consistency, digital twin consistency, explanation fidelity, uncertainty preservation, robustness, traceability, safe deferral, latency, data sensitivity, and computational requirements to edge, on premises, cloud, and hybrid implementations. An illustrative battery state-of-health and remaining useful life use case demonstrates the resulting information flow. The foundation model layer is primarily intended for slow-timescale, human-supervised functions such as diagnostic explanation, degradation interpretation, maintenance prioritization, inspection planning, and fleet-level assessment, rather than protection or real-time control. The Perspective also examines complementary roles for small language models, tiny recursive models, world models, large language models, and multimodal foundation models and identifies priorities for their reliable evaluation and deployment in power and energy prognostics and health management. © 2026 The Author(s). Published by Elsevier Ltd. This is an open access article under the CC BY license. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

title: HIRA-DGA: Hierarchical Invariant Representations and Abstention for Cross-Source Power Transformer Fault Diagnosis
authors: Adilbekov, Alibek; de Jesus, Luigi Carlo; Lucena, Joe Robert Paul; Baigulbayeva, Moldir; Alnazirov, Ruslan; Moldakhmetov, Sayat
venue: Journal of Intelligent Decision Making and Information Science
abstract: High within-dataset accuracy does not establish that a dissolved-gas analysis model will remain valid in an independently sourced transformer population, especially when gas magnitudes, case mix, and label structures differ. This study proposes HIRA-DGA, a Hierarchical Invariant-Representation and Abstention framework, and evaluates it using two public real-data sources: 200 Malaysian development records and 25 Ukrainian cases, of which 19 represented single mechanisms and six were mixed or composite. Five common gases were harmonized. HIRA-DGA separates locally calibrated normal/fault screening from portable fault typing: Stage 0 uses centered log-ratio composition plus total gas magnitude; Stage 1 uses three log gas-ratios for thermal-versus-discharge recognition; Stage 2 uses centered log-ratio composition for discharge severity; and Stage 3 returns HOLD for unsupported label structures. Duplicate-aware 10-by-5 grouped validation, and a one-way, no-target-tuning external challenge were used. Median total gas magnitude differed by 65 to 1,322 times across harmonized classes. With logistic regression, direct four-class absolute-log and ratio models achieved 2/19 and 7/19 external accuracy, whereas HIRA-DGA achieved 18/19 (94.7%; Wilson 95% CI 75.4-99.1%). Stage 2 centered log-ratio features classified 11/11 discharge-severity cases versus 5/11 for its absolute-log ablation. A fixed LightGBM robustness check showed the same architectural direction, improving from 5/19 for direct ratio classification to 13/19 for the hierarchical path. All six mixed cases were assigned HOLD. The contribution is a representation-by-decision technology architecture, not a new classifier: it localizes magnitude-sensitive screening, transfers scale-reduced chemistry and makes abstention an explicit engineering output. © 2026, Nexora Academic Press. All rights reserved.

title: Hierarchical Stroke-Level Clustering and Step-Level Segmentation for Automatic Scoring of Geometric Construction Answers with an Electronic Drawing Compass
authors: Truong, Thanh-Nghia; Nguyen, Hung Tuan; Ly, Nam Tuan; Tsuchida, Yoichi; Miyazawa, Hiroshi; Asakura, Tomo; Ito, Masamitsu; Horie, Toshihiko; Yasuno, Fumiko; Nakagawa, Masaki
abstract: Geometric construction is a fundamental component of school mathematics that tests students’ understanding of geometric properties and their logically organized problem-solving processes. It requires students to follow correct procedural steps; however, the construction process is not observable in traditional paper-based examinations, making it difficult to verify whether the required steps were followed. Electronic pen-and-paper systems can record complete stroke histories, enabling process-based assessment and automated grading. Recently, an electronic drawing compass (e-compass) comprising a digital stylus pen and a needle sensor was developed to replace the conventional compasses, enabling students to construct on paper-like media while recording time-stamped compass, pencil, and eraser strokes. This study proposed an automatic scoring method for e-compass answers under practical challenges, including fragmented compass arcs, mixed drawing orders across tools, and variations in individual construction strategies. This method leverages the temporal order of strokes to identify meaningful drawing actions from fragmented inputs, reconstruct arcs and lines, and extract geometric features such as centers, radii, and intersections. By analyzing the temporal relationships between the extracted features and subsequent drawing actions, the method evaluates whether the prescribed procedures are correctly followed and outputs partial-credit levels with an explicit reject option for uncertain cases. Experiments on 2,000 student answers from 20 geometric construction tasks, including detailed analyses of three representative tasks, achieved an overall binary accuracy of 0.722 and an F1 score of 0.754, while maintaining high precision for non-rejected answers (0.935) under a reject option for uncertain cases. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

title: SMISMP: Stable Scoring for Few-Shot 3D Anomaly Detection via Stochastic Metric Modeling
authors: Li, Jiayi; Zhang, Jianhua; Dong, Chen
abstract: Few-shot 3D anomaly detection is challenging because memory-bank methods usually rely on deterministic k-nearest-neighbor (KNN) scoring, which is sensitive to sparse memory coverage and local perturbations. We propose SMISMP, a stochastic scoring method that estimates anomaly scores by Monte Carlo integration of Gaussian-weighted query-neighbor distances. The sample mean serves as the final score, while the sample variance provides an uncertainty estimate. As a plug-and-play modification of the scoring layer, SMISMP integrates into existing memory-based 3D anomaly detection pipelines without retraining. Experiments on 12 industrial point-cloud categories show that SMISMP improves Image-AUROC from 0.6210 to 0.6470 and reduces the cross-seed standard deviation of Pixel-AUROC from 0.0194 to 0.0106. In the selective-prediction evaluation, filtering out the top 10% most uncertain samples improves the corresponding image-level AUROC from 0.6215 to 0.6317. These results demonstrate that SMISMP enhances the robustness and reliability of few-shot 3D anomaly detection. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

title: Leakage-aware, calibrated, and explainable deep learning for robust almond disease classification
authors: Workneh, Abebaw Degu; Elkari, Badr; El Mouhtadi, Meryam; Ali, Mohammad Furqan
abstract: Reliable assessment of plant-disease classifiers requires evaluation units that reflect the intended scope of generalization. Using a field-acquired dataset of 1,717 images, we present a protocol-centred study integrating correlation-aware validation, probability calibration, selective prediction, and explainability for eight-class almond disease classification. Moving from a conventional random hold-out to grouped five-fold validation produced only a modest change in macro-F1, from 0.9941 to 0.9797, while preserving strong within-domain discrimination. Temperature scaling reduced expected calibration error from 0.036 to 0.025, and selective prediction achieved 99.7% accuracy at approximately 90% coverage. On a representative grouped fold, grayscale perturbation reduced macro-F1 to 0.8388, showing that chromatic information contributes substantially to discrimination while leaving biological and acquisition-related color effects unresolved. A complementary source-disjoint stress test based on equal weighting of independent sources yielded macro-F1 0.5587 on a single hold-out of 46 source representatives (95% bootstrap CI [0.44, 0.60]) under markedly reduced training support. Given the small sample and wide interval, this value is exploratory and does not constitute a stable cross-source estimate. Because provenance separation and effective training support changed together, this diagnostic addresses a different inferential target from grouped internal validation and identifies source diversity as a critical determinant of broader transfer. The contribution is an integrated evaluation framework that separates discrimination, calibration, abstention, interpretation, and provenance-aware generalization claims. The results support strong internal performance while motivating larger source-, acquisition-, and orchard-independent validation before operational use. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

title: Purging the Gray Zone: Latent-Geometric Denoising for Precise Knowledge Boundary Awareness
authors: An, Hao; Lou, Yibin; Guo, Jiayi; Xu, Yang
venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit hallucinations due to their inability to accurately perceive their own knowledge boundaries. Existing abstention fine-tuning methods typically partition datasets directly based on response accuracy, causing models to suffer from severe label noise near the decision boundaries and consequently exhibit high rates of abstentions or hallucinations. This paper adopts a latent space representation perspective, revealing a “gray zone” near the decision hyperplane where internal belief ambiguity constitutes the core performance bottleneck. Based on this insight, we propose the GeoDe (Geometric Denoising) framework for abstention fine-tuning. This method constructs a truth hyperplane using linear probes and performs “geometric denoising” by employing geometric distance as a confidence signal for abstention decisions. This approach filters out ambiguous boundary samples while retaining high-fidelity signals for fine-tuning. Experiments across multiple models (Llama3, Qwen3) and benchmark datasets (TriviaQA, NQ, SciQ, SimpleQA) demonstrate that GeoDe significantly enhances model truthfulness and demonstrates strong generalization in out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/Notbesidemoon/GeoDe. © 2026 Association for Computational Linguistics.

title: Robust post-selection reliability acceptance under right censoring: Closed-form feasibility optimization and familywise risk control
authors: Thavorn, Erawin; Witthayapraphakorn, Aphisak
abstract: Reliability qualification may select and evaluate a candidate using the same right-censored lifetime data, in which observation can end before failure. Without assuming independent failure and censoring times, these data identify a range of compatible fixed-horizon survival probabilities. Qualification is represented by the minimum slack across an absolute survival requirement and prespecified pairwise superiority margins. Over the primary rectangular identified set, coordinatewise monotonicity yields sharp closed-form lower and upper feasibility margins, their width, and the binding constraint. Scientifically justified cross-candidate restrictions use finite linear programs; sensitivity analysis shows when deferral changes to robust feasibility. Simultaneous one-sided Clopper–Pearson bounds formed before selection control familywise false acceptance for any measurable selector that accepts at most one candidate. A 270-cell simulation crossed censoring, candidate-set size, sample size, dependence, and survival pattern. Among 162 null or equality-boundary cells per count-based selector, 144 had no false acceptance; the maximum was 32/50,000=0.064%, and minimum simultaneous coverage was 95.335%. Four count-based selectors produced identical aggregate actions, and a Kaplan–Meier selector matched its count-based comparator across 48 continuous-time cells. Power planning found 18 identification-limited configurations; 12 attainable strong alternatives reached 80% correct acceptance at 800–4800 units per candidate. Descriptive Backblaze analyses with unverified sampling assumptions accepted four of nine exploratory pairwise comparisons but deferred all nine prespecified three-model analyses. The certificate separates incomplete identification from sampling uncertainty and model sensitivity. © 2026

title: MRQF-MAS: A Multiscale Relativistic Quantum Finance Framework for Cooperative Multi-Agent Trading Systems with Shared Knowledge Base
authors: Iovane, Gerardo; di Palma, Gabriele
abstract: Featured Application: MRQF-MAS provides an interpretable, agent-traceable high-volatility regime filter on the energy–entropy plane that can serve as a regime-aware abstention pre-filter upstream of scalar volatility estimators in risk-management and algorithmic trading pipelines. Background: price dynamics in financial markets exhibit scale-invariant volatility, quantized liquidity and collective behaviour that resist single-paradigm models; Multiscale Relativistic Quantum Finance (MRQF) reconciles these facets on an energy–entropy (Formula presented.) plane, but its translation into a deployable decision system has remained open. Methods: we propose MRQF-MAS, a cooperative multi-agent system (MAS) in which institutional, commercial and retail operators become first-class agents, each decomposed into signal, energy, entropy, risk and execution sub-agents that share beliefs through a horizontal cooperation layer and a shared knowledge base (SKB) of (Formula presented.) trajectories. The framework is benchmarked as a high-volatility regime classifier on 6978 daily EUR/USD reference rates published by the European Central Bank (ECB) over 1999–2026 against four baselines including Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroscedasticity (GARCH)(1,1). Results: on the full official ECB EUR/USD series, MRQF-MAS attains 83.0% accuracy, precision 0.552 and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) 0.479 with 95% bootstrap CI [0.46, 0.51] and a one-day median detection latency, improving slightly on a rolling-volatility baseline while remaining below a GARCH(1,1) reference. Conclusions: MRQF-MAS delivers a structurally interpretable, agent-traceable regime decomposition complementary to scalar volatility estimators. © 2026 by the authors.

title: AquaSelect: Learning when to abstain via score fusion for reliable underwater species classification
authors: Daga, Miit; Naole, Saransh; Ramu, Swarna Priya
abstract: Deep learning classifiers for fine-grained visual recognition provide no per-prediction reliability estimate, yet selective prediction methods that allow classifiers to abstain remain evaluated only on standard benchmarks, untested in domains where visual degradation drives failure patterns. We present AquaSelect, a post-hoc selective prediction framework that learns when to abstain rather than risk a misclassification. AquaSelect trains a lightweight binary selection head of 213K parameters on a frozen backbone to predict classifier correctness, fusing this with temperature-calibrated confidence and image quality features via interpretable logistic regression. Because the backbone remains frozen, the selection head can be retrained for new environments without touching the base classifier. Evaluated on two underwater species datasets, AQUA20 with 8,171 images across 20 classes and Sea Animals with 13,711 images across 23 classes, using ConvNeXt-Tiny and DeiT-Small backbones across three seeds, AquaSelect outperforms Softmax Response and Monte Carlo Dropout on all six seed-backbone evaluations on AQUA20 and improves mean coverage metrics on Sea Animals. At 80% coverage, accuracy rises from 87.3% to 94.8% and Macro F1 from 81.5% to 88.6%, surpassing the benchmark full-data accuracy of 90.69% despite using 15% less training data. We also report that RAPS conformal prediction sets averaging 3.7 to 5.0 classes are impractical for single-label classification, and fusing set sizes with learned scores degrades selection quality. Ablation identifies the learned selection head as the dominant component. The framework runs at 149 FPS, 2.8 times faster than Deep Ensembles, and applies to any classification system where errors carry asymmetric costs. © 2026

title: Comparative evaluation of embedding and generative model combinations in retrieval-augmented generation pipelines
authors: Hitl, Mateo; Bagić Babac, Marina; Mornar, Vedran
abstract: Purpose – Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems integrate information retrieval with generative language models to improve the relevance, accuracy and explainability of AI-driven responses. This study evaluates how different configurations of embedding and generative models nfluence the performance of RAGpipelines for knowledge management (KM) scenarios. Design/methodology/approach – The study combines a broad benchmark of embedding and generation components with a contemporary open-weight comparison centered on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 and Gemma-2-9B-It. Retrieval configurations are evaluated through recall, latency and storage trade-offs, while generation quality is assessed using ROUGE-L, exact match (EM), token-level F1, BERTScore F1, semantic similarity, answer relevance and faithfulness. The benchmark also includes complementary evaluation on SQuAD and HotpotQA, grounded prompting, abstention prompting, error analysis and long-context stress testing. Findings – Retrieval quality remained the main determinant of end-to-end RAG quality. The strongest shared retrieval setup combined all-mpnet-base-v2, 256-token chunking with 64-token overlap and top-1 retrieval, reaching Recall@1 = 0.938. Among the open-weight generators, Gemma-2-9B-It achieved the strongest lexical and semantic matching, with its best grounded-abstain configuration reaching ROUGE-L = 0.631, EM = 0.456, token-F1 = 0.631 and BERTScore F1 = 0.767. Llama-3-8B-Instruct produced the strongest faithfulness score in the best grounded setting (0.241), while Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 occupied a more conservative operating point with lower answer matching but stronger abstention behavior. HNSW matched exact-search quality for equivalent retrieval configurations while reducing query latency. Practical implications – The findings support retrieval chunking, top-1 retrieval and grounded prompting as robust design choices for question-answering-oriented RAG. They also suggest that safer abstention-oriented prompting should be treated as a different operating point rather than as a universal default. Social implications – More reliable RAG systems can improve access to institutional knowledge, support organizational learning and reduce barriers to expertise discovery, especially when system designs balance quality, latency and computational cost. Originality/value – The paper contributes a component-level benchmark for RAG in KM settings, richer evaluation dimensions and a more explicit treatment of retrieval/generation trade-offs across historical and contemporary open-weight baselines. The design narrows practical claims to what is supported by multi-dataset evidence, error analysis and long-context testing. © 2026, Emerald Publishing Limited

title: SCOPE: Subgroup-Calibrated Selective Prediction for Compact Vision-Language Models in Edge Chest X-Ray View Classification
authors: Wang, Ziwei; Zhu, Di; Zhang, Yanyan; Huang, Yuxuan; Zhong, Jiachen; Wang, Yiting; Li, Weiyi
venue: 2026 11th International Conference on Machine Learning Technologies, ICMLT 2026
abstract: Compact vision-language models (VLMs) are attractive for privacy-aware healthcare deployment, but their reliability is difficult to control when APIs expose generated text rather than trustworthy class probabilities. We study AP/PA chest Xray view classification as a controlled testbed and present SCOPE, a subgroup-calibrated selective prediction framework for scorelimited compact VLMs. SCOPE uses prompt-constrained JSON inference, confidence-proxy extraction with isotonic calibration, and subgroup-specific threshold selection. We evaluate Qwen2.5-VL, MiniCPM-V, Gemma-7B, and LLaVA-7B on a patient-level benchmark and compare against standard vision-only baselines for context. Tier-0 compact-VLM accuracy ranges from 0.54 to 0.63. After calibration and subgroup-aware selective prediction, holdout operating points reach 0.75-0.88 coverage, 0.69-0.74 accepted-case accuracy, and 0.04-0.07 subgroup ECE. Compared with a single global threshold, subgroup-aware deployment improves accepted-case accuracy and calibration with modest coverage loss. The results suggest that compact multimodal models are more dependable when deployed as calibrated selective predictors rather than unconditional classifiers. © 2026 IEEE.

title: Remind Me of Something? Zero-Shot Learning for Trustworthy Image Comparison in Rolling Stock
authors: Papini, Oscar; Corso, Giulio Del; Bulotta, Davide; Carboni, Andrea; Gravili, Silvia; Leone, Giuseppe Riccardo; Pascali, Maria Antonietta; Moroni, Davide; Colantonio, Sara
abstract: This paper discusses the need for trustworthy AI in urban mobility, focusing on high-stakes security applications such as anomaly detection in public transportation. Because the accuracy required to identify potentially dangerous objects often surpasses the capabilities of current models, there is an unavoidable incidence of false positives. We suggest a “learning to defer” approach as a solution. Our technique uses the deep features and label relative importance of a pre-trained classifier (DenseNet/ImageNET-1k) to create a unique item “fingerprint”. We then employ a zero-shot meta-learning approach to calibrate the system, enabling it to distinguish between normal background items and genuine anomalies by assigning a similarity score. This method significantly reduces the false “new object” alarms that would otherwise overwhelm human operators. Our proof-of-concept demonstrates that the system is computationally light and can be easily adapted to specific environments and integrated into existing classification modules. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

title: Transparent Self-Calibrating Neurointerfaces for Visual Information Substitution
authors: Kimura, Akira
abstract: Restorative neurotechnologies demand individual training, yet sensory substitution lacks an empirical doctrine for how long training should last and for whom. We propose a transparent self-calibration framework in which the quantities used for adaptation and the assumptions linking them to design are stated as falsifiable hypotheses before adaptive control. The central latent quantity is the cumulative period of functional vision. Estimation fragility is assessed with Metric-T, while a critical-period hypothesis links visual history to decoding latency and behavioural fragility. A latency-distribution model converts that fragility into a warning-lead-time specification and dual-pathway hazard design. We then interrogate the measurement layer using 128-Hz pilot EEG from 13 blind (4 congenital, 9 acquired) and 6 blindfolded sighted participants, together with conditional simulation. The prespecified frontopolar gamma-latency candidate did not meet the reliability requirement; exploratory power-adjusted analysis instead identified left-lateralised alpha connections T7–Pz and AF3–T7 as candidates for prospective replication. Simulations show how few-shot acquisition, adaptive duration, and confidence-based deferral would operate if reliable measurements were available. The contribution is therefore a falsifiable theory-to-measurement architecture: autonomous calibration should proceed only after the quantities required by the model are measurable and analytically robust. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

title: Estimating Causal Effects from Tabular Data with Assumption Gates and Automated Estimator Selection for Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence
authors: Berti, Alessandro
abstract: Causal analysis can guide decisions by estimating how interventions change outcomes and making the assumptions behind those estimates explicit. We present the Causal World Foundation Model, a framework for answering causal questions from tabular data. It checks declared conditions, combines classical estimators, and calibrates uncertainty. Effect queries receive an estimate with diagnostics or an explanation for refusal. A pretrained neural router serves as a baseline for comparing estimator selection and aggregation policies. The evaluation covers treatment effects, observed regimes, and network interference, alongside a semi-synthetic test using energy sensor covariates. In confirmatory experiments, a shallow selector and a convex stack improve accuracy over the evaluated deep router. Stress tests demonstrate consistent refusal when declared conditions fail, while causal interpretation remains conditional on truthful and complete declarations. A separate audit clarifies the strengths and limitations of empirical support checks. Together, these findings support a practical approach to transparent causal artificial intelligence through flexible estimator selection and clear reporting of assumptions, uncertainty, and decision reasons. © 2026 by the author.

title: Learning Selective Deferral Policies for Reliable Medical Text Classification
authors: Albalawi, Tahani; Alzahrani, Amani
abstract: Medical text classification is an important task in biomedical natural language processing, but prediction errors remain problematic in high-stakes settings where reliability matters in addition to accuracy. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a learned selective deferral framework for biomedical sentence classification that allows uncertain predictions to be deferred under constrained review budgets. The framework combines a transformer-based classifier with uncertainty estimation, temperature scaling, and a learned deferral policy that predicts the likelihood of model error from multiple signals, including confidence, entropy, calibration-aware features, and Monte Carlo Dropout descriptors. Deferral decisions are applied under fixed budgets to improve the use of limited review capacity. Experiments on the PubMed 200k RCT dataset show that budget-constrained deferral reduces system-level risk. Using PubMedBERT as the primary backbone, deferring 20% of the highest-risk cases reduces system risk from 0.1108 to 0.0360. Compared with a calibrated confidence-threshold baseline, the learned policy provides modest but generally favorable improvements, with statistical significance observed at the 20% budget. Additional experiments across PubMedBERT, BioBERT, and SciBERT suggest that the framework transfers across biomedical transformer backbones, while calibration improves the reliability of confidence estimates and learned policies outperform random deferral. © 2026 by the authors.

title: A Modality-Adaptive System for Real-World Colorectal Polyp Classification
authors: Chen, Erdong; Chen, Qilei; Yang, Yingyun; Hu, Wenmo; Wu, Dong; Yang, Aiming; Liang, Xiaolong; Cao, Yu; Liu, Benyuan
venue: Proceedings - 2026 IEEE/ACM Conference on Connected Health: Applications, Systems and Engineering Technologies, CHASE 2026
abstract: Colorectal polyps are precursors to colorectal cancer, a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. While early detection and removal during colonoscopy are effective preventive measures, automated polyp classification remains challenging due to substantial appearance variability and the domain gap between curated public datasets and artifact-heavy real-world clinical frames. In this study, we propose a context-aware AI system for three-class polyp classification - adenomas, hyperplastic polyps, and sessile serrated lesions (SSLs) - using a large-scale private dataset of 4,094 real-world colonoscopy images collected under routine clinical conditions. Unlike conventional pipelines that apply uniform preprocessing across modalities, our unified framework introduces Modality-Adaptive Context Expansion, which tailors contextual scaling to modality-specific imaging characteristics. Specifically, we integrate YOLOv8-based field-of-view extraction, Mask R-CNN-based localization, and a Swin Transformer classifier with modality-specific context scaling (1.5× for WLI and 2.0× for NBI) to better balance noise suppression and discriminative contextual cues. Furthermore, we incorporate a confidence-based abstention mechanism (threshold > 0.8) to defer low-confidence predictions for human review, enabling a practical reliability-coverage tradeoff in a clinical decision-support workflow. Extensive experiments and ablation studies show that, on NBI images, the proposed system achieves high specificity (91.21%) on real-world clinical frames. Moreover, compared to standard fixed-crop pipelines, Modality-Adaptive Context Expansion improves NBI classification performance, increasing accuracy by +9.2% and specificity by +4.6%. © 2026 IEEE.

title: Research on calibrated and cost-sensitive vulnerability alert governance for open-source software auditing
authors: Feng, Xiaorong; Gao, Ying; Gu, Xin; Jian, Zhibin
abstract: Context: Open-source vulnerability auditing increasingly combines static analyzers, rule-based scanners, and learning-based detectors, but triage workflows often treat raw detector scores as if they were reliable probabilities. Objective: This paper studies how security teams can turn heterogeneous detector outputs into auditable decisions that account for uncertainty, review cost, and unsafe-ignore risk. Methods: We propose a calibrated and cost-sensitive governance framework that separates detector scoring from final action selection and explicitly models three actions: Fix, Review, and Ignore. The main experiment evaluates 2740 registered OWASP Benchmark Java prediction rows with independent train, calibration, and test splits, using outputs from CodeBERT, CodeQL, Semgrep, and SpotBugs/FindSecBugs. Results: The registered CodeBERT executor collapses under the fixed 0.5 threshold because its scores are concentrated around 0.997. A calibration-split threshold produces TP/FP/TN/FN = 139/124/61/69 on the test split, with F1 = 0.5902, AUROC = 0.5256, and AUPRC = 0.5455. Under the registered baseline protocol, Semgrep outperforms the rectified CodeBERT output. Calibration reduces overconfidence, hybrid review-oriented policies eliminate unsafe auto-ignore on the test split by routing nearly all samples to review, and a review-budget simulation shows that increasing review capacity from 10% to 100% reduces false-positive fixes from 167 to 0 under the selected rule-union policy. A Vul4J real-project study further executes three Java project cases, producing Semgrep JSON, SpotBugs XML, compiled CodeQL SARIF artifacts, and official target-test evidence for the selected vulnerable and fixed revisions. Conclusion: The results indicate that calibrated and cost-sensitive governance provides a practical decision layer for vulnerability auditing by improving auditability, reducing unsafe automatic dismissal under review-aware policies, and making review workload and safety-cost trade-offs explicit. © 2026 The Authors

title: Knowing when to escalate: Prompt-based uncertainty quantification for selective automation of LLM-based intrusion detection
authors: Assidiqi, Mohammad Hasbi; Alghazzawi, Daniyal; Alarifi, Suaad; Cheng, Li
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can classify network flows for intrusion detection, but safe deployment depends less on raw accuracy than on knowing when to defer to a human: a model must flag which decisions to automate and which to escalate. We study whether black-box, prompt-based uncertainty quantification (UQ) can support such a selective-automation (accept/escalate/reject) policy. We present the first systematic comparison of seven prompt-based UQ methods across five LLMs and two benchmarks (CIC-IDS2017, CIC-IDS2018) with stratified sampling (n=750 per dataset), spanning self-report confidence, multi-prompt voting, Monte Carlo prompting, Cross-Variant Sampling, and three penalty-adjusted variants. Three findings emerge. First, the binding constraint on safe automation is classification accuracy, not calibration: with a mean accepted accuracy of 0.630 — well below the 0.95 operational target — even well-calibrated uncertainty cannot license autonomous acceptance, so UQ's value here is escalation, not full automation. Second, Penalty-Adjusted Multi-Prompt Voting (PA-MPV) attains the lowest mean calibration error (ECE = 0.217) at zero additional API cost over plain multi-prompt voting (ECE = 0.243), whereas Monte Carlo prompting severely degrades calibration (ECE = 0.597); penalty adjustment lowers ECE for all base methods, but only deterministic ones beat baseline. The modest PA-MPV and MPV gains are not significant after multiple-comparison correction, whereas the stochastic-method degradations are. Third, reasoning-specialized models are more accurate than general-purpose models (0.675 versus 0.604), but their calibration advantage largely vanishes at scale. These results reframe prompt-based UQ as a triage mechanism—valuable for routing uncertain cases to human analysts, but not, at current accuracy, for unsupervised automation. © 2026 The Authors

title: Detecting AI-Generated Vietnamese Essays with Calibrated Uncertainty and Explainable AI
authors: Nguyen, Hoang-Anh; Hoang, Ngoc-Tuan; Huynh, Minh-Phuc; Le, Anh-Cuong
abstract: The proliferation of large language models (LLMs) capable of generating human-quality text poses unprecedented challenges for academic integrity in secondary education. However, AI text detection in educational settings is fundamentally a decision-making problem under uncertainty, as classifiers inevitably produce errors and naive binary predictions fail to communicate prediction reliability. Despite extensive research, two critical gaps remain: limited exploration of Vietnamese, a morphologically distinct language central to national curricula; and insufficient integration of principled uncertainty quantification for risk-aware selective prediction. We address these gaps through three contributions. First, we construct ViLitDetect, a balanced dataset of 10,000 Vietnamese literary essays spanning seven grade levels, with 5,000 human essays paired with 5,000 AI-generated counterparts from five frontier LLMs. Second, we propose an uncertainty-aware detection framework combining Qwen3-Embedding-4B with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning, a two-layer multilayer perceptron (MLP) with Supervised Contrastive (SupCon) loss, and Monte Carlo (MC) Dropout for calibrated uncertainty estimates. The framework achieves 99.40% accuracy. Critically, MC Dropout enables selective prediction; by deferring only the 1.1% most uncertain samples to human review, the system maintains 99.697% accuracy on the automated subset. Third, sentence-level explainability analysis provides educators with interpretable rationales for each prediction. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

title: DRIFTBENCH: Long-Horizon Memory Benchmark For AI Agents
authors: Sunil Kumar, P.; Reddi, Seethi Venkata Sai Gowtham; Sai Chaitanya, P.
venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
abstract: Persistent memory is essential for AI agents expected to operate across extended, multi-session interactions; however, conventional benchmarks often emphasize bounded-context recall and provide limited insight into how memory performance changes over time. This study introduces DRIFTBENCH, a controlled benchmark for evaluating long-horizon agent memory through repeated factual updates, increasing memory interference, and delayed retrieval. The benchmark comprised 120 synthetic scenarios distributed across personal assistance, project-state management, travel and logistics, and collaborative workflows. Each scenario extended over 35 days and included stable facts, mutable attributes, timestamped revisions, graded distractor loads, delayed probes, and unanswerable queries. Five memory architectures were evaluated: sliding window, Vector RAG, graph memory, temporal slots, and Hybrid fusion. Performance was assessed using update fidelity, interference resistance, normalized decay area, abstention accuracy, retrieval latency, and an overall DRIFTBENCH score. Hybrid fusion achieved the highest overall score (0.920), update fidelity (0.918), interference resistance (0.946), and decay AUC (0.922). It retained an accuracy of 0.882 under 1,000 distractor memories and a day-35 recall of 0.877. Temporal slots ranked second overall (0.874) and achieved the lowest median retrieval latency of 116 ms, indicating the most favourable accuracy–efficiency balance. Graph memory showed intermediate robustness, whereas Vector RAG and the sliding-window baseline deteriorated more sharply under repeated revisions, distractor accumulation, and longer retention intervals. The findings demonstrate that reliable long-horizon agent memory requires explicit temporal validity, version control, selective retrieval, and resistance to interference rather than reliance on context length or semantic similarity alone. DRIFTBENCH provides a reproducible framework for diagnosing memory degradation and comparing persistent-memory architectures across controlled longitudinal conditions. © 2026, SvedbergOpen. All rights reserved.

title: Empirical fair auditing of high-confidence failures under distribution shift
authors: Bastola, Laxmi Prasad; Luo, Senlin; Munna, Md Minhazul Islam; Khan, Sohrab
abstract: Fair auditing of high-confidence failures is crucial for validating the trustworthiness of machine-learning decision-support systems operating under distribution shift. While selective classification and out-of-distribution detection have attracted growing interest, three core challenges remain unresolved. Existing abstention methods suffer from the following limitations: they do not explicitly target high-confidence errors and therefore waste review budget on lower-confidence regions where such failures are unlikely; they are typically evaluated only at a single deployment snapshot, making them brittle under progressive distribution shift; and they ignore fairness, allowing subgroup disparities in high-confidence failures to remain hidden. To address these issues, we propose an empirical fair-auditing framework for budget-constrained review under distribution shift. In particular, τ-gating confines monitoring to the τ-target eligible high-confidence region, aligning alert selection with the audit objective and reducing budget waste, while fairness-aware alert allocation combines risk-based prioritization with parity and bounded group-allocation policies to reduce disparities across sensitive groups. The proposed approach is evaluated on ACSIncome, Diabetic Readmission, CivilComments, and a cross-domain text shift (CivilComments → Jigsaw) over 20 random seeds against standard baselines. The experimental results demonstrate an HC-AUC of 0.944 on Diabetic Readmission, Lift@5 of 9.518 on Diabetic Readmission and 4.561 on ACSIncome, and a reduction in alert-rate disparity of up to 99.8% under parity allocation at negligible utility cost, establishing a practical foundation for knowledge-driven, fairness-aware decision support in high-stakes AI systems. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

title: Evaluating Case Selection for Human Oversight in Clinical AI
authors: Cha, Yu-Jung

title: One Signature, Two Threats: Grammar Scored Cross-Channel Disagreement for Robust Traffic Sign Recognition
authors: Fayzullaev, Mirjalol; Axmedova, Aziza; Oh, Ryumduck
abstract: Traffic sign recognition (TSR) sits on the critical path of advanced driver assistance and autonomous driving, yet deployed classifiers fail in two qualitatively distinct regimes that prior work has largely defended against in isolation worst case adversarial manipulation from imperceptible digital perturbations to physically realizable stickers, patches, and outline-conforming edge attacks and average case environmental degradation such as fog, glare, motion blur, fading, and occlusion. We observe that, despite their differing origins, both regimes leave the same observable signature on the over specified structure of a sign whose class is redundantly encoded by the silhouette, color scheme, and central pictogram: a spatially localized disagreement among otherwise independent cues, scored against a small, enumerable grammar of physically valid attribute tuples. Recasting robustness as detection of this signature rather than defense against any single threat, we propose SAFER-Sign, which integrates four components that each repair a documented failure mode of prior approaches: (i) class conditionally decorrelated shape, color, and glyph encoders that render over the specification genuine rather than nominal; (ii) evidential per channel uncertainty that lets a degraded cue abstain instead of voting confidently wrong; (iii) a soft, factorized, confidence gated sign grammar prior that rewards jointly consistent tuples without becoming a single attribute attack surface; and (iv) a jointly trained spatial reliability gate anchored to a parameter-free cross-channel disagreement signal, so it cannot be suppressed like a decoupled front end. Taken together, these components mean that a successful adaptive attack in our evaluated settings had to jointly address class evidence, cross channel consistency, grammar compatibility, reliability gating, and abstention. This raises the number of coupled attack objectives, but we emphasize that it does not guarantee that all three channels must be corrupted. © 2026 by the authors.

title: Calibration-Aware Lightweight Model Selection for Trustworthy Skin Lesion Classification
authors: Oladele, Daniel Ayo; Akinyemi, Lateef Adesola; Sumbwanyambe, Mbuyu; Luo, Yifan; Mnkandla, Ernest; Sibiya, Malusi
abstract: Lightweight skin-lesion classifiers are attractive for resource-constrained dermatology support, but accuracy-only selection can be unsafe when predictions are miscalibrated, rare classes are unstable, or uncertain cases should be referred. This paper presents a calibration-aware benchmark across HAM10000, ISIC 2019, and PAD-UFES-20. We evaluate ResNet18, MobileNetV2, MobileNetV3-Small, MobileViT-XXS, EfficientNet-B0, EfficientNetV2-B0, EfficientNetV2-S, and the proposed compact distillation student UAX-Distill-Lite under a shared multi-seed protocol. Beyond accuracy, the study reports macro-F1, balanced accuracy, AUROC, ECE, Brier score, sensitivity/specificity, malignant-versus-benign risk, uncertainty-based abstention, corruption robustness, cross-dataset transfer, test-time augmentation, deployment cost, and Grad-CAM auditing. EfficientNetV2-S is strongest on HAM10000 (macro-F1 0.708, AUROC 0.953) and ISIC 2019 (macro-F1 0.632, AUROC 0.911), while EfficientNet-B0 leads PAD-UFES-20 clinical-photo classification (macro-F1 0.720, AUROC 0.922). At 60% coverage, selective prediction improves retained-case macro-F1 to 0.876, 0.758, and 0.811 on the three datasets. The results show that preferred lightweight classifiers change when calibration, referral behavior, binary clinical risk, domain shift, and deployment cost are evaluated jointly. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

title: SPID: A Security Principle Instantiation Detector for Security Explanation Text
authors: Brown, Caitlin; Morisset, Charles
abstract: We present SPID, a Security Principle Instantiation Detector for security explanation text. Whether a security explanation is right or wrong is hard to judge, because explanation quality has no ground truth. Whether a unit of text instantiates a security design principle is a more tractable question, and one that any principle-grounded account of explanation quality must answer first. Security principles encode community consensus on why specific design properties improve security. Identifying the principle a unit argues for therefore connects it to reasoning that can be assessed independently of the individual explanation: a reader who accepts the principle has reason to accept the argument. SPID labels each sentence-level unit of an explanation with the Basin et al. principle it instantiates, abstaining when the text only describes a mechanism. A unit instantiates a principle when it argues that the design property the principle names improves security, not merely when it mentions a related concept. The tool combines a fine-tuned Claims-Evidence (CE) classifier with a three-stage principle detector. The staged design separates abstention from classification across three inference calls: SPID reaches macro F1 of 0.879 on a controlled synthetic set of 1,798 responses while abstaining on 100% of principle-free text, whereas a single-call variant produces a 67% false positive rate and a zero-shot NLI baseline reaches only 0.696. Three lines of evidence support the tool’s validity. Detection rates track the expected density of principle instantiation across eight corpora. Within NIST 800-53, a fourteen-fold gap between rationale sections and requirement sections isolates argumentative function from topic. As a demonstration, applying SPID to 500 Security Stack Exchange comments surfaces principle instantiations in fewer than 13% of them, illustrating the analysis the tool supports in educational, community, and assurance settings. We release the code, the prompts, and the evaluation data. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

title: Answering the Unanswerable Is to Err Knowingly: Analyzing and Mitigating Abstention Failures in Large Reasoning Models
authors: Liu, Yi; Liu, Xiangyu; Sun, Zequn; Hu, Wei
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have shown remarkable progress on complex reasoning tasks. However, some questions posed to LRMs are inherently unanswerable, such as math problems lacking sufficient conditions. We find that LRMs continually fail to provide appropriate abstentions when confronted with these unanswerable questions. In this paper, we systematically analyze, investigate, and resolve this issue for trustworthy AI. We first conduct a detailed analysis of the distinct response behaviors of LRMs when facing unanswerable questions. Then, we show that LRMs possess sufficient cognitive capabilities to recognize the flaws in these questions. However, they fail to exhibit appropriate abstention behavior, revealing a misalignment between their internal cognition and external response. Finally, to resolve this issue, we propose a lightweight, two-stage method that combines cognitive monitoring with inference-time intervention. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly improves the abstention rate while maintaining the reasoning performance. © 2026, Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (www.aaai.org). All rights reserved.

title: MaGOS-IDS: A Mahalanobis-Enhanced OpenMax Method for Graph Neural Network-Based Intrusion Detection
authors: Nguyen, Thanh-Tung; Park, Minho
