Experimental results demonstrate strong performance (0.91 accuracy, 0.90 F1-score, 0.95 AUC), along with improved calibration (ECE 0.041) and reliable uncertainty handling (0.84 coverage), making it suitable for clinical risk assessment and decision support. © 2026 IEEE.

abstract: The proceedings contain 33 papers. The special focus in this conference is on Social Networks Analysis and Mining. title: Human–AI Deferral under Limited Expert Availability: A Study in Intraoperative Ischemia Detection
authors: Murali, Nihal; Elzokm, Karim; Thirumala, Parthasarathy; Batmanghelich, Kayhan; Visweswaran, Shyam
abstract: Intraoperative neuromonitoring (IONM) during carotid endarterectomy (CEA) is used to monitor cerebral ischemia, but reliable interpretation depends on scarce expert neurophysiologists. Because many medical tasks are safety-critical, relying solely on artificial intelligence (AI) is impractical. We study how human–AI deferral methods perform in this setting and also introduce Learning to Augment (L2A), a simple method that selectively incorporates human input into AI predictions. We evaluate these methods on intraoperative electroencephalographic data from 400 CEA cases in a large U.S. academic health system. Unlike prior deferral work that focuses on non-clinical tasks and relies on expert humans, we use novice monitors with no prior IONM experience and only brief training. We use these novices as a conservative lower-bound test of whether non-expert human input contains complementary information, not as a proposed replacement for clinically trained personnel. Across methods, human–AI deferral shows that substantial gains over the AI alone can be achieved with minimal human involvement, even when the human is a novice. With just 5–10% novice involvement, L2A improves precision and sensitivity by ∼40%, and the area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) by ∼20% compared to the AI model alone. Importantly, while some deferral methods degrade with less experienced human input, others such as L2A remain robust with better calibration. We further observe that these methods produce sparse and temporally clustered deferral decisions, enabling long periods without human intervention. These properties make human–AI deferral approaches practical in settings where expert neurophysiologists are not available. .

title: Sinkhorn-Regularized Uncertainty Quantification for LLMs via entropic optimal transport
authors: Cong, Jin
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve remarkable performance but exhibit poorly calibrated confidence estimates. Existing calibration methods ignore the semantic geometry of token spaces, treating semantically similar predictions (e.g., “correct” vs. “right”) as entirely distinct, and lack formal guarantees under distribution shift. We propose Sinkhorn-Regularized Uncertainty Quantification for Calibration (SUQC), recasting LLM calibration as an entropy-regularized optimal transport problem. Our contributions include: (1) the Sinkhorn Calibration Metric (SCM), quantifying miscalibration via minimum-cost alignment between predicted confidence and empirical accuracy distributions using semantic token embeddings; (2) information-theoretic generalization bounds characterizing the calibration-transfer tradeoff with explicit regularization dependence; and (3) an efficient O(Vk) inference-time algorithm using sparse Sinkhorn iterations with k-nearest-neighbor semantic kernels. Experiments on TruthfulQA, MMLU, Natural Questions, and TriviaQA demonstrate a 17.7–22.4% reduction in Expected Calibration Error relative to the strongest baseline (up to 25% relative to Deep Ensembles) and improved selective prediction AUROC. SUQC shows enhanced robustness under domain shift, establishing optimal transport as a principled foundation for LLM uncertainty quantification. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Cervical Cancer Dataset Catalog (CCDCAT-U_v1.0; Release v0.1): A Machine-Readable, Reproducible Catalog of Discoverable Human Cervical Cancer and Pre-Cancer Datasets Across Modalities
authors: Tune, Kula Kekeba; Mohammed, Foziya Ahmed; Mohammed, Juhar Ahmed; Muhie, Seid
abstract: Human cervical cancer and pre-cancer research relies on datasets scattered across modality-specific archives, imaging repositories, benchmark platforms, trial registries, and controlled-access catalogs. This fragmentation—combined with heterogeneous metadata, ambiguous use of “cervical” terminology, and inconsistent indexing of pre-cancer and screening/triage resources—limits reproducible discovery, access planning, and cross-modal benchmarking. We present the Cervical Cancer Dataset Catalog (CCDCAT), a machine-readable, versioned dataset of datasets that enumerates host-specific dataset-instance records anchored to stable identifiers and resolvable landing records within an explicitly declared discoverable source universe (U_v1.0) and a frozen discovery/labeling lexicon (Q_v1.0). The CCDCAT spans invasive cervical cancer, pre-cancer/dysplasia, and cervix-focused screening and triage phenotypes, and it covers molecular omics, imaging and microscopy (including cervix photography, cytology, and digital pathology), trial registry records, benchmark resources, and controlled-access catalogs represented as metadata with explicit access pathways. Eligibility and labels are assigned conservatively from source-provided metadata; when evidence is insufficient, the CCDCAT abstains rather than infers. In the initial release (CCDCAT-U_v1.0; v0.1), we enumerate 14 eligible dataset instances across 11 host systems within a declared universe of 21 sources. Releases include manuscript-ready tables and interoperable artifacts (schema, controlled vocabularies, provenance logs, abstention ledgers, and a queryable database), enabling reproducible filtering, linkage, and auditable reuse planning. Dataset: The Cervical Cancer Dataset Catalog (CCDCAT-U_v1.0, v0.1) is a versioned, machine-readable dataset of datasets for discoverable human cervical cancer and pre-cancer resources across modalities (omics; imaging and microscopy, including cervix photography, cytology, and digital pathology; clinical trial registry records; benchmark resources; and controlled-access catalogs). The release contains normalized metadata tables, the CCDCAT schema and controlled vocabularies, provenance and query logs, an abstention ledger, and a queryable database. The CCDCAT is metadata-only: it provides stable host identifiers and resolvable landing-page references to original source records, together with access pathways and requirements, but it does not host or redistribute participant-level primary data (e.g., omics files, images, or other protected files) governed by external repositories. The DOI/link was submitted as supplementary material to this manuscript. Dataset License: CC0 1.0 Universal (applies to CCDCAT metadata and release artifacts only). Underlying source datasets remain under their original repository-specific licenses and access/governance conditions. © 2026 by the authors.

title: Trustworthy Generation and Verification-Guided Correction for ChatGPT-Type Large Language Models: Symmetry-Aware Technical Mechanisms and Ethical Risk Analysis
authors: Gong, Xihan; Zhu, Chunyan
abstract: Reliable retrieval-augmented generation requires consistency across query interpretation, evidence selection, and final answer generation. This study defines computational symmetry as bidirectional coverage among canonical query constraints, traceable evidence, and answer claims, with residual asymmetry triggering correction or abstention. The proposed framework integrates a source-linked raw text/entity/event knowledge graph, hybrid dense–sparse retrieval, cross-encoder reranking, pre-retrieval semantic alignment, and a post-retrieval verification gate. DeepSeek-V3 serves as the implementation backbone, while “ChatGPT-type” denotes the broader class of instruction-following conversational large language models. Experiments use T2Ranking for retrieval and reranking, ATIS for diagnostic intent–slot evaluation, and controlled dialogue scenarios derived from T2Ranking. The hierarchical representation improves retrieval F1 from 0.586 to 0.660, while the complete pipeline increases average answer correctness from 0.530 to 0.611 compared with direct LLM answering and from 0.559 to 0.611 compared with graph retrieval. On ATIS, the controller achieves 92.61% intent accuracy, below Joint BERT at 95.18%, and is therefore treated as a reusable orchestration module rather than a superior classifier. The results support the proposed verification correction framework within the tested settings, without claiming superiority over untested adaptive RAG systems. © 2026 by the authors.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Single-Channel Surface EMG Classification for Low-Resource Hand Gesture Recognition: A Subject-Independent Evaluation
authors: Aydoğan, Yiğit; Cantürk, İsmail
venue: Medical and Biological Engineering and Computing
abstract: Abstract: Single-channel surface electromyography (sEMG) could reduce the cost and complexity of hand-gesture interfaces, but performance commonly degrades when models are tested on unseen subjects. We evaluated five-class hand gesture classification using only the Flexor Carpi Radialis (FCR) channel from 83 quality-screened subjects drawn from 113 recordings. Time-domain (TD) features were classified with multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) and three uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods: Monte Carlo (MC) Dropout, Deep Ensembles, and Evidential Deep Learning (EDL). A raw-window one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN) and a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) were included as end-to-end comparators. The best within-subject result was obtained by Random Forest at, while full-coverage leave-one-subject-out cross-validation (LOSOCV) accuracy was for the MLP baseline; all UQ methods were statistically indistinguishable from this baseline after Holm correction. Confidence-based selective prediction improved per-subject accuracy to at coverage and at coverage, but this gain was achieved equally by plain MLP softmax confidence and by MC Dropout, indicating that the improvement arises from the confidence-ordering property of softmax outputs rather than from stochastic inference. The deterministic MLP achieved the best calibration (Expected Calibration Error, ECE), while EDL showed vacuity collapse and was the only method to degrade under selective prediction (ECE). Both 1D-CNN and TCN showed numerically lower LOSOCV accuracy than the TD+MLP pipeline under the evaluated preprocessing configuration, though the differences were not statistically significant after Holm correction; loss of amplitude information through per-sample normalisation is a plausible contributing factor. Per-class analysis revealed that selective prediction gains are structurally concentrated in the rest class, which is retained at coverage with near-perfect accuracy (); excluding rest, active-gesture accuracy at coverage was only. This rest-class dominance effect has direct implications for how selective prediction should be evaluated in sEMG datasets that include a rest class. External validation on NinaPro DB2 (40 subjects, one circumferential forearm channel) confirmed above-chance classification () but showed no meaningful correlation between uncertainty and per-subject accuracy (), indicating that the UQ mechanism does not generalise to this dataset. These results indicate that standard softmax confidence, requiring no additional training or inference overhead, is sufficient for rejection-based low-resource sEMG deployment under the evaluated conditions; computationally expensive stochastic inference methods provide no measurable additional benefit on low-dimensional tabular features. © The Author(s) 2026.

title: Anatomy-Aware Routing for Robust Medical Image Segmentation: A Failure-Detectable Alternative to Mixed Models
authors: Khan, Musab Ahmed; Salem, Mohammed Sateh
venue: SIU 2026 - 34th Signal Processing and Communications Applications Conference, Conference Proceedings
abstract: Heterogeneous medical segmentation pipelines that use a single shared model lose organ-specific feature learning and degrade silently under distribution shift. We propose an anatomy-aware framework where an upstream classifier routes inputs to dedicated specialist networks, combined with a composite post-hoc failure detector based on MC-Dropout uncertainty, domain-shift detection, and plausibility checking. Using chest X-ray pneumothorax and brain MRI datasets, we show anatomy-aware routing yields higher segmentation accuracy (+8.6-14.4 Dice points) compared to a mixed-organ baseline. Our failure detector achieves flag rates of 1.000 on misrouted pneumothorax cases and 0.963 on brain cases. In contrast, under identical noise, the mixed model produces flag rates of only 0.173 and 0.156. Anatomy-aware pipelines offer superior accuracy and the ability to fail loudly, allowing safer clinical deployment through explicit abstention. © 2026 IEEE.

title: Not all Errors are Equal: Improving Worst-Group Accuracy with Disagreement-Based Selective Prediction: A Post-Hoc Abstention Mechanism for Reliable Prediction Under Biased Training Data
authors: Varsh, Amogh; Anand, Ankita; Joshi, Ashwini M.
venue: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
abstract: Deep learning models trained with empirical risk minimization often achieve high average accuracy while systematically failing on underrepresented subgroups. This disparity arises from spurious correlations in the training data and creates a reliability risk. We propose a lightweight, post-hoc disagreement-based selective prediction framework that abstains on inputs where subgroup-specific failure is likely, without requiring group annotations at training or inference time, aside from optional validation-time tuning. Our approach pairs a standard empirical risk minimization model with a class-balanced, last-layer retrained model and abstains when they disagree, a signal that empirically concentrates on minority-group samples where spurious decision boundaries between the models diverge. On Waterbirds, CelebA, and HAM10000, disagreement improves worst-group accuracy over entropy-based abstention by 11.4, 19.5, and 2.3 percentage points, respectively at matched coverage. On CelebA, confidence-based abstention degrades worst-group accuracy below the baseline, while our method improves it, showing that standard uncertainty signals are not aligned with subgroup risk. Because the method is post-hoc and annotation-free at deployment, it can be applied to already-deployed models where retraining is infeasible, providing a practical mechanism for improving subgroup reliability using existing models without retraining. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

title: Cross-Cohort Reliability of Machine Learning for Breast Cancer Survival Prediction
authors: Nadir, Younes; Rachdi, Mohamed; Amhaimar, Lahcen; Bakhouyi, Abdellah; Khalidi, Abderrahim; Azouazi, Mohamed
venue: International Journal of Advanced Computer Science and Applications
abstract: —Transportability limitations can affect discrimination, probability calibration, and uncertainty estimates even when machine-learning pipelines use the same input variables. This study evaluated 5-year breast cancer survival models across METABRIC and TCGA-BRCA using age and ER, PR, and HER2 status. Logistic regression, radial-basis-function support vector machine, random forest, XGBoost, and soft voting underwent bidirectional external validation. The METABRIC soft-voting model was further assessed with source-only Platt scaling, split conformal prediction, selective prediction by singleton sets, cohort classification, and exploratory few-shot target adaptation. The principal contribution is an integrated reliability framework. METABRIC-to-TCGA ROC-AUC decreased numerically from 0.732 to 0.643, an observed difference of approximately 0.088 with a 95 percent confidence interval from minus 0.015 to 0.196. TCGA-to-METABRIC ROC-AUC decreased numerically from 0.674 to 0.586, also by approximately 0.088, with a 95 percent confidence interval from minus 0.127 to 0.282. Neither interval excluded zero. Source Platt scaling improved the observed internal Brier score and expected calibration error but produced worse observed values for both metrics externally. TCGA empirical conformal coverage was 81.8 percent versus nominal 90 percent. Exploratory target recalibration improved mean locked-test Brier score and expected calibration error at larger target sample sizes, whereas updating only the conformal threshold did not restore nominal mean coverage. These findings support separate evaluation of ranking, probability accuracy, and uncertainty under cohort shift and do not establish model superiority, clinical usefulness, or deployment readiness. © (2026), (Science and Information Organization). All rights reserved.

title: Selective classification under imbalance in multiclass settings: A novel metric for bias-aware risk–coverage evaluation
authors: Sağlam, Fatih; Özgen, Ünsal; Uygun, Alper; Dinçer, Oğuz Salih; Albayrak, Canan
abstract: Objective Selective classification improves reliability by allowing models to abstain on uncertain inputs, which is critical in safety-sensitive domains such as healthcare. However, commonly used evaluation metrics obscure fairness issues under class imbalance, leading to disproportionately high rejection of minority classes and misleadingly favorable assessments of selective strategies. Methods We introduce two imbalance-aware evaluation metrics, Class-Averaged AURC (CA-AURC) and Class-Averaged AUGRC (CA-AUGRC), which integrate risk against class-specific coverage and then average across classes, alongside the Area under the IAM-coverage curve (AUIC) as a complementary imbalance-aware performance metric. In addition, we propose a class-conditional coverage-matching selection strategy that enforces balanced rejection across diagnostic categories. The proposed framework is evaluated on a clinical complete blood count dataset comprising 3316 patient records, 11 laboratory features, and 9 diagnostic classes, and validated on three additional publicly available benchmark datasets covering different domains, class structures, and imbalance levels. Results While conventional metrics such as AURC and AUGRC favor classical selective strategies, the proposed class-averaged metrics reveal substantial disparities in rejection behavior under class imbalance. Using CA-AUGRC and AUIC, the class-conditional strategy consistently outperforms both the classical approach and LABEL, a theoretically principled set-valued baseline, across all four datasets and five uncertainty measures. Rank-based statistical comparisons confirm significant advantages of the class-conditional strategy on CA-AUGRC (p=0.009, r=0.638) and AUIC (p<0.001, r=0.957). Conclusion The results demonstrate that both evaluation and selection in selective classification must be class-aware to ensure fairness and clinical usefulness. Class-averaged metrics and class-conditional selection provide a more reliable basis for assessing selective classifiers in imbalanced medical data, with consistent generalizability across diverse datasets and uncertainty measures. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

title: TRACE-Med: Policy-based Abstention to Mitigate Hallucinations in LLM-Generated Clinical Case Analysis
authors: Dakshit, Sagnik; Suryadevara, Bhavani; Stockton, Lindsey
venue: Proceedings - 2026 IEEE 14th International Conference on Healthcare Informatics, ICHI 2026
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored as tools for supporting clinical reasoning and case-based learning in healthcare education. When applied to clinical case analysis, however, these systems often generate statements that extend beyond the information provided in the case description, introducing plausible but unsupported reasoning. Preserving the integrity of case-based learning therefore requires mechanisms that ensure generated analyses remain grounded in the evidence available to the learner. This paper introduces TRACE-Med, a policy-based governance framework for enforcing evidential grounding in LLM-generated clinical case analyses. TRACEMed operates as a post-generation governance layer under a closed-evidence assumption in which the case narrative defines the complete admissible evidence universe. The framework separates generation from governance, where model outputs are decomposed into claims, evaluated against the case text using semantic similarity, and subjected to section-aware epistemic policies that regulate evidence reporting, diagnostic reasoning, etiological explanations, differential diagnoses, and management recommendations. We evaluate TRACE-Med through controlled prompting experiments on a corpus of approximately 998 clinical case studies. Prior to enforcement, unsupported reasoning occurs consistently across prompting strategies, with boundary violation rates ranging from 29.5% to 48.5%. After applying TRACE-Med governance, unsupported claims are systematically transformed through policy-driven remediation actions such that no unsupported claims are emitted unchanged. These findings suggest that reliable use of LLMs in case-based healthcare education requires architectural governance mechanisms rather than reliance on prompt design alone. By operationalizing closed-world evidential constraints, this provides a practical pathway for aligning language model reasoning with the evidential standards expected in clinical environments. © 2026 IEEE.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: Evolution, Architectures, Applications, and Challenges (2020–2025)
authors: Faridi, Arman Rasool; Masood, Faraz; Keshvi; Yunus, Tabassum
venue: Wiley Interdisciplinary Reviews: Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generate fluent text but remain vulnerable to hallucinations, outdated knowledge, weak provenance, and costly model updates in knowledge-intensive settings. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) addresses these limitations by grounding generation in external evidence retrieved at inference time. This Advanced Review presents a PRISMA-guided synthesis of 91 studies published between January 2020 and December 2025. It traces the evolution of RAG from early retrieve-then-generate pipelines to a broader design space that includes sparse, dense, and hybrid retrieval; multi-stage reranking; evidence fusion; retrieval-aware pre-training; non-parametric memory; iterative and agentic workflows; GraphRAG; multimodal RAG; multilingual retrieval; and privacy-preserving deployment. The review examines how retrieval granularity, indexing, reranking, context construction, and retriever-generator integration affect recall, precision, latency, robustness, and governance. It also compares explicit retrieval with long-context prompting, vector-based retrieval with graph-based retrieval, and fixed pipelines with adaptive or agentic architectures. Domain requirements shape these choices: healthcare systems require evidence quality and privacy protection; legal and policy applications prioritize authoritative sources and citation fidelity; enterprise systems require freshness and access control; and educational systems must combine factual grounding with pedagogically appropriate explanations. Evaluation remains a central challenge. End-task accuracy alone does not capture retrieval quality, faithfulness, attribution, calibration, abstention, efficiency, or resilience to prompt injection and knowledge-base poisoning. The review therefore synthesizes current evaluation practices, promotes reproducibility-oriented reporting through RAG Cards, and identifies open research directions for secure, efficient, transparent, and domain-aware RAG systems. © 2026 Wiley Periodicals LLC.

title: Variational Visual Question Answering for Uncertainty-Aware Selective Prediction
authors: Wieczorek, Tobias Jan; Daun, Nathalie; Khan, Mohammad Emtiyaz; Rohrbach, Marcus
abstract: Despite remarkable progress in recent years, Vision Language Models (VLMs) remain prone to overconfidence and hallucinations on tasks such as Visual Question Answering (VQA) and Visual Reasoning. Bayesian methods can potentially improve reliability by helping models predict selectively, that is, models respond only when they are sufficiently confident. Unfortunately, such approaches can be costly and ineffective for large models, and there exists little evidence to show otherwise for multimodal applications. Here, we show for the first time the effectiveness and competitive edge of variational Bayes for selective prediction in VQA. We build on recent advances in variational methods for deep learning and propose an extension called “Variational VQA”. This method improves calibration and yields significant gains for selective prediction on VQA and Visual Reasoning, particularly when the error tolerance is low (≤ 1%). Often, just one posterior sample yields more reliable answers than those given by models trained with AdamW. In addition, we propose a new risk-averse selector that outperforms standard sample averaging by considering the variance of predictions. Overall, we present compelling evidence that variational learning is a viable option to make large VLMs safer and more trustworthy. © 2026, Transactions on Machine Learning Research. All rights reserved.

title: Teacher-anchored, disagreement-weighted confidence learning: Suppressing overconfident bypasses in budgeted small-to-large language model cascades
authors: Li, Peng; Pei, Yang
abstract: Budgeted small-to-large cascades reduce LLM serving cost by letting a small language model (SLM) answer locally and escalating only a limited fraction of queries to a larger model. Existing approaches largely optimize the online routing rule, implicitly assuming that the SLM already provides a meaningful retain-versus-escalate score. We show that this assumption fails in a structured and deployment-critical way. In a two-coordinate failure geometry, the most damaging cases lie in an overtrust region: the base SLM assigns high confidence, while teacher-supported evidence indicates that the trajectory is unsafe to keep. These overconfident bypasses leave wrong local answers on the retained path despite an available fallback budget. We propose TAD-CL (Teacher-Anchored Disagreement-weighted Confidence Learning), a confidence-learning framework that reshapes this score geometry before routing. A bounded query-adaptive construction rule spends fewer teacher-scored trajectories on internally consistent queries and retains a larger supervision budget for ambiguous ones. The teacher anchor then defines a soft local-retention target from answer verification and LLM support, while a one-sided disagreement weight amplifies only the positive overtrust gap [ωbase−c * ]+[jls-end-space/], where the frozen SLM is more confident than the teacher target permits. This targeted surrogate emphasizes teacher-identified overtrust while retaining a base fitting loss on every trajectory. The learned trajectory-conditioned confidence is then served by a lightweight SLM-first cascade with a validation-calibrated budget gate. Across MATH, GSM8K, and ARC-Challenge with three SLM families, TAD-CL improves over MaxProb and RouteLLM under matched LLM call-rate budgets. In the core two-backbone setting, it improves RouteLLM by 1.4–4.2 accuracy points. Mechanistic analysis reduces calibration error from 0.230 to 0.061 and unconditional bypass rate from 34.0% to 12.3% on the MATH pilot. An ASQA extension further demonstrates graded semantic verification beyond exact-match reasoning. These results suggest that reliable collaboration depends not only on the serving-time router, but also on learning a confidence geometry in which unsafe high-confidence local answers are less likely to bypass the LLM. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. All rights are reserved, including those for text and data mining, AI training, and similar technologies.

title: An Evidence-Gated KCMVP Pre-Certification Decision-Support Prototype: Rule-Based Analysis, Evidence Retrieval, and Constrained LLM Review
authors: Cho, Su-Been; Park, Do-Yun; Lim, Da-Eun; Kim, Jae-Hwan; Jeong, Su-Min; Hyoung, Yu-Lim; Seo, Hwa-Jeong
abstract: The Korean Cryptographic Module Validation Program (KCMVP) requires the joint review of source code, submission documents, and their traceability. This study presents an evidence-gated decision-support prototype combining rule-based candidate generation (L1), rule-bound evidence retrieval (L2), program-fact verification, and constrained LLM-assisted review (L3). Its 166 YAML rule assets, comprising 97 code rules, 65 document rules, and four traceability rules, were developed with reference to official KCMVP procedures and National Intelligence Service guidance on submission preparation and cryptographic algorithm implementation. On an LEA-centered development corpus, L1 matched 115 of 128 author-annotated positive file–rule pairs (89.84%). However, because these annotations were created during system development, independent expert validation is required before interpreting this value as detection accuracy. In nine source-derived mutation groups, the baseline and improved-evidence conditions each produced six binary dispositions and three holds (exact McNemar test, (Formula presented.)). This result defines the current role of L2 as supplying traceable evidence, validating citations, and withholding unsupported decisions rather than independently determining compliance. L3 reviews only residual candidates supported by validated evidence and program facts under a structured output contract; failure to satisfy input, evidence, citation, or output-validation conditions results in a hold. Overall, the results demonstrate a feasible and auditable architecture that preserves evidence provenance and explicitly holds unresolved cases instead of forcing unsupported decisions. © 2026 by the authors.

title: Progressive Diabetes Risk Prediction Using Attention-Based Deep Representation Learning
authors: Sharma, Sachin; Mehra, Ritika; Upreti, Kamal
venue: 2026 International Conference on NextGen Data Science and Analytics, ICNDSA 2026
abstract: The study presents a very modern and sophisticated deep learning architecture of progressive diabetes risk prediction using representation learning and adaptive interaction modeling of features. Rather than binary screening, diabetes risk is expressed as a three-class staging problem to include latent disease progression. Denoising autoencoders are used to train powerful clinical embeddings and an attention-based model dynamically captures patient-specific feature relevance. Extensive analysis based on macro-averaged measures shows that the suggested attention model is always more accurate than the baseline deep networks, and ranking, resistance to measurement noise, and selective prediction that is aware of uncertainty. Additional evidence to support smooth progression of risks and clinically significant behavior of misclassification is in the form of latent space and error pattern analyses. The findings provide a valid and deployment-capable deep learning framework in terms of early and progressive monitoring of diabetic risk. © 2026 IEEE.

title: Provable Limits and Certified Deferral for Verbalized Uncertainty in Small Language Models
authors: Shen, Jianru
abstract: Small open-weight language models increasingly run in private, offline, and cost-sensitive settings, where the key deployment question is not only what a model answers but when it should defer to a human. We evaluate verbalized confidence for risk-controlled deferral in eleven instruction-tuned models from three families, 0.5B to 14B parameters, on ARC-Challenge and TruthfulQA with 25,168 local predictions. We separate three roles that are often conflated. Strictly increasing calibration supplies probability semantics but preserves confidence ranking, error-detection AUROC, and every threshold-induced operating point. Temperature scaling carries a nonzero ECE lower bound when every stated confidence exceeds one half while accuracy falls below it; five of the eight model–task pairs that saturate the temperature search land within one percentage point of the corresponding benchmark, and all within three. Building on finite-sample risk-control methods, we certify the prespecified family of all 101 integer confidence cutoffs with simultaneous Clopper–Pearson bounds: at a 20% retained-risk budget only Qwen2.5-14B obtains a non-null policy, on both tasks, at 10% none of the 22 pairs do, and repeated-split analysis shows certification availability is governed by calibration-set size. Platt scaling reduces test ECE to as low as 0.02 yet, as predicted, creates no new retained sets. We also identify and repair an answer-ordering artifact in multiple-choice TruthfulQA. Calibration makes small-model confidence interpretable; valid certification often concludes that small models should defer. Code and data are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21944368. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

title: Stable Discrimination Can Hide Reliability Failures in AI Decision Support Under Distribution Shift and Changing Target Definitions
authors: Kovari, Attila
abstract: Stable discrimination can coexist with unreliable probabilities, abstention policies, and uncertainty sets under distribution shift. We evaluate this mismatch with CRIT-AID, an executable multi-domain reliability-audit framework that separates model fitting, probability calibration, operating-rule calibration, and testing and then transports source-derived rules unchanged to target domains. Across four public tabular domains, stable discrimination did not imply stable probability quality, selective operating points, or conformal uncertainty. On identical ACS 2024 records, changing the income target definition left AUROC nearly unchanged, while ECE differed by 0.083; prevalence-intercept alignment reduced this difference to −0.004, showing that target semantics can alter probability reliability without materially changing ranking. Across 27 primary 90% conformal conditions, label-conditional calibration improved worst-class coverage in 18 but worsened it in 9 and usually increased prediction-set size. LightGBM sensitivity changed absolute discrimination without removing the mismatch among reliability dimensions. These findings show that discrimination alone is insufficient evidence for reliable AI decision support: audits should test the transportability of probability mappings, operating rules, class-specific validity, and uncertainty informativeness when deployment conditions or target meanings change. © 2026 by the author.

title: Refined generation-based framework for consistent and reliable visual question answering
authors: Xu, Quanxing; Zhou, Ling; Zhong, Xian; Zhang, Feifei; Tian, Jinyu; Yu, Xiaohan; Huang, Rubing
abstract: Distribution shift, defined as discrepancies between training and testing answer distributions, poses a fundamental challenge in multimodal learning. Despite the progress of visual question answering (VQA) and the availability of powerful pretrained large models (PLMs), such shifts continue to undermine generalization and prediction stability. Existing VQA methods typically perform well on in-distribution (ID) data but exhibit pronounced degradation on out-of-distribution (OOD) samples, rendering adaptation under continuous shifts unreliable. Although PLMs achieve strong performance across diverse multimodal tasks, their predictions remain insufficiently robust, and most reliability-oriented VQA approaches focus on data partitioning rather than data augmentation. To address these limitations, we propose Refined Generation-based Training (RGT), a unified framework that jointly enhances model consistency and reliability. RGT comprises two key components: (1) a self-consistency mechanism embedded within the VQA model to enforce coherent predictions and improve image understanding, and (2) a selection function trained with synthetic data to strengthen reliability. Specifically, a generation-based augmentation pipeline compensates for weaknesses across data subsets, thereby facilitating effective training of the selection function. In parallel, the self-consistency scheme encourages the model to produce multiple answers for a single image, refining cross-question reasoning. The proposed framework is model-agnostic and can be readily integrated into existing VQA architectures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RGT achieves state-of-the-art performance and substantially improves robustness under continuous distribution shift. The code will be released at https://github.com/xqx23/RGT. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Bias and Fairness in Radiomics: A Comparative Analysis of Machine Learning Models on Four Oncology Datasets
authors: Ruiz Pujadas, Esmeralda; Hernández-González, Jerónimo; Dang, Vien Ngoc; Camacho, Marina; Lekadir, Karim; Starmans, Martijn P. A.
venue: International Journal of Imaging Systems and Technology
abstract: Radiomics, the practice of mining quantitative features from medical imaging, has gained increasing popularity in diagnosing and treating cancer. However, clinical deployment and adoption of radiomics tools in real-world practice remain limited. To increase trust in radiomics models, one of the main remaining challenges is ensuring fairness by addressing algorithmic bias and promoting equitable outcomes. This study aims to identify key fairness challenges in radiomics and demonstrate how state-of-the-art mitigation techniques can be applied to address them. Moreover, we aim to provide new guidelines for both the selection of mitigation techniques and procedural recommendations for future directions in fairness. This study evaluates the fairness of radiomics models using six machine learning algorithms applied to four publicly available oncology datasets: Liver, Gastrointestinal, Desmoid-type fibromatosis, and Liposarcoma. Fairness was assessed using Equal Opportunity Difference (EOD) with respect to two protected attributes: age and sex. We employed three bias mitigation techniques—Disparate Impact Remover (DIR), Reweighting, and Reject Option Classification (ROC)—to examine their effect on fairness metrics and model performance. DIR, Reweighting, and ROC each showed dataset- and attribute-specific improvements in fairness. For example, DIR notably reduced sex-related bias in the Liposarcoma dataset, while ROC offered the best fairness–performance trade-off in the Liver dataset. Reweighting was effective in mitigating age-related bias in Liposarcoma. In the Desmoid dataset, applying ROC to Extra Trees marginally improved fairness; however, age-related bias persisted. Overall, the applied techniques reduced disparities in true positive rates between groups, enhancing fairness. Our findings show that while radiomics models can be accurate, they often exhibit bias with respect to demographic groups. Carefully addressing this trade-off is crucial for developing radiomics models that are accurate but also trustworthy for clinical deployment. © 2026 The Author(s). International Journal of Imaging Systems and Technology published by Wiley Periodicals LLC.

title: Risk-Aware Fruit Ripeness Recognition under Synthetic Distribution Shift via Selective Classification and Conformal Prediction Sets
authors: Daniel Cevallos, V.; Garcia, Erasmo; Torres, Miguel; Cevallos, Holger
venue: 2026 3rd International Conference on Digital Image Processing and Computer Applications, DIPCA 2026
abstract: Deep image classifiers can reach high accuracy on curated test sets, yet their reliability can degrade under distribution shift and when decisions are made at scale. This paper studies risk-Aware fruit ripeness recognition from RGB images by combining (i) selective classification-A reject option that trades coverage for reduced error-And (ii) conformal prediction sets that provide distribution-free guarantees on set coverage. Using a nine-class fruit ripeness dataset, we train three ImageNet-pretrained backbones (MobileNetV3-Large [1], ConvNeXt-Tiny [2], EfficientNetV2-S [3]) with a unified twostage fine-Tuning recipe and evaluate robustness under four synthetic shifts (lighting, noise, blur, JPEG compression). We report standard accuracy metrics together with calibration (ECE), risk-coverage curves (AURC and risk at fixed coverages), conformal coverage and set sizes for APS/RAPS, and end-To-end inference latency with and without test-Time augmentation (TTA). Across backbones, in-domain Top-1 accuracy exceeds 99% while selective classification sharply reduces retained-set error at high confidence. Under shift, accuracy degrades most under additive noise, yet conformal sets maintain at least nominal coverage with compact average set sizes. Our findings highlight practical tradeoffs among accuracy, calibration, abstention, prediction-set size, and latency for deploying ripeness recognition in the wild. © 2026 IEEE.

title: Evaluating Multimodal LLMs for Context-Aware Forensic Image Interpretation
authors: Fedynyshyn, Taras; Partyka, Olha; Opirskyy, Ivan; Konakbayev, Olzhas
venue: International Journal of Networked and Distributed Computing
abstract: Digital forensics is vital for analyzing extensive image data from mobile devices to identify individuals and activities in investigations. Traditional methods struggle with complex real-world images, particularly distinguishing military personnel from military-themed mannequins. This study assesses multimodal Large Language Models (LLMs) - Google’s Gemini 1.5 Pro, open-source LLAVA, and GPT-4o - for detecting military personnel in 434 mobile device images, including military personnel, mannequins, and civilians. The models achieved strong recall (0.99 for Gemini, 0.98 for LLAVA, and 0.91 for GPT-4o) but only moderate precision (0.69, 0.69, and 0.67 respectively), reflecting a notable rate of mannequin-induced false positives.] Accuracy varied from 0.793 for Gemini and LLAVA to 0.770 for GPT-4o, aligning with observed differences in contextual understanding. Contextual classification also posed challenges: Gemini achieved 0.787 accuracy for country identification, followed by GPT-4o (0.385) and LLAVA (0.121). Unit name recognition remained weak across models. Misclassification of mannequins was the primary source of error, confirming that current multimodal models overemphasize uniform and equipment cues without verifying human authenticity. To enhance interpretability and reduce false positives, we integrated an agentic orchestration layer using CrewAI and LangGraph, which structured multimodal reasoning through dedicated sub-agents for provenance validation, perception, mannequin discrimination, and evidence-grounded attribution. These agentic frameworks substantially improved forensic reliability: CrewAI achieved 0.88 precision with a mannequin false-positive rate of 0.12, while LangGraph reached 0.90 precision and reduced false positives to 0.08. Country attribution accuracy rose to 0.58 and 0.62 respectively. Although recall decreased slightly due to conservative abstention logic (CrewAI 0.74, LangGraph 0.73), this trade-off yielded higher forensic confidence and reproducible, audit-ready decision traces. The results demonstrate that integrating agentic architectures transforms multimodal LLMs from opaque classifiers into transparent, evidence-driven forensic tools - enhancing both analytic precision and the evidentiary defensibility of AI-assisted investigations. © The Author(s) 2026.

title: Scope: Stochastic Consensus Purification with Explanation Consistency for Adversarially Robust Image Classification
authors: Honey Diana, P.; Supriya, N.
venue: Journal of Theoretical and Applied Information Technology
abstract: Adversarial perturbations are very effective at fooling deep neural image classifiers: adding subtle noise to the image can lead to unreliable predictions. Current defenses typically have three drawbacks: low clean accuracy, low defense strength against high-level adaptive attacks, and a lack of evidence of semantically meaningful visual regions recovered from recovered predictions. In response to these challenges, we present a novel adversarial defense framework called SCOPE: Stochastic Consensus Purification with Explanation Consistency for robust and explainable image classification. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel adversarial defense framework, called Stochastic Consensus Purification with Explanation Consistency (SCOPE), for robust and explainable image classification. SCOPE combines stochastic image purification, randomized consensus classification and explanation alignment via Grad-CAM into a single optimization framework. The proposed approach is based on a stochastic robustness objective which combines clean risk, adversarial risk, purification error, prediction variance, margin loss, and explanation inconsistency. Moreover, multiple stochastic forward passes are aggregated by a consensus inference mechanism, to get more stable predictions, estimate uncertainty and enable abstention for unstable inputs. The framework is tested on publicly available datasets such as a balanced subset of 10,000 images from the ImageNet dataset, 4,000 of which are used for purifier training, 1,000 for validation and 5,000 for independent testing. Comprehensive evaluation is made on FGSM, BIM, PGD-20, PGD-100, DeepFool, C&W, AutoAttack, Transfer Attack and Adaptive BPDA+EOT. Experimental results demonstrate that SCOPE gains the clean accuracy of 94.62%, the FGSM accuracy of 89.42%, the PGD-100 accuracy of 79.64%, the AutoAttack accuracy of 75.48% and the BPDA+EOT accuracy of 71.36%, outperforming PGD-AT, TRADES, SmoothAdv, DiffPure, RDC, and ADBM. Moreover, SCOPE's interpretability is enhanced by its explanation stability score of 0.892, pointing-game accuracy of 82.75%, and its AUC for insertion and deletion of 0.742 and 0.218 respectively. The findings in this work confirm the ability of SCOPE to deliver high-quality trustworthy image classification with all the above-mentioned properties. © 2026, Little Lion Scientific.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Paw-Tip Localization in Animal Pose Estimation via Gaussian Regression
authors: Li, Zy
abstract: Animal pose estimation methods predict keypoint locations without quantifying localizationuncertainty, limiting their use in applications where prediction reliability matters. We focus on paw-tipkeypoints, the most ambiguous and biomechanically distinctive joints in AP-10K, and validate the methodon all body keypoints. We show that a simple modification to standard pose regressors, replacing L 2 losswith a 2D Gaussian negative log-likelihood (NLL) head, yields interpretable uncertainty at a modest 5.2%accuracy difference relative to the L 2 baseline. Without any explicit supervision, the model learns structureduncertainty consistent with biomechanical motion patterns: back-paw predictions exhibit horizontally-elongated covariance (σ x /σ y ≈ 1.8), while front paws are near-isotropic. The learned uncertainty enablessingle-pass selective prediction that outperforms multi-pass MC Dropout, achieving roughly 22% lowerRMSE on the retained predictions at half retention. We further evaluate held-out-species generalization(Felidae), hybrid L2/NLL losses, and isotropic-covariance variants on CNN and transformer backbones,characterizing where each is appropriate. © 2013 IEEE.

title: Reject Option for Medical Image Classification Using CNN-Derived Latent-Space Neighbourhood Analysis
authors: Arcangeli, Andrea; De Santi, Lisa Anita; Santarelli, Maria Filomena; Celi, Simona; Positano, Vincenzo
venue: Journal of Imaging Informatics in Medicine
abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimation is a key requirement for the clinical adoption of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in biomedical imaging. We propose a reject option framework that assesses prediction reliability by leveraging the local structure of the latent space. The method is based on three latent-space features: Simple Data Point Target Density (DPTDS), defined as the proportion of a sample’s nearest neighbours sharing its label, a distance-weighted extension (DPTDW), and the k∗ value. These metrics characterise local label agreement and intra-class consistency without relying on explicit parametric assumptions. A logistic regression rejector is trained post hoc using features derived from the latent representations of the base CNN. Experiments were conducted on two public neuroimaging datasets: ADNI (FDG-PET for Alzheimer’s disease) and PPMI (DaTSCAN SPECT for Parkinson’s disease). Using all three latent-space features, the rejector achieved AUC-ROC values of 0.843 (95% CI: 0.809–0.874) on ADNI and 0.884 (95% CI: 0.867–0.900) on PPMI, with corresponding eAURC values of 0.0278 (95% CI: 0.0193–0.0370) and 0.0169 (95% CI: 0.0133–0.0209), respectively. For the full-feature configuration, no significant difference from maximum softmax probability (MSP) was detected on ADNI for either AUC-ROC or eAURC, whereas MSP performed significantly better on PPMI for both metrics. The proposed framework provides a representation-based mechanism to assess prediction reliability through local latent-space structure. As a post-hoc approach, it can be integrated into existing CNN pipelines without modifying the underlying model, offering a practical tool for uncertainty-aware decision support in biomedical imaging. © The Author(s) under exclusive licence to Society for Imaging Informatics in Medicine 2026.

title: Knowing When Not to Answer: Mitigating Social Bias in LLMs via Epistemic Abstention
authors: Suman, Chanchal; Rana, Kapil; Kumar, Sanjit; Singh, Gopendra Vikram
abstract: The growing application of Large Language Models (LLMs) to social contexts has led to an increase in unjustifiable social group attributions through their own stereotype-based responses; especially when responding to questions where there is little evidence to support a response or ambiguity to context. The lack of sufficient evidence often leads models to hallucinate socially grounded inferences, undermining fairness and trust. In this work, we attempt to mitigate social bias under ambiguity via epistemic uncertainty. We further introduce BHARATBBQ-R, a rationale-augmented extension of BHARATBBQ that explicitly annotates evidential sufficiency or absence. We propose EPIK (Epistemic Pruning under Implicit Knowledge), an epistemic calibration framework for detecting contextual insufficiency and enforceing principled abstention in case of inadequate evidences. Our framework enforces principled abstention in cases of inadequate evidence, while maintaining the performance for unambiguous cases. Prior bias mitigation technique focuses on suppressing stereotypes or debiasing representations; our proposed framework reframes biased behavior as a failure of epistemic humility. Experiments across five open-source LLMs show that EPIK substantially reduces the bias score for ambiguous contexts (from 1.41–1.52 to 0.86–0.98), while maintaining accuracy on unambiguous instances. From results, we establish the epistemic calibration enables selective suppression of stereotype-driven inference without indiscriminately refusing valid social reasoning. © 2026, Transactions on Machine Learning Research. All rights reserved.

title: An Engineering-Oriented Machine Learning Decision Support System for Outcome Prediction in Dynamic Environments
authors: Detroja, Vraj; Verma, Yash; Veena R.s; Sushmitha S
abstract: Accurate outcome prediction in real-world dynamic systems is challenging due to temporal evolution, contextual variability, and uncertainty in historical data. Many existing approaches rely on static indicators and algorithm-centric optimization, limiting their robustness as decision-support tools. This paper presents an engineering-oriented, machine-learning-based decision support system designed from a system-level perspective. The proposed framework integrates engineered temporal, contextual, physical load, and opponent-aware features within a modular and reproducible pipeline, complemented by structured ablation analysis and uncertainty-aware decision logic. Classical machine learning models: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and Linear Support Vector Machine, are evaluated using professional tennis match data. Results show that engineered features, particularly contextual adaptability, substantially improve performance, with Random Forest achieving the strongest results. Beyond accuracy, probability-based thresholds and an explicit abstention mechanism enhance reliability, demonstrating how machine learning can be systematically embedded within robust decision support systems. © 2026 The Authors.

title: Interpretable Subgroup Discovery with Abstention in Small, Heterogeneous Clinical Trials: A Retrospective Multi-Dataset Study
authors: Geraci, Joseph; Qorri, Bessi; Cumbaa, Christian; Tsay, Mike; Marrella, Christopher Alexander; Zappulla, Seb; Leonczyk, Paul; Gogacz, Adam; Pani, Luca
abstract: Small, heterogeneous clinical datasets pose a challenge for whole-cohort prediction because clinically meaningful treatment or response patterns may be diluted across biologically diverse patients. We describe and evaluate NetraAI, an interpretable dynamical-systems framework for selective subgroup discovery that uses finite-iteration contraction-inspired dynamics and long-range memory (LRM) to identify stable, outcome-linked Model-Derived Subgroups (MDS). This system can abstain by assigning No Call when a stable subgroup assignment is not supported. A large language model (LLM) Strategist is outlined only as a possible future extension; it is not evaluated here and contributes nothing to the results reported. Foundation and language models asked to perform subgroup discovery directly did not recover the structure the specialized discovery step recovered. We demonstrate this framework across three retrospective clinical trial datasets: Clinical Antipsychotic Trials of Intervention Effectiveness (CATIE) schizophrenia (olanzapine vs. perphenazine comparative treatment-preference benchmark), Canadian Biomarker Integration Network in Depression (CAN-BIND) depression (escitalopram response), and Comprehensive Molecular Characterization of Advanced Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma for Better Treatment Selection (COMPASS) pancreatic cancer (GnP vs. FOLFIRINOX observational regimen-associated response). The benchmark is not a contest between NetraAI and competing predictors: the same eight downstream methods are evaluated with and without what NetraAI discovered. Given the full feature sets and their own selection procedures, those methods were at or near chance on all three datasets, and blind de novo searches by an independent interaction model and by a pretrained tabular foundation model did not recover an equivalent signature or subpopulation. In internal downstream evaluation, given the discovered variables alone—the same patients, the same classifiers, the full cohort and no abstention of any kind—every one of the eight methods improved on every dataset, 24 of 24 method-dataset comparisons, moving from a raw-feature range of 0.46–0.62 AUC to 0.54–0.78. Restricting further to the subpopulation in which those variables hold improved all eight methods again in CAN-BIND and in COMPASS, 16 of 16 comparisons, reaching 0.66–0.83 and 0.96–1.00, respectively; in CATIE, where the called subgroups are the least outcome-homogeneous of the three, it improved only one of eight. Taking the framework as a whole, 23 of 24 method-dataset combinations improved over the raw-feature baseline. NetraAI abstains on patients without stable subgroup structure, calling 27.7% to 40.4% of each cohort. The contribution demonstrated is therefore subgroup discovery rather than downstream prediction, and its beneficiaries are the conventional methods themselves. In COMPASS, NetraAI identified a three-SNV signature associated with regimen-linked response ranking among called patients; because the cohort was observational and the permutation test was conditional on the selected signature, this finding is exploratory. The two mechanisms are complementary rather than competing: variable discovery establishes which features carry the structure, and abstention establishes in which patients it holds. Neither mechanism replaces conventional modeling. Variable discovery improved every method on every dataset, the pretrained tabular foundation model included; identifying the population in which those variables hold conferred further benefit in two of the three datasets and not in the third. These findings support NetraAI as an exploratory system for generating compact, inspectable subgroup hypotheses that may inform future enrichment strategies after external validation, and indicate that its value lies in what it contributes to other methods rather than in competing with them. © 2026 by the authors.

title: Enhancing multimodal sentiment analysis reliability: SentiGuard+ with Dirichlet evidence and selective prediction
authors: Narejo, Komal Rani; Zan, Hongying; Mostafa, Samih M.; Karim, Faten Khalid; Mehmood, Faisal; Yaseen, Ayesha
venue: Journal of King Saud University - Computer and Information Sciences
abstract: Real-world image–text posts mix subtle visual signals with short, informal language, making multimodal sentiment analysis susceptible to label noise, miscalibration, and brittle decisions. We present SentiGuard+, a reliability-aware model that processes images with a Swin Transformer and text with RoBERTa-large, fusing them via a bi-directional cross-attention module (CrossWeave). For each input, the system produces three interpretable outputs: class probabilities, a calibrated reliability score, and an accept/abstain decision for risk-controlled deployment. The fused representation is equipped with an evidential Dirichlet head and a hierarchical noisy-label channel (HD-SIT); we then apply reliability-preserving evidence calibration and a simple two-feature gate (P-Gate) that bases acceptance on predicted entropy and calibrated variance. Across standard multimodal sentiment benchmarks, SentiGuard+ improves overall accuracy and F1 while reducing calibration error, and it delivers stronger accepted-set performance at matched coverage. We find evidence that a single calibrated-and-gated operating point transfers between two datasets with minimal drift. These results indicate that combining Swin Transformer and RoBERTa-large with evidential modeling and selective gating yields better-conditioned probabilities, higher accepted-set F1, and portable operating points suitable for real-world use. © The Author(s) 2026.

title: When Not to Answer: Evaluating Prompts on Reasoning Models for Effective Abstention in Unanswerable Math Word Problems
authors: Saadat, Asir; Sogir, Tasmia Binte; Chowdhury, Md. Taukir Azam; Aziz, Syem
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to solve complex mathematical word problems, but their susceptibility to hallucination raises concerns, especially when faced with unanswerable questions. Despite their widespread use, little is known about how effectively these models can abstain from answering unsolvable problems. In this work, we investigate whether LLMs and mathematical reasoning models can appropriately handle unanswerable math word problems when prompted as if they were solvable. Using the Unanswerable Word Math Problem (UWMP) dataset, we evaluate GPT-based models and the NuminaMath model with metrics that integrate abstention, correctness, and confidence. Our results reveal that current models often hallucinate answers for unsolvable problems, highlighting critical gaps and emphasizing the need for models capable of better uncertainty management and complex mathematical reasoning. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

title: Research on Economic Benefits of the Jinghan Canal: A Valuation Based on Real Options Model
authors: Wang, Zuohua; Wang, Bufang; He, Xuerong
venue: Proceedings of SPIE - The International Society for Optical Engineering
abstract: To address the inherent limitations of the traditional Net Present Value (NPV) method in evaluating the Jinghan Canal project, this study applies real options theory to develop a deferral option (estimated via the Black-Scholes model) and an abandonment option (calculated using the binomial tree model), thereby systematically assessing the project’ s economic benefits and investment risks. Even with the integration of flexible option strategies — including "delayed decision-making" and "abandonment clauses"—the project fails to meet the threshold of economic feasibility due to two critical structural constraints: substantial initial capital outlays and ongoing rigid maintenance expenditures. Sensitivity analysis further validates the robustness of this conclusion: adjustments to key parameters, including freight volume, maintenance cost ratio, and the risk-free rate, do not reverse the negativity of the total project value. Based on these findings, this paper recommends conducting additional pragmatic feasibility studies and promptly suspending preliminary investment activities to avoid irreversible risk exposure. This research contributes theoretically by applying real options in large-scale water transport infrastructure valuation and practically by providing a scientific basis for project investment planning, offering a replicable framework for quantifying decision flexibility in similar projects. © 2026 SPIE.

title: Design and Evaluation of a RAG-Based Educational Assistant Grounded in Course Materials: A Case Study in Vocational Training
authors: Burillo, Jaime Dionisio; Hijón-Neira, Raquel; Borrás-Gené, Oriol
abstract: This study presents the design, implementation, and exploratory classroom evaluation of a course-constrained educational assistant combining Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with large language models (LLMs) in Vocational Education and Training (VET). The platform retrieves teacher-provided materials, generates course-aligned responses, displays source references, and returns a predefined abstention message when evidence appears insufficient. It was deployed during a practical session in the Spanish Higher Vocational Training programme Administración de Sistemas Informáticos en Red (ASIR; Network and Information Systems Administration). Nineteen students and one instructor completed a post-session questionnaire. Students reported positive perceptions of usability, clarity, perceived reliability, and learning support, while restricted corpus coverage and the absence of conversational memory emerged as limitations. To complement the perception-based classroom study, a separate post hoc technical assessment used 30 predefined queries with the same prototype and corpus. All 16 fully answerable prompts received substantive responses; 13 were rated fully correct and three partially correct by the first author. Seven of eight deliberately out-of-corpus prompts triggered abstention, whereas one OpenShift Route query produced an unsupported answer from semantically adjacent but non-supporting Kubernetes evidence. The contribution is empirical and design-oriented rather than algorithmic. The findings are context-specific and show both the potential and limitations of bounded cognitive support grounded in instructor-selected materials. © 2026 by the authors.

title: Question Selection and Answer Scoring Shape Revision Risk in Recurrent Language Models
authors: Lei, Ruian; Ren, Yazhou; Xu, Zenglin
abstract: An evaluation of early answers must choose which questions to release and how to read their answers. Using one scoring convention for both choices can make two procedures look similar while concealing their sensitivity to either choice. We measured this dependence on stored trajectories from Huginn and Ouro, using cloze scoring on three filtered benchmarks with 200 questions per task and cohort. The historical cohorts share questions; the three cohorts are not independent replications. At 50% release in the headline windows, changing the selection margin with the answer readout fixed changed revision risk by 9.33 to 12.00 percentage points (pp). Changing the readout with the margin fixed changed it by 9.67 to 13.00 pp. Yet changing both together gave only 0.33 to 3.00 pp. Similar risks for complete procedures therefore did not establish interchangeable selection margins. Separate sum-to-mean grids within each length unit also placed the lowest tested risks near matching rules. At the headline windows, final-depth disagreement retained the fixed-readout margin effect, although its magnitude depended on the outcome definition and observation window. Lower revision risk established neither an accuracy gain nor better stopping decisions. The results support a practical evaluation check: hold the answer rule fixed when comparing selectors, then cross the rules to measure dependence on the target. © 2026 by the authors.

title: Reasonable Doubt in the Face of Bias: Fair Flagging with Dirichlet-Based Models
authors: Barker, Charmaine; Kazakov, Dimitar
venue: Proceedings of the ACM Symposium on Applied Computing
abstract: Ensuring safety in machine learning requires not only robustness to adversarial or distributional uncertainty but also protection against systematic bias. Models that produce unfair or group-dependent predictions pose critical risks when deployed in socially sensitive domains such as credit, justice, or healthcare. This work introduces EviFair, a fairness-aware safety monitor that flags predictions exhibiting excessive dependence on protected attributes. EviFair combines evidential uncertainty modelling with sensitivity analysis to detect biased decision paths, flagging predictions where fairness cannot be guaranteed. We also show that EviFair's bias scores can effectively guide post-processing fairness methods. Results on standard fairness benchmark datasets show that EviFair achieves substantial reductions in group disparities with minimal impact on predictive performance, demonstrating its promise as a practical, inference-time mechanism for bias-sensitive, safety-aware model oversight. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

title: Selective band-gap prediction for lead-free A2BB'X6 halides under unseen B-site chemistry
authors: Chen, Ge
abstract: Screening the large composition space of lead-free halides by first-principles calculations is costly. Composition-based models can help prioritize calculations, but their value depends on performance in unfamiliar chemistry. Using 1931 A 2 BB'X 6 records from the Materials Project spanning 353 B/B′ pairs, we combined grouped validation, selective prediction, external classification tests and analysis of existing DFT calculations. Complete-pair holdout increased the mean absolute error (MAE) of the Hurdle ExtraTrees reference model from 0.256 to 0.515 eV relative to random-row validation. On the same folds, Magpie–random-forest regression achieved 0.431 eV MAE. Retaining 80% of predictions by tree dispersion reduced the retained-set MAE to 0.305 eV. When targeting Materials Project-reported gaps of 1.1–1.8 eV, dispersion-assisted ranking increased target hits from 33 to 54 at 100 checks compared with gap-only ranking, with a paired 95% interval of 5–30 additional hits. This gain depended on the verification budget. In external tests of the reference classifier, accuracy remained higher for pairs represented in training after excluding Fe compounds. DFT analysis of three compounds showed direct gaps for Rb 2 LiInBr 6 under PBE and PBE + SOC, while gap interpretation for K 2 AgFeCl 6 and Rb 2 AgFeCl 6 depended on electron-correlation treatment and band occupations. These results support more efficient allocation of computational resources in lead-free halide screening and provide an auditable basis for model use under incomplete chemical coverage. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier B.V.

title: Elastic TDMA Overlay for Dense Wi-Fi Networks
authors: Mueller, Reuven; Xie, Ying
venue: 2026 International Conference on Intelligent Multimedia, Networking, and Security, IMNS 2026
abstract: Dense Wi-Fi networks can lose efficiency when many uplink stations contend at the same time. This paper presents an access-policy study of an AP-managed elastic TDMA-style scheduled-access overlay for dense WLANs. The intended policy reserves protected airtime for active hybrid-capable stations while leaving fallback CSMA/CA available for regular stations and new reservation requests. We evaluate the policy with a policy-level ns-3 model layered over stock Wi-Fi behavior. The model uses scheduled queue release and NAV-like regular-station deferral to isolate access-policy behavior before full MAC integration. In a matched 16-station high-load campaign, a mixed 8 hybrid / 8 regular configuration with NAV-like deferral improves throughput by 6.51%, delivery by 5.74 percentage points, Wi-Fi TX failures by 60.34%, and retransmissions by 28.18% relative to all-regular standard Wi-Fi. Paired five-run differences give preliminary statistical support for the protected mixed case, including throughput gains of 1.175 ± 0.372 Mbps and delivery gains of 5.743 ± 1.820 percentage points. A NAV-like-off stress case degrades, representing missed or unenforced protection. A fixed 8H/8R timing sweep shows that protected airtime must be sized carefully: 5 ms is best among the tested block durations, while oversized protected blocks starve fallback contention. These results support AP-managed elastic TDMA-style access policy and motivate future MAC-integrated validation. © 2026 IEEE.

title: Scene-verified negatives for selective 3D visual grounding
authors: Zhu, Songyuan; Zhang, Zhihao; Wang, Haolan; Wang, Zixuan
abstract: Three-dimensional visual grounding must determine when a natural-language description is satisfiable within a scene and localize the referent only in those cases. To address this requirement, we cast the task as selective prediction with scene-verified true negatives and paired supervision. From each positive description, our method creates a single-factor edit and retains it only when a global scene graph verifies that no object in the same scene satisfies the edited text, yielding auditable negatives that fix visual context while isolating semantics. Utilizing these pairs, a hierarchical selective module produces voxel-level keep maps that gate pruning and aggregates a global keep probability, while the detection pathway remains unchanged. The training process uses a unified sigmoid focal objective with a flip-consistency margin that orders each positive above its edited counterpart, so that correct rejection depends on precise reasoning over negation, composition, and counting. On a predefined subset of difficult examples and across twenty-five linguistic slices, the approach improves intersection-over-union accuracy, reduces false rejections at a fixed true negative rate, increases the area under the keep probability curve, and lowers expected calibration error, indicating better calibration and more reliable abstention. Our code is available at https://github.com/Zsongyuan/TNS_for_3DVG. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Systems for Human-AI Collaboration
authors: Pearson, Vasco; Alves, Jean V.; Bono, Jacopo; Figueiredo, Mário A.T.; Bizarro, Pedro
abstract: Learning to defer (L2D) algorithms improve human-AI collaboration (HAIC) by deferring decisions to human experts when they are more likely to be correct than the AI model. This framework hinges on machine learning (ML) models’ ability to assess their own certainty and that of human experts. L2D struggles in dynamic environments, where distribution shifts impair deferral. We argue that robust HAIC in dynamic environments requires uncertainty-driven policy switching rather than reliance on a single deferral strategy. To operationalize this principle, we introduce two uncertainty-aware approaches that estimate epistemic uncertainty to guide the deferral policy choice. Both methods are the first uncertainty-aware approaches for HAIC that also address limitations of L2D systems including cost-sensitive scenarios, limited human predictions, and capacity constraints. Empirical evaluation in fraud detection shows both approaches outperform state-of-the-art baselines while improving calibration and supporting real-world adoption. © 2026, Transactions on Machine Learning Research. All rights reserved.

title: AI-Driven Decision-Oriented Scholarly Influence Forecasting With Calibrated Confidence and Abstention
authors: Tobaly, Lior; Zalevsky, Zeev
abstract: Forecasting the future influence of scholarly articles can enable earlier, more actionable decisions in research management, editorial triage, and funding oversight. However, most citation forecasting pipelines are evaluated purely as predictive models and often rely heavily on “prestige” proxies (e.g., author history), limiting their suitability as decision-support systems and raising concerns about robustness, fairness, and temporal stability. In this work, we extend our prior AI-CITE framework into a decision-oriented forecasting pipeline that adds calibrated confidence, structured abstention, and explicit controls on prestige dependence—without requiring any additional data collection (AI-CITE2). Building on publication-time inputs, the system fuses neural text representations (title+abstract) with auditable, time-truncated metadata descriptors, and supports both (a) top-quantile influence classification at horizon H and (b) regression of stabilized citation counts via \log (1+\text citations). To make forecasts operationally reliable, we introduce calibrated confidence using post-hoc temperature scaling and an abstention mechanism that allows the model to output “I don’t know” when uncertainty is high. We evaluate selective prediction through coverage–risk and selective performance curves, demonstrating how abstention can reduce decision risk while retaining strong ranking ability on the accepted subset. To audit and reduce measured dependence on prestige proxies, we conduct structured prestige ablations and report influence forecasting performance under progressively restricted descriptor sets, alongside metrics that quantify dependence on author-derived features. Finally, we add decision-relevant evaluation beyond standard AUROC/AUPRC, including ranking metrics and temporal robustness checks across publication years, with drift diagnostics that identify distribution shifts affecting confidence and operating thresholds. Across controlled temporal splits with strict identity-leakage prevention, the proposed decision-oriented AI-CITE2 variant maintains competitive forecasting performance while providing calibrated, abstention-aware outputs and reduced measured dependence on prestige-related proxies (as quantified by controlled ablations). These results position citation forecasting as a practical decision-support tool rather than a purely retrospective prediction benchmark. © 2013 IEEE.

title: E3-Guarded Generation: Provably Mitigating Hallucinations in Large Language Models
authors: Wang, Gang; Nixon, Mark
venue: 2026 International Conference on Computing, Networking and Communications, ICNC 2026
abstract: Large language models generate fluent text but frequently hallucinate - producing factually incorrect or unsupported claims. Existing approaches like retrieval-augmented generation and post-hoc verification lack formal guarantees needed for high-stakes deployment. We present E 3 -Guarded Generation, a unified framework that provably reduces hallucinations by enforcing three principles: Evidence grounding, logical Entailment, and Executable verification. Our framework integrates five synergistic components - Provenance-First Decoding, Speculative Verification Decoding, Counterfactual Cross-Examination, KWIK-Calibrated Abstention, and Semantic Constraint Grammars - achieving exponential decay in hallucination probability: P[halluc] ≤ ϵ r + α v · (1-γ s ) T . We prove soundness and completeness guarantees while maintaining polynomial-time complexity O(n log |E|), establish connections to program verification and PAC learning, and demonstrate the framework approaches information-theoretic optimality. This work provides the first comprehensive theoretical treatment of hallucination mitigation with provable guarantees, showing faithful generation is tractable when verification and generation are co-designed. © 2026 IEEE.

title: Reliability-Aware Benchmarking of Visual LOS and Single-Frame Range for Guidance-Oriented Measurement Handoff
authors: Yasar, Huseyin Avni; Akif Ahrazoglu, Mehmet
venue: RAST 2026 - 11th International Conference on Recent Advances in Air and Space Technologies, Conference Program
abstract: Guidance-facing visual measurement handoff depends on online line-of-sight and range measurements, but these channels do not share the same reliability profile. This paper presents a reliability-aware benchmark to quantify where a practical visual stack remains accurate, calibrated, and usable, and where it fails. The benchmark uses grouped held-out evaluation with stratification over altitude difference, LOS geometry, apparent target size, range, and visual family. A full-coverage baseline is compared against a reliability-gated practical branch. The results show a clear asymmetry: single-frame range requires abstention for risk control, while LOS remains stable when support exists (valid fraction 0.893, MAE 0.00164 rad). On held-out test data, reliability-gated acceptance reduces RMSE from 732.9 m to 113.4 m at 0.664 coverage, with p95 relative error reduction from 0.477 to 0.139 and sMAPE/WAPE reductions from 14.31%/18.70% to 5.58%/5.71%. Coverage-risk and calibration analyses further define an operating envelope with supported, conditional, and unsupported regions (9/2/40 over 51 combined bins, respectively). The paper therefore characterizes where the current measurement stack is practical for handoff and where it remains unreliable. © 2026 IEEE.

title: Multi-strategy enhanced dung beetle optimizer for reliable hyperparameter search in multimodal emotion recognition
authors: Rui, Yajin
abstract: Hyperparameter selection in multimodal emotion recognition is challenging because heterogeneous and incomplete modalities can produce noisy validation responses, while configurations selected primarily for peak predictive performance may exhibit poor probability calibration, limited robustness, or unnecessary computational cost. Reliable model selection therefore requires jointly considering discrimination, probability quality, robustness to modality loss, and search efficiency under a limited evaluation budget. To address this problem, this study proposes a multi-strategy enhanced dung beetle optimizer (MSA-DBO) that combines opposition-based initialization, diversity- and remaining-budget-dependent behavioral-role allocation, stagnation-triggered bounded chaotic escape, feasibility repair, and an uncertainty-aware validation objective. The method was evaluated against six hyperparameter-search baselines across four controlled MELD-derived feature domains. MSA-DBO achieved the highest mean weighted F1 of 79.85%, exceeding standard DBO by 4.63% points while showing lower between-run variability.
