title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Sensing of Cross-Border Trade Risks Through Declaration-to-Physical-Fact Alignment and Evidence-Grounded Question Answering
authors: Chen, Meitong; Huang, Jiayi; Zhou, Zilang; Zhang, Zhonghao; Lei, Kele; Tang, Yongxin; Li, Manzhou
abstract: Cross-border trade security risks are often embedded in inconsistencies among trade documents, logistics trajectories, hardware sensor states, and financial settlement activities. Existing methods primarily rely on structured declaration fields, making it difficult to verify digital declarations against actual physical processes or to generate complete evidence suitable for regulatory review. To address these challenges, TradeSense-EQA is proposed as a cross-border trade security anomaly detection and evidence-grounded English question-answering framework. Multisource sensing information, including trade documents, GPS/AIS trajectories, RFID records, electronic seal events, port weighing data, temperature and humidity measurements, vibration signals, container door states, and visual images, is jointly modeled within the framework. The reliability-aware representation module dynamically adjusts sensing-channel weights according to data missingness, sampling intervals, device health states, and communication quality. The trade-process-constrained module identifies anomalies across declaration, packing, transportation, transshipment, arrival, and customs clearance stages and generates process-consistent evidence chains. The evidence-grounded question-answering module answers English trade risk questions on the basis of verified documentary fields and sensor records, while confidence estimation and abstention mechanisms are incorporated to reduce factual hallucinations. Experimental results demonstrate that TradeSense-EQA achieved an Accuracy of (Formula presented.), a Precision of (Formula presented.), a Recall of (Formula presented.), a Macro-F1 of (Formula presented.), and a ROC-AUC of (Formula presented.) on the cross-border trade anomaly detection task, outperforming baseline methods including XGBoost, LightGBM, TCN, Transformer, BERT, CLIP, and VisualBERT. On the English trade risk question-answering task, Exact Match, Token-level F1, BLEU, ROUGE-L, and BERTScore reached (Formula presented.), (Formula presented.), (Formula presented.), (Formula presented.), and (Formula presented.), respectively. Ablation results further confirmed the effectiveness of hardware sensing input, reliability-aware weighting, declaration–fact alignment, process-graph reasoning, and evidence-constrained generation. The proposed framework provides a reliable, interpretable, and auditable artificial intelligence-driven sensing solution for customs supervision, port security, international logistics review, and trade-background investigation. © 2026 by the authors.

title: Do Large Language Models Link to Incorrect Citations? A PubMed and DOI Benchmark
authors: Ozkan, Goktug
abstract: Background Large language models can return citations whose PubMed Identifier (PMID), digital object identifier (DOI), title, and journal appear plausible but identify different papers. Checking one valid identifier may therefore fail to detect an incorrect citation bundle. Objective This study aimed to measure citation metadata incoherence in responses from five large language model snapshots to an internal medicine prompt benchmark. Methods Five models answered 30 synthetic prompts each, producing 150 model-by-prompt responses. Twenty-six prompts per model requested citations, and four were designed to elicit abstention. A corrected parser extracted 300 citation units. We checked reported PMIDs against PubMed metadata, queried reported DOIs separately, and rechecked DOI strings not found in PubMed through Crossref. Response-level outcomes were primary because citation units were nested within responses. The author reviewed a deterministic stratified sample of 50 units for parser capture and citation identity. Results Among 130 citation-expected responses, 69 contained a DOI that resolved to a different PMID than the PMID supplied by the model, 100 contained at least one automated metadata mismatch, and 28 contained no citation. Those 100 were 69 DOI-PMID, 29 other, and 2 unresolvable. All 20 abstention trap responses abstained. Among 116 units whose reported DOI resolved in PubMed, 99 resolved to a different PMID and 17 to the reported PMID. Human review found correct parser capture in 48 of 50 sampled units. Two section boundary errors were corrected before the final rerun; the primary counts did not change. Human review classified 32 sampled units as incoherent, 7 as coherent, 6 as having an unresolvable PMID, and 5 as containing no citation. Clinical claim support was not assessed. Conclusion Citation identity failures occurred in all five tested model snapshots. Evaluation and clinical evidence workflows should confirm that the PMID, DOI, title, and journal identify the same source before treating a model-supplied citation as evidence. © 2026. Thieme. All rights reserved.

title: Visual reasoning consistency and robustness analysis of multimodal LLMs
authors: Jegham, Nidhal; Abdelatti, Marwan; Hendawi, Abdeltawab
abstract: Traditional evaluations of multimodal large language models (LLMs) have been limited by their focus on single-image reasoning, failing to assess crucial aspects like contextual understanding, reasoning stability, and uncertainty calibration. This study addresses these limitations by introducing a novel benchmark that uniquely integrates multi-image reasoning tasks with rejection-based evaluation and positional bias detection. We further introduce entropy as a novel metric for quantifying reasoning consistency across reordered answer variants and abstention rate to measure a model's tendency to avoid uncertain answers. We assess 8 state-of-the-art models, such as Grok 3, ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 2.0 Flash Experimental, and DeepSeek's Janus models, across eight visual reasoning tasks. Our findings reveal ChatGPT-o1 leading in overall accuracy (82.5 %) and rejection accuracy (70.0 %), closely followed by Gemini 2.0 Flash Experimental (70.8 %). On the other hand, Janus models exhibited challenges in bias and uncertainty calibration, reflected in low rejection accuracies (Janus 7B: 25.0 %, Janus 1B: 30.0 %) and high entropy scores (Janus 7B: 0.839, Janus 1B: 0.787), underscoring their susceptibility to positional bias and unstable reasoning. By employing multi-image contexts, rejection mechanisms, and entropy-based consistency metrics, this benchmark sets a new standard for evaluating multimodal LLMs, enabling a more robust and reliable assessment of next-generation AI systems. © 2025 The Author(s)

title: Hardware Lazy PAT: Making Memory Encryption with Integrity Verification Unobtrusive
authors: Furukawa, Jun; Goshima, Masahiro; Ohata, Satsuya; Takamaeda-Yamazaki, Shinya; Matsumi, Wakuto
abstract: Authenticated memory encryption (AME) protects memory confidentiality and integrity through cryptographic authentication trees while allowing block-by-block updates. Our analysis demonstrates that existing AME designs suffer serious performance degradation for memory-intensive workloads because they fail to execute multiple memory requests in parallel. The fundamental challenge is that manipulations of each authentication tree node cannot be made independently per request: when one request decides to refill a node to reduce future memory accesses, a parallel request may require that node to be uncached to avoid cascading evictions or even deadlock. We present “Hardware Lazy PAT”, a mechanism that enables full multi-request parallelization. Our architecture tracks inter-request dependencies and defers refill decisions until cryptographic operations complete, dynamically balancing refills against evictions across parallel tree node updates. Moreover, we modified the AME protocol to separate the detection of rare events, called counter overflows, from their processing, enabling this deferral. Our gem5 simulations with RISC-V out-of-order cores show overhead grows from 8.8% on 1 core to only 23.8% on 32 cores for DAXPY (versus 9.4% to 1,104% without our technique), and similar scalability on SPECspeed® 2017 benchmarks with only a 64KiB dedicated cache. Our results show multi-request parallelization—not faster crypto engines—is critical for scalable AME. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

title: CRISP: Conformal Resilient Intrusion Detection with Selective Prediction
authors: Moccardi, Alberto; Amato, Alessandra; Ghosh, Rajib Chandra; Cirillo, Egidia
venue: 2026 6th International Conference on Machine Learning and Intelligent Systems Engineering, MLISE 2026
abstract: Intrusion detection systems on Internet of Things (IoT) networks experience high class imbalance, manipulation from attackers, and lack of human supervision. In this framework, the majority of deep learning-based classifiers are not suitable for such an environment, as they usually provide singlelabel predictions with no way to abstain, defer to the human analyst, or detect potential unknown attacks classes. We propose the CRISP (Conformal Resilient Intrusion Detection with Selective Prediction) framework, which introduces operational prediction sets which size reflects the system uncertainty, potentially indicating unknown class of attacks, while preventing overconfident classification. In detail, we propose a composite class-conditional nonconformity mechanism that acts as an adversarial detector. We validate the framework on two large-scale IoT benchmarks - ACI-IoT-2023 (1.2M flows, 11 classes) and CICIDS2017 (2.1M flows, 8 classes) - using a 1D-CNN and an Attention-DNN as backbone classifiers. Across all tested configurations, empirical per-class coverage deviates from the theoretical target by at most $pm 0.25 %$, and within this guaranteed framework the integrated adversarial detector attains a ROC-AUC of 0.87. Selective accuracy exceeds the base classifier's raw performance at every significance level $α$ through principled abstention. Cross-dataset generalization on CICIDS2017 and an open-set evaluation via conformal entropy further demonstrate the breadth of the conformal approach. To the best of our knowledge, this constitutes the first application of class-conditional conformal prediction to network intrusion detection. © 2026 IEEE.

title: Detecting (Un)answerability in Large Language Models with Linear Directions
authors: Lavi, Maor Juliet; Milo, Tova; Geva, Mor
venue: EACL 2026 - 19th Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics, Proceedings of the Conference, Vol. 1 - (Long Papers)
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often respond confidently to questions even when they lack the necessary information, leading to hallucinated answers. In this work, we study the problem of (un)answerability detection, focusing on extractive question answering (QA) where the model should determine if a passage contains sufficient information to answer a given question. We propose a simple approach for identifying a direction in the model’s activation space that captures unanswerability and uses it for classification. This direction is selected by applying activation additions during inference and measuring their impact on the model’s abstention behavior. We show that projecting hidden activations onto this direction yields a reliable score for (un)answerability classification. Experiments on two open-weight LLMs and four extractive QA benchmarks show that our method effectively detects unanswerable questions and generalizes better across datasets than existing prompt-based and classifier-based approaches. Moreover, the obtained directions extend beyond extractive QA to unanswerability that stems from factors, such as lack of scientific consensus and subjectivity. Last, causal interventions show that adding or ablating the directions effectively controls the abstention behavior of the model. We release our code at: https://github.com/MaorLavi/unanswerability-directions. © 2026 Association for Computational Linguistics.

title: TheraTime: a reliability-aware software framework for therapeutic timing evaluation in mental-health response retrieval
authors: Briouya, Asmae; Briouya, Hasnae; Choukri, Ali; Amnai, Mohamed
abstract: Mental-health response retrieval is usually evaluated using semantic relevance or retrieval rank, but these measures do not directly assess whether a retrieved response is therapeutically appropriate for the user's current need. A response may be semantically related while still being poorly timed, for example by giving advice before validation, missing a safety concern, or offering only empathy when concrete steps are requested. This paper presents TheraTime, an offline software framework for therapeutic timing evaluation in mental-health response retrieval. TheraTime separates evaluation into support-stage classification for the user query, support-move classification for the retrieved response, and rule-based timing assessment through a stage–move compatibility taxonomy. The framework uses pre-trained sentence-transformer encoders and prototype descriptions rather than supervised fine-tuning. Dense retrieval uses all-MiniLM-L6-v2, while the default timing classifiers use paraphrase-mpnet-base-v2, reducing circular encoder bias between retrieval and timing evaluation. In an illustrative experiment with 2250 query-level retrieval examples and 11,250 ranked judgments from ESConv, CounselChat, and MentalChat16 K, BM25 achieved the highest automatic top-1 timing rate (TTA@1 = 0.6053), followed by TF-IDF (0.5760) and dense MiniLM retrieval (0.4187). Human validation was conducted in two stages. An exploratory two-annotator study assessed 150 examples, followed by a primary study of 300 rank-1 examples independently assessed by three annotators, including one annotator external to the author team. Under majority consensus, the raw automatic timing labels agreed with the primary human reference in 50.3% of cases. In pooled five-fold out-of-fold evaluation, a validation-gated correction policy increased timing-label accuracy from 50.3% to 61.7%, with a paired absolute gain of 11.3 percentage points. TheraTime is intended for screening, comparative analysis, error inspection, and human-review support. It is not a reliable final automatic judge, is not a clinical decision-support system, and is not validated for deployment with real users. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

title: Calibrated selective prediction using deep ensembles for thyroid nodule ultrasound classification under dataset shift
authors: Sadib, Md. Sadibul Hasan; Mukit, Md. Mohayminul; Sarker, Rahmatul Kabir Rasel; Tamim, Tahmid Alam; Hasan, Md. Nazmul; Shimul, Md. Monir Hossain
abstract: Background Deep learning can accurately classify thyroid nodules on ultrasound, but discrimination alone does not establish clinical reliability. We developed a calibrated deep-ensemble framework incorporating uncertainty-aware selective prediction and conservative image-based triage. Methods Backbone selection used nested five-fold cross-validation with three-fold inner architecture selection. ConvNeXt-Tiny with a squeeze-and-excitation block was selected consistently and used to construct a deterministic five-member ensemble. Within each outer-development partition, images were separated into training, early-stopping, calibration, and threshold-selection subsets, while the outer-test data remained isolated. Mutual information (MI), predictive variance, and maximum-softmax-probability (MSP)-derived uncertainty were compared using risk–coverage and triage analyses. Predictive values were assessed across assumed malignancy prevalences of 5%–70%. External evaluation applied the frozen TN5000-derived ensemble and operating parameters to TN3K without recalibration. Results On TN5000, pooled out-of-fold AUC-ROC was 0.9377, average precision 0.9708, expected calibration error 0.0138, and Brier score 0.0827. Under the primary MI-guided policy, 8.86% of images received a No-FNA suggestion, 60.00% an FNA recommendation, and 31.14% radiologist review. Among 3574 malignant images, 14 (0.39%) received a No-FNA suggestion and 708 (19.81%) were assigned for review. Predictive variance and MSP-derived uncertainty showed better error-ranking performance than MI on AURC and AUGRC, although no measure consistently optimized all triage outcomes. Across malignancy prevalences of 5%–70%, NPV ranged from 99.95% to 97.93%, while PPV increased from 29.28% to 94.75%. On TN3K, the frozen policy achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.7870, average precision of 0.7254, expected calibration error of 0.1899, and an 83.7% radiologist-review rate. Conclusion The ensemble demonstrated strong internal discrimination and calibration with conservative selective prediction. However, performance and calibration deteriorated substantially on TN3K, indicating limited transportability under dataset shift. Multicentre validation, site-specific recalibration, threshold validation, and prospective workflow evaluation are needed before clinical implementation. © 2026 The Authors.

title: EPRAG: An epistemic policy framework for action selection in multi-source enterprise retrieval-augmented generation
authors: Kinalioglu, Ismail Hakki
abstract: Background and Objective: Enterprise retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems must select an appropriate action when retrieved sources differ in freshness, authority, access, or evidential compatibility. Methods: We propose EPRAG (Epistemic Policy RAG), an executable framework that separates evidence-state diagnosis from response selection through a six-state taxonomy and a deterministic five-action policy. Counterfactual answerability is implemented as a practical LLM/NLI-based approximation, while provenance is treated primarily as an auditability feature. Evaluation: EPRAG is evaluated on Spider2-derived (n=504) and BIRD-derived (n=720) benchmark adaptations, a manual adjudication study (n=400), a single-site enterprise helpdesk cohort (n=400), and a taxonomy-blind public audit (n=200). A structured GPT-5 judge is also evaluated on BIRD (n=240) and helpdesk (n=100) subsets using the same inputs and five-action space. Results: EPRAG achieves 91.7%–96.8% action accuracy on the public benchmarks and 76.0% against operationally derived helpdesk labels. In the taxonomy-blind audit, annotator agreement was 93.5% (κ=0.916), and EPRAG achieved 85.0% agreement with the trusted action (macro-F1 =0.849). EPRAG also outperformed the structured GPT-5 judge on BIRD (97.9% vs. 40.8%) and helpdesk (80.0% vs. 23.0%). Conclusions: EPRAG provides a bounded, auditable decision-policy baseline for multi-source enterprise RAG. The helpdesk evidence is single-site and label-dependent, the GPT-5 comparison is not an upper bound, and broader validation remains necessary. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

title: The différance engine: large language models and poststructuralism
authors: Gunkel, David J.
abstract: This essay argues that large language models (LLMs), such as GPT-type transformer architectures, actualize Jacques Derrida’s concept of différance. Originally introduced within the context of poststructuralist theory and semiotics, différance designates the way meaning is produced through a system of differences and deferrals, rather than stable reference. Drawing on this framework, the essay examines how LLMs generate meaningful content by calculating statistical differences across massive textual corpora—foregrounding processes of spacing, temporalization, and trace. It proposes that LLMs can be understood as “différance engines” that computationally enact the very mechanisms Derrida theorized. In addition to tracing these points of intersection, the essay reflects on the philosophical consequences of this alignment, including challenges to logocentrism, authorship, and the metaphysics of presence. It then addresses three potential criticisms of this approach, arguing that the use of Derrida’s work in this context is not a misappropriation, but a continuation and reiteration of its logic. And it concludes by identifying three systemic limitations and by charting opportunities for future research in this domain. The essay thus shows, on the one hand, how LLMs can be read through poststructuralist theory, and on the other, how poststructuralist theory can be clarified and rendered accessible through the technical operations of contemporary AI. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer-Verlag London Ltd., part of Springer Nature 2025.

title: PRISM: A Calibrated Multi-Signal Trust Framework for KG-Based Selective Prediction in API Service Ecosystems
authors: Far, Parimehr Morassa; Beheshti, Amin; Taeb, Kamyar; Shammasi, Alireza; Shahsavandi, Ali; Newton, M. A. Hakim
venue: Proceedings of the IEEE International Conference on Web Services, ICWS
abstract: Reliable knowledge graph (KG) reasoning is increasingly important for service ecosystems driven by application programming interfaces (APIs). In such ecosystems, typed relational graphs can represent service capabilities, dependencies, and invocation relationships, and link prediction can inform downstream service selection decisions. Existing KG reasoning models, particularly link prediction models, achieve strong ranking performance but do not produce calibrated trust scores, incorporate provenance directly into reasoning, or quantify structural fragility. Together, these limitations reduce their usefulness for deployment decisions. This paper proposes PRISM (Provenance, Robustness, and Inference-based Service trust Mechanism), a trust-aware framework for selective KG link prediction. The framework uses Neural Bellman-Ford Networks as a path-based inference backbone and derives three complementary trust signals: epistemic uncertainty, provenance quality, and counterfactual fragility. These signals are combined through a learned query-adaptive aggregator into a single calibrated trust score that supports selective prediction, allowing a reasoner to abstain on low-trust link predictions under a user-defined precision target. Evaluated on benchmark knowledge graphs, PRISM achieves strong calibration with an Expected Calibration Error (ECE) of 0.034 and reaches Hits@1=0.943 on Hetionet (from a baseline of 0.102) in the high-confidence regime (τ=0.9), suitable for selective decisions where coverage is deliberately traded for precision. At broader coverage levels, PRISM improves Hits@1 by up to 31% on FB15k-237. These findings suggest that PRISM provides a practical basis for trust-aware selective reasoning in dependency-rich service ecosystems. Code is available on GitHub. 1 1 https://github.com/parimehrmorassa/PRISM.git © 2026 IEEE.

title: Q-RAD: a gated residual architecture for quantum-assisted fraud detection, and why its quantum branch does not pay
authors: Sindayigaya, Jean Marie Vianney
venue: International Journal of Electronics and Telecommunications
abstract: —Hybrid quantum–classical detectors are usually evaluated as monolithic alternatives to classical models, which conflates two separable questions: whether the hard cases can be identified, and whether a quantum model can resolve them. We introduce Q-RAD, a gated residual architecture that separates these questions by construction. A quantum-blind, quantum-cost-free gating function routes only ambiguous transactions to a financial-transaction-specific quantum-kernel branch, whose scores are fused residually with a classical trunk under an explicit finite-shot budget. We predeclare the architecture, an eight-comparison confirmatory family with Holm–Bonferroni correction, a cost metric in quantum circuit executions, and a refutation posture, then evaluate on the Kaggle Credit-Card Fraud dataset over ten repeated case-control splits under three blocking validity gates, including exact-equality replay of pre-viously published results. The routing half of the architecture succeeds: the gate attains 0.889 AUROC against realized classical errors and captures 77% of them within a 22% routing budget. The quantum half fails: handed exactly those hard cases, the quantum residual produced zero net corrections in nine of ten seeds and one net regression in the tenth. Q-RAD attains mean case-control test F1 0.916 against 0.918 for the classical trunk and 0.922 for an otherwise identical classical second opinion; the hypotheses of improvement over the classical trunk, over random routing, and over a classical second opinion are all refuted after correction. We report this refutation as predeclared, and localise it: ambiguity in this task is identifiable from classical signals alone, but the quantum kernel cannot exploit that signal at any tested shot budget. Balanced-cohort metrics are benchmark values, not deployment-prevalence estimates. © The Author(s). title: Three-way decision oriented rational behavior multi-attribute decision-making
authors: Deng, Tingquan; Wang, Wenjie; Wang, Chaoyue; Zhan, Jianming
abstract: Three-way decision is a methodology that utilizes human cognitive thinking to handle multi-attribute decision-making with deferral decision-making. The key to achieving this goal is to reasonably fuse evaluation values from multiple attributes of alternatives to extract rules for classifying and ranking alternatives. There have been already lots of literature addressing this issue by considering the regret psychology of decision-makers. However, the regret theory oriented multi-attribute decision-making may lead to irrational or incomplete decision strategies. To tackle such a challenge, this paper introduces the idea of game theory into behavior three-way decision based multi-attribute decision-making (GBMADM) to weighted fuse regret and rejoice values of each alternative across all attributes to extract game rules for classifying and ranking alternatives. Firstly, a decision state set is fuzzified with the idea of TOPSIS and the weight of each attribute is determined based on the self-information of approximate accuracy from generalized fuzzy rough set theory. Secondly, a pair of utility functions is introduced to act as players to play in game. Two pairs of weighted regret functions and weighted rejoice functions are achieved by fusing the regret values and rejoice values of each alternative across all attributes, respectively. A payoff matrix for each alternative is then constructed by fusing the weighted regret value and weighted rejoice value. All decision rules for classification and ranking are thereafter extracted from the payoff matrix through optimal Nash equilibrium solutions. Finally, a practical example and simulation experiments on two benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method compared to representative methods. © 2025 Elsevier B.V.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Class-Contrast Evidence Audit for Reliable Cross-Subject Wearable Activity Recognition
authors: Li, Qiang; Qu, Zhirong; Yan, Meng; Zhang, Xiaohong
abstract: Reliable wearable activity recognition requires not only a class label but also an auditable indication of whether that label is supported by historical sensor evidence. We present CC-NSIEA, a label-preserving neural-plus-rule-based class-contrast evidence audit for cross-subject wearable activity recognition. A Temporal Residual Perception Network supplies the sole activity label, posterior probabilities, and a normalized temporal embedding. A read-only Training-Subject Evidence Memory retrieves global, predicted-class, and competing-class records. A rule-based Evidence Consistency Audit combines data validity, dynamic/static motion coherence, retrieval support, and class separation. When first-round evidence is insufficient, Class-Contrast Evidence Refinement performs one deterministic contrast between the predicted class and the strongest posterior competitor; the audit cannot change the neural label. The term neuro-symbolic is used only in this restricted architectural sense: a neural predictor is coupled to explicitly represent deterministic predicates and a finite rule-based controller; the method does not perform symbolic inference, theorem proving, or knowledge-graph reasoning. On five subject-disjoint outer folds of the UCI HAR official training partition, the shared perception model achieved 90.13% accuracy and 90.55% macro-F1 across 7352 out-of-fold windows from 21 subjects. Relative to a matched dynamic deterministic controller, CC-NSIEA increased Error AUPRC from 0.423802 to 0.433057 and reduced AURC from 0.035941 to 0.035913. The 10,000-resample subject-cluster bootstrap interval for the AUPRC difference was [0.001595, 0.019547]. CC-NSIEA provides an evidence-centered complement to confidence-based reliability estimation. © 2026 by the authors.

title: Auditable multimodal decision support for ordinal real estate price-band classification: Source-aware and leakage-controlled fusion
authors: Kim, Jae Hyung; Kim, Jinhwa
abstract: Residential decision-support systems increasingly combine structured property attributes, listing descriptions, and photographs. With small labeled samples, however, an additional representation may duplicate its source rather than add reproducible signal. This study presents a source-aware, leakage-controlled framework for five-class ordinal classification of posted asking-price bands. Structured attributes (N), native listing text (L), photo-derived caption text (C), and frozen verified-photo features (P) are evaluated separately, while C and P are recognized as representations of the same visual source. The final analysis set contains 422 unique address–photo entities. Ten-fold entity/image-safe outer validation prevents related cases from crossing the train–test boundary, and stream-model and fusion-weight selection are confined to three-fold inner splits. Structured attributes achieved 0.666 accuracy and 0.894 quadratic weighted kappa (QWK). Photo-derived caption text was the weakest individual stream, with 0.329 accuracy and 0.439 QWK. The caption-excluded N+L+P configuration produced the best multimodal point estimates, with 0.680 accuracy and 0.892 QWK, whereas the complete N+L+C+P diagnostic configuration attained 0.664 and 0.889, respectively. The complete diagnostic configuration showed no statistically detectable advantage over the predefined controls after Holm adjustment, and fixed XGBoost produced the highest overall point estimates, with 0.697 accuracy and 0.906 QWK. Global-band performance degraded sharply in held-out markets, identifying a clear need for local recalibration and revalidation. Integrated CPU inference beginning with a model-ready listing record and an archived background-removed photograph averaged 12.96 s per listing; the preceding third-party background-removal operation was outside the measured interval. The framework therefore provides an auditable basis for evidence-based representation selection: it separates representation format from source lineage, identifies redundant streams, preserves traceable uncertainty and case-level decision paths, and exposes conditions that require deferral or external revalidation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. All rights are reserved, including those for text and data mining, AI training, and similar technologies.

title: When Models Hesitate: Answer Instability as a Label-Free Uncertainty Signal for LLMs
authors: Arana, Jasper Meynard P.; Carandang, Kristine Ann M.; Casin, Ethan Robert A.; Alis, Christian M.; Monterola, Christopher P.
venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings, yet reliably estimating when their outputs should be trusted remains an open challenge. Existing uncertainty estimation approaches-such as calibration, token-level probabilities, or semantic entropy-typically require access to model internals, additional supervision, or computationally intensive pipelines. We propose answer instability, defined as the variability of a model’s final answer across repeated stochastic generations of the same prompt, as a simple, label-free, and black-box uncertainty signal. Evaluated across three task types - reasoning, multiple-choice QA, and constraint-following - using four LLMs and 520 prompt-model pairs, our approach achieves performance competitive with semantic entropy while requiring no semantic similarity model. Our results show that instability strongly correlates with prediction errors and reliably discriminates correct from incorrect outputs. We further demonstrate its utility for selective prediction and targeted repair, improving reliability without access to internal probabilities or additional training. © 2026 Association for Computational Linguistics.

title: An Explainable and Uncertainty-Aware Lightweight Dynamic Attention-Based Deep Learning Architecture for COVID-19 Detection from Chest X-Rays
authors: Hossain, Moinul; Khaleque, Taskin; Islam, Md Jahidul; Mahmood, Mohammad Sakib; Haque, Fahima; Ashiquzzaman, Md.; Arman, Mohammad Alif; Chisty, Nafiz Ahmed; Bhuyan, Muhibul Haque; Fattah, Shaikh Anowarul
venue: 14th IEEE Region 10 Symposium, TENSYMP 2026 - Shaping The Future: Unleashing Innovation to Elevate Technologies for The Betterment of Humanity
abstract: Automated COVID-19 detection from chest X-rays faces four barriers: dataset bias, limited cross-distribution generalization, absent uncertainty quantification, and computational overhead. RobustXAI-COVID addresses all four through five contributions: (i) DAM - a per-sample gating scalar α adaptively fuses channel and spatial attention, surpassing fixed CBAM by +1.10%; (ii) CDRT - weighted joint training on COVIDx CXR-4 and ChestX-ray14 yields +0.68% at zero inference overhead; (iii) UE - Shannon entropy deferral reduces misclassification by 45% on flagged samples; (iv) EGT (core XAI contribution) - Grad-CAM++ alignment loss makes anatomically faithful explanations intrinsic, jointly improving accuracy (+0.50%) and heatmap fidelity; (v) KD from ResNet-18 with hybrid CE+Focal loss achieves +1.32%. On COVIDx CXR-4 (n=1,000): 95.40% accuracy, 97.00% COVID-19 sensitivity, 0.9531 F1, 0.9901 AUC at 5.6M parameters and 12.1ms CPU latency. © 2026 IEEE.

title: SiCal-CytoNet: A Stain-Invariant, Calibrated Multi-Scale Network for Trustworthy Cytology on SIPaKMeD
authors: Vasudevan, Gokula Krishnan; Tiwari, Arvind Kumar; Sankaran, Sankar Krishnamurthy; Jayakaran, Lydia Pancy; Azizur, Alima Beevi; Boddula, Prathusha Laxmi
abstract: Background and Objectives: Cervical cancer screening through Pap-smear cytology remains a cornerstone of early diagnosis. However, its large-scale deployment is constrained by stain and illumination variability, morphological complexity across spatial scales, class imbalance, and unreliable confidence estimation in automated systems. Although deep learning models have achieved high classification accuracy on cytology benchmarks, many lack robustness to domain shifts and produce poorly calibrated probabilities, limiting their suitability for clinical triage. The objective of this research was to develop a stain-invariant, multi-scale, and well-calibrated deep learning framework that delivers both strong discrimination and trustworthy probability estimates for cervical cell classification, thereby enabling safe and effective decision support in screening workflows. Methodology: This study proposes SiCal-CytoNet, a stain-aware and calibrated multi-scale network designed for Pap-smear cytology analysis. This framework employs optical-density– based stain deconvolution with controlled perturbations to address stain variability in combination with domain generalization strategies, including Fourier Domain Adaptation and MixStyle. Morphological features are learned at multiple resolutions and adaptively fused using a learnable resolution gate. A prototype-guided metric head improves class compactness under imbalance, while probability reliability is enhanced through a combination of Brier loss, evidential Dirichlet modeling, and post-hoc temperature scaling. A selective prediction mechanism based on calibrated confidence is integrated to support clinically meaningful abstention. Main Results: On the SIPaKMeD five-class benchmark, SiCal-CytoNet achieves a test accuracy of 98.9% and a macro-F1 score of 98.7%, with excellent ranking performance reflected by an AUROC of 99.7% and an AUPRC of 99.4%. This model demonstrates strong probability calibration, attaining a low Brier score of 0.012 and an expected calibration error of 1.7%, while maintaining high discrimination under simulated stain, style, blur, and illumination shifts. Ablation experiments confirm the importance of multi-scale fusion, domain generalization, and calibration components. Using a utility-optimized selective prediction strategy, the system confidently automates 88.1% of cases while preserving high sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values for clinical triage. Conclusions: The findings show that combining stain physics, adaptive multi-scale learning, prototype-guided classification, and explicit calibration produces a cytology model that is both highly accurate and clinically trustworthy. SiCal-CytoNet moves beyond accuracy-centric evaluation by delivering reliable probability estimates and robust performance under domain shifts, addressing critical requirements for real-world deployment in cervical cancer screening. Practical Application: SiCal-CytoNet can be deployed as an automated triage system in cytology laboratories to assist pathologists by rapidly classifying routine Pap-smear samples while referring uncertain cases for expert review. Its calibrated outputs support transparent threshold selection, reduce screening workload, and enhance consistency across laboratories with heterogeneous staining conditions, offering tangible benefits to public health screening programs and AI-assisted diagnostic platforms. © 2026, School of Liberal Arts, King Mongkut's University of Technology Thonburi. All rights reserved.

title: CalStack-SP: Calibration-First Class-Wise Stacking with Selective Prediction for Φ-OTDR DAS event classification
authors: Liu, Zhidong; Chen, Xiaojuan; Wang, Huan
abstract: Distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) based on phase-sensitive optical time-domain reflectometry (Φ-OTDR) enables large-scale monitoring of pipelines, transportation corridors, and perimeter security. However, field DAS measurements are often affected by low and heterogeneous signal-to-noise ratios (SNR), environmental noise, and temporal drift, which may lead to overconfident but unreliable recognition outputs. To support reliable threshold-based alarming, this paper proposes Calibration-First Class-Wise Stacking with Selective Prediction (CalStack-SP), a confidence-aware measurement interpretation framework tailored to Φ-OTDR DAS event classification. CalStack-SP first applies branch-wise temperature scaling to align predicted confidence with empirical correctness, thereby producing uncertainty-calibrated sensing outputs. It then performs class-wise simplex-constrained convex stacking on the probability simplex to fuse heterogeneous learners in a stable and interpretable manner. A lightweight top-2 margin gate further enables selective prediction by accepting high-confidence segments and deferring ambiguous measurements to the calibrated ensemble, supporting risk-aware trade-offs among coverage, missed detections, and false-alarm control. To address Φ-OTDR distributed sensing constraints, DAS-specific feature stabilization and training augmentations, including SNR-targeted noise injection, temporal shifts, and class-conditional mixup, are incorporated. On a public nine-class Φ-OTDR benchmark, CalStack-SP achieves 95.06% accuracy and 95.51% Macro-F1, with a Brier score of 0.0832 and an ECE of 0.0081. On an open metro-tunnel intrusion dataset, it reaches 98.91% accuracy and 97.21% Macro-F1, suggesting favorable cross-scenario effectiveness with low additional inference cost. © 2026

title: Bootstrap Wasserstein alignment for stable feature attribution in low-data regimes
authors: Islam, Mujahidul; Dubey, Priya
abstract: Feature attribution methods become unreliable in low-data regimes (N≪d), producing inconsistent explanations across bootstrap replicates. We propose BWA (Bootstrap Wasserstein Alignment), a geometric framework that projects each bootstrap-replicate attribution to a probability measure on the feature simplex and aggregates the replicates via a Wasserstein-barycenter consensus paired with a per-feature sign-abstention mechanism. We present two versions: BWA-v1 with a hard binomial sign test, and BWA-v2 with a magnitude-weighted soft sign and a per-feature median-absolute-value scale that preserves natural attribution magnitudes. BWA-v2 closes a documented sign-accuracy deficit of BWA-v1 by 5–15 percentage points across eight experiments spanning synthetic data (N=20, d=100, B=50, 100 trials), MNIST saliency (N=100, d=784, 5 seeds × 50 images), Golub leukemia gene expression (N=72, d∈500,2000), and four UCI tabular datasets (N∈20,50, d∈13,30,34,60). On sparse-signal domains BWA-v2 produces significantly sparser attribution maps than every Euclidean baseline: MNIST Gini 0.645 vs. 0.613 Vanilla Mean and 0.584 budget-matched SmoothGrad; gene-expression Gini 0.417 at d=500 and 0.427 at d=2000 vs. Vanilla Mean 0.397/0.405 (all p bonf ≪0.001). On dense tabular UCI data BWA-v2 ties Vanilla Mean on every metric – a scope limitation we disclose explicitly. We pair the method with a bootstrap-level uncertainty σ UQ (model-retraining variance, an order of magnitude larger than SmoothGrad's input-noise variance) and a continuous per-feature soft-sign confidence signal, supporting explicit reliability estimation of attributions under data scarcity. Theoretically, Lemma 1 formalizes the worst-case norm-collapse failure of Euclidean averaging under sign-flip symmetry, motivating the geometric approach. We also clarify precisely what the Wasserstein barycenter contributes to each version: we prove that BWA-v2’s soft sign is an exact per-feature positive rescaling of the bootstrap mean (Proposition 2) and hence provably preserves its sign (Proposition 3) and is provably independent of the cost matrix (Proposition 4) – v2 closes BWA-v1’s sign-accuracy deficit by algebraic construction, not by geometric estimation, and the barycenter enters v2 only as an auxiliary uncertainty diagnostic. We verify this identity numerically with zero sign disagreements across 8465 features. BWA-v1’s barycenter remains load-bearing, and we report the one regime – domain-informed pathway recovery – where it demonstrably earns its cost. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

title: From Defect Prediction to Defect Triage: Evaluating Accepted Risk and Review Effort With CReST-DP
authors: Alsawalqah, Hamad; Abadleh, Ahmad; Al-Shboul, Bashar; Al-Tawil, Marwan; Aljarah, Ibrahim; Alshamaileh, Yazn; Alaydaa, Mohammed Saad
abstract: Software defect prediction is commonly evaluated as classification, although quality-assurance use also requires a decision about which model outputs need an additional review escalation. We present Cost-Risk-Effort Software Triage for Defect Prediction (CReST-DP), a decision-layer evaluation framework rather than a new defect classifier or reject-option principle. The primary evaluation track (Track A) covers 18 static datasets, 5 seeds, and 5 outer folds (450 settings) using mutually disjoint model-fit, learner/threshold-validation, and policy-validation subsets; all settings completed with zero processing errors and zero selection-policy overlap. The no-routing backbone achieved mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) 0.834 and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) 0.388. Inspection left 70.13% of artifacts without an additional triage-triggered review, with accepted error (AE) 0.0842, accepted false-negative exposure (AFNE) 0.2444, and routed-effort fraction 0.3385 under the line-change workload proxy. Matched random routing at the identical coverage yielded AE 0.1359 and AFNE 0.3708; dataset-bootstrap mean differences (Inspection minus random) were -0.0518 for AE and -0.1263 for AFNE. Deterministic single-signal rules can attain lower AE or AFNE but route more of the line-change workload proxy, so Inspection is interpreted as a risk-workload compromise rather than a universally superior rejection rule. Risk-coverage, signal, effort-score, policy-constant, alternative-effort, and uncapped-Camel sensitivities support this bounded interpretation. The secondary evaluation track (Track B), an ApacheJIT semantic-evidence analysis, remains exploratory because its original semantic extraction stage cannot be prospectively reconstructed from the preserved artifacts. © 2013 IEEE.

title: VCCV: conservative transcriptomic corroboration for measurement prioritization of computational drug–target hypotheses
authors: Huang, Haihui; Zhou, Yanan; Kang, Dingkui; Liang, Yong
abstract: Motivation: Computational drug-target interaction (DTI) models nominate plausible binders but cannot determine which candidate best accounts for an observed cellular response. Perturbational transcriptomics offers orthogonal mechanistic evidence, yet pharmacology-to-genetics mismatch, incomplete reference coverage, and non-specific stress programs make simple signature matching unreliable. This motivates a principled integration layer that corroborates hypotheses conservatively, abstains under global mismatch, and prioritizes informative follow-up measurements when the evidence remains ambiguous. Results: We present Virtual-to-Cellular Corroboration for Validation (VCCV), a model-agnostic posterior-triage layer for pre-trained DTI models. VCCV updates calibrated DTI working weights with context-aligned perturbational evidence using a near-identity affine map and exact covariance transport. Within the stated Gaussian class, exact transport is the unique uncertainty update that preserves posterior-odds comparisons under invertible affine changes of measurement coordinates. VCCV also introduces an empirical warning branch for abstention and converts residual ambiguity into compact follow-up gene panels, using a submodular objective for deep near-ties. Each query is assigned one of three actionable states: a target-resolved hypothesis, an abstention, or a prioritized panel. Across five DTI models, VCCV improved discrimination (paired ROC-AUC gains 0.021–0.037) and reduced negative log-likelihood in every case. Additional evaluations showed improved ranking on the same-cell-supported endpoint, warning-score discrimination of strong-response profiles (ROC-AUC 0.876), and better recovery of full-coordinate leading hypotheses by selected panels than by random panels. Across these retrospective kinase-focused evaluations, VCCV provides a principled bridge from computational nomination to conservative, measurement-directed cellular corroboration. Availability and implementation: Source code of VCCV is publicly available at https://github.com/bio-ai-source/VCCV. © The Author(s) 2026. Published by Oxford University Press.
